News.title: UK’s gloomiest cities ahead of clocks going back as spot with just TWO hours of sunshine a day steals unwanted crown
News.content:
Next

DARKER evenings are set to return from tomorrow (October 25) as Brits prepare for the clocks to go back.

However, some UK cities are gloomier than others, with one location averaging just two hours of sunshine a day in winter.



All 197 of the UK’s towns and cities have been given a gloom score out of 100, compiled by premium appliance brand AEG.

The company has examined Met Office data on rainfall, sunshine and humidity between September and February to find out where has the bleakest weather conditions during autumn and winter.



Derry/Londonderry has received the unwanted crown of being the UK’s gloomiest location, receiving a gloom score of 86.8 with over 102 rainy days every autumn and winter.

Residents in the Northern Irish city receive just 366.5 hours of sunshine a day, working out at just two hours a day during autumn and winter.

Following closely behind is the Scottish town of Cumbernauld, located in between Edinburgh and Glasgow, which received a gloom score of 83.5.

Over 99 days of the year in Cumbernauld are filled with rainfall, amounting to 774.5mm, with only 397 hours of sunshine during the winter.



Historic market town Rochdale in Greater Manchester ranks third most gloomy, with Burnley closely behind then East Kilbride in Scotland.

All of these locations endure a minimum of 95 rainy days between September and February, as well as minimal sunshine.

UK's gloomiest locations in autumn and winter Derry/Londonderry, Northern Ireland Cumbernauld, Scotland Rochdale, England Burnley, England East Kilbride, Scotland Paisley, Scotland Halifax, England Lisburn, Northern Ireland Oldham, England Blackburn, England Bury, England Huddersfield, England, Glasgow, Scotland Newtownabbey, Northern Ireland Hamilton, Scotland Craigavon, Northern Ireland Bolton, England Stoke-on-Trent, England Bridgend, Wales Bradford, England Belfast, Northern Ireland Castlereagh, Northern Ireland & Preston, England Macclesfield, England Lancaster, England Newcastle-under-Lyme Swansea, Wales Blackpool, England Plymouth, England Taunton, England & Cardiff, Wales Wigan, England

Weather isn’t much brighter in Paisley in Scotland, Halifax in West Yorkshire or Lisburn in eastern Northern Ireland – which all experience at least 15 days more rain on average alongside high humidity.

Oldham and Blackburn in the North West of England round off the gloomy top 10, receiving Gloom Scores of 74 and 75 respectively.

On the other end of the spectrum, the coastal city of Southend-on-Sea is officially the most ungloomy location in the UK, followed by Clacton-on-Sea and Margate – receiving scores between 20 and 25.



Despite having 70 rainy days throughout winter, Weymouth’s 518 hours of sunshine between September and February help it rank fourth ungloomy in the UK.

News.title: What is the exact time the clocks change tonight?
News.content:
Next

BRITS are getting an extra hour in bed tonight as the clocks go back, but evenings are about to get darker even earlier.

Here’s everything you need to know about the exact time of the changeover and which clocks you might have to reset yourself.



What exact time do the clocks change tonight?

British Summer Time (BST) is drawing to a close, and the UK is returning to Greenwich Mean Time (GMT).

The clocks go back at 2am on Sunday, October 25, 2026, when the time jumps back to 1am.



That means the switch happens overnight from Saturday, October 24, into Sunday morning, rather than at midnight.

Anyone awake through the switch will experience the hour between 1am and 2am twice, so travellers or those working overnight should be careful.



The Sunday morning slot was chosen to minimise disruption to schools and businesses.

Do the clocks go forward or back tonight?

The clocks go back in autumn, so Sunday will be a 25-hour day as the hour from 1am to 2am repeats itself.

But there is no extra sunshine; the daylight is simply shifted to a different part of the day.

In London, for example, sunrise moves from 7.39am on Saturday to 6.41am on Sunday, while sunset slips from 5.48pm to 4.46pm.



So although early risers get a little more light, those heading home in the late afternoon will notice it getting dark far sooner.

Will my phone change automatically?

Most smartphones, tablets and computers automatically switch to GMT, provided their date and time settings are configured to update automatically.

However, traditional alarm clocks, wall clocks, ovens, microwaves, older stereo systems and some car dashboards may still need a manual reset.

It is also worth checking heating and hot water timers, especially if they are programmed to come on at set hours.

Anyone relying on an alarm for work or an early train on Sunday should double-check the displayed time.



The change can also throw off your sleep pattern, despite the extra hour in bed.

Norfolk and Suffolk NHS Foundation Trust recommends getting daylight in the morning to help reset your body clock.

There’s no need to stay up until 2am to adjust an old-fashioned clock; you can simply turn it back an hour before bed.

When do the clocks go forward again?

The UK will remain on GMT throughout the winter, until the clocks go forward on Sunday, March 28, 2027.

At 1am that morning, the time will jump to 2am as BST returns.



This time, we lose an hour rather than gaining one, although lighter evenings lie ahead.

The tradition dates back to 1916, when summer time was introduced during World War I.

It followed years of campaigning by builder William Willett, who argued that people were wasting precious daylight in summer.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Clocks always go forward an hour at 1am on the last Sunday of March each year, and then they move back an hour at 2am on the last Sunday in October.

An easy way to remember which way the time changes is “spring forward, fall back”.

News.title: Man in his 70s and dog die after being hit by bus as driver arrested & police appeal for dashcam video
News.content:
DOG CRASH DEATH Man in his 70s and dog die after being hit by bus as driver arrested & police appeal for dashcam video







Next

A MAN and a dog died after being hit by a bus.

The pedestrian, in his 70s, was critically injured following the incident in Bristol at 11pm on Thursday.

Cops confirmed both he and dog died at the scene on the junction between Stockwood Road and Holloway Road.

Avon and Somerset Police have arrested the bus driver, a man in his 30s, and he remains in custody while enquiries continue.





The force said: “We are appealing for witnesses and dashcam footage after a pedestrian died after he was involved in a collision with a bus in Bristol last night (Thursday 22 October).

“The collision happened at the junction for Stockwood Road and Hollway Road at around 11.10pm.

“The road has since reopened after enquiries were carried out at the scene.

“The pedestrian, a man in his seventies, was critically injured and died at the scene.

“While formal identification is yet to take place, his next of kin have been informed and will be supported by a specialist family liaison officer.

“Our thoughts are with them at this traumatic time. A dog also died in the incident.

“The driver of the bus, a man in his thirties, has been arrested and remains in custody while enquiries continue.

“Any witnesses and those with CCTV and dashcam footage from around the time of the incident are asked to contact us on 101 quoting reference number 5226345957 or complete our online appeals form.”

News.title: Nazi’s WW2 ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain guest retreat engulfed by flames in Germany – as suspect arrested
News.content:
MOUNTAIN BLAZE Nazi’s WW2 ‘Eagle’s Nest’ mountain guest retreat engulfed by flames in Germany – as suspect arrested







Next

A SUSPECT has been arrested after a fire erupted at Adolf Hitler’s “Eagle’s Nest” mountain retreat in Germany.

Around 200 firefighters battled the roaring blaze at the Nazi dictator’s remote and hard-to-reach compound in the Bavarian Alps.



They saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, before finding the building “completely ablaze,” police said.

“A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody,” they said in a later statement, adding that nobody has been injured.



Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the inferno due to the building’s location at an altitude of around 6,000ft.

The complex, known in Germany as the Kehlsteinhaus, was only accessible with “heavy breathing apparatus”, she added.



Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered an alarm at around 9:50pm local time, police said.

No cause for the fire was given, but investigators suspect arson.

As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle’s Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of Saturday, a weather camera showed.

Officers were also seen blocking access to the road leading to the retreat.



The firefighters found no one inside the building.

Maier, the police spokeswoman, said the investigation was still ongoing, while a news conference is expected later today.

A motorcyclist was arrested after police came across them on their way to the scene, according to Bild.

The Eagle’s Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler’s Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews along with Roma, LGBTQ people and Communists in the Holocaust.



Workers were forced forced to work long nights in the winter of 1938 to complete the retreat in time for Hitler’s birthday in April 1939.

It was designed to serve as a monument to the dictator’s rule, though the dictator himself rarely visited the complex.

Built of stone and granite, the residence offers an exceptional view of the picturesque Bavarian Alpine landscape and was designed to impress foreign diplomats.

It survived the Second World War undamaged.

Since 1952, it has hosted both an exhibition recounting the house’s Nazi history and a restaurant.

News.title: Inside Burnham’s two-speed revolution and why Labour MPs fear voters won’t wait
News.content:
Next

THE man who promised to bury Thatcherism has a rather more immediate enemy in his sights: the bloke blasting music on the bus.

It is not quite the revolution Andy Burnham advertised when he swept into No10 pledging the biggest transformation in 40 years.



But three months into his premiership, a curious two-speed strategy is emerging behind the famous black door.

While the PM wages war on rip-off parking fines, nuisance vaping and other everyday irritations, the truly radical stuff is being given rather more time to breathe.



Brexit, social care, electoral reform and greater public ownership of water are all part of a much longer political game.

And with Chancellor John Healey expected to deliver a relatively cautious Budget next week, the real centrepiece of Burnham’s ambitions will be his forthcoming ten-year plan for Britain.



There is just one issue.

Some Labour MPs are already wondering whether an electorate desperate for change will stick around long enough to see it.

“He comes in, promises biggest change in 40 years,” one Labour MP told The Sun.

“People were tired of waiting under Starmer. They will be tired of waiting under Burnham too.”



But those closest to the PM insist this is no ordinary case of kicking difficult decisions into the long grass.

Instead, the Prime Minister believes he can tackle problems that have defeated successive governments by changing not just what politicians do, but how they do it.

And while the biggest reforms are being developed, Downing Street is determined to prove government can still deliver results people notice.

A senior Government source explained: “He wants to do the big things and the small things. “There’s a real focus on everyday fixes, whether that’s taking VAT off electricity bills, making bus fares £2 or changing the car parking fine system.

“It’s about showing people that government can actually get stuff done. People have, to an extent, stopped believing in government, and he wants to show them that it can have a direct impact on their lives and make things better now.



“But he also wants to take on the big issues. He calls it getting Britain believing in itself again…showing that we can tackle these big problems and sort them out.”

This week offered a glimpse of the approach, with new protections against unfair private parking charges and a crackdown on passengers blasting music or vaping on public transport.

The calculation is that a steady drumbeat of crowd-pleasing announcements can buy Burnham the political breathing space needed to pursue something considerably more ambitious.

But there is a deeper reason for his approach, rooted in one of the most bruising episodes of his career.

During an early question-and-answer session with journalists in July, Burnham was asked what he had learned from his time as Gordon Brown‘s Health Secretary.



His mind went straight back to 2010, when his plans for a National Care Service became engulfed in a toxic pre-election row over a so-called “death tax”.

Explaining why he was accelerating Baroness Louise Casey’s social care review, Burnham said: “I think it’s better to do it sooner and further away from an election… Engage now. Don’t have cross-party talks when a solution is emerging, which is what we did back then. Build it with people.”

It was an unusually revealing glimpse into the thinking of a Prime Minister who appears convinced that building consent is the key to delivering lasting reform.

Those around him insist the cross-party discussions are genuine, with Burnham determined to involve people at the beginning rather than present them with policies cooked up in Whitehall.

There are echoes of Tony Blair‘s “Big Conversation” before the 2005 election, while Theresa May‘s disastrous 2017 social care manifesto offered a brutal lesson in the dangers of unveiling controversial policies at the eleventh hour.



One senior Labour MP acknowledged the competing interpretations, saying: “Some people may say we’re putting off decisions. Others would say we are being extremely thoughtful about what we’re doing.”

Another argued the aim was to enter the next election with detailed policies ready to implement, rather than squander the first two years of another government working out how to deliver them.

But the trouble with political conversations is that not everyone agrees on the answer.

Just ask Miatta Fahnbulleh.

The Energy Secretary spent much of this week tying herself in knots over Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood‘s controversial plans to make some migrants wait up to 15 years for permanent settlement.



After repeatedly refusing to endorse the proposals on Sky News, she joked that her determination never to lie had landed her in some “awkward moments”.

She later insisted she fully supported the Government’s position.

But her discomfort with the policy goes back further.

The Sun understands that while serving as a junior communities minister, Fahnbulleh would refuse to undertake lengthy interviews on social cohesion because she felt unable to publicly defend Mahmood’s settlement proposals.

And there are signs of impatience on Labour’s industrial flank too.



At a meeting of MPs campaigning for reindustrialisation this week, one backbencher is understood to have walked out following a frustrating exchange with Treasury minister Dan Tomlinson.

The flashpoint was the plight of areas without elected mayors, with MPs demanding economic support now rather than having to wait for new devolution arrangements.

Tomlinson was unable to offer firm answers ahead of Wednesday’s Budget, leaving some MPs frustrated.

For those watching industrial jobs disappear in their constituencies, the promise of transformation over ten years can seem painfully distant.

The Budget itself, meanwhile, is being prepared with military precision.



Insiders say Healey has imported a Ministry of Defence-style need-to-know approach to the Treasury, with even ministers being kept largely in the dark about its contents.

One decision is settled, though: after toying with the idea of a pint at the despatch box, the Chancellor has opted for water – perhaps fitting for a Budget expected to be a rather sober affair.

Former Starmer ally Darren Jones has already warned that the Budget must “meet the moment” or risk eroding public support.

And that is the fundamental tension in Burnham’s grand experiment.

He wants to restore faith in government by proving that politicians can finally solve the problems their predecessors ducked.



But social care will still need funding, Brexit will still divide opinion and reindustrialising Britain will still require uncomfortable choices.

David Cameron discovered that starting a national conversation about Europe is considerably easier than controlling where it ends.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Burnham is betting that taking time to build agreement now will make lasting change possible later but after years of being promised change, voters may be rather less interested in the conversations he starts than the results he delivers.

News.title: Labour set to deploy 2,000 new anti-fraud specialists to clampdown on benefits cheats
News.content:
Next

CHANCELLOR John Healey will deploy 2,000 new anti-fraud specialists as part of a major clampdown on benefits cheats.

Officers will be put in Jobcentres to spot suspicious Universal Credit claims early — which is hoped to save £1.4billion.



These employees will work closely with existing staff that handle benefit claims.

Mr Healey’s move, to be announced at the Budget, comes as he faces growing pressure to cut the welfare bill, which is forecast to hit £400billion at the start of the next decade.



Trials have already started, with one claimant’s application rejected for using a digitally altered document and giving conflicting accounts of their ability to work.

A Treasury spokesperson said: “We need to make the most of every pound of taxpayers’ money and cut fraud to ensure the welfare system is fair and sustainable. We’re rooting out those who abuse the system, while protecting those who need it most.”

Currently, 78 staff are working on the project, rising to 250 by the end of the year and 2,000 by 2030.

Mr Healey will also be targeting “abroad fraud” where people claim taxpayer cash after leaving the UK. One individual held on to £39,000 despite living in Zimbabwe.

But the welfare blitz comes after Sir Keir Starmer climbed down from his own attempted reforms due to a backbench rebellion.

A key priority for the overhaul will be the nearly one million Neets aged 16-24 who are not currently in education, employment, or training.



Meanwhile, the Budget will also see Mr Healey unveil an AI safety package to guard against cyber threats.

This will include £165million going to an AI Biosecurity Lab, and £10million to study AI’s impact on jobs.

News.title: Brit mum, 36, who drowned while desperately trying to save her two children in Bahamas snorkelling horror is pictured
News.content:
HOLS TRAGEDY Brit mum, 36, who drowned while desperately trying to save her two children in Bahamas snorkelling horror is pictured







Next

A BRIT mum who drowned while trying to save her two children has been pictured for the first time.

Leanne Gregory, 36, was snorkelling with her family in the Bahamas when a strong current suddenly swept the two youngsters away.



Filled with fear she dived after her two sons in a desperate bid to save them.

But tragically Leanne was pulled unconscious from the water in the horror incident on Tuesday.



Husband Nathan Gregory, 36, tried to resuscitate her as emergency services were called.

Police rushed to the ferry dock in Bimini shortly after 10am – but the mum-of-two had already been taken away for treatment.

Doctors later pronounced her dead.

Her two boys were safely rescued from the water by emergency services.

A spokesman for the Royal Bahamas Police Force said foul play was “not suspected”.

Witness Katie Resciniti wrote on Facebook: “I was there for all of it. She’s a hero.



She added: “Also pray for her husband. He went out to save the other boy but a bystander was able to get him.

“It was truly terrible and nobody’s fault. Just two boys who were eager to get in the water and then things went crazy fast.

“Two of the best parents I’ve ever seen in my entire life.”



The captain of the snorkelling expedition boat Linty Stuart told local news outlet ZNS that he “saw two boys and a mum” in the water but that powerful tides stopped them from being able to reach the mother.

The outlet reported that “one of her children got in distress” when Leanne jumped in to save him.

Speaking to The Telegraph, the boys’ grandma Mrs Jones said: “It is devastating. Leanne drowned trying to save her two boys who got into trouble in choppy waters.

“They can both swim, they’re good swimmers, but the current was too strong”, she added.

Giving a heartbreaking detail, she said: “Nathan tried to save her, by giving her the kiss of life. Sadly, it was too late.”



The husband’s dad and brother are flying out to support the family, according to Nathan’s nephew Gail Parker.

The family lived in Stapleford, Nottinghamshire and had been on holiday in the Bahamas over half term.

Nathan and Leanne were childhood sweethearts who had been together for more than 20 years, having first met in school.

A spokesman for the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office said: “Our thoughts are with the family of a British woman who has died in the Bahamas.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“We are in contact with the local authorities and providing support to her family.”



At least four people have drowned off the coast of hols hotspot Bimini since 2024.

News.title: Andy Burnham says booze shouldn’t be a priority in an emergency kit in case of attack by Russia
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has warned Brits not to prioritise booze in their emergency rations in case of a Russian attack.

But they can still have a “glass or two” to help them deal with the stress.



Minister Angela Rayner had joked a bottle of sauvignon blanc and mascara would be in her stash.

Quizzed on BBC Radio 5 Live, the PM said wine should not be your “best first port of call” in a crisis.



He added: “It probably helps when you’ve done the hard work, but I’ll stick to the basics, I think.”

On his own top picks for emergency supplies, he said: “I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.

“I think those are the kinds of things I would recommend people to have. As well as Twiglets. I’m not sure I can get by without those for too long.”

Houses are being told to stock up on long-lasting food, water, cash, and medicines in case of an attack or natural disaster.



The warning was reiterated more strongly this week, as government and business websites were taken down to address cyber-security flaws.

Defence Secretary Wes Streeting urged people to be ready and has been launching a “national resilience conversation”.

Military bigwigs will address the nation in the coming days to explain why we need to spend more on defence, Mr Streeting added.



He spoke again about the “Be Ready” campaign at a new factory in Shropshire where Britain will be producing parts for tanks for the first time in 20 years.

News.title: Met investigates reports of letter detailing claims about Meghan's father
News.content:
Instead, Scotland Yard has opened an inquiry to confirm the claim that the Met's royal protection unit passed on the letter to the Duchess eight years ago.

According to the Sun, the letter was sent to a Met Police unit tasked with dealing with individuals posing a threat to Royals and politicians - the Fixated Threat Assessment Centre.

A Met spokesperson said: "We are aware of media reports that officers from the Met's Royalty and Specialist Protection Command were involved in the passing on of a letter in 2018.

"We are undertaking inquiries internally in an effort to confirm this."

Thomas Markle moved to the Philippines in 2025 after a series of strokes.

He is reportedly now living in a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk again, after having a leg amputated during surgery in December 2025.

In her statement on Friday, Meghan said that when she received the letter outlining allegations against her father in 2018, she was "given assurance that these were being investigated".

Meghan's half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told the Sun that he had allegedly found child abuse images at his father's home in the Philippines and reported it to the police.

The Undersecretary for the Philippines Department of Justice, Nicholas Ty, told the BBC that "the matter is currently being investigated" by an anti-human trafficking and child sexual exploitation task force in Cebu.

Philippines Interior Minister Jonvic Remulla separately told the BBC that national police had secured Thomas Markle Snr's computer to conduct a comprehensive digital forensic examination.

Investigators there are currently analysing the data to determine the full scope and extent of his alleged criminal activities, with the minister saying it would take one week to get the forensic results.

The US Federal Bureau of Investigations said it was "aware of the allegations", adding it would "provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities".

The FBI's statement continued: "We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law."

Meghan is the only child of Thomas Markle's marriage to her mother, Doria Ragland, but he has two other children - Samantha and Thomas Markle Jr - from an earlier marriage.

The relationship between Meghan and her father, a former TV lighting director, broke down in the run-up to her wedding in 2018.

At the time, Thomas Markle was found to have colluded with photographers, accepting payment to stage photographs of him preparing for the wedding.

It is understood that Meghan first learnt about the allegations against her father shortly after she married the Duke of Sussex Prince Harry.

Sources close to the Sussexes said Meghan could not speak publicly about the allegations when she first learned of them, in order to avoid jeopardising any future investigation.

Speaking out could have resulted in legal action against her, the sources said.

News.title: UK to invest £100m in 'world first' AI Biosecurity Lab
News.content:
The UK says it will establish a national AI Biosecurity Lab (AIBL) to help strengthen its defences against emerging biological threats.

As part of Wednesday's Budget, the government will commit Â£100m to establishing the new, "world first" institute with the support of leading AI firms.

The chancellor will also pledge millions of pounds in spending across a range of initiatives aimed at shoring up the UK's ability to respond to evolving cyber, biological and AI-enabled threats.

"AI will transform daily life: every firm, community, hospital, school, and every aspect of our economy can benefit," John Healey said.

"I understand and share the concerns of working people, so I am setting out a distinctively British approach to AI.

"One that doesn't leave workers behind and defends our national interest, while ensuring the benefits of AI-enabled growth are felt right across the country."

The full details about the role and remit of the new lab are yet to emerge.

But the AI Minister Kanishka Narayan said it would be a "major new global institution" that brings together "world-leading scientific expertise" to ensure the UK can safeguard its citizens and goals as AI develops.

"That means staying ahead of emerging threats, from cyber attacks to biological risks, while building more of the critical technology our security depends on," he said.

"By backing British science, advanced chips and our own AI companies, we can strengthen our national security, rebuild Britain's industrial strength and create good, skilled jobs across the country."

The AI Biosecurity Lab's creation will also be supported by leading AI developers, with OpenAI and Anthropic providing Â£200m worth of AI model credits that can be spent on the use of their models.

News.title: Father who killed Oregon school shooter describes anguish over children he couldn't save
News.content:
A father who fatally shot a gunman at his daughters' school in the US state of Oregon has described his anguish over being unable to save more pupils after "hearing children pleading for their lives".

Three students and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student at Silver Rail Elementary School earlier this month. The attacker was then killed by Kaylub Giamanco.

"I want to apologise for not saving their babies," Giamanco, who has been hailed as a hero, said of his thoughts for the parents of the children killed, in an interview with Oregon Public Broadcasting (OPB) that aired on Friday.

"The gratitude for saving people's children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn't save."

Giamanco, 36, said he wanted to meet the victims' families and "cry with them and hold them".

He credited a teacher who fought the attacker with giving him the chance to intervene without losing his own life.

"I would love to give her a hug because that's a real true hero," he said.

The students who were killed were all boys, aged five, eight and 11. They were among six people in total who were shot in a classroom at the school, police said. Alongside the teacher who was killed, another child and a teacher were wounded.

Giamanco told OPB that the day of the attack began with breakfast and making packed lunches. He and his wife had spent extra time getting their daughters ready because it was school picture day.

The carpenter had taken lunch to work but decided to go home to eat with his wife instead. That decision brought him past the school as the attack began.

He initially wondered whether someone carrying a long gun was playing a prank. Then he saw him fire at a pickup truck and head towards the school.

Giamanco retrieved a handgun from his vehicle and called emergency services.

"I said, 'I'm sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die'," he told the broadcaster.

He followed the attacker, who shot through the school's locked glass doors. Hearing children pleading for their lives and more gunfire, Giamanco crawled towards the building.

"I told myself this is probably the last thing that I'm ever going to do," he said.

News.title: Celebrity Traitors left on a knife edge after a trip to the field of screams
News.content:
Spoiler warning: This article reveals details from episode eight of The Celebrity Traitors, series two.

Original Celebrity Traitor Maya Jama, latest recruit King Kenny and now even the reluctant James Acaster - hurrah! - have developed a real appetite for murder this week.

And going into Friday's episode we knew that their collective cruel intention was to see that one of three faithfuls, Miranda Hart, Romesh Ranganathan or Sebastian "Bash" Croft, did not make it to breakfast.

When it became clear that the murdered Miranda had danced her last dance in the castle - leaving only 10 of the initial 21 players - the pressure began to mount and speculation was rife as to whodunnit and why?

The self-declared Miss Marple wannabe had been stitched up, of course. "Miranda is a good detective," noted James A in a flashback to the turret talk from the night before.

"I don't know who I'm becoming," responded Maya - who has taken to treachery like a duck to water - "but I feel it in my loins, and Miranda is the only one that makes sense."

Miranda, who had been in her element sleuthing away on the show, did not take the news of her untimely death at all well, throwing her murder note to the ground. "No! Absolutely not," she cried.

"Oh bottoms!"

"I'm so cross with myself, I was wholly focusing on my Joanne issue," she added, with reference to her theory about Joanne McNally being a traitor. One that even Miranda herself had - unwisely - "debunked" at the roundtable.

Ending on a more positive note, the comedian, who has had health issues in recent years, reflected: "Ultimately, in my little personal story, this has been quite extraordinary that I've been able to get back and do the thing that I love professionally and do the things that I love personally.

"Like wandering around a Scottish island and being in nature and laughing and connecting. There were times that I didn't think that would be possible again".

News.title: Are California voters about to impose 'world's first' tax on billionaires?
News.content:
While the ballot measure has many supporters - including some billionaires like Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang - it has faced fierce opposition from a variety of figures, from billionaires to the state's liberal governor.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin has given more than $100m to a political organisation funding ballot measures that could block the wealth tax, the Los Angeles Times reports, external.

California Governor Gavin Newsom, whose tenure is coming to an end, is perhaps the most notable political leader opposing it. He has voiced concerns that the measure could cause the wealthy to leave the state and drive out their crucial income tax revenue.

A September poll, external from the Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times found the proposition has not clearly won over a majority of voters, with 45% of likely voters in favour of the tax, 42% opposed and 13% undecided.

The statewide ballot measure would need to be approved by a majority of residents.

California is not the first place to toy with the idea of taxing the rich. Also on the West Coast, voters in US state of Washington are considering whether to accept or reject a "millionaires tax" - a 9.9% tax on income over $1m a year.

While wealth taxes were once a fairly common form of taxation in Europe, they have rapidly fallen out of favour and now only exist in three European countries â Spain, Norway and Switzerland, says Dr Kristian Niemietz, head of political economy at the Institute of Economic Affairs.

Niemietz believes wealth taxes are "more trouble than they are worth" because they cause administrative issues, suppress investment, lead to capital flight and, in the end, do not raise much revenue.

In the case of Norway, a local news organisation found that an increase in the wealth tax led to more super wealthy people leaving the country in 2022, external than in the preceding 13 years combined. A study on Switzerland, external found that a 0.1 percentage point increase in a wealth tax reduced taxable wealth by 3.5%.

News.title: Strictly's new presenters - after frosty reviews have they warmed up?
News.content:
Strictly Come Dancing's new hosting trio received a very mixed reception when the latest series began a month ago. Ratings have dipped and the jury's still out, but critics say they are slowly getting into the groove.

Changing the hosting team on the BBC's flagship Saturday night entertainment show was never likely to be a waltz in the park.

And going from two presenters to three, and giving them slightly different roles, upset the show's rhythm even more.

Tess Daly and Claudia Winkleman were always going to be a hard act to follow.

Into their sparkly shoes have stepped the safe and smooth Emma Willis; the flamboyant former professional dancer Johannes Radebe; and cheeky comedian Josh Widdicombe, a wildcard who was not hitherto associated with either the dance world or prime-time TV.

Willis and Widdicombe have been paired on the live shows, where he is tasked with injecting humour into the moments before and after each dance - with mixed results, say critics.

Radebe, meanwhile, has taken over from Winkleman upstairs on the mezzanine, bringing his warmth and dance expertise to the celebrity interviews following each routine.

News.title: Ruins of Limoges city hall a symbol of France divided by national protests
News.content:
"Of course it was really sad, it's a symbol of the republic, but what is more important: a town hall or people living in poverty?" asks Alexander, 24.

It is student night at the Lord John pub, and Alexander is one of several wearing a faluche, a colourful, traditional French student beret. Many chatting under the mist from their vapes took part in the demonstrations last weekend.

I ask Alexander whether the widespread looting and fires seen last weekend, with â¬500,000 (Â£420,000) of reported damage in Limoges, helped his argument?

"For some people it's a catastrophe and some things are not acceptable," he admits.

Jade, a 19-year-old, medical student, has a similar opinion: "I think burning the town hall is sad, but it's not the saddest part of the protests."

She complains of having to live on â¬300 per month.

"I feel we are not respected as young adults."

Their views on the town hall's fate are not replicated in Limoges' imposing market halls, where neat, narrow timbers sitting upon studded steel girders have been painted a duck-egg blue, using the same engineering approach as the Eiffel Tower.

This has been a "week of chaos" that 63-year-old Jean Roger Faucher would like to forget.

In a region renowned for producing beef, his family has run his fishmonger stool here for more than a century.

"It left us stunned," he says. "I got married in the town hall, so it had an unimaginable effect on us."

News.title: Before you crank up the thermostat, try these tips to keep your house warmer for longer
News.content:
With the clocks going back this weekend, the nights will be drawing in.

So if you have a thicker duvet, now is the time to bring it out. Some supermarkets sell winter duvets for under Â£20 - look for 10.5 tog or higher.

But there's something to be said for a craftily placed blanket, too. When it gets cold, Rebecca, 44, from Hertfordshire, sleeps with a blanket underneath her mattress, which she says stops draughts. "This was passed to me by my nan, she swore by it," she says. Others swear by placing a blanket above the mattress but under the bedsheet.

You can heat your bed before getting in with a hot water bottle, but make sure you check the expiry date. A guide by NHS Scotland, external says to let the water from the kettle cool for a few minutes before filling, only fill it two-thirds full, squeeze air out of the top before putting the stopper on, and don't hold it directly against your skin.

Using an electric blanket - to heat your bed before you get in or to wrap around yourself on the sofa - is "one of the cheapest ways" to stay warm, says Emily Seymour, energy editor at consumer organisation Which?. Testing by Which?, external shows it typically costs between 2p and 8p an hour to run an electric blanket at its highest setting. The London Fire Brigade, external says to unplug your blanket before you get into bed unless it has a thermostat control, not to use a hot water bottle at the same time, and replace it every 10 years.

News.title: Tory activist in 'contract killing broker' claim had worked for party HQ
News.content:
A former Tory activist who appeared to offer to "broker" the hiring of contract killers in an undercover film report previously worked for Conservative headquarters.

Jack Ross was contracted to do social media work for the party until earlier this year, the BBC has been told.

It comes after Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch referred to them as "shocking allegations", adding that she did not "believe that person is a member anymore".

A Conservative spokesman said Ross's party membership had "been suspended with immediate effect pending an investigation". It has reported that Ross said his words were not meant to be taken seriously.

Ross was paid to provide social media advice to the party for a brief period, the BBC has been told. He was never an employee or Conservative Campaign Headquarters pass holder.

However, he met Badenoch on several occasions as part of his role as chief executive of Turning Point UK, an offshoot of a right-wing American organisation.

Ross has also met several other right-wing politicians including the former Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Nigel Farage, the Reform UK leader.

In undercover filming broadcast this week by Al Jazeera, Ross appears to offer to "broker" the services of contract killers.

The Al Jazeera report said its undercover journalist approached Ross in 2022 with a fictitious situation of a family business at risk of being taken over by a criminal gang.

Ross is alleged to have asked the undercover reporter what was needed from him, and listed violent options that could be bought including stabbing, shooting and killing.

Al Jazeera said Ross denied the finding "completely" and claimed everything he said to the reporter was not meant seriously.

Turning Point UK has been approached for comment.

News.title: How does the UK state pension compare with other countries?
News.content:
Getting older is something few of us want to think about. Yet how we fund our later years, and how much we'll get, has been a hot topic.

The triple lock formula - state pensions increasing by the greatest of 2.5%, earnings growth, or inflation - means those benefits have risen far faster than the earnings of workers since its introduction in 2011.

But as housing costs have also been rising fast, pensioner poverty has actually increased slightly in the last decade.

Nevertheless, even if you take those costs into consideration, pensioners are less likely to be in relative poverty - that is, having to get by on less than 60% of the income of the typical household - than families with children or working-age people.

News.title: GP says she was forced out of job after raising concerns about gender treatment
News.content:
Although Doyle at first denied to the tribunal he knew Hall before this, it emerged during the tribunal that he had previously had a number of mentoring meetings with the GP.

The GMC investigation was not taken forward. However, the NHS launched an investigation into Redvers, bringing in an external investigator.

The tribunal heard she was called to what she described as a "brutal" four-hour interrogation.

"It was oppressive, very upsetting. I didn't feel I had the chance at all to explain what had happened," she said. "I broke down at one point".

She said she was off sick for several months as a result and received treatment for trauma.

Other colleagues who were interviewed as part of the investigation into Redvers also complained about the process and the NHS upheld most of their complaints.

The investigation concluded the CEO and trust should apologise to Redvers.

It also warned that Redvers' treatment would have a "broader negative impact" on the willingness of staff to raise concerns.

In 2023, a year after the grievance outcome, when a trans campaigner suggested in an NHS meeting that she was transphobic, Redvers told the tribunal she felt the NHS did not do enough to support her. She felt she had no choice but to leave her job as a safeguarding GP.

"I just felt there's no way I could carry on working in this organisation," she told the BBC.

At about that time, a group of parents, school governors and social workers began raising concerns about WellBn and Hall.

The co-founder of campaign group PSHE Brighton, Rachel Cashman, said: "It is a travesty that Sarah Redvers was punished for doing her job safeguarding and expecting the best standards of care for gender distressed children."

Redvers is now waiting for the outcome of her employment tribunal. She may not get the judgment for several months.

She described what has happened as "personally and professionally difficult" and said the NHS "needs to remember that patients come first" and it should "listen to staff who raise legitimate concerns."

In a statement NHS Surrey and Sussex said: "We engaged professionally and supportively with the Employment Tribunal. We recognise that some employment processes should have been handled differently and have apologised whilst Dr Redvers was employed with us, before, and during the hearings. We await the findings of the tribunal to make any further comment."

NHS England said: "When concerns about prescribing practices by an individual GP were escalated to NHS England national directors in 2023, they met directly with an affected family and asked regional professional standards leads to undertake formal investigations.

"Wider concerns were subsequently identified, and the WellBN practice was asked to stop providing a specialised prescribing service. Further new information led to NHS England and NHS Sussex initiating an independent patient safety investigation in 2025."

Dr Sam Hall and WellBN have been contacted for comment.

In response to the investigation report in June, WellBN said it recognised "the seriousness and sensitivity of the matters raised" and that its priority remained providing "compassionate, safe and effective care for all patients".

News.title: Burnham suggests stocking up on tinned food and bottled water
News.content:
The prime minister has advised people to stock up on tinned food and bottled water in order to be prepared for emergencies.

With storms battering the UK, and in the wake of online disruption caused by a major security flaw, Andy Burnham said "unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common".

The government has drawn up recommendations for households to have three days' worth of bottled water and tinned food to deal with a crisis such as a war, an online attack or a natural disaster.

Burnham added: "It's not about panicking... It's about just taking sensible measures to have enough in the house to tide you over should there be a difficult situation."

At Labour's conference last month, Housing Secretary Angela Rayner joked that her emergency box, external would include a bottle of wine.

She said she'd include: "Mascara, concealer, I don't know, a bottle of Sauvignon Blanc, a tin of baked beans because you've gotta have some baked beans, and I like a good tin of custard as well so I think that'll keep me going for a while."

Asked whether he agreed with her, Burnham told BBC Radio 5 Live's Matt Chorley: "Well, I'm not sure a bottle of wine is your best first port of call if you're in a slightly crisis situation, but it probably helps when you've done the hard work.

"But I'll stick to the basics I think - I do like my beans, so I have plenty of those in the cupboard, and soup.

"I think those are the kind of things that I would recommend people to have, as well as Twiglets, I'm not sure I can get by for too long without those."

Last month, the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis and said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

The chief executive of the Cold Chain Federation, which represents firms transporting temperature-controlled foods, also told the BBC the UK is being targeted by Russian cyber-hackers who "know that there are pinch points in the food supply system".

Speaking at a wildfire resilience summit in Liverpool, Burnham denied the government had failed to properly prepare, saying: "No, we're having the conversation with people about being better prepared because we're living in a world where unexpected events seem to be becoming more and more common.

"Obviously, weather events, and we're in a situation today where the UK is facing storms and obviously, we feel for the people without power in Cornwall right now.

"It is just having those supplies in the house to get you through those moments. So we are having that conversation about resilience."

News.title: Trump says Burnham 'getting it done' after Jackdaw decision
News.content:
Burnham announced the decision to approve the drilling of the Jackdaw gas field earlier this week.

Jackdaw is situated 150 miles (241km) east of Aberdeen and is operated by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Norwegian state energy firm Equinor.

Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.

Environmental campaigners say the decision would hamper efforts to tackle climate change and make "no meaningful difference" to UK energy security.

Based on official forecasts for the amount of gas the UK will need over the next decade, that suggests Jackdaw has the potential to meet around 1.6% of total projected national gas demand between 2026 and 2036.

Operators say it could be connected to the Great British gas network within weeks and could produce gas for the next 11 years.

Trump responded to the decision on Friday, but appeared to confuse oil and gas.

He said: "They're opening up the North Sea oil. I've been after them to do that for two years."

Trump added: "Andy is getting it done, and I guess it's against the liberal principle, but he knows what's right. It's going to make UK a very wealthy country."

In a discussion on Friday, Burnham and Trump spoke about the decision to approve Jackdaw.

The two leaders "agreed on the significant benefits this will bring to the UK, boosting the economy and supporting jobs for British workers", a statement from Number 10 read.

It added that Trump and Burnham "welcomed the continued collaboration between UK and US companies, especially on nuclear power".

Earlier this week, on Wednesday, Trump said the decision was "great news for the wealth and prosperity" of the UK.

Writing on his Truth Social platform, Trump urged the UK to go "full blast" and called the North Sea "one of the greatest and most prosperous areas of oil in the world".

A decision is yet to be taken on whether production can begin at Rosebank, the UK's largest known untapped oil field, which is located off the coast of Shetland in the North Atlantic.

News.title: Green councillors face Labour deadline to disown Zionism policy
News.content:
Labour is set to decide whether to end power-sharing with Green councillors after demanding they disown their party's policy that Zionism is a form of racism.

The BBC has been told Green groups have been given until Sunday to respond to the demand, after which Labour's ruling National Executive Committee (NEC) will decide whether the party will continue with local deals to share power.

Green groups in some areas have publicly stated they do not agree with the policy or have distanced themselves from it, reducing the likelihood the pacts will end.

But in other areas Green councillors are yet to specify where they stand on the issue, meaning local alliances appear more vulnerable to collapse.

The issue is the most acute in nine local authorities where Greens are key partners in power-sharing arrangements, such as making up majorities that enable budgets to be passed and policy decisions to be made.

These include Sheffield City Council, Warwick District Council and Lewes District Council, three authorities where Labour and the Greens are in direct coalition.

The other areas where the Greens play a key role are: West Oxfordshire District Council, Stafford Borough Council, Havant Borough Council, Broadland District Council, Derbyshire Dales District Council and Wealden District Council.

In other areas, Green councillors are not central to local alliances continuing to function. These include Runnymede Borough Council, where Green councillors have left the local ruling alliance folllowing Labour's ultimatum.

In some areas, such as Lewes, Wealden, Broadland, West Sussex and North Somerset, local Green groups have distanced themselves from their party's Zionism policy, or said they do not agree with it.

But other Green groups are yet to publicly respond to Labour's demands, meaning there is greater uncertainty over the future of their co-operation with the party.

In Stafford, the power-sharing arrangement means the Greens have one cabinet member on the authority, councillor Tony Pearce, who holds the climate change portfolio.

Councillor Pearce has been contacted for comment but has not yet responded.

The leader of the Stafford Green group, Doug Rouxel told the BBC they were "formulating a response" to Labour's letter which they would like to put to party members first.

Labour confirmed the if the Greens refused to reject the Zionism policy, a process would then be triggered to remove Pearce from his cabinet position in Stafford.

Elsewhere, the leader of the Labour group on the Green-led Lewes District Council has resigned from the party, following his own party's ultimatum.

Chris Collier, who has been contacted for comment, will now sit as an independent cabinet member on the Labour-Green alliance that was formed to run the council in May 2023.

The BBC has been told Collier did not agree with the tone of Labour's ultimatum to the Green Party over the Zionism policy.

News.title: Man dies after car crashes into Lidl supermarket
News.content:
A man in his 30s has died after a car crashed through the entrance of a Lidl shop in Wolverhampton.

Police were called to the supermarket in Finchfield Hill shortly before 18:00 BST on Friday.

West Midlands Police said the man was pronounced dead at the scene and a number of other people were treated for injuries.

West Midlands Fire Service said it dispatched four crews to the incident at 17:51 BST with two crews still at the scene at 20:05 BST.

News.title: First personalised cancer vaccine cuts risk of disease returning in major trial
News.content:
Shares in the drugmakers MSD (known as Merck in the US) and Moderna have surged since both companies first hinted at the success of the vaccine in the summer.

But investors sold off stock on Thursday after financial analysts said the results were not quite as strong as those seen in an earlier, much smaller trial.

Both companies said they were now "engaging with authorities" suggesting they could file for approval from medicine regulators as soon as next year.

Widespread NHS use will also depend on cost, given that each individual patient will need to have their tumour genetically analysed and a personalised vaccine made for them.

The trial will continue so that the patients involved can be monitored â both to see if the cancer returns over time and to assess whether the drug ultimately helps them live longer.

Professor Alan Melcher from the Institute of Cancer Research in London, who wasn't involved in the research, described the results as "very impressive".

"It is an important proof of principle for the field, although we shouldn't get ahead of the evidence," he said.

"We can't assume from one melanoma trial that the same approach will work across all cancers, and longer follow-up will be important to understand the effect on overall survival."

The full trial results are due to be presented at the European Society of Medical Oncology (ESMO) cancer conference in Madrid on Saturday.

They have yet to be published in a peer-reviewed medical journal, where they can be scrutinised by independent experts.

News.title: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visits China, South Korean news agency reports
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has visited China in his first visit to the country in a year, according to South Korea’s Yonhap news agency.

The agency cited an unidentified government source saying Kim arrived in the Chinese border city of Dandong after crossing a newly opened bridge between the countries.

South Korea’s presidential office and Unification Ministry, which deals with inter-Korean affairs, didn’t immediately confirm the report. North Korean and Chinese state media didn't immediately report on a visit by Kim.

Yonhap said Kim used the New Yalu River Bridge, which opened earlier this month after more than a decade of delay, to arrive in Dandong.

After years of prioritizing Russia, sending thousands of troops and conventional weapons to support President Vladimir Putin’s war in Ukraine, possibly in exchange for military and economic assistance, Kim has more recently sought to strengthen ties with China, the North's traditional main ally and economic lifeline.

Kim’s visit comes months after Chinese President Xi Jinping traveled to Pyongyang in June for a meeting with Kim. During their summit, Xi expressed Beijing’s willingness to expand bilateral cooperation in trade, agriculture, construction and technology, while Kim described ties with China as a top strategic priority.

Kim last visited Beijing in September 2025, when he met with Xi and watched a military parade alongside Putin and other foreign leaders.

News.title: Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.

The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.

Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.

“We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily,” al-Shahid said in a phone interview.

Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.

The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn’t only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.

Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to “the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster.”

Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents’ access to wells

Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country’s north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.

War-related damage to Taiz’s aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.

By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.

As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents’ access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.

The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.

As Taiz’s fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.

The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food

Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.

Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.

Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.

These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.

“The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises,” Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.

Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.

Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.

“We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food,” he said in a phone interview.

Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.

Why Taiz matters to the Houthis

While the Yemeni government still controls the center of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city.

Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south toward Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that won’t be easy.

“Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters,” said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.

Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city. The Associated Press couldn’t independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren’t allowed to brief the media, but Yemen’s foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group's tightening grip on the city.

The Houthis' fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials said.

Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians.

Abdel Gaber said he can hear loud explosions every day from fighting that is happening roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away. The family isn't returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety.

Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive.

“Staying in our home is inevitable — whether it be a matter of life or death,” al-Shahid said.

___

Associated Press writer Ahmed al-Haj in Aden, Yemen, contributed to this report.

News.title: Table for one: Could dining alone be the unlikely cure for loneliness?
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Dining alone is supposed to be having a moment, though you wouldn’t know it from Franco’s terrace, where I appear to be the only person without a companion. Around me are convivial little groups of two and three, deep in conversation. I have no company and, as if that weren’t enough, I have also decided to spend the entire lunch without looking at my phone. No scrolling, no messages, not even a quick photograph of my food.

Despite writing about food and wine for a living, I rarely give my own meals the attention they deserve. The frenetic pace of freelance life in London means lunch is usually gobbled down over emails at home or eaten while distractedly chatting when out. The only pause comes when I whip out my phone to take a shot of a plate with the usual apologetic quip: “The phone eats first!” My phone is never far from my hand; my notifications are always on. And yet, surely good food and excellent restaurants deserve better than half our attention?

In an age of endless distractions, solo dining is becoming an act of self-care. Today, it is just me and my food. This is going to be a challenge.

Which is why I have chosen Jermyn Street’s Franco’s, London’s oldest Italian restaurant, for my experiment. Partly because you always receive a warm welcome – Boban, the restaurant manager, greets many of the arriving clientele by name – and partly because the terrace allows for excellent people-watching. It seems as good a place as any to learn how to enjoy my own company.

Boban immediately brings me a glass of their house champagne, and I take in my surroundings rather than doomscroll everyone’s “autumnal feels” reels on Instagram.

Everyone here has amazing hair. The women’s thick locks cascade like waterfalls down their Loro Piana-clad backs, while the men’s are just as lustrous, pushed back with that slight flop of the public-school boy elite. I have rarely studied my fellow diners so closely, but by now I could probably give you a fairly accurate inventory of everyone’s wardrobe. I note I am the only person in trainers and slide my feet further under the table as a stuffed courgette flower arrives.

It is October but the sun is shining, creating dapples of light across the white tablecloth. My Champagne catches the light beside a potted olive tree, and the little plate in front of me is so pretty that my hand automatically goes for my bag. Then I remember my rules. I can’t take a photograph. I am just going to have to remember it. Oddly, as I write this, I can still picture the whole scene in detail, probably far better than if I had posted it on Instagram and immediately forgotten about it.

Without anyone to talk to, my mouth and mind are fully focused on the flavours. I notice the crispness of the batter, the saltiness of the ricotta cheese. Damn, I think. If I had cooked this, this is exactly how I would want somebody to eat it. A dish that would usually have taken me two bites takes me five. I am chewing properly, as we are forever being told to do and almost never do. My eating has slowed right down. My Champagne, however, is going fast.

As I leave the warm embrace of Franco’s, I realise I have appreciated this meal more than almost any I can remember. Not because it was the fanciest lunch I’ve ever had – although the Champagne and truffle certainly helped – but because, for once, I was properly there for it

A bowl of mussels arrives with a glass of Chablis, the shells piled up on a thick slice of bread to soak up the white wine sauce. I use an empty shell to pinch up the chubby little molluscs and suck them in with the salty, chilli, garlicky sauce. I am thinking about how I am going to write about this and realise I have never thought about the colour of a mussel before. These are not quite orange, or beige, or pink. They are the colour of the terracotta buildings of Toulouse, and suddenly lunch feels rather like a holiday. I must have eaten hundreds of mussels in my time, but I have never looked at them quite like this.

It feels a bit like meditation, and I am getting a little smug about how much I am enjoying my meal more than anyone else here. My first instinct is to message my friend Anna to boast of my newfound mindfulness. My second is to message my partner to tell him this is now my favourite restaurant in London. I hadn’t realised quite how often I send people every passing thought, simply because my phone is there in my hand. For once, these thoughts will have to wait until I see them in person.

I look around and realise that almost no one else is drinking at lunch. It is all sparkling water and I wonder when boozy lunches stopped happening. Then an American woman on a date behind me cries, “I’m a psychic! And I know we’re meant to be together, here, right now!” I feel reassured that at least one other table appears to be embracing the spirit of a long lunch.

Other people’s conversations float around me. The shirtmaker Emma Willis is at the next table talking business with the men with the great hair. A trio arrive, the women entirely clad in Gucci, from sunglasses and bags to red-striped trousers and shoes. The man has matched his red gilet to his socks. They order still wine as they have “had a lot of fizz today already”. It is 3.15pm. A couple more solo diners have arrived, and the wine is beginning to flow.

When my pasta arrives, it is all thick ribbons of al dente tagliatelle coated in butter, topped with mushrooms and generous, scallop-edged slivers of truffle. I feel a slight pang as the parmesan is grated over it – ordinarily, I would have filmed that. But the feeling passes. The sommelier, Rae, keeps flitting by for a quick chat, and between her friendly banter and the food I haven’t felt a lack of company at all. If anyone has noticed I am by myself, I imagine they are wondering who the cool, enigmatic woman is confidently dining by herself. This is almost certainly wishful thinking, but I am enjoying myself too much to care.

By the time I have finished, Emma Willis has left and the two gentlemen ask if I would like to join them. Having managed more than two hours in my own company, I decide I have earned a conversation. They have noticed my leather notebook and tell me about their luxury leather goods brand Balfour Cairns. Rae tops us all up with the impeccable Isole e Olena Chardonnay, and it turns out we have mutual friends. They ask if I would join them for rooftop drinks, but I have to go. As I depart, two men sitting alone look up and smile; one gestures to the empty seat at his table.

Have I found the cure for the loneliness epidemic? Is this the new (old) way for people to meet in real life? Put down those dating apps and book a table for one, as apparently nothing makes you more attractive as a dining companion than being happy in your own company.

As I leave the warm embrace of Franco’s, I realise I have appreciated this meal more than almost any I can remember. Not because it was the fanciest lunch I’ve ever had – although the Champagne and truffle certainly helped – but because, for once, I was properly there for it. I can remember every course, more than a few outfits and a surprising amount of excellent hair.

For someone who spends so much time writing about eating and drinking, it has been a useful reminder to enjoy the business of doing both. I shall be pencilling in a few more lunches for one because the ultimate luxury isn’t Michelin-starred dining; it’s having the time to give the present my uninterrupted attention.

Franco’s can be found at 61 Jermyn Street, St James’s, London SW1Y 6LX. For more information, visit their website.

Libby Brodie is a freelance wine writer, founder of Bacchus & Brodie Wine Consultancy and co-host of ‘The Inner Table: The Art of Living Well’ podcast. She was recently named in the Top 100 Most Influential in Drinks list by Drinks Retailing. Her Instagram handle is @libbybrodie.

News.title: Back to Black at 20: The hidden story behind the iconic cover of Amy Winehouse’s final album
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

To label a release one of the greatest albums of the 21st century is, generally, a hyperbolic accolade. Not in the case of Back to Black.

The bluntly beautiful 11-track masterpiece, with its jangling Sixties melodies, catapulted Amy Winehouse into the mainstream and elevated the 23-year-old to heights of the artists who’d inspired her: Prince began performing “Love Is a Losing Game” on stage. Ronnie Spector covered the album’s title track live alongside The Ronettes’ hits. It was the bestselling album of the year – and won Amy five Grammy awards in one night. “I am so proud of this album,” she responded, quietly shell-shocked after her historic sweep. “I put my heart and soul into it.”

open image in gallery Amy Winehouse on Back to Black: ‘I put my heart and soul into it’ ( Getty )

Wander through Amy’s home borough of Camden on the record’s 20th anniversary and the singer is everywhere; remembered in smiling images taken for Back to Black, and her first album Frank, installed in an open-air exhibition above benches on Granary Square and King’s Boulevard. Among recent visitors is the star’s first stylist, Lou Wood, who took Amy shopping at Selfridges for many of her early photoshoots. “One day she turned up in a massive pair of high heels and hot pants, carrying a guitar. We were walking for five hours,” she says, laughing. “She wasn't a manufactured artist. She had her own mind definitely, and her own style.”

Hilariously funny and down to earth, Amy was a dream to go shopping with. “She liked retro polo shirts, bits of denim, pedal pushers and she used to personify all the clothes,” says Wood. “She’d be like, ‘I don’t like him. I like him.’” All the selected items would then get flung into piles on Amy’s bed, from which they’d cobble together looks for her second album’s promo shots. Any designer items were begged and borrowed from Wood’s contacts. “You had to go cap in hand,” she says. “Amy’s first album was a success, but she wasn’t a household name.“

One such borrowed dress, by Thai designer Disaya Sorakraikitikul, was worn in the eventual Back to Black cover shot – and auctioned for £43,200 (quadruple its estimated price) for charity in 2011. Accessories, though, were done “on the cheap”: A red belt from Topshop, Amy’s own necklaces, plus heaps of “gold and fake” bling from Shepherd’s Bush Market.

Wood had no clue about the success Amy would go on to have when she played Back to Black in her car, blown away by its brilliance before its official release. “We can’t tell the future,” she says. “You do the job that you’re employed to do. You’ve got no idea.”

open image in gallery Winehouse on the night ‘Back to Black’ won five Grammys ( Getty )

At a time when designers were dragging their feet over lending Amy apparel, photographer Mischa Richter leapt at the chance to work with her when propositioned by Island Records. He’d seen Amy live at a jazz lounge charity gig at The Serpentine, where she was starstruck by Missy Elliot in the front row. “She just kept saying, ‘I can’t believe that you’re here,” he says. “She was adorable. Such an incredible voice. I was blown away.”

On the day of the shoot, Amy was hours late. She’d been at one of her best friend’s weddings the night before and hadn’t been to bed. She wanted the day to be done and was self-conscious in front of the camera, asking Richter whether her friend could stand near the lens with her head facing her to put her at ease. “I said, ‘absolutely not. No way. I can’t work like that,’” he says. “So, we talked for a while, and then she was cool.”

Once the shoot relocated from a bar on Portobello Road to Richter’s home in Kensal Rise alongside the photographer’s young children, Amy relaxed. There wasn’t a big team. There were no studio lights, just the blind-free windows. Naturally, they gravitated towards a room where Richter stored negatives and contact sheets. He took the last shot of the day there, in front of a cupboard that had blackboard paint on its sliding doors, which was selected for the Back to Black cover. “That was serendipitous,” he says of the choice. “We hadn’t had any conversation about the name.”

That day was the last time Richter ever saw Amy. “I see that photo now and I just feel sad,” he says, retrospectively. “I didn’t pick it for the cover. The label did. I think it really shows that she was vulnerable. When I met her in her apartment, then at the photoshoot, you could feel her excitement about what she’d just made; what she’d achieved as an artist before all the b******t that basically killed her. Personally, selfishly, I’m sort of glad that I wasn’t privy to any of that stuff... It swallowed her up.”

After the release of Back to Black, Wood styled Amy for the “Rehab” music video and other gigs and TV appearances. She stopped midway through promotion for the album, after the “You Know I’m No Good” video, where the singer is seen drinking whisky, arguing with a man, and crying on the bathroom floor. “Things had become quite difficult for her,” she says. “It was starting to feel quite uncomfortable for me.”

open image in gallery ‘She was vulnerable’: Winehouse died from alcohol poisoning in 2011 ( PA )

Today, as the world prepares to celebrate 20 years of Back to Black with a big BBC anniversary concert at Camden’s Roundhouse, Wood still struggles to listen to Amy’s music or see her as any form of entertainment. “Even if I’m out at the pub, I go outside and have a cigarette because I find it difficult,” she says. “Amy wasn’t an icon to me. She was a human being, a young woman, someone with huge talent, who tragically died.”

More than the musician, Wood lost a warmhearted colleague and friend. A deeply compassionate person, who’d invite friends round to her flat and make them all chicken soup. Wood’s main memory of the Back to Black shoot day isn’t the outfits, the artistic difference, or the images – but that her two-year-old son had been in casualty with a high temperature.

“Amy had met my son and was going ‘Oh, can I hold him? Can I hold him? Oh my God, he’s so lovely. Can I babysit?’” she says. “She loved children. So, when I turned up to the shoot after being in hospital all morning, she was like, ‘Why are you here? Why aren’t you at home looking after your baby?’ She was more concerned about him than herself or the photoshoot. She was lovely, caring. Those are the memories I have of her.”

News.title: Welcome back: Mitsubishi Outlander
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in
