When my companion climbed into the new Mitsubishi Outlander, she was immediately struck by the comfortable, well-appointed interior of this highly capable SUV. It has immense “showroom appeal”. You are immediately impressed by the sumptuous leather seats, a warm tan shade in my test example, and a solidly built interior. Mitsubishis have long been popular with rural types for their durability, with the rugged L200 pick-up probably second only to the Toyota HiLux in durability, and the Outlander imbues its users with that sense that it will look after them whatever the circumstances.

Its reputation goes before it, and even though the marque has been absent from the UK for five years, thanks to stiff competition and some disadvantageous changes to taxation of plug- in hybrids, it’s not been forgotten by a fairly loyal band of customers.

open image in gallery Dialled up: the switch in the centre console automatically optimises for different terrain, while ‘Power’ mode boosts performance ( Sean O'Grady )

Now, with fuel prices being where they are, the cars are back, and it’s a very welcome return. Here is an excellent blend of luxury, go-anywhere adjustable four-wheel drive and reliability that is actually quite uncommon. More reliable than a Land Rover, more of a known quantity than a Jaecoo, cheaper than a Mercedes-Benz, if you will. Plus an outstanding range on a single tank of petrol and a fully charged battery – about 50 miles in EV only, and 500-plus in total.

Go anywhere indeed, with a big switch in the centre console that will automatically optimise for tarmac, snow, gravel, mud, power and fuel-saving “eco”. “Power” mode gives the beast a fair old chunk of extra performance, but at greatly disproportionate cost in mpg. For off-road, there’s the choice of low and standard range gears. The choice extends to two trim levels, Nativa and Diamond (which is extra lush), and you can choose a five- or seven-seater.

The Spec Mitsubishi Outlander Diamond PHEV Price: £49,995 (as tested, range starts at £46,995) Engine capacity: 2.4lpetrol, 4-cyl + 22.7kWh battery, CVT auto 4WD Power output (PS): 299 Top speed (mph): 106 0 to 60 (seconds): 7.9 Fuel economy (mpg): 313, with full plug-in usage CO2 emissions (WLTP, g/km): 20 with full plug-in usage

All and any of the many potential driving adventures take place in a welcoming cabin. That, indeed, is a great attraction in this model, and especially if you’ve found yourself over-exposed to the stark, overly sombre and simplified interiors that have grown so fashionable in recent years.

Partly under the influence of the very advanced electronics favoured by the Chinese makes, but also because the world’s car designers became obsessed with the iPad as the apogee of good taste and efficiency, common sense, durability and safety were all compromised. It’s an old theme of mine, but every time I see the pendulum swinging back to the more conventional style of controls, ie knobs, buttons and dials, I feel like the automotive world is healing.

open image in gallery Tan and relaxing: sumptuous leather seats and a solidly built interior add to the considerable ‘showroom appeal’ of the Outlander ( Sean O'Grady )

So it is with this Outlander. Mitsubishi’s UK importers, International Motor Group claim that this model is new “from the ground up”, and it is, but there are a couple of important caveats to add. First, this iteration of the Outlander series dates back to 2021, just when Mitsubishi gave up on the British market – so not entirely fresh, and I believe there’s a facelift on the way.

Second, the Outlander shares a good deal of its underpinnings with the Nissan X-Trail, even if the siblings have different drivetrains (the makes have financial links). Both essentially work with their respective petrol engines generating the electricity to motors that drive the wheels, supplementing the charge emanating from the 22.7kWh battery. But, if needs be, unlike the Nissan, the Outlander’s engine can also supply varying amounts of propulsion direct to the wheels.

open image in gallery All-round potential: to get the best from the Outlander, like most hybrids, it should be plugged in and charged up ( Sean O'Grady )

Both, therefore, offer most of the economy, smoothness and refinement found in true electric cars. The Mitsubishi also draws upon long experience of PHEV technology, and the Outlander was a pioneer when first introduced in 2014. Then everyone copied it, which became a problem, and still is.

The choice of vehicles in this sector is legion, but I’d feel obliged to mention the Jaecoo 8, Mazda CX-5, stunning Hyundai Santa Fe, trad Volvo XC90 and Skoda Kodiaq as some of the more interesting alternatives, broadly speaking (plus the Nissan X-Trail). In the case of any PHEVs, the usual rule applies; to get the best out of them they should be plugged in and charged up. Otherwise you’ve just got a petrol vehicle carrying a heavy battery pack doing 35mpg.

As you can gather, I like the Mitsubishi because, despite the Nissan links, there’s something very authentic about it, and it’s an unpretentious affair. It doesn’t have to try too hard to be what it is, and I found it lends that self-confidence to its keeper.

The “face” is a bit challenging, I’ll admit, a little “too outlandish”, but with a long partnership of human and machine ahead, you will have time to grow accustomed to it. Nothing outlandish about that, you know.

News.title: Naomi Ackie: ‘I got whiplash. I played Whitney Houston then went straight back to my damp little basement flat’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

When I go through hectic times, I end up wiping my memory,” Naomi Ackie explains. It’s a good thing, she insists. “I do it if I’m overwhelmed, or if I’m around people I don’t like. I can just lift them out of my mind without effort.”

We’re talking about selective amnesia because we’re talking about Whitney Houston, who Ackie played in a 2022 biopic called I Wanna Dance with Somebody. It was an enormous opportunity, one that promised to propel the London-born actor – then having just turned 31 – into the big leagues. But with it came extra scrutiny, extra commitments. “Pray I don’t get thrown into some lion’s den,” she had told me back then, before being whisked away for more press junkets and radio appearances. The reviews for the film came out soon afterwards, praising her performance but criticising everything else about it. It made no real money. Ackie went home. “I got real whiplash,” she recalls now. “I was Whitney Houston and then I’m just back sitting in my damp little basement flat in [North London district] Angel.”

For Ackie, that whiplash meant unemployment or, at least, a return to the endless hustle – for parts, for recognition, for a shot. But now she appreciates it. “Everything was brand-new back then, and I didn’t know who I was going to be within it,” she says. “But it turned out that not much changed. I didn’t change.”

Today, Ackie is one of Britain’s most successful movie stars, even if she hasn’t yet become a household name. This weekend she stars as the scientist responsible for creating a gloopy Gotham City anti-hero in the DC Comics movie Clayface, and next weekend she’s a radical feminist shoplifter in Boots Riley’s gonzo black comedy I Love Boosters. Recently, she’s also led Zoe Kravitz’s rape-revenge thriller Blink Twice, romanced Robert Pattinson and Robert Pattinson in Bong Joon-ho’s dystopian duplicate tale Mickey 17, and provided oceans of empathy as the best friend to Eva Victor’s withdrawn assault survivor in last year’s award-winning Sorry, Baby.

Clayface fans are definitely like, ‘oh no, it’s not canon!’ But who needs normal canon?

“I think Naomi is honestly the best actor in the world,” Victor tells me. “I always said that my character in Sorry, Baby is the moon, and what we needed was our sun. And Naomi walked in and immediately I was like, ‘Oh God – there it is.’”

Ackie does radiate. She arrives in a suite at Soho Hotel dressed to the nines and trailed by an elaborate entourage – publicists, agents, hair and make-up. But she’s very much a passenger in it, still speaking in that straight-to-the-point east London accent and quick to dismantle any worry that Hollywood has got its claws in her. She has a big, gappy smile that envelops everyone in her immediate vicinity. She’s 35 now, and cringes when I remind her that she was once terrified at the prospect of being in her thirties.

“Thirty is a baby!” she shrieks. “I’m sure women older than me would have been like, shut aaap!” She runs her nails down the sleeves of her taupe jacket. “I was convinced that I’d get less opportunities the older I got. I remember thinking, ‘Oh no, have I missed my window?’ But I’ve got so much more life to live!” She cringes again, then cackles. “That sounds so dumb, please don’t write that.”

open image in gallery Ackie, Keke Palmer, Poppy Liu and Taylour Paige in Boots Riley’s ‘I Love Boosters’ ( Neon )

In I Love Boosters, she is Sade, a resolutely earthbound communist in a succession of outrageous wigs, who spends her nights as part of The Velvet Gang, a troupe of women (Keke Palmer, Eiza Gonzalez and Zola’s Taylour Paige are among them) who rob luxury stores and then flog their pilfered wares for a discount. The women collide with Demi Moore’s ruthless fashion maven, before becoming embroiled in a scheme involving blackmail, teleportation and Chinese sweatshops. Boots Riley, its writer/director – he broke out with 2018’s gig-economy comedy Sorry to Bother You – has a unique ability to slip progressive politics into the most easily digestible and visually inventive forms, and it’s no different here. It made Ackie think about community, and who gets credit for work and who can make an actual living off it.

“Take my clothes,” she says. “What I’m wearing isn’t just a reflection of me but also the team around me. The clothes are from a brand, but on top of that were made by someone else. We don’t think about the labour behind all of these things, and the work that goes into it. It all comes from somewhere, and absolutely everyone deserves a chance to be appreciated and paid appropriately for their work.”

Riley said he cast Ackie and her co-stars for their “specificness”. “Some actors have sanded their edges down so much that they can be whoever,” he explained. “But it comes off as a lot of nothing to me.”

Ackie smiles when I repeat this. “There’s a Spice Girl-y vibe about us,” she laughs. “We each come with a different story, and what I see in us – and I think what Boots is talking about – is that we’re authentic and honest. Because now I try to be as honest as I can.”

open image in gallery Ackie as Whitney Houston in 2022’s ‘I Wanna Dance with Somebody’ ( Sony )

After studying at the Royal Central School of Speech and Drama and bagging a role as Florence Pugh’s handmaid in the period thriller Lady Macbeth, there were the initial years of nothing. She spent much of that time trying to be somebody else – speak a different way, express herself differently. “But it doesn’t work,” she says. “You can’t fake being whatever you think the zeitgeist is looking for. I’ve been in this business for nearly 11 years and been told no hundreds of times. I know I have limits, but the job of an artist is to find out what those limits are, and then try and push through them.”

She’s been great at picking projects, and fighting for roles that feel novel and original. We’re speaking in the week of the Paramount-Warner Bros studio merger, which has raised concerns about the future of original films and a possible mandate to focus on franchises and intellectual property. Warner Bros chiefs Pam Abdy and Mike De Luca were two of the merger’s biggest fatalities – they lost their jobs, despite being the people who greenlit ambitious and often commercially successful original movies including Sinners, Weapons, One Battle After Another and Mickey 17. Ackie sighs and shakes her head when I mention their exits.

“I can understand that going with an IP works, but I think it’s running out,” she says. “People are getting bored of it. And it’s about passing down the gauntlet, and investing in filmmakers with something to say. It doesn’t even take as much money – look at Obsession! That was like a cute little 20-quid movie!” (Curry Barker’s spooky wish fulfillment horror cost $750,000 to make and has to date earned a colossal $523m at the box office.) “Every single film is a gamble. I’ve never signed onto anything that I’m convinced will be a surefire win. But why not take the risk on things that are big swings?”

Which brings us nicely to Clayface. It’s an example of taking a piece of IP and having fun with it – Clayface is traditionally a Batman villain capable of extraordinary shapeshifting, but James Watkins’ film axes Batman and instead uses the character as the jumping-off point for a tale of madness and Cronenbergian ooze. The movie is subsequently disgusting, full of sludgy body freakiness and scissors taken to fused eyelids.

open image in gallery Ackie stars alongside Tom Rhys Harries in ‘Clayface’ ( Warner Bros )

“People are definitely like, ‘Oh no, it’s not canon!’,” Ackie says. “But who needs normal canon? I don’t want to say anything controversial, but adding new things to the conversation is so important. Film is something that needs to evolve over time. It’s why so many remakes don’t work. Yes, it worked in the Nineties or the Eighties, but that’s because it was a different time. We need to be present with what’s going on in the world now, so that we can reflect it.”

Ackie tends to oscillate between conviction and catastrophising. She admits that it usually takes her dad, a Transport for London worker, to talk her down off the ledge – it was him who convinced her to keep acting when she nearly walked away from it in the years after Lady Macbeth, and it’s him who always lets her know when he thinks she’s travelling too much. “That’s his main thing right now,” she says. “He’s very used to my life otherwise. Like he doesn’t even come to the premieres any more – no wait, don’t put that. He’ll be like, ‘What the hell, Nay?’” Ackie’s mother, who worked for the NHS, died when she was 22, and didn’t get to see the accomplished career her daughter would go on to build. But she’s grateful that her father has. “I know he’s proud of me, but I hope he’s proud of my ordinary-life stuff more so,” she says. “I dip in, have a little fun, wear some nice clothes and talk about a job that I love, and then I go back home and daydream about getting a dog.”

Her dad won’t like it, but she’s due in Los Angeles imminently for more Clayface promotion, then New York, then back to London again. Before that, though, she’s headed to a screen talk thrown in her honour as part of the London Film Festival. “I’m scared!” she admits. “What if I show up and there’s only, like, 10 people there?”

The next day, of course, hundreds gather to hear Ackie speak. True to form, she really didn’t have anything to worry about.

‘Clayface’ is in cinemas, and ‘I Love Boosters’ is in cinemas from 30 October

News.title: Paris shuts museums and police deploy in big numbers for new protests across France
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Major museums in Paris closed and authorities deployed a sizable police force for a round of new protests Saturday across France, hoping to prevent a repeat of last week’s violent unrest that shocked the country.

Scenes of looting, burned-out cars and attacks on public buildings left the impression that the government had lost control, as groups of masked vandals targeted businesses in Paris and other city centers.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.

A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.

Museums are closed and shopkeepers are worried

Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.

Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend’s hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.

Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.

Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.

Some protests have been banned

Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.

Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.

President Emmanuel Macron, a centrist, entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.

Saturday’s demonstration in the city of Orléans, about 110 kilometers (70 miles) south of Paris, will also be closely watched.

About 50 organizations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Organizers include labor unions, left-wing parties, student and anti-racism groups.

Students and workers are angry

The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school southeast of Paris over a lack of staff.

From there, class boycotts and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and nationwide, including smaller towns. High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.

With the government seemingly unable to respond to students’ demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron’s successor.

“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. “And it’s not possible anymore.”

News.title: France protests latest: 70,000 police deployed as Macron’s last-ditch talks to halt potential riots fail

News.title: How an aid initiative killed thousands of children in war-torn Africa
News.content:
Tormented by pain from severe internal burns, Amza Kebbie is one of thousands of children in Sierra Leone damaged for life by an aid intervention which went horribly wrong.

It has been five days since the four-year-old boy drank caustic soda, one of the two main ingredients for making soap, after mistaking it for drinking water. The highly corrosive liquid, also known as sodium hydroxide, has stripped the lining of his oesophagus and part of his stomach, causing life changing damage.

He’s now in intensive care, clinging precariously to life. An intravenous drip provides fluids and there’s a nasal cannula that enables him to breathe. Medics and relatives look over him around the clock.

If he can gather enough strength (which the nurses say is by no means guaranteed) the dangerously sick child will undergo a gastrostomy, an operation that will see a tube directly inserted into his stomach so that he can be fed long term.

Amza drank caustic soda while being looked after by a neighbour who was making soap at home Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

He can no longer swallow properly and may never be able to do so again, say his doctors.

This is not an isolated tragedy. Across Sierra Leone, there are thousands of children like Amza, and their number is growing every year.

At the Goderich Surgical Centre in the capital Freetown, around 200 children are admitted annually with caustic soda poisoning. Many more are thought to die in remote regions where emergency medical treatment is unavailable.

Behind the calamity is a humanitarian initiative that has spectacularly backfired. It’s a prime example of the law of unintended consequences; of a seemingly sensible and undoubtedly well meaning public health intervention doing more harm than good.

Fatmata Kamara accidentally drank caustic soda at her grandmother’s house in 2014 and has had a feeding tube ever since Credit : SImon Townsley

The story starts in the aftermath of Sierra Leone’s vicious civil war, which ran between 1991 and 2002.

Fought between the government and the Revolutionary United Front – backed by Liberian warlord Charles Taylor – the war claimed an estimated 50,000 to 70,000 lives, displaced 2.5 million people and left the country brutalised and in ruins.

In its aftermath, international aid agencies and NGOs desperately sought ways to revive the country and alighted on DIY soap making as a way of killing two birds with one stone.

Siblings Aminata Fofana and Salieu Bangura help out with the family soap-making business Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Organisations including UNHCR, UNICEF and World Vision thought the practice would both improve sanitation in the country’s disease-ridden shanty towns and provide home-bound women with the means to earn a sustainable income.

It seemed like an obvious “win-win”, and schemes to help women set up in the soap making business rapidly proliferated.

An annual report by the International Federation of the Red Cross, published in May 2002, promoted a micro-finance scheme to fund small-scale soapmaking.

Saieu Bangura, 13, with a tub of soap flakes Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

In 2005, the Centre for War Affected Women in Sierra Leone’s Kono district, backed by the UNHCR, listed soap making as one of the main training courses for war widows and female amputees.

And at about the same time, the Freetown-based Safer Future Youth Development Programme, supported by UNICEF and the charity War Child, provided “a tool kit for soap production” at its training workshops.

As recently as 2020, Action Aid ran a promotional article on its Sierra Leone website showing how soap making had enabled women to become financially independent of their husbands.

The article ran under the headline: “With Soap Making Skills – I'm Empowered!”

Mabinty Bangura is taken to theatre for an endoscopy Credit : Simon Townsley

It is for good reason that the ancient Greek physician Hippocrates urged doctors “first, do no harm”.

To follow the rule literally is not possible as all health interventions entail some risk but it's a reminder never to underestimate the capacity of a new intervention to backfire.

There are plenty of examples from history to choose from.

The surgical team examine the internal damage via an endoscopy Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A child’s gastrostomy scar with a feeding tube in place Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Giuseppe Meucci, chief surgeon at the Goderich Surgical Centre Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Ibrahim Kerah is fed by his father Mohamed Credit : SImon Townsley

The hospital has many of these gastrostomy patients.

In a ward dedicated to soda burns, four-year-old Ibrahim Kerah is being fed through his stomach tube by his father Mohamed.

The Telegraph watches as Mohamed carefully prepares his son’s meal, adding spinach leaves to the porridge-like mix which is fed into a syringe at the end of the tube.

Pregnant Isatu Alie now works as a patient ambassador Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

A small proportion of the patients needing treatment following caustic soda burns are adults.

Mothers are taught how to prepare liquid food; Junisa Bundeh shows his feeding tube Credit : SImon Townsley

In the muddy lanes of Freetown’s Waterloo district there are makeshift soap making operations all over.

The coloured plastic buckets full of either soda or water are everywhere.

Against the backdrop of the rainy season’s persistent gloom, the containers symbolise a measure of cleanliness for families sheltering from torrential downpours under mouldy concrete awnings.

As the Telegraph watches Yabom Kapro, a village elder, making soap, the risks involved are immediately obvious.

Chief Yabom Kapro makes soap at her Waterloo town home, near Freetown Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

As she tips a purple bucket of caustic soda solution into a large basin and then adds palm oil from a plastic jerrycan, local children hover round the cluster of colourful containers.

“When you dilute the caustic soda, it is completely clear like water at first,” says another soap maker, 43-year-old Cilina Bangura.

“I want my children to continue making soap when I stop working,” she says. “I took out a loan to buy everything I needed, and now it is the only way I can make a living.

“Of course, I know how dangerous soda is – it has burned my skin many times – but I don’t have another option.”

Home-made soap, in Waterloo Credit : The Telegraph/SImon Townsley

Maimunatu Sankoh, three, whose family lives in a nearby tin-roof shack, is sadly too well aware of that danger from her own bitter experience of soda poisoning.

As she feeds her daughter through a stomach tube, Maimunatu’s mum Iyesatu complains: “I have never seen any public information about soda.

“There are warnings on the packets but that is no use once the product is dissolved in water. They need to tell people to keep buckets out of the way.”

Iyesatu Kamara feeds her daughter Maimunatu Sankoh at their home Credit : SImon Townsley

Incidents of children consuming harmful chemicals are not confined to developing countries and were once common in the west.

In the US, the Poison Prevention Packaging Act was introduced in 1970, mandating childproof containers and the labelling of harmful household products.

The UK followed suit in 1975 with the introduction of child-resistant safety caps on containers of caustic soda and most other noxious household substances.

Despite the risks, Cilina says she can't afford to stop making soap Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Such legislation is still a long way off in Sierra Leone and is anyway far too late for four-year-old Amza.

Under heavy sedation in the intensive care unit, his glazed eyes open only occasionally.

The only visible evidence of his injuries is some scarring on his lips, but the doctors say his throat, oesophagus and stomach have all been seared by several large gulps of soda.

The boy’s mother, Mamie Kebbie, 30, keeps a watchful vigil, stroking his listless head tenderly. She says he used to be a playful and vivacious child.

If they are taken to hospital quickly, children with soda burns are normally given an oesophageal dilation endoscopy – a procedure which aims to keep the oesophagus open – but for Amza this has not been possible.

Freetown, Sierra Leone Credit : Simon Townsley

“This is a very severe case,” explains nurse Annette Turay, who heads the hospital’s intensive care unit. “When he was brought in, about 10 hours after he had ingested the soda, we were unable to conduct an endoscopy because he already had respiratory problems.

“He has pneumonia and he cannot feed through his mouth. He cannot even swallow his own saliva.

Mamie Kebbie keeps a vigil at her son's bedside Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“It will be a week before he is strong enough for us to be able to operate. We will insert a gastric tube into his stomach. He will have to keep this as his main way of being fed for a long time, potentially forever.”

But nurse Turay has seen worse.

“I have seen so many children suffering a lot after ingesting soda, so many dying too.

“A few weeks ago, we had a child in the ward who died because his stomach was completely gone”.

The Telegraph contacted all the NGOs involved in the setting up of and promotion of soap making schemes in Sierra Leone that are mentioned in this story for comment.

News.title: Carrick weighs up stripping Bruno Fernandes of Man Utd captaincy
News.content:
A defiant Michael Carrick refused to rule out stripping Bruno Fernandes of the captaincy as the Manchester United manager told his players to cut out their public sniping and start doing their talking on the pitch.

Carrick struck a bullish tone as he came out fighting and moved to reassert his authority after a tumultuous past fortnight that has left him battling to save his job ahead of Sunday’s must-win game against Bournemouth at Old Trafford.

The United manager began his press conference on Friday afternoon with a stirring five-and-a-half-minute monologue in which he issued an emotional call to arms to his players to demonstrate the values of hard work, sacrifice, humility and resilience that define the club.

Referencing Sir Matt Busby, Sir Alex Ferguson, Sir Bobby Charlton, Ryan Giggs and Wayne Rooney, Carrick warned there could be no “entitlement” culture in echoes of complaints from his predecessor Ruben Amorim.

United are actively considering their options in the event Carrick cannot quickly arrest a shocking start to the season that hit a new low with Wednesday’s 4-1 humiliation by Como. The likes of Julian Nagelsmann, Eddie Howe, Unai Emery, Fabian Hürzeler and Antonio Conte are in the frame.

But Carrick insisted he was “100 per cent” convinced he was the right man to take United forward and, while he claimed the dressing room was “not divided”, he has had to contend with first defender Lisandro Martínez and then Fernandes venting in public.

Martínez was fined and publicly apologised for an extraordinary tirade at Jason Wilcox, the director of football, and the Old Trafford board last week before Fernandes appeared to call out Carrick’s tactics in the wake of the Como debacle.

Carrick responded at the time to having his set-up and approach questioned by suggesting tactics count for little if players are unprepared to run.

Asked if he would consider taking the captaincy off Fernandes, Carrick said: “I’m just saying I’ll always – whatever the situation is – do what’s best for the club.”

News.title: Oil hits five-month high amid fears of fresh strikes on Iran
News.content:
The price of oil has hit a five-month high amid fears Donald Trump will ramp up strikes in the Middle East following the midterm elections.

Brent crude, the international benchmark, climbed as much as 2.8pc to more than $116 a barrel, pushing down stock markets in the US and Europe.

It followed a New York Times report that the US and Israel had drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iran after the midterm elections.

Oil has climbed more than 4pc this week, increasing pressure on stock markets at the same time as fears grow about the valuations of AI companies.

European shares fell on Friday, with the FTSE 100 down as much as 0.8pc, the Cac 40 in Paris down 1pc and the Dax in Frankfurt down 1.1pc.

On Wall Street, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell as much as 1pc, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite fell at a slower pace than the previous day.

Traders were rattled on Thursday after Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, warned that a “scarcity of capital” was hampering the rollout of the technology.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq in New York dropped by 2.6pc on Thursday while the S&P 500 fell 1.2pc on its worst day since July.

Mark Zuckerberg’s Meta was one of the worse hit in the sell-off, as its shares finished trading almost 7pc lower.

Overnight, the sell-off spread into Asian markets. Japan’s Nikkei 225 dropped by as much as 2.3pc and was down more than 4pc on the week.

The Kospi index in South Korea declined as much as 4.1pc on Friday but recovered to be marginally higher as markets closed.

The stock market turmoil led to a jump in safe haven assets like bonds.

The yield on 10-year US Treasury bonds, a benchmark for the cost of borrowing for governments around the world, fell by the largest amount since March 2023.

News.title: Europe’s record-breaking summer heat estimated to have killed 50,000 people
News.content:
More than 50,000 people are estimated to have died across Europe as a result of this summer’s record-breaking heatwaves, according to research.

In the UK alone, researchers estimate there were 4,354 excess deaths this summer.

The number of excess deaths across Europe is double the number recorded in 2025 and it is also far higher than the previous record of 29,000 deaths. This was recorded in 2022 when the continent also endured exceptionally high temperatures, with the mercury hitting 40 degrees celsius for the first time in the UK.

According to the Met Office the UK saw its hottest ever summer this year with five widespread heatwaves and 40 days where the temperature was above 30 degrees celsius. Mainland Europe experienced its third hottest summer, with temperatures particularly high in the south and west.

Researchers from Imperial College, London and the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine (LSHTM) looked at 854 urban areas in 30 countries across Europe. Using temperature records and modelling based on the relationship between heat and mortality they estimated the number of heat-related deaths that occurred between June and August.

They said findings from previous years’ excess heat mortality modelling matched official figures released later by national health authorities.

Because the study only looked at urban areas – making up 40 per cent of the population of the countries studied – researchers believe the number of deaths is likely to be an underestimate.

According to the study, published in Nature Health, southern and western Europe were hardest hit. Italy experienced the highest number of excess deaths (13,303), followed by France (7,268), Spain (6,824), Germany (6,340) then the UK.

There were an estimated 22,000 deaths among those aged 85 and over but researchers pointed out that an estimated 6,000 people under the age of 65 are also likely to have died as a result of the heat.

Around a third of the deaths took place in late June, when average temperatures across Europe were more than 5°C above what would be expected during this time of year. Researchers say in early summer people were less likely to have acclimatised to the sweltering weather. This period was marked by both extremely high humidity and unusually high night-time temperatures, making it difficult for people to cool down.

Researchers also estimated that more than two thirds of the total excess deaths were attributable to climate change. Across the continent as a whole Europe was an average 2.9°C higher than would have been expected. However, in some places temperatures were as much as 12°C higher.

Dr Clair Barnes, extreme weather and climate change researcher at Imperial College, said extreme heat was having a severe impact on public health.

“It is yet another reminder both of the imperative of rolling out targeted interventions to protect those who are most vulnerable to this increasingly extreme heat, and of the growing need to rapidly transition away from fossil fuels to slow the pace of change and limit future warming.”

Dr Pierre Masselot, assistant professor of statistics and epidemiology at LSHTM and one of the study’s authors, said “climate change is everybody’s problem”.

“It is not just hot regions that are suffering any more with some parts of Western and Northern Europe experiencing extreme heat and historically high health burden. And the whole population is affected, as shown by the significant death toll among younger age groups.

“It is becoming increasingly clear our cities are poorly adapted to rising heat, and it is critical we improve our efforts towards adaptation. This means cooling the cities through more green spaces and less pollution, and providing health care for affected populations.”

News.title: Bournemouth thrash Milan to seal greatest win in club’s history
News.content:
Milan could not even point to being down to 10 men for the last hour as mitigation; long before, Bournemouth had treated the Rossoneri with contempt. When Ruben Amorim’s side trudged off, soaked and silenced, they had not mustered a single shot on target.

Few nights have better encapsulated the Premier League’s power. Bournemouth have never finished higher than last season’s sixth in the top flight of English football; AC Milan have won seven European Cups. But the Premier League’s financial clout is such that, each season, the bottom club earns more than the champions of Serie A.

The Premier League’s shared riches, allied to years of astute recruitment and management, have underpinned the Bournemouth’s ascent. Even Andoni Iraola’s departure has not stalled the progress at the Vitality Stadium; Marco Rose has relished the new European adventure.

Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz had already been toppled in Bournemouth’s first two European games. Now, Bournemouth have won their first three matches in Europe. Despite middling Premier League form, Rose’s ambitions will extend far beyond securing a berth in the knockout stages of the Europa League. On this evidence, Bournemouth are legitimate contenders to win the competition, and earn a berth in next season’s Champions League.

“It’s a special night for the club,” Ryan Christie, Bournemouth captain, said. “It’s mega – in terms of the story of the club, it’s ridiculous.”

Evanilson, perhaps, was Bournemouth’s standout player against AC Milan, combining intricate linkup play with a constant threat in front of goal. Centre-back Antonio Silva, controlling play from deep while marauding forward, also possessed a calmness that any of Milan’s beleaguered team lacked.

His side’s fate swiftly sealed, Amorim did not bother to summon Luka Modric or Christian Pulisic. Bournemouth’s own bench showed the depth that the club now possesses. Rayan showed off his trickery and directness; Adli – a substitute for substitute Alex Toth, who suffered a hamstring injury – then ensured that Bournemouth secured the margin of victory that their dominance deserved.

News.title: Harry Brook hits historic double century – but England still lose to Sri Lanka
News.content:
Good morning and welcome to the fourth match of the autumn tri-series in Pakistan. After two wins for the hosts, the two touring sides face each other for the first time in Rawalpindi, the last match here before the circus leaves for Lahore. England and Sri Lanka played each other only last month in this format, England winning at Chester-le-Street and the Oval by a distance, those victories sandwiching a narrow defeat at Headingley where, if you remember, Harry Brook’s side were cruising until Jos Buttler ripped his left hamstring. He did eventually come back out to bat on one leg as his rattled team-mates flapped and fell to Asitha Fernando, Dilshan Madushanka and Eshan Malinga.

On Tuesday against Pakistan, England again were flying with both ball and bat but they let the middle-order rebuild, losing control of the rate. Their two most experienced white-ball bowlers, Adil Rashid, who looked rusty after breaking his hand in August, and Sam Curran, who missed the end of August and all of September following groin surgery, went for 6.87 and eight runs an over respectively. Then, after a promising opening partnership, Ben Duckett top-edged a pull, Tom Banton flicked straight to midwicket and Will Jacks later fell in identical fashion when well-set to marshal the chase. Arafat Minhas ended up with six for 40, bowling Harry Brook with a beauty, and there will be more trial by spin today.

Although there was some talk of England failing in end-of-days Bazball fashion, it most reminded me of the teething troubles of Eoin Morgan’s side in 2015 and 2016 when they were experimenting with players, viz this Rose Bowl collapse. We have to acknowledge that Joe Root, the best player of spin, was undone by one that kept low from Naseem Shah and both Brook and Jordan Cox lost their wickets to very good deliveries from Arafat, a bowler, on a feast day. Dunith Welllalage will return to try to replicate his line of attack today but he is a bowler that England know well. He has had his days against them but they have also given him some tap in the past.

As the Telegraph Fantasy Football season heads further into 2026-27, the award-winning experts at Fantasy Football Hub ccontinue to bring you the very best in fantasy football knowledge, tips and tools to help you rise up the ranks and win your mini-leagues.

Telegraph Fantasy Football: last week's insights



1-0 to the Arsenal



The reigning champions put in a resolute performance at the City Ground to keep the pressure on leaders Manchester City, grinding out a narrow victory thanks to a late Noni Madueke (£3.8m) strike. While Gunners attackers aren’t currently on the menu, the upcoming fixture run and style of play should see further defensive returns. Adopting a similar approach to last season, with two, three or even four of their defensive assets, is therefore a strategy likely to yield returns.

Running out of superlatives for the Seagulls

After putting five goals past M23 rivals Crystal Palace, it’s now 23 goals in seven Premier League games this season for Fabian Hurzeler’s side. However, TFF managers without Brighton assets may want to hold off for a couple more weeks, with trips to Anfield and the Etihad still to come before the fixture schedule eases again.

Semenyo setback

The former Bournemouth star finds himself on the sidelines for approximately eight weeks after picking up a knee injury against Ipswich last time out. Summer recruit Iliman Ndiaye (£3.3m) could be a budget-enabling midfielder who benefits from the Ghanian’s absence by gaining more minutes.

Visit the Telegraph Fantasy Football Stats Centre for all player points >



Telegraph Fantasy Football Tips: Game Week 8



The Telegraph Fantasy Football player list has been analysed ahead of the upcoming games, and these look like the best players to transfer in:



1. Cole Palmer (£6.2m)

With the likes of Bruno Fernandes (£6.5m) and Bukayo Saka (£6.0m), flattering to deceive so far, Chelsea’s No.10 looks like the second premium player to own behind Erling Haaland (£8.3m). With a home tie against Spurs before a likely appearance in the Carabao Cup in midweek, Saturday could be the ideal time to invest.

2. Kevin Schade (£3.6m)

The German was on fire before his short-term injury, and his return against Liverpool last week should put him in contention to start against Hull this weekend. The Tigers appear to have lost some momentum after their impressive start to the season, so the midfielder could find himself among the attacking returns once more at the MKM Stadium.

3. Jack Rudoni (£2.7m)

The third midfielder in this week’s picks has 31 points from his seven appearances so far this season, is the penalty taker, has his share of set-pieces, and embarks on the best fixture run in the league over the next six. Coventry host Fulham this weekend, and TFF managers should be considering the entry point for the one-per-cent-owned differential.

Arsenal vs Everton preview

Champions Arsenal are in action this afternoon against Everton as they look to close the gap on Premier League leaders Manchester City.

The Gunners arrive in second place having won six of their opening seven league matches, with defeat at Brighton the only blot on their record.

Arsenal have more Premier League points this season than at the same stage last season, have won 10 of their 12 games this season and earned a 2-2 Champions League draw with Bayern Munich midweek.

That said, they are increasingly under the microscope for their overly pragmatic and, at times, wearisome playing style, especially when trying to break down teams who sit deep.



That’s exactly the opponent they’ll be facing today in David Moyes’ Everton, but history suggests another three points could be on the cards.

Under Moyes, the Toffees have never won away at the Gunners in 13 league attempts (D3 L10). Arsenal are also unbeaten in their last seven Premier League matches against Everton, winning five of those.

In fact, Everton have won just one of their last 30 away Premier League matches against Arsenal and are winless in their last eight Premier League away games, with all three on the road this season ending level.

Furthermore, David Moyes has lost 11 of his last 12 Premier League matches against the reigning champions, while away from home, he has never beaten the previous season’s champions in 19 attempts.



The Toffees lost their unbeaten record against Chelsea last weekend and find themselves in eighth place, having collected two wins from their opening seven games.

Sports.title: Inside the making of Iliman Ndiaye, from warnings over showboating to Man City star’s real best position
Sports.content:
Next

SIX years ago, Iliman Ndiaye was catching the train from Sheffield to Hyde to play non-league football.

But now the “showman” has got his chance to become a £60million superstar at Manchester City.



Ndiaye, who left Everton in the summer, is set for a run in City’s side — starting tomorrow lunchtime at Aston Villa — after right winger Antoine Semenyo was ruled out for eight weeks with a knee injury.

It is only eight miles from Hyde to the Etihad — but Ndiaye has come a long way.



And nobody knows how extraordinary the Senegal international’s journey has been better than David McGurk.

Former York and Darlington defender McGurk was the boss of seventh-tier Hyde United who signed Ndiaye on loan from Sheffield United in January, 2020.



Within weeks, McGurk and his players realised they had something special on their hands.

McGurk, 44, who also spent the 2016-17 season turning out for Hyde, said: “I played professionally for 16 years and had never seen anything like him.

“It is always hard to tell if a player is going to reach the very top.

“Iliman came to Hyde, did well, and then went straight into the plans of Paul Heckingbottom, who was United manager at the time.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

“He adapted to that level and quickly became one of their best players.”

At Manchester-based Hyde — who were then in the Northern Premier League — Ndiaye arrived at a level where defenders were seasoned pros, hardened by years of non-league football. But, according to McGurk, once he received the ball, the age gap looked meaningless.

McGurk said: “He was a really quiet lad, but not on the pitch.

“He was aggressive, just got on with his game and spoke with his football.

“The defenders either couldn’t get near him or he was too skilful to get away from them.



“Some of them did go after him in terms of being aggressive and kicking him, but at a young age he was a strong boy. He had a real core strength to him, so he rode a lot of the tackles.

“A lot of people were unaware of him so they didn’t really know what they were coming up against. By the time he had gone past them it was too late.”

McGurk could see that France-raised Ndiaye, whose father Mouhamadou Abdoulaye was a professional choreographer, still had things to learn and there was one game when he missed a couple of chances and was feeling sorry for himself.

But McGurk did not sugar-coat and stated: “I told him he was going to play at the very top level but to get there he needed to take them chances.



“You could see there were parts of his game that needed work, with his end product and final decision making.”

Off the pitch, McGurk remembered a quiet and humble youngster who simply wanted to play football and who travelled by train most days from Sheffield.

McGurk said: “Iliman had no airs and graces.

“He was really streetwise, managed everything he needed to and did anything he could just to come and play football.”



Ndiaye, who also spent a season in France with Marseille, only played nine games for Hyde before the Covid pandemic brought the season to an abrupt halt.

But those matches were enough to leave a lasting impression.

And there was even one occasion when McGurk had to tell his young star to tone down the flair.

He said: “We did have to warn Iliman in one game to be careful with his tricks and flicks. We were leading the game 5-2 and he was sort of showboating, but it was just his natural game.”

Former Blades boss Heckingbottom is backing Ndiaye to live up to his price tag after City bought him from the Toffees on September 1 for £60m up front with £5m in possible add-ons.



He said: “He’s quiet and he’s shy but on the pitch it’s his stage and he becomes a showman.

“He has no problem conducting a whole stadium with his goal celebrations or when he’s got the ball at his feet.

“Everyone likes him wide but I like him in the middle of the pitch.

“I say that to everyone who is working with him. ‘Play in the middle, play in the middle’. I just think the smaller the space, the tighter the margins.

“He’s a fantastic kid and obviously we had a lot of time together and his journey has been really good and enjoyable for me.



“He’s always rose to the challenge and I’m sure he will do the same there.

“He was probably on his way out at Sheffield United. There was no way you could let someone like that go, you know.

“When I was in charge of the Under-23s I copied what the first team was doing and started working with him.

“I saw how bright and what a talent he was then.

“One of my favourite memories was when they were announcing the 2022 World Cup squad when he’d just got in the Senegalese team and all the Sheffield United boys were around him when they announced it.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

“His was the last name read out and a big cheer went up. Everyone likes him and that showed it.”

McGurk and co-founder, former York manager Michael Morton, own Tactx, which analyses games and develops coaching sessions for grassroots coaches through a subscription service.

Sports.title: Fabian Hurzeler breaks silence on Man Utd job links with Brighton manager among frontrunners for job
Sports.content:

FABIAN HURZELER has “unfinished business” with Brighton despite being in the frame for the Manchester United job.

The German boss is among the frontrunners if under-fire Red Devils manager Michael Carrick is sacked.



Hurzeler, 33, has taken the Seagulls to third in the Premier League. They also knocked United out of the Carabao Cup, fighting back to win 3-2 at Old Trafford last month.

But Hurzeler, whose side visit Liverpool on Sunday, said: “I am fully focused on my job here. I have no time to think about these rumours because we play every three days.



“And besides that I have a lot of respect for Michael Carrick, for what he has done with Manchester United last season. He’s a great human being, he’s a great personality.

“Every time we meet each other we have a really good relationship so therefore I really respect him and there’s nothing more to say about that.”

Brighton owner Tony Bloom and chief executive Paul Barber stood by Hurzeler when he was under pressure last term.

United’s dressing room is far more volatile, with outspoken stars Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes criticising the hierarchy and Carrick over recruitment and tactics.

Hurzeler hinted he would not want to swap the good thing he has going at Brighton for that.

He said: “I think I’m really privileged to be in this situation here and I always mention that I’m part of a journey.

“I always emphasise as well I still have this feeling when I go to bed that we are not finished with our journey.

“I’m not 100 per cent satisfied and happy where we are. There are still improvements we can do.

“There’s still a lot of potential to get out of the players and therefore I really want to work on that.

“I have a great group of players who support me, who give everything for this club and we built this over the last years.

“We had tough periods, we have good periods but I think to build these kinds of relationships you need time, you need connections.



“In the end it’s a people’s business and making a people’s business out of this very pressure business is something I don’t take for granted and I don’t throw it away that fast.”

Brighton visit the Reds before two trips in four days to the Etihad to face Manchester City, first in the Carabao Cup and then the Premier League.

Sports.title: Football has invented a wonderful job for people who want all the power without the pressure – the sporting director
Sports.content:
Next

FOOTBALL has invented a wonderful job for people who want all the power without the pressure. It is called sporting director.

The sporting director assembles the squad, chooses the targets and decides which players are worth £50million.



While the manager must turn them into a team, win matches and explain why it has all gone wrong.

When the experiment fails, it is usually the manager shown the door. A neat arrangement, particularly if you are the sporting director.



At Manchester United, Jason Wilcox is under scrutiny while boss Michael Carrick must find a way to get results with the squad at his disposal.

The question is familiar: Who is responsible for the football when the man recruiting the players is not the man picking the team?



Ruben Amorim’s departure at Old Trafford exposed the problem.

He wanted to be Manchester United’s manager, not merely their coach — and made little secret of his frustrations with the hierarchy.

His successor inherits the same fundamental question. Carrick can coach, motivate and organise but he cannot conjure players out of thin air.

Modern football needs structure. No sensible club should leave every transfer decision to one individual, however distinguished his CV.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Managers leave; player contracts remain. Rebuilding recruitment every time a manager departs is not a strategy. It is a very expensive revolving door.

But the opposite arrangement is equally dangerous. A sporting director cannot demand authority over recruitment and then disclaim responsibility when it fails.

I know how this can end. At West Ham, Tim Steidten arrived in 2023 to modernise recruitment but clashed with David Moyes, who had delivered three successive top-ten finishes and a European trophy.

Moyes quite rightly wanted a say in signings; Steidten favoured a director-led approach. By May 2024, relations had collapsed so badly that Steidten was told to stay away from first-team areas.

Moyes left that summer. Julen Lopetegui arrived, the club spent heavily and the dysfunction resurfaced. Lopetegui was sacked in January 2025; Steidten followed him out.



Two managers, two breakdowns, one sporting director.

At some point, you have to stop blaming the man in the dugout and start questioning the man responsible for recruitment. The irony is sporting directors are supposed to provide continuity. West Ham failed to achieve it.

Recruitment is not successful because signings look impressive on a private jet or a spreadsheet predicts their resale value will rise.



It succeeds when players improve the team, suit the manager’s requirements and deliver on the pitch.

Look at Brighton. They have sold some of their finest players for enormous fees, yet keep finding ways to compete near the top of the table.

Their secret is not a succession of lucky guesses but a recruitment model built on data, long-term planning and a clear footballing philosophy.

Tony Bloom’s much-discussed algorithm helps identify talent but numbers alone cannot build a team.

Human judgement still matters. Brighton demonstrate what happens when recruitment is a key strategy, rather than a power struggle.



Sporting directors and managers need complementary responsibilities, clear authority, a shared vision and mutual trust.

If they disagree fundamentally about recruitment, the owners must resolve it before the training ground becomes a battleground.

United is a reminder that grand titles and organisational charts cannot substitute for sound judgement.

West Ham shows changing the manager does not necessarily solve the problem.

Football loves talking about projects, long-term planning and modern structures.



All are sensible. But a structure is only as good as the people operating it — and somebody must be accountable for the outcome.

A sporting director cannot claim credit for assembling the squad while leaving the manager to carry the can for their shortcomings.

Nor can a manager demand control of everything and blame others when his choices fail.



There is room for both jobs. There is no room for two competing football departments in the same club, each convinced it knows best.

When the relationship works, the club win. When it fails, supporters pay for the mistakes and owners discover that the most expensive position in football may be the one nobody can quite explain.

So, the real test of a sporting director is not how many players he signs or how cleverly he describes his philosophy.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It is whether he builds a club that can succeed beyond the tenure of any one manager.

Anything less is just an expensive way of moving the blame around.

Sports.title: Glamorous female football photographer forces club to back down as they attempt to ban her revealing outfits
Sports.content:
Next

A GLAM football photographer forced a club to back down on its attempt to ban revealing outfits at the ground.

Paraguayan first-division outfit Sportivo Ameliano requested members of the press to follow a dress code “in order to maintain… the club’s institutional image”.



Photographer Adriana Caballero felt targeted by Sportivo’s request, whose ban was addressed to both men and women.

Ameliano’s rule also banned “low-cut blouses” and the “exposure of the navel”.



Female journalists and photographers are also banned from wearing leggings that aren’t black or dark blue.

Adriana, 29, claims all this drama started after a photo of her went viral.

She added that the controversial measure could hinder her colleagues’ work.

Adriana said: “I always want to wear the most comfortable clothes possible for my job. Sooner or later it probably had to come to this.”



The Paraguayan outfit ultimately backtracked after fierce criticism across social media.

Adriana has over 200,000 followers on Instagram alone where she shares a series of glam snaps.

Sportivo’s president Hector Melgarejo, tried to distance himself from all the controversy.

Melgarejo claimed the dress code had been published without club management’s approval.

He described the measure as “madness” and said members of the press should dress however they wish.

Sports.title: 'Roy Keane ripped into me in blazing row – but I had the perfect response'
Sports.content:
'Roy Keane ripped into me in blazing row – but I had the perfect response'

Roy Keane launched a furious rant at a player who responded in the best possible way

View 2 Images Roy Keane launched a verbal tirade at James McClean in 2017 (Image: Getty )

Roy Keane once ripped into James McClean during a foul-mouthed dressing room row while on Republic of Ireland duty. But the winger, now 37, responded perfectly to his then-assistant manager Keane’s criticism about his application levels by scoring in the following game.

‌



‌



McClean celebrated his 50th international cap for Ireland by captaining his nation in a friendly against Mexico back in June 2017. But the then-West Bromwich Albion star had a poor game as his side lost 3-1, having conceded a penalty himself in the first half.

‌



Manchester United legend Keane, who was Martin O’Neill’s assistant at the time, unleashed his wrath on McClean and his team-mates in the dressing room at half-time. The pundit appeared to be especially triggered by a meeting with Irish boxer Mick Conlan before the New Jersey match.

‌



Writing in his autobiography The Walls, as per the Irish Independent, McClean said: "Martin [O’Neill] had just finished his bit when Roy came over, got right in my face and started f***ing me out of it.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Roy Keane finally breaks golden rule as Gary Neville mocks 'fawning' Man Utd legend READ MORE :

Sir Alex Ferguson was one day from becoming Arsenal boss as contract offer revealed READ MORE :

"'Look at you, the f***ing captain, f***ing giving off, yeah? You were taking pictures before the game with f***ing Mick Conlan. Your head isn’t f***ing in it.'"

‌



McClean remained silent during Keane’s dressing room scolding. But the ex-United skipper doubled down by accusing him of "having a big ego" in another furious rant during a gym session.

McClean continued: "He said he’d never been critical of me in the press or around the group, and now, the first time he’d said anything, I’d pulled him up over it.

‌



View 2 Images McClean had a poor game against Mexico (Image: Getty )

"Then he started going off about the Lamborghini at Sunderland, which was f***ing six years earlier. I was thinking he must have been seething for the afternoon, gathering information."

‌



That was in relation to then-Sunderland manager O’Neill having allegedly dropped the Irishman for buying a supercar. But McClean responded to Keane's comments in the best possible way, scoring in Ireland’s 3-1 friendly win over Uruguay in the following game and performing a selfie celebration.

McClean went on to reach 103 caps for Ireland, scoring 11 goals for the Boys in Green. He returned to his hometown club Derry City in January 2026 but has not played for the side since August due to a bitter public dispute with the club hierarchy.

Article continues below

Keane, meanwhile, left his role as Ireland's assistant manager in November 2018, departing alongside O’Neill and the rest of the coaching staff after a poor run of form where they failed to win across the entire year. His last managerial role was his five-month tenure as O’Neill’s assistant at Nottingham Forest, after which he has focused solely on his successful media career.

Sports.title: Man Utd dream defence next season with £160million duo signed and two stars axed
Sports.content:
Man Utd dream defence next season with £160million duo signed and two stars axed

Manchester United's season has got off to a disastrous start, and the pressure is on for Michael Carrick to turn things around

View 4 Images Michael Carrick can turn things around at Manchester United with the right recruitment (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Two arrivals and two departures could give Michael Carrick a very different Manchester United defence to work with next season. The priority should be to bring in Lewis Hall and Jarrad Branthwaite for a combined £160million, with Luke Shaw and Lisandro Martinez making way.

‌



‌



That would leave Carrick able to field a back four of Diogo Dalot, Leny Yoro, Branthwaite and Hall. Matthijs de Ligt and Harry Maguire would offer experienced alternatives in the middle, while Ayden Heaven could continue his development.

‌



United's miserable start to the 2026/27 campaign has made the case for defensive investment increasingly difficult to ignore. Just two months into the season, the optimism generated by last term's surprise third-place finish has faded. United are in the bottom half of the table and struggling in the Champions League, leaving Carrick under intense pressure only months after his permanent appointment.

‌



The problems extend beyond just results. Captain Bruno Fernandes appeared to question Carrick's tactics after the midweek Champions League drubbing at Como. A week earlier, Martinez had criticised senior club figures for failing to strengthen the squad adequately over the summer.

FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

United signed Carlos Baleba, Youri Tielemans and Andrey Santos, concentrating their recruitment on midfield after focusing on the attack the previous summer. That strategy has left the defence short of the improvements it needed, while problems persist going forward.

‌



Left-back is the most obvious place to start. United entered the campaign relying on 31-year-old Luke Shaw as their first choice despite his long-standing fitness concerns. It is a gamble that has not paid off.

Signing Hall from Newcastle would be a solid starting point. The 22-year-old England international remains a primary target for director of football Jason Wilcox and Ineos, having been monitored by United in recent months. The Magpies told United he was unavailable in the summer, so securing him would require a substantial offer.

‌



View 4 Images Lewis Hall is a long-term target of Manchester United (Image: Stu Forster, Getty Images)

Hall was reportedly interested in moving to Manchester and remains keen, giving United reason to test Newcastle's resolve again in the next transfer window. Recent reports claim he could cost north of £80m.

‌



Shaw could still feature for the rest of this season. Beyond that, United should look to sell him in the summer, recognising his 12 years of service while moving towards a more reliable long-term option. With 12 months left on his deal, a decision on his future is approaching.

The other major change should come on the left side of central defence. Lisandro Martinez was reportedly considering his departure even before his criticism of Wilcox and the club hierarchy.

‌



View 4 Images Lisandro Martinez has reportedly been put up for transfer (Image: Michael Steele, Getty Images)

Atletico Madrid were linked with him during the summer and interest from Spanish clubs remains. The 28-year-old favours La Liga, with United said to be weighing up whether to let him leave. His contract expires next year, though the club can trigger a 12-month extension to help secure a transfer fee.

‌



Branthwaite, who TEAMtalk claim costs around £80m, is the obvious player to replace him. United are understood to be considering another approach for the Everton defender after having two bids worth up to £50m rejected in 2024.

Aged 24, the left-footed centre-back brings crucial Premier League experience and would seamlessly slot into United's new-look defence, accelerating their much-needed overhaul. His performances so far this season earned him a place in England’s recent Nations League squad, strengthening the argument for United to renew their interest.

‌



View 4 Images Everton's Jarrad Branthwaite would be a top signing (Image: NurPhoto, NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Alongside him, Yoro is showing signs of progress despite his red card against Atletico Madrid. De Ligt remains a useful option when fit, while Maguire offers the leadership and professionalism that this unsettled dressing room needs.

Article continues below

United are expected to activate the extra year in the 33-year-old's contract, allowing him to help guide Yoro and Heaven. Keeping that experience would make sense while changing two other key positions.

Dalot and Mazraoui may not be outstanding options at right-back, but it is less urgent than the problems on the opposite flank and at centre-back. Hall and Branthwaite would address those priorities directly - and give Carrick a stronger platform from which to rebuild.

Sports.title: Arsenal news: £50million wonderkid wows scouts as Cristiano Ronaldo heir on radar
Sports.content:
Arsenal news: £50million wonderkid wows scouts as Cristiano Ronaldo heir on radar

Mikel Arteta has already got some top talent joining him at Arsenal but transfer talk hasn't slowed down

View 3 Images More young talents could join Mikel Arteta at Arsenal in the not-too-distant future (Image: Angelika Warmuth/DPA via AP)

Arsenal kept their unbeaten Champions League record alive in midweek but it came at a cost. Bukayo Saka was forced off early with a quad injury against Bayern Munich and looks set to be out for some time.

‌



‌



Mikel Arteta will need to take a different approach on Saturday when Everton visit the Emirates Stadium. Looking further ahead, though, further investment could follow in the January transfer window.

‌



The Gunners have a number of young talents on the way already. Victor Ozhianvuna will join from Shamrock Rovers in January while the Quintero twins will follow over the summer, and a deal has also been agreed for Georgian talent Andria Bartishvili.

‌



They might not be the only new arrivals, though. We've taken a look at a couple of other stars reported to be capturing Arsenal's attention.

Jamie Carragher pinpoints Mikel Arteta change as he bids to end 92-year Arsenal hoodoo READ MORE :

Scouts keep tabs on Russian wonderkid

Arsenal scouts were in France this week to watch Aleksey Batrakov, according to TEAMtalk. The Russian international scored Galatasaray's second goal as they came from behind to beat Lille 4-2 - their first away win in Europe for more than 11 months.

Batrakov, an attacking midfielder, joined the Turkish side for a little over £20million after hitting double-figures for Lokomotiv Moscow in each of the last two Russian Premier League seasons. He has already found the net twice this term, also netting against Barcelona.

‌



Make sure you don't miss the best Arsenal coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

View 3 Images Aleksey Batrakov has scored in each of his last two Champions League games (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Liverpool are among the other clubs said to be scouting the 21-year-old, who is reported to have a £50m release clause. He already has four goals and four assists across 15 senior international caps for Russia and set up the opener in a 2-0 victory over Iran during the last international break.

Portuguese goal machine eyed

Portuguese youngster Gustavo Varela has been making a big impression in Serie A this season and Arsenal have taken note. According to Gazzetta dello Sport, the Gunners are among several top European sides keen on the Monza star.

‌



Varela, 21, has been touted as a potential long-term heir to Cristiano Ronaldo at international level. He has scored four goals in just seven outings for the Under-21s, helping Portugal qualify for next summer's finals in Albania and Serbia.

View 3 Images Gustavo Varela has made a fast start at Monza (Image: Getty Images)

‌



At club level, he's scored six goals in his first six Serie A appearances and also bagged a brace on his Coppa Italia debut. Arsenal could face a battle for his signature, though, with Italian giants Napoli and former club Benfica both keeping close tabs on the hotshot.

Sports.title: Jadon Sancho given crushing reality check with contract offer after Man Utd and Chelsea flops
Sports.content:
Jadon Sancho given crushing reality check with contract offer after Man Utd and Chelsea flops

Jadon Sancho's contract with Manchester United expired this summer, with the winger remaining a free agent since - but that could soon change

View 2 Images Getafe have reportedly offered Jadon Sancho a contract (Image: 2024 Marc Atkins)

Manchester United flop Jadon Sancho has been handed a contract offer of around £10,000-per-week by Getafe as he searches for his next club. The 26-year-old may have excelled with Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga during his early years as a professional, but fell well short of expectations at Old Trafford.

‌



‌



United brought in the winger in a £73million deal in 2021, but to say that the Camberwell-born player underwhelmed would be putting it mildly. Sancho mustered just three goals and three assists in his first campaign on English shores, before recording six and three in 26 games throughout 2022/23.

‌



Sancho ended up heading back to Dortmund on loan the following season, but was ultimately unable to recapture his earlier form in the Bundesliga. A further loan switch to Chelsea followed in 2024/25, with the west London outfit holding a £25m obligation to sign him permanently the next summer.

‌



Andre Onana in terrifying car crash as update on Man Utd star's condition released READ MORE :

Following a disappointing stint in the capital, Chelsea chose not to proceed, instead paying a £5m penalty to return Sancho to Greater Manchester. Another season-long loan to Aston Villa then came Sancho's way last term, with the Villans showing no interest in securing the player at its conclusion.

Consequently, Sancho was let go by United this summer, and has been without a club ever since. That situation could soon alter, though, with several sides reportedly interested in handing the versatile attacker a deal.

Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



Matching the eye-watering £250,000-per-week he is understood to have earned during his spell at Manchester United, however, appears highly improbable. According to the Telegraph, Getafe have tabled a deal running until the end of the season, proposing to pay him just £10,000-per-week.

While Sancho has not completely dismissed a switch to the La Liga outfit, it is understood that he wants to hold talks with head coach Jose Bordalas before reaching a verdict on the proposal.

‌



FOLLOW OUR MAN UTD FB PAGE! Latest United news and more on our dedicated Facebook page

At present, Getafe occupy 15th place in the Spanish top division, having secured just two victories from their first nine fixtures of the season.

‌



Bordalas has also endured a challenging period with the club recently. Brought in during 2023, 'Pepe' has openly criticised Getafe's leadership this term over insufficient squad resources.

This comes despite him having previously expressed doubts about his first-team's capacity to perform at the elite level every three days - with both La Liga and Conference League commitments to juggle.

‌



View 2 Images Jadon Sancho was released by Manchester United this summer (Image: 2024 Allstar)

He told the media: "I feel deceived because what has been promised year after year hasn't been fulfilled. I'm angry. I've been warning about this since May, that it was going to be a very difficult season with matches every three days. It's been proven that we don't have the squad for it."

‌



Club president Angel Torres has now fired back, making it clear the manager is free to walk away should he wish. Speaking to Cadena SER, Torres said: "He signed because he wanted to. Anyway, he's free to leave. If we're so bad, what can we do? This is Getafe.

"What I don't understand is what you're doing here if you're unhappy and I already knew it. To say that I deceived him...you have to be as shameless as stone to tell me, after 30 years, that I deceived him. But well, what he needs to do is respect the players, just as the players respect him."

Sports.title: Ex-Arsenal chief Edu lands new role at League Two side after move fails to work out
Sports.content:
Ex-Arsenal chief Edu lands new role at League Two side after move fails to work out

Edu's stint at Nottingham Forest ended prematurely with the ex-Arsenal chief now taking on a surprise advisory role at Northampton, who are second bottom of the Football League

View 2 Images Edu has secured a shock role near the bottom of the Football League

Former Arsenal sporting director Edu has landed himself a new role with Northampton Town, who are sitting 23rd in League Two.

‌



‌



The Brazilian was crucial in beginning the recent rise of the Gunners during his time at the Emirates, choosing to hire Mikel Arteta and then backing the Spaniard in the market. However he left north London to join Evangelos Marinakis‘ group of clubs, including Nottingham Forest, last year.

‌



That move has not worked out for Edu, who cited a desire to work in a multi-club model, and he was quickly moved on from the City Ground.

‌



He's since become a member of the board of directors at Bulgarian side Levski Sofia and will now combine that with becoming a senior advisor to Northampton - a role that was confirmed by the club's co-chair Joao Xavier.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



The Cobblers have recently been taken over by a Brazilian consortium including former Chelsea and AC Milan star Alexandre Pato. Xavier said an open forum on Thursday: “We are very proud to have Alex [Pato] with us and Edu with us too. We became friends as he had a role at Nottingham Forest and I asked him to help me learn more about English football.

“Edu is a senior advisor for one of our partners, acting as an advisor for Levski Sofia and also here, helping us navigate the sporting questions here at the club, not day to day, just when we ask him and when we need him.”

‌



Edu's decision to quit Arsenal came as a surprise to the club, who had become serial challengers for honours towards the end of his tenure. He presided over several landmark deals, including the club-record signing of Declan Rice from West Ham.

View 2 Images Northampton have won two of their 10 games this season

‌



Martin Odegaard, Kai Havertz and Jurrien Timber were also signed under his watch as Arsenal morphed into one of the best teams in Europe. Their upward trajectory has continued despite his departure.

Now he faces new challenges, with clubs of a far lesser stature than Arsenal. It may only be early in the season but Northampton face the prospect of relegation to the National League. The club have jumped between the third and fourth tiers of the pyramid for years but haven't been a non-league outfit for more than a century.
