Tottenham, four points above their neighbours before Saturday’s meeting, may have been humbled in consecutive Women’s Super League matches but all eyes are on Renée Slegers.

Arsenal are winless in five WSL matches for the first time, and the most decorated club in English women’s football desperately need a turning point. Their failure to beat Birmingham at home last Saturday, dropping points against a promoted side for the second time this season, again demonstrated the team’s inability to convert possession into goals. They increasingly look like a team stuck in Groundhog Day.

The Arsenal hierarchy are understood to remain behind Slegers, but for how long? The answer may hinge on Saturday lunchtime’s result. However much goodwill the Dutchwoman gained for guiding Arsenal to Champions League glory in May 2025, the simple truth is, it is unacceptable for a club with one of the biggest budgets in the world to be 12 points behind the leaders after six games.

That gap is why the draw with Birmingham not only pretty much extinguished Arsenal’s title hopes but also burned a hole in their secondary domestic objective – Champions League qualification. The unthinkable prospect of failure appears a genuine possibility: they are nine points adrift of third-placed London City. Arsenal need a derby win on Saturday but also a winning run to reverse the slide, and there is little evidence to suggest such a turnaround is close.

Arsenal have the worst shot conversion rate in the league (4.1%) and, according to Stats Perform, the third-worst shooting accuracy (30.6%) and third-lowest average xG per shot (0.09) despite averaging over 60% possession. Slegers’s persistence in deploying Alessia Russo – widely regarded as one of Europe’s best No 9s – in the No 10 role has baffled supporters and commentators alike. Russo has scored more WSL goals against Tottenham (eight) than any other player so Saturday’s game may be the perfect moment for that to change.

View image in fullscreen Arsenal’s Alessia Russo and Caitlin Foord wheel away after a goal against Tottenham in February 2025 – however, Russo has not flourished as a No 10 this season. Photograph: Matthew Childs/Action Images/Reuters

Arsenal have struggled against low blocks for a number of seasons, though, so not all fault lies at Slegers’s door. Nonetheless, the 37-year-old was substantially backed in the summer, with Arsenal enjoying perhaps their strongest transfer window in recent memory. So far though they have looked confounded tactically, bruised mentally and lacking the self-belief to grab a game by the scruff of its neck.

Asked if she was surprised to still be in her job, Slegers said: “That’s not something I think about. It’s about, ‘where are we as a group?’ and ‘what are we working towards?’ It’s absolutely not what we expected [our recent results] or what we wanted. But I’m in the here and now, and we are preparing for the north London derby. We have the group together. Everyone is going in the same direction and the fuel and motivation is sky high, because of the fans that will be there for us. That’s where my focus will be.”

Asked how imperative it is that Arsenal climb back up into a Champions League place this season, Slegers added: “Of course that’s in the back of our heads, but what we need right now is to get back to winning ways. We can only do that with the next game in front of us so that’s why the next game in front of us is the most important right now.”

Slegers has maintained after last weekend’s draw that Arsenal will recover when they fix some “details and margins”. Perhaps taking on a Tottenham side who have become only the second team in history to concede six or more goals in consecutive WSL games is the perfect opportunity.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

“It is a little bit of game intelligence and smartness in moments,” said the Spurs head coach, Martin Ho, insisting he is not worried about his team’s defending in the long-term. “There have been certain aspects that, collectively, players and staff, we were not happy with in certain moments, and we have to make sure we correct them. At the moment we’re getting heavily punished for some small errors with the ball that we’re making.”

The Englishman also only had praise for Arsenal’s qualities when speaking on Friday morning. “If you try and underestimate a team with Arsenal’s quality you’re in for trouble,” he said. Asked about Arsenal’s poor run, Ho added: “Arsenal aren’t a bad side. Their possession stats are probably the highest in the league, alongside Manchester City. Their goalscoring chances and touches in the opposition box are very, very high. They have world-class players.”

Last season’s runners-up do have world-class players but it is high time for them to play like a cohesive team.

Sports.title: How Erling Haaland's dad has masterminded the Man City's star meteoric rise: Alf-Inge Haaland has reinvented himself after Roy Keane feud - but wanted his son to pursue GOLF before plotting his football career
Sports.content:
How Erling Haaland's dad has masterminded the Man City's star meteoric rise: Alf-Inge Haaland has reinvented himself after Roy Keane feud - but wanted his son to pursue GOLF before plotting his football career

Alf-Inge Haaland enjoyed an admirable career in English football, playing for Nottingham Forest, Leeds United and Manchester City, but he never reached the heights of his superstar son.

It wasn't his football ability that made his name but rather his bad blood with Manchester United legend Roy Keane.

The 53-year-old stood united with City fans at Anfield only a few weeks ago, in their first game after they were found guilty of the vast majority of financial charges against them. He watched on as City won 3-0 with his son scoring the third goal, in a massive win for the whole football club.

Erling was born in 2000, just a few months after one of the most brutal tackles in Premier League history.

Haaland Sr and Keane's conflict ignited in 1997 when the former was furious with the way Keane went down under his challenge as his Leeds team overcame bitter rivals United.

Keane injured his ACL and four years later the feud caught fire as the ex-United midfielder exacted his revenge with an aggressive and dangerous high-kick tackle on Haaland, who was playing for City at the time.

Alf-Inge Haaland, 53 with son Erling with the former a key part to the latter's success. Source: Alfie Haaland/Instagram

Haaland Snr, then at Leeds United, pictured with Erling shortly after he was born in July 2000

Haaland Sr retired from the game just two years later as the project to turn his son into one of the best footballers in the world began. And for a younger generation of football fans, Alf-Inge is only known for being the father of the prolific striker.

The family moved back to Norway in 2003, where Erling turned his hand to all sports. His mother, Gry Marita Braut, was a national heptathlon champion. With parents boasting exceptional athletic prowess, it was only natural for attention to turn to Erling's prospects of success.

While Erling dreamt of following in his father's footsteps, Alf-Inge had different plans for his young son.

‘My dad’s biggest dream was for me to become a golfer… but eventually I told my parents, "I want to play football",' he revealed on his YouTube channel.

Pushy parents are rife throughout elite sport but, despite his parents' enviable sporting background, Erling only felt pressure from himself to reach elite level.

And it quickly became apparent that Erling was going to follow in his father's footsteps as a professional footballer.

Using his in-depth knowledge and connections in the game, Alf-Inge was able to encourage Erling to make strong career decisions, all designed with the ultimate goal of becoming one of the most dominant players in the game.

Alf-Inge applied this savvy approach to Erling's transfer moves – prioritising clubs where his son would be exposed to as much playing time as possible.

Alf-Inge is known for his feud with Manchester United legend Roy Keane from their playing days. Keane took revenge for a tackle with a dangerous high-kick in 2001

Alf-Inge, a young Erling and his older brother Astor (right) watch Manchester City as fans. Source: Gabrielle Haaland/Instagram

From a teenager, when transferring clubs, Erling has always been in a position where he has been able to play. In only one season at RB Salzburg, Haaland registered 44 goals, in 40 appearances, and this was followed by two incredible years at Borussia Dortmund where he scored 70 goals in 71 games. The natural progression and careful selection of teams was heavily influenced by his dad.

Out and out strikers have been heavily sought after in recent years and Alf-Inge assessed specific criteria to ensure his son received the best opportunity. This became clear when Erling was linked with both Manchester City and Real Madrid.

In Manchester there was family legacy, playing in the Premier League under Pep Guardiola, with a young team. However, in Madrid there was arguably the biggest club in the world, with a massive history of winning trophies.

The difference was, one of those clubs needed a No 9.

‘We had established a first criterion which was: "Who needs a number nine?" Manchester City had 10/10 at this level, it was the perfect option. Real, we gave him more of a 5 or a 6 out of 10 because of how Karim Benzema was playing’, Alf-Inge said in the documentary Haaland: The Choice.

The move to Manchester City wasn’t just because of Alf-Inge's time there, it was because he knew that it would be the best place for his talented son to be as successful as possible.

The decision made by the Haaland family is proving to be incredibly successful, with Erling winning two Premier Leagues, two FA Cups, a League Cup, one Champions League and one UEFA Super Cup.

The switch to the blue side of Manchester has allowed Alf-Inge to continue to support his son while also supporting his former club, but his presence has sparked criticism from none other than old rival Keane.

The father and son duo celebrate after the latter's Premier League title win in the 2022-23 term

Alf-Inge watches on from the stands in Istanbul as Erling goes on to win the Champions League

After Norway were knocked out of the 2026 World Cup, at the hands of England, Alf-Inge wrote on X: 'Well done Bellingham and referee’.

‘Is that sour grapes from Alf-Inge Haaland, saying well done to Bellingham and the referee? I think that was just a bit of a low blow from him’, Ian Wright said on the Stick to Football podcast.

In the same podcast, old foe Keane added: ‘Will he remember the game? Because he always seems to be drinking alcohol at the matches, the dad.’

The rivalry between Alf-Inge and Keane rumbles on while the former enjoys his son's success in England.

Sports.title: Ric Flair now doing 'OK,' daughter Charlotte says after wrestling icon, 77, was rushed to Florida hospital
Sports.content:
Ric Flair now doing 'OK,' daughter Charlotte says after wrestling icon, 77, was rushed to Florida hospital

Wrestling legend Ric Flair was rushed to a Florida hospital shortly after canceling an appearance due to blood clots, but is now said to be doing 'OK.'

The 77-year-old born Richard Morgan Fliehr was at a Tampa restaurant on Friday morning, according to a report by TMZ. Flair is said to have stood up from the bar, leaving his phone and drink behind, before walking across the street and falling. TMZ further reported that Flair cut his face and the area around his eye, adding that he may have suffered a concussion.

He was taken into an ambulance and rushed to a nearby hospital.

The Daily Mail has sought comment from a Flair spokesperson.

Flair's daughter Charlotte, herself a wrestler, has since issued an update, saying her father is 'going to be ok.'

Earlier Friday, Flair released a statement saying he would not be attending a fan convention in Seattle on the advice of his doctors, who are worried about some recently discovered blood clots.

Wrestling legend Ric Flair (pictured here in 2025) has been rushed to a Florida hospital shortly after canceling an appearance due to blood clots

Ric Flair posted a photo of himself outside of an emergency room back in May

Flair's daughter, Charlotte, has updated fans on her father's condition, saying he's 'OK'

'Blood Clots Are Extremely Serious And Can Be Life-Threatening,' Flair wrote online, capitalizing the first letter of every word. 'We Have Seen This Recently With [Philadelphia Eagles quarterback] Jalen Hurts And The Complications Involving Blood Clots In His Lungs. It Is A Reminder That This Is Not Something To Take Lightly, And I Must Follow Medical Advice.'

Flair said he can resume traveling after he undergoes a procedure on the affected vein.

He previously revealed a skin cancer battle in 2025, as well as unspecified health issues back in May.

'If you understood the health issues that I deal with and am currently dealing with, you would understand why I get frustrated in life with a lot of people,' he wrote online at the time. 'I'm sorry for the frustration. I am taking time to focus on my health.'

Flair also revealed a legal battle with his family.

In a series of since-deleted posts, the 'Nature Boy' claimed there is 'someone that I'm very familiar with' who is using 'my own trademark, FLAIR.'

He warned them that he is 'well represented by a reputable $1,000 per-hour attorney' who 'makes a living suing people that abuse my trademark.'

Flair is known for his years across the WWF/WWE, the WCW and other wrestling promotions.

Sports.title: Tearful Simone Biles struggles to come to terms with quick sale of $1M mansion she shared with NFL star husband
Sports.content:
Simone Biles broke down in tears as she said an emotional goodbye to her stunning Texas home where she spent six years alongside NFL star husband Jonathan Owens.

The 29-year-old took to TikTok to share the bittersweet moment with fans after the 3,998sq ft property was snapped up just four days after hitting the market.

'Why the f*** am I boohoo crying? F***,' Biles said through tears as she panned around the empty residence.

'This house will be on the market for the first time and I don't know why I'm boohoo crying. I was here for six years and I feel like there were so many good memories.

'I feel like I grew up in this house. It's made me a real adult so I'm going to miss it. Ugh, I didn't think I'd be emotional about a house', the gymnastics icon added.

Biles walked through the vacant rooms before stepping outside to the spacious backyard before sharing a warm message for the future homeowners.

Simone Biles broke down in tears as she said an emotional goodbye to her Texas home

The 29-year-old took to TikTok to share the bittersweet moment with fans after the 3,998-square-foot property was snapped up just four days after hitting the market

'Whoever buys this house, I hope it brings you as much joy as it did for me', she said.

Biles captioned the video: “I was so excited to put in air fresheners for the potential buyers & showing Jonathan the last look. I just cried instead… anyone else?”

The property was initially listed for $1.275 million before eventually being sold for a fee between $1.08 million and $1.24 million, according to the Houston Association of Realtors.

Spanning nearly 4,000sq ft in a gated community near Spring, Texas, the four-bedroom, 3.5-bathroom estate sits on just over an acre of land.

The luxury residence features a heated backyard swimming pool, an in-home sauna, a dedicated dog-washing station and a custom wine display wall.

Inside, the home boasts a waterfall island kitchen with quartz countertops, a hidden walk-in pantry and an oversized three-car garage.

The property went under contract just four days after the listing went live on September 22, with the sale officially closing on October 15.

Join the discussion Have you ever been unexpectedly emotional about leaving a home, or is it just bricks and mortar to you?

The gymnastics icon spent six years in the home alongside NFL star husband Jonathan Owens

Earlier this year, Biles shared a glimpse at the stunning property in a series of online posts

The update comes one month after Biles revealed three masked intruders broke into her Chicago home and stole her luxurious Porsche.

The legendary Team USA gymnast dropped the bombshell news during a TikTok video. It remains unclear when the burglary happened or if the police have made any arrests but Biles confirmed the car was recovered.

'Feel like I need a new car because during our last few months in Chicago, three men in masks came to our house and stole my Porsche,' she said.

'Stole the GTS. But that's another story. If you guys want to know, I'll do a story time on that.'

Sports.title: Why WOULDN'T a top manager want the Man United gig? The club is so dysfunctional, they won't get the blame when it goes wrong. And if they get it right, they're a genius, writes RIATH AL-SAMARRAI
Sports.content:
Erik ten Hag came across pretty well this week. And of course he did, because anyone would look and sound a little wiser when they’re not in the process of being passed through the bowels of a bloated, belching beast.

Thankfully for Ten Hag, he has long since wiggled free of Manchester United. Like Andy Dufresne, having crawled through 500 yards of sewer to escape Shawshank, he has found redemption on the other side and is enjoying the cold rain of freedom on his face.

Those two trophies United won under him? They’re ageing better by the hour. His body of work? Almost two years to the day after his sacking, it no longer seems too shabby.

And so he is cutting loose. In an interview with The Athletic, he went to town on his former club, detailing everything from broken promises and toxic cultures to Cristiano Ronaldo’s work-rate and the voids of communication within the vast, dysfunctional Ineos machine. Withering stuff.

Settling scores into an open goal, he took his chances. Good on him. And good for the Ten Hag brand, too, because for the first time in a while he was able to sound like the smart man in the room. As in, who else could possibly deliver two trophies with so many monkeys loose in the rafters of this circus?

Erik ten Hag struggled for answers during the end of his Manchester United tenure but had plenty to say this week in an interview about his time at the helm at Old Trafford

Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s narcissism wasn’t behind the £72m wasted on Rasmus Hojlund. That was Ten Hag’s wish

Here’s the problem, though: Ten Hag’s football was dreadful. For the second half of his reign, he stank the place out. With £600million spent on the squad, his final season saw United fall from third in 2023 to eighth in 2024. When the trigger was finally pulled, they were 14th after nine games and that wasn’t all a symptom of his environment.

Sir Dave Brailsford, an over-promoted chancer, didn’t drive the spending of £82m on Antony. Ten Hag did. Sir Jim Ratcliffe’s narcissism wasn’t behind the £72m wasted on Rasmus Hojlund. That was Ten Hag’s wish as well. And Jason Wilcox, the latest bug-ridden update to a broken operating system, wasn’t even there when Liverpool put seven on United at Anfield.

The point being, Ten Hag had plenty of cock-ups, too many to list, but there is no greater gift to an error-prone manager than the whole world knowing that those above you were incompetent. There is no thicker shield and no insurance policy so favourable.

In other words, I don’t buy into the idea that United are too toxic for a serious manager to touch. Quite the opposite, in fact.

Several excellent arguments have been made this week about why it would be an impossible job, assuming it is vacated in the near future by Michael Carrick. If Bournemouth resemble Como on Sunday, that change might even be imminent, and Bayern Munich’s CEO, Oliver Kahn, has spoken for many in his warnings to Julian Nagelsmann: ‘Essentially every (United) manager in recent years has failed.’

That is true, of course. If we are to invoke Sir Alex Ferguson, as we seemingly must in these discussions, we would remember his time-worn wisdom to other managers: ‘Pick your owner.’

But if you can’t pick a good one, there is presumably some benefit in ownership so very bad that they absorb responsibility for your own shortcomings. We could call it the Ten Hag phenomenon.

Ruben Amorim landed the plum job of AC Milan manager despite his woeful run at United

Jose Mourinho has somehow argued his way to another stint at Real Madrid

The depths to which United have fallen are such that Carrick’s replacement, whoever it may be and whenever that might occur, would arrive with a pre-packaged case for mitigation. A free swing and a free pass.

If you fail, collect your pay-off and blame the monkeys. If you succeed, you’re the genius who saved United; it’s either a golden ticket or a golden parachute.

To date, no one has unwrapped the ticket, but nor has anyone shattered their legs on landing. It hasn’t been terminal to any who tried.

David Moyes is back at Everton and thriving. At West Ham, he won a European trophy. Jose Mourinho has somehow argued his way to another stint at Real Madrid. Ralf Rangnick has taken Austria to a European Championship and World Cup.

Ruben Amorim landed at AC Milan, Louis van Gaal got another crack with Netherlands, and Ten Hag was gifted Bayer Leverkusen, one year after they won the Bundesliga.

He lasted three games, as it happens, and today he has another gig as technical director at FC Twente. Reading that interview with The Athletic, he seems happy. If there is one outlier in the list, it is Ole Gunnar Solskjaer, but even he got another go with Besiktas.

In summary, Old Trafford isn’t Chernobyl, and United’s financial power means someone ought to get it right eventually. The queue to be that person is already forming and no second-rate chumps among them.

Eddie Howe is a serious, ambitious man who has always valued his reputation. But the word on the grapevine is that he is happy to stand as a candidate

So is Antonio Conte. He could have an argument in an empty room and fill another with his trophies, but he also fancies a trip to the United roulette table

Eddie Howe is a serious, ambitious man who has always valued his reputation. But the word on the grapevine is that he is happy to stand as a candidate. So is Antonio Conte. He could have an argument in an empty room and fill another with his trophies, but he also fancies a trip to the United roulette table.

Nagelsmann, too. He has had multiple options for his next step post-Germany but likes the sound of United.

The grandest delusion of all might be the one that coaxes any of them into believing it will be different under them. That they have the clout and nous and force of personality to tame all those monkeys.

But there is an advantage to operating at a club that is forever finding new ways to lose: failure is now so common that it doesn’t kill a reputation. Part of the shambles of the modern United is that such twisted logic might now be a saving grace.

Sports.title: Brighton's 30-year story from brink of extinction to high-fliers told by those who saved the club: From a rogue owner, a newspaper exposé and court cases to life-saving goal, play-off glory and Tony Bloom's maths wizards
Sports.content:
Take a walk through the gallery space in Brighton’s Royal Pavilion and you encounter a vivid sense of the extraordinary creative energy behind the fight for the local football club’s survival, 30 years ago. An exhibition called ‘Stand or Fall’ charts Brighton and Hove Albion’s 125-year history, and it is the early years of the three-decade metamorphosis from near extinction to one of the Premier League’s most outstanding clubs – third in the table and Champions League prospects, ahead of Sunday’s visit to Liverpool – which produces the greatest examples of innovation and imagination on display at the Brighton Museum and Art Gallery. Campaign T-shirts became an art form back then and the 1997 ‘They Think it’s all Over’ classic takes pride of place, alongside back issues of the fearless satirical Goals Eye fanzine, heartbeat of the legions of great writing which highlighted the activities of the nefarious and detested owner, Bill Archer. And then there is wonderful photography of Stewart Weir, who chronicled it all. That intelligence and attention to detail is the thread which binds the modern Brighton to what has gone before. Though a meticulous attention to detail by Tony Bloom’s mathematical wizards has seen the club invest so well and soar, it can be reasonably argued that the same relentless study of facts by a Brighton-supporting chartered accountant in the late 1990s still means more. Paul Samrah was a partner at mid-tier accountancy firm Kingston Smith when the club’s mismanagement by Archer led him to investigate the club’s accounts, filed at Companies House. And to discover that Archer had quietly changed the club’s ‘articles of association’ to ensure that he – and not the local community – would be allocated any surplus cash if the club went bust. ‘It was pre-email, remember,’ Samrah tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘You would contact Companies House for information, receive a microfiche of documents and have to go to a library to print out the relevant pages and make sure you didn’t miss anything. I was acutely worried that while I’d found this change they’d put in place, maybe there was another set of documents.' Fabian Hurzeler's flying Brighton side are third in the Premier League - but it has been some journey by the club over the last 30 years to get there Brighton-supporting accountant Paul Samrah (second right) was influential in exposing the mismanagement of the Seagulls' former owner Bill Archer But current owner Tony Bloom has been the driving force behind the club's meteoric rise He found out a lot more besides. Archer and his business partner, who had bought the club for £56.25 in 1993, had sold the Goldstone Ground to property developers for £7.4million without disclosing the fact and were raking in interest from the club on loans they’d made. ‘My professional reputation was on the line,’ Samrah says of these findings. ‘You’ve got to be very careful when you go around saying these things. I was thinking, “Here’s something really big. Now what do I do?”’ The answer was provided by a journalist with the intellectual curiosity to act on all this – the Brighton Argus’ chief reporter Paul Bracchi, now a Daily Mail journalist, who immediately saw the significance and persuaded his editors of it. ‘We didn’t have a team of lawyers,’ relates Bracchi. ‘As I recall, it was one external lawyer who we sometimes gave a call to, but our journalistic instincts told us that Paul had something.’ With its 100,000 circulation, the Argus’ story had an immense impact. In what would become a year’s work on the story, Bracchi turned up at Archer’s house in Lancashire and offered to buy his shareholding for the original £56.25. Archer’s ally David Bellotti, Albion chief executive, banned the Argus and all its employees from the ground. Including Fred Oliver, an Argus seller who was over 80 years old and had been selling the newspaper at the Goldstone Ground for as long as anyone could remember. The Goals Eye fanzine, edited by Ian Hart, a local undertaker, came into play. It was Hart who doorstepped Bellotti at the ground after discovering that Archer had struck an agreement that Brighton would play home games in 1996-97 at the home of fierce local rivals Portsmouth. ‘I parked the hearse outside and went in and told Bellotti I had this from an impeccable source,’ Hart tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘You could see the colour draining from his face. Archer tried to bring us inside the camp and eventually he sued us.’ Hart, whose book Brighton & Hove Albion: From Every Angle charts this extraordinary period, was in the High Court on the same day that Sonia Sutcliffe, wife of Yorkshire Ripper Peter Sutcliffe, received libel damages from Private Eye. He, too, was ordered to pay damages for allegations published about the Brighton directors’ activities and then became a cause celebre.

Your browser does not support iframes.

A fighting fund was set up to help pay the £6,000. But the momentum of the nascent fan campaign could not prevent the side’s slide to the jaws of relegation to non-League, knowing that defeat on a rock-hard, grassless surface at Hereford’s Edgar Street in May 1997 would end 77 years of Football League presence. Thousands of Brighton fans will tell you that the 63rd-minute equaliser by Robbie Reinelt that day still means more to them than anything Pascal Gross might fashion at Anfield on Sunday. ‘Who knows where we would be now if we’d vanished from the Football League,’ says Hart. He, like many others, will swear until their dying day that Mark Ormerod, the Brighton goalkeeper, is among the most important figures in this 30-year resurrection story because of his save from Hereford’s Adrian Foster in the dying minutes. ‘Too many people forget him,’ Hart says. Dick Knight certainly features extremely substantially, too. It was he who, having built a successful career in advertising, agreed to take over the club in 1997 after Archer was forced out. Knight’s brilliant memoir, Mad Man, demonstrates how ousting Archer was just the beginning. The battle to be permitted to relocate to the Withdean athletics stadium in Brighton from Gillingham’s Priestfields, 70 miles away in north Kent, was a rehearsal for the longer campaign to develop the Amex Stadium at Falmer, on the edge of the South Downs. By 2003, when Mark McGhee arrived as manager, almost every penny was being spent to fund the near £3million it cost simply to get through the series of planning inquiries required to get the club to Falmer. ‘We were doing talks, marching on the sea front, generally “making a scene”,’ McGhee tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘Every penny I was earning on players was going on the planning inquiries and money was going down the sinkhole, really. It was some cost. At that time, we were still scratching our heads about how we were actually going to build that stadium.’ Withdean – a 5,000-capacity ground with no cover on three of its sides – seemed bleak to outsiders. ‘But I weaponised the place,’ says McGhee. ‘We made it what we had to fight other people with. We made the best of it. We enjoyed beating Leeds and Wolves there. We were in portaloos but they were good portaloos!’ Mark Ormerod, the Brighton goalkeeper, is among the most important figures in this 30-year resurrection story, because of his save from Hereford’s Adrian Foster in the dying minutes of that 1997 match Brighton fans celebrate their stay of execution at Edgar Street in 1997 Some of a Brighton persuasion will tell you that the most significant win down all these years was the shootout victory over Swindon Town in the second leg of the 2004 play-off semi-final, when McGhee’s side had been rescued by a last-gasp Adam Virgo equaliser in torrential rain. It took them to a triumphant Millennium Stadium final appearance against Bristol City which was a stage to project the club’s Falmer stadium campaign to the world. ‘That was a springboard for us,’ says Samrah. But McGhee says his greatest Brighton day of all was the win at Ipswich the following season which kept them up in the second tier. ‘In some ways, staying up with Brighton that season is the greatest achievement of my management career,’ he says. Knight sold to Bloom in 2009 and remains a local legend. Nick Szczepanik, who helped him with his memoir, tells of walking down the street past a trench in which two workmen were labouring. ‘One of them recognised Dick and climbed out to shake his hand.’ It was by no means a linear path to the Premier League, of course. Szczepanik’s own excellent book, Brighton Up, vividly depicts the desolation of the play-off semi-final defeat by Sheffield Wednesday in 2016, and how Chris Hughton’s side finally reached the promised land. It also relates how the devastating Shoreham air crash of August 2015, in which a jet from a local airshow exploded into a fireball and crashed, killing 11 people, bound club and community together. Among those killed were Matt Grimstone, an assistant groundsman at Brighton’s training ground and his friend Jacob Schilt, who had played in the same school team as Lewis Dunk. Some of the details are heartbreaking. Albion staff picked up a video on the internet which seemed to show Grimstone’s car. Its number plate was matched with the one on the club’s system. ‘The club slogan at that time was #Together and what happened that day turned it into something with real meaning,’ says Szczepanik. ‘It had such resonance in the community.’ Brighton fans protest about needing a stadium of their own back in 2004 Some will tell you the most significant win down all these years was the shootout victory over Swindon Town in the second leg of the 2004 play-off semi-final when Chris Iwelumo scored It was the following season that Brighton took the final step. Though the money now is unimaginable to all there through the foothills of the story, there is a significance to the fact that Bloom is a diehard Brighton fan, just like Knight, Samrah, Hart and all the others who have been a part of it. ‘There is still this shared journey that not all clubs have,’ says Samrah. Thirty years ago this weekend, Brighton and Fulham supporters marched together in solidarity from Brighton Railway Station to the Goldstone Ground before kick-off in their fourth-tier game and only when the detested Bellotti had been forced to leave his seat did attention turn to what was a 0-0 draw, before around 8,000 people. Though the club’s world has turned beyond belief, McGhee sees the golden thread between then and now. ‘There’s this appreciation of what difficulty and struggle means,’ he says. ‘We were always the underdog – it was something we tried to use in our favour – and I think they’ve tried to keep that. The mentality where, regardless of how many games they’ve won, they are still not the favourites. They try to take that out with them, just like we did.’

Sports.title: Return of the Mac: How Andoni Iraola unlocked the real Alexis Mac Allister, why Argentine is a man transformed this season - and the latest on his Liverpool future after being hurt by contract snub
Sports.content:
Given the amount of trading done at England’s best-run club, Brighton play against a former player most weeks. Some get a little clap, some are booed, some prompt no reaction at all – but one always gets a rousing reception, whether back at the Amex Stadium or Anfield: Alexis Mac Allister. The Argentine is still adored by Seagulls fans and will be welcomed if he goes over to the away end on Sunday. But funnily enough, said affection was not always shared by Liverpool fans. Not last year, anyway. In 2026, people demand instant results. From next-day parcel deliveries to managers being sacked after a few bad games, modern life is all about now, now, now. So when Mac Allister’s form dipped last season, many fans were quick to be vocal in their criticism. The evidence is all over social media. That is not to castigate those supporters – more to highlight how drastic a U-turn Mac Allister has performed in the last few months. Alexis Mac Allister (left) has looked back to his best at Liverpool this season. The Argentine's two goals against Villarreal mean he is one goal off his tally for the entire 2025-26 campaign The 27-year-old looks fitter, sharper and more tactically aware than at any point in the last 18 months At the back end of last season, many observers, even those more reluctant to rush to judgment, would not have grumbled had Mac Allister been sold. Now, he is once again the first midfielder on the Liverpool team sheet. So how has he done it? And does his resurgence warrant a new contract, that he has publicly admitted is not yet forthcoming? After scoring goals three and four of the season with a brace against Villarreal on Tuesday, the 27-year-old is already just one strike away from matching last season’s tally – with about seven months to spare. But this resurgence is about much more than Mac Allister's goal-scoring. He looks fitter, sharper and more tactically aware than at any point in the last 18 months. ‘Last year was a really difficult year for all of us,’ he told Amazon Prime on Tuesday. ‘It was clear that I was not at the level. I am the first one to say, I have no problem (admitting that). ‘Something wasn't right in the group. This manager (Andoni Iraola) changed it, and that's really important. The way we play is quite different. I don't like to compare. ‘I feel good, that's what I want and that's what I enjoy.’ One reason for Mac Allister’s rise is a tactical shift. Last season, Arne Slot followed a zonal pressing structure, whereas Iraola’s off-the-ball system is more man-to-man orientated. It means his players have to communicate and co-ordinate less, which in turn makes them less susceptible to being played through and picked apart. There is undoubtedly still a balance issue with Iraola’s midfield and they are played through far too easily – Liverpool have conceded ten goals in their last four games – but it is improving and Mac Allister’s tenacity is helping them win the ball high up the pitch and start attacks.

Your browser does not support iframes.

Mac Allister is transformed physically - he looks fresher, more robust and more confident after a summer at the World Cup then resting Mac Allister is winning 5.1 duels per 90 minutes this season and has a duel success rate of 53.2 per cent – up from 4.2 and 46.6 respectively last campaign. He is winning possession 4.7 times per game (up from 3.9) and making more tackles. On the ball, Mac Allister is taking 2.7 shots per game (up from 1.8 last year), scoring 0.49 goals (an increase from 0.12), creating more chances (1.7, was 1.3) and making more successful passes (46.6 per game, up from 43.5). Those stats confirm what Liverpool fans have seen with their own eyes. But Mac Allister's resurgence is about more than tactics. It is also down to physical reasons. Last year, he came into the campaign nursing an injury, missed a lot of pre-season and never really caught up. It felt like he had lost several yards of pace. Mac Allister, part of the Argentina side who reached the World Cup final, was the last person to report to the AXA Training Centre for pre-season in the summer. He skipped the tour of the United States and had a proper rest. The World Cup was good for Mac Allister mentally. He regained confidence and enjoyed life in camp with Lionel Messi, Julian Alvarez et al. Atletico Madrid came calling in the summer and Argentine boss Diego Simeone tried to tempt his compatriot to join. Manchester City were mooted as suitors, too. But Mac Allister and his father, Carlos, wanted to stay at Liverpool. The Reds might have entertained offers had they reached a suitable price but none were forthcoming. Mac Allister’s desire to stay and prove people wrong came at a time when the club's hierarchy informed him they were not willing to extend his contract, which runs until summer 2028. The player felt hurt given his midfield partners, Ryan Gravenberch and Dominik Szoboszlai, both penned new deals and Cody Gakpo, who is also 27, renewed until 2030. Publicly, Mac Allister said he was ‘very sad’ about his deal but vowed to give ‘100 per cent’ until his last day at the club. Ever since that press conference in early September, he has delivered on his word and put in perhaps his best run of form since his first season. Since publicly complaining about not being offered a new contract, Mac Allister has put in his best run of form in years Andoni Iraola is loving his all-action midfielder. ‘I am very happy, his performances have been very good' For this reason, the contract issue is not done and dusted. Should Mac Allister continue his impressive form, his hand will be significantly strengthened but Liverpool are realistic that he will be 29 by the time his deal expires. They want more evidence that his resurgence is not just a temporary purple patch. Right now, though, Iraola is loving his all-action midfielder. The boss said yesterday: ‘I am very happy, his performances have been very good since day one when I arrived. He takes all the information and is smart. You don’t need to explain the same things seven times to Alexis. ‘He is one of the players that understands things very quickly. He gets things from opposition, gets information on what we need to do against each team, what we need from every position. He helps his team-mates a lot because he understands the overall picture. ‘He is another of the leaders we have. He has experience. He is not as old but he has been involved in top-level games, has won titles for club and country and he has been really good. ‘Sometimes players play well, other times not so much, but I think Alexis is in a place where he has consistently been playing well. I hope he can stay there.’

Sports.title: Stephen Fleming is right - it's embarrassing that England can't produce their own elite coach. This is what the ECB are doing to fix their broken pipeline, reveals LAWRENCE BOOTH
Sports.content:
As so often in English cricket, it took an outsider to say the quiet bit out loud – even if Stephen Fleming’s contention that ‘the national team should be coached by a national representative’ seemed an odd thing to hear from a New Zealander who had just been handed the reins to the England Test side.

Fleming, though, has always been a class act, and his comments to the BBC earlier this week reflected his priority, which is to help English cricket – not just himself. Clearly, he was on to something.

After all, England’s 21st-century zeniths have all coincided with foreign coaches. Duncan Fletcher (Zimbabwe) regained the Ashes in 2005 after an 18-year gap; Andy Flower (Zimbabwe) won Test series in Australia and India, and took England to the top of the rankings; Trevor Bayliss (Australia) won England men’s first one-day World Cup.

That’s before we mention Matthew Mott (Australia), whose tenure as white-ball coach ended in disappointment but not before he had won the T20 World Cup in Australia, and Brendon McCullum (New Zealand), whose win-rate as Test coach of 55 per cent should not be overlooked because of the excesses that brought down Bazball.

Amid that quintet were three Englishmen: Peter Moores, who had two largely unsuccessful stints; Ashley Giles, who never got a fair crack of the whip in charge of the white-ball set-up; and Chris Silverwood, whose tenure was ended by the 4–0 Ashes thrashing of 2021-22.

Fleming, then, is not just articulating a view held by many: that international cricket should in part be about the fascination of pitting one country’s system against another, coaching staff included. He is also querying what at times has looked like a policy decision by the ECB, who appear to have taken one look at the English coaches fostered by the 18-team county structure, and decided they prefer the view abroad.

Stephen Fleming (left) has highlighted English cricket's difficulties in producing elite coaches, with Fleming himself and white-ball coach Brendon McCullum (right) both Kiwis

Almost all of the high-points in England's recent history have come under a foreign coach, such as the 2005 Ashes triumph masterminded by Zimbabwean Duncan Fletcher (left)

They have, in short, concluded that the innate conservatism of the county game is ill-suited to the task of producing coaches capable of making the big, bold calls required to thrive at international level. It is the same philosophy that has driven them to select players in spite of their county record, not because of it.

Plainly, the job of Rob Key, the ECB’s managing director of men’s cricket, is to select the best candidate. But the two nations with whom England like to seek comparison have either stopped looking abroad, or have had little need to do so.

The last non-Indian to coach India was Fletcher, whose four-year reign ended in 2015. Australia, meanwhile, have had eight head coaches, starting with Bob Simpson in 1986, and only one – the South African Mickey Arthur, who lasted just two years – was not a native.

The English game, by contrast, has always borrowed from abroad, from the players themselves – more than one in seven of their Test cricketers were born outside the UK – to their latest national selector, Australia’s Marcus North. This pragmatic multiculturalism is both a function of England’s colonial past, and a statement of insecurity.

Yet the idea that the coach of the England cricket team should be English need not be dismissed as nationalistic tub-thumping. In theory, at least, an English coach will be more instinctively in tune with an English approach to the game, and it’s not a stretch to suggest that the appointment of Fleming appears to confirm the ECB’s lack of faith in their own system.

The board can argue reasonably enough that the best person for the main job need not be dictated by their nationality: look at Thomas Tuchel in football or, not so long ago, Eddie Jones in rugby. But when only one head coach in the eight-team Hundred tournament this year was English – Moores at Trent Rockets – it suggests a deeper malaise.

When The Hundred began in 2021, Paul Farbrace, the former England assistant coach who was recently appointed director of cricket at Lancashire, suggested that four of the eight franchises should have an English coach. He recently told the Daily Telegraph: ‘I was shouted down. One of the guys in the ECB at the time said: “Oh, I couldn’t name you four who were capable of doing the job.”’

But times may be changing. For one thing, Fleming has surrounded himself with more English coaches than McCullum, whose white-ball coaching team includes fellow New Zealanders Tim Southee and Jeetan Patel, as well as Kevin Pietersen, an adopted South African.

Fleming’s new-look Test entourage consists of a trio of locals – Richard Dawson, Marcus Trescothick and Sarah Taylor (centre)

Rob Key (left) is keen for top players like Ben Stokes (right) to be mentored into coaching roles rather than head for the Sky Sports commentary box

Fleming’s new-look Test entourage consists of a trio of locals – Richard Dawson, Marcus Trescothick and Sarah Taylor – plus the experienced South African bowling coach Eric Simons. Mike Yardy, formerly of England and Sussex, was recently appointed as the ECB’s new ‘elite national batting lead’.

And the shift in emphasis is mirrored by the bespoke coaching courses overseen by the ECB’s performance director, Ed Barney, and delivered by the head of coach development, the former rugby player Diccon Edwards, which caters to international cricketers who have not had the time to do the traditional Level 3 and 4 coaching programmes.

Among those to have benefited are Ben Stokes, Andrew Flintoff – who until recently coached England Lions – Mark Wood, Chris Woakes, Moeen Ali and Jonny Bairstow. Female players include Heather Knight, Georgia Elwiss and Alice Davidson-Richards.

One part of the course is a practical element where the intake are monitored by ‘developers’ who can advise them on aspects of the job that go beyond batting and bowling technique. These players end up with a Level 3 qualification that is tailored to their schedule and ensures good cricketing brains are not automatically lost to the Sky Sports commentary box.

Key’s role, then, is to look after both the needs of the present and to lay the groundwork for a future in which the England set-up is a more accurate reflection of the English system.

‘With McCullum and Fleming, we’ve got two of the best coaches in the world,’ he tells Daily Mail Sport. ‘The national side should always take the best person for the job. Where we want to get it to in the future when these jobs come up is the best option are English candidates.’

As Fleming has intimated, English cricket is not quite ready to stand on its own two feet. But that moment may not be far away.

Sports.title: 'It's been seamless... I'm over the moon': JAMES PATER, Northampton's 19-year-old 'Slim Reaper' on his rapid rise into the first team, taking Jonny Wilkinson's advice and how he's trying to bulk up
Sports.content:
'It's been seamless... I'm over the moon': JAMES PATER, Northampton's 19-year-old 'Slim Reaper' on his rapid rise into the first team, taking Jonny Wilkinson's advice and how he's trying to bulk up

When James Pater was 15, his team-mates at Shelford RFC clubbed together to bid for a training session with Jonny Wilkinson in a charity auction. To their amazement, they won – and suddenly found themselves sharing a pitch with English rugby’s most famous man.

‘It was an auction prize at a big memorial match between the two local schools, Perse and The Leys,’ Pater tells Daily Mail Sport.

‘One of the dads drove us to Pennyhill Park in the Shelford minibus. We had breakfast in the hotel and then we went out on the pitch with him. I brought my kicking tee. It was funny because there were props and hookers and second rows doing a kicking session with Jonny Wilkinson.

‘He went through everyone individually and talked about how he deals with challenges. He was quite insightful on how to control your emotions and manage things that don’t go your way.

'Don’t dwell on it. Move onto the next thing. We have a similar mindset here at Northampton so it’s something I take into everyday life.’

James Pater, 19, has made an astonishingly quick rise into the Northampton first team and is now their go-to full-back

A 15-year-old Pater does some kicking under the watchful eye of Jonny Wilkinson (Source: Instagram/Jamespater_)

Pater has carried Wilkinson’s advice into his fledgling career. Now 19, the rangy 6ft 3in full-back is showing composure beyond his years, thrusting himself into contention for an England A call-up next week.

But rugby was not always his destiny. ‘I hadn’t played academy rugby at the time we met Jonny Wilkinson. I played football for Cambridge Academy until I was 15 or 16. We played Chelsea when I was like 12 years old but more often we played teams like Luton and Peterborough.

'I played central defensive midfield or centre back. I liked Sergio Busquets in that 4-3-3 formation at Barcelona – or the quick centre backs like (former PSG man) Presnel Kimpembe. I grew up wanting to be a footballer, 100 per cent, but GCSEs came along and I didn't really progress any further. That’s when I called it.’

Rugby was never far away. Throughout secondary school, Pater played for the Huntingdon Stags – the junior club that brought through George Furbank. He joined Shelford at Colts level and his rugby snowballed when he starred at Warwick Festival as a 16-year-old.

‘I was picked for Ireland IQ, which is for Irish-qualified English people,’ reveals Pater. ‘My mum’s from Letterkenny, County Donegal. She’s one of 10 so I’ve got 40 or 50 cousins. We’d go down to the beach with any kind of ball. We’d have enough of us to play our own match!

'I played for Ireland IQ against Ealing Trailfinders and a week later I got a call-up for England Under 18s. I started playing in the Under 18s Academy League for Northampton and that’s when rugby became something to really go after. Charlie Reed, the manager, said, “If you keep playing well then you could get offered a contract”.

‘We won the Academy League and then I made my PREM debut a few weeks after that against Gloucester, when I was still at school, which was pretty sick.

'I was doing my A Levels at the time. It was half-term, I was revising, and I got the message saying I might be travelling with the team. I came up and trained on the Thursday and it was announced that I was on the bench. It all happened so quickly.’

'We won the Academy League and then I made my PREM debut a few weeks after that against Gloucester, when I was still at school, which was pretty sick'

‘It’s been pretty seamless,' Pater says. 'I didn't feel like I was the next in line. I just got an opportunity at the start of the season and played well'

At the time, Pater was only on a part-time contract with Northampton. A highflyer at the Leys School, he secured the grades required for a three-year economics degree at the University of Bath.

‘I had my accommodation sorted and everything was ready to go. I would play BUCS University rugby there on Wednesdays and come back every few weeks to train as part of a uni deal.

‘That was the plan. I stayed with Northampton for pre-season and that summer I had conversations with Sam Vesty and Phil Dowson about staying on and doing this full time. It got to late August – a few weeks before uni started – and I decided to defer my first year at Bath. I put all my eggs in one basket and decided to go for it.’

Pater has not looked back. He had been earmarked as the club’s long-term successor to Furbank, who joined Harlequins during the summer. He opted not to move to Bath, instead enrolling with the Open University for an online course.

He scored a hat-trick in the opening game of the season and has been praised for his unflappable abilities as a ball-playing 15.

‘It’s been pretty seamless,' he says. 'I didn't feel like I was the next in line. I just got an opportunity at the start of the season and played well. My aim was actually to make more than half of the matchday 23s. I've been pretty over the moon with how it’s gone so far.

‘Furbs is an idol of mine. When I joined the academy, the players I liked to watch were the dual playmakers like Dan Carter and Beauden Barrett. I’d watch their YouTube highlights. Now I look at guys like Sascha Feinberg-Mngomezulu, Ruben Love and Will Jordan.

‘But when you’re with someone 24/7 in this environment, you learn so much quicker than watching online. Furbs taught me so much. When you're training against him, you learn so much, like what he does positionally.

Pater celebrates a try with his Northampton team-mates Tommy Freeman (left) and Fin Smith

Pater scores Northampton's fifth try during their remarkably high-scoring PREM match against Bath earlier this month

‘I want to be involved all the time. I want to get my hands to the ball. I don't want to miss moments and I want to have a triple threat: run, pass, kick. I don’t want to feel like I’m watching the game.

'I never have targets, but I always look at the stats sheets. Especially at Under 20s, I’d want to have the most carries and play 80 minutes every game.’

Pater has played his way into Test conversations. Furbank, Freddie Steward and Marcus Smith are England’s senior full-backs but, if he continues on the same trajectory, then Pater could be their longer-term successor.

Weighing 86kg, the willowy teenager is nicknamed ‘The Slim Reaper’ by his club-mates. On Northampton's pre-season tour to Sri Lanka, the senior players ribbed the youngster about bulking up for the demands of senior rugby.

‘That nickname actually came from Chunya Munga,’ laughs Pater. ‘He started calling me it because I’m tall and thin, but it’s also what they call Kevin Durant in the NBA. It's not a terrible nickname, to be fair.

'I’m trying to put a bit of weight on but it's hard when you're playing every weekend and running a lot. I’m just trying to put more on my plate at dinner time, speaking to the nutritionist.’

Still living in the club’s academy house, dinners are an unglamorous affair. ‘You hear about Tigers putting 20 people in an academy house with two kitchens but we just have three or four people. It’s quite civil.'

Pater touches down against Newcastle Red Bulls on the opening day of the season, when he grabbed a hat-trick

‘You’re brought up knowing that Leicester’s a big game,' Pater says about this weekend's opponents. 'That’s never lost on you in the academy'

Which means he might stay with his mates in the house even if the academy contract he's on should shortly be upgraded, what with him now being the club’s first-choice full-back. His ball-playing skills have fitted seamlessly into Northampton’s expansive attack and this weekend he will be taking on Leicester in the East Midlands derby.

‘You’re brought up knowing that Leicester’s a big game,' he says. 'That’s never lost on you in the academy. If you look at the scores, we used to put 70 points on them in the academy!

'We had Tim Rodber, our old forward, come in and talk to us this week about these being the best times of your life. He talked about what it means for yourself, the club, and the town.’

Pater, still carrying Wilkinson’s unflappable advice, will no doubt take it all in his long stride.

Sports.title: Liverpool news: Club chiefs jet out on £50m scouting mission as talks set for January switch
Sports.content:
Liverpool news: Club chiefs jet out on £50m scouting mission as talks set for January switch

Liverpool may have fallen short in their recruitment efforts over the summer but will reportedly be busy in January as a string of potential deals emerge

View 2 Images Andoni Iraola's staff are reportedly hard at work scouting Valencia's David Otorbi (Image: Getty Images)

Andoni Iraola is beginning to leave his mark as Liverpool manager after piecing together three straight wins for the first time at Anfield. However, the Reds look set to continue their evolution in January as several major deals start to gather traction.

‌



‌



Sunday's clash against Brighton will be a fierce test of just how well things are truly going under Iraola's command. The Seagulls have soared up to third in the Premier League table, two places above Liverpool, after enjoying the fruits of their own transfer labour.

‌



Ahead of a hectic week that also comprises an EFL Cup showdown with Chelsea, the transfer rumour mill remains hard at work. Mirror Football has dissected the latest transfer headlines around Anfield heading into a key weekend clash.

‌



Reds scout £50m gem

Liverpool are reportedly escalating their interest in Valencia winger David Otorbi and have had scouts in attendance to watch the youngster. Their interest comes amid reports the 19-year-old will soon see his price-tag double after impressing this term.

Otorbi put pen to paper on a two-year contract back in April, complete with a £25million release clause and the option of another three-year extension. Reports in Spain now suggest Los Che are on the verge of triggering that option, which would also increase the forward's release clause valuation to £50m.

It would mean Valencia will have the bargaining security to demand that entire fee for his signature. Although Rio Ngumoha has started to show extreme promise as Liverpool's new star on the right wing, more competition for the role wouldn't go astray.

‌



Make sure you don't miss the best Liverpool coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Liverpool have had scouts in attendance at Valencia games to monitor the progress of Harvey Elliott during his loan. However, they may have identified another fine prospect in the process, one Valencia appear eager to keep out of the clutches of English suitors.

‌



As part of keeping tabs on Elliott, Liverpool are also reported to have met with Valencia manager Javier Aguirre and sporting director Braulio Vazquez to discuss the matter. However, it's plausible exploratory talks have also taken place regarding Otorbi's future and whether there's a place for him at Anfield.

Agents meet over Ndukwe solution

View 2 Images Liverpool are meeting with Ifeanyi Ndukwe's representatives to discuss bringing the Levante loanee back in January (Image: Getty Images)

‌



Ifeanyi Ndukwe's stellar start to life in Spain could be set to earn him an Anfield lifeline sooner than expected. In fact, the player's agents are due for talks with his parent club about potentially ending his loan spell at Levante early, according to reports.

After a super pre-season, Ifeanyi was farmed out due to the fact he couldn't obtain a UK work permit and Liverpool had already used up their quota of non-eligible players. He's since started pulling up trees in La Liga and established himself as an increasingly prominent member of Levante's starting XI.

‌



Sky Sports Austria has reported the Reds will discuss the matter with Ndukwe's representatives this weekend. After shining in La Liga, the 18-year-old has accumulated enough points necessary to obtain the proper work permit and is eligible to play in England.

‌



Despite the recent rise in results at Anfield, defensive solidity remains an area of concern for Liverpool. In that sense, another option at centre-back wouldn't go astray, especially after loanee Ronald Araujo has impressed while playing on the right side of defence.

Rave reviews in Spain suggest Ndukwe could soon outgrow Levante, who will not be keen on the idea of losing the player. However, Liverpool could execute a masterstroke after including a clause in his contract to recall the player this winter.

Sports.title: Man Utd manager candidates highlight outside view of club as dressing room chaos raised
Sports.content:
Man Utd manager candidates highlight outside view of club as dressing room chaos raised

Manchester United's dressing room has been cited as a concern by potential candidates to replace Michael Carrick with some claiming the players are too vocal following two recent outburst

View 2 Images Man Utd's dressing room conduct has been raised as an issue by potential future managers

Those who are being considered to replace Michael Carrick at Manchester United claim that the squad "talk too much" whilst also believing that the dressing room "needs order and discipline".

‌



‌



The Red Devils have endured a miserable start to the season, winning just one of their opening seven Premier League games, which is their worst start to a campaign in 40 years.

‌



That has seen the pressure ramp up on Carrick, who was also appointed in the summer, but his latest blow came in Italy, where his United side were hammered 4-1 by Como in the Champions League.

‌



The dire run of results has already led to talk of Carrick being replaced, but several of the candidates who are being considered have raised red flags with how the players act. Over the past fortnight Lisandro Martinez and Bruno Fernandes have both spoken out, taking aim at senior figures at Old Trafford.

Following the loss in Atletico Madrid Martinez said that he expected more from the technical director, Jason Wilcox, who had not given them the squad required to fight across four competitions. Then on Wednesday night Fernandes blamed United's tactics, which were continually ripped apart, on Carrick.

‌

The Telegraph reports that a source close to one of United’s managerial candidates has said: “It’s clear they need order and discipline. The dressing room is out of control and that is the first thing to fix.”

‌



Meanwhile a friend of another candidate clearly feels similarly and claimed that the players are too vocal and need to be more respect of United's stature.

The players on the red side of Manchester, some of whom have had four or more different permanent managers at Old Trafford, have been accused of playing major roles in the dismissals of previous bosses. Difficult periods, of which there have been many, have been marred by players who've been accused of downing tools.

‌



View 2 Images Bruno Fernandes became the latest player to air his views in public (Image: TNT Sports)

Carrick came out fighting on Friday ahead of United's clash with Bournemouth this week, underlining the need for his players to work hard, something he had mentioned in the aftermath of their loss in Como.

‌



But despite his show of defiance, United have had to consider the prospect of another change in the dugout. It is understood former Germany and Bayern Munich boss Julian Nagelsmann would be high on the club's list, with the 39-year-old open to any approach.

Eddie Howe is another name that is highly regarded, but he has only been out of work for a matter of months. He left Newcastle during the summer and did want time away from the game, yet could be lured in by the prospect of leading such a massive outfit.

Article continues below

Other at Old Trafford are known to be admirers of Antonio Conte, Unai Emery or Fabian Hurzeler. Conte is another man out of a job and is a previous Premier League winner following his spell at Chelsea.

Sports.title: Premier League clubs learn individual cost of independent regulator after fees double
Sports.content:
Premier League clubs learn individual cost of independent regulator after fees double

Premier League clubs have learnt the cost of funding the Independent Football Regulator which, whilst doubling, will still be a drop in the water when compared to their mammoth revenues

View 2 Images Some Premier League clubs will pay less than a million to fund the Independent Football Regulator (Image: James Gill - Danehouse/Getty Images)

Clubs have been told the cost of the Independent Football Regulator has doubled. The regulator set out the reasons why the annual running costs figure has gone up to £20m which is twice the figure originally estimated by the Government.

‌



‌



They will employ around 100 staff with the cost being met by a new levy on clubs with Premier League clubs shouldering most of the burden.

‌



It comes just a week after the IFR published its State of the Game report which revealed the huge financial issues facing English football which has an annual revenue of £9billion.

‌



They say the cost of the regulator will only represent 0.1 per cent of revenues for some clubs with the highest-earning Premier league clubs having to contribute £1.8m-a-season.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



The highest-earning Premier League clubs, which play in Europe or generate more than £150m in commercial income, will be expected to contribute up to £1.8m a season, with the majority of top-flight clubs paying £600,000 a season. Championship clubs not in receipt of parachute payments would pay around £45,000 per season.

The IFR chief executive, Richard Monks, said: “The announcement of the levy is another big moment for the IFR. Over the last year we have been busy laying the ground for the world ’s first independent football regulator.

‌



“We have already started to deliver real change in football – whether that’s through the stringent suitability checks we are running on owners and directors or through the State of the Game report which shone a light on how the football industry needs to change.

View 2 Images Championship clubs will also chip in, but their fees depend on whether they are enjoying the benefit of parachute payments (Image: Getty Images)

‌



“The levy we are proposing today represents a fair and balanced approach and will ensure that most clubs pay around 0.1% of their annual revenues.

“We are confident football will see this is a relatively modest investment to help achieve a more sustainable ecosystem which will provide peace of mind for fans, clubs and the communities they serve.”

Article continues below

The total set-up costs for the regulator have run to £45m with the bulk being recovered over time from the clubs via the levy.

Sports.title: Man Utd fans sent new stadium survey as 100,000-seater ground gathers pace
Sports.content:
Man Utd fans sent new stadium survey as 100,000-seater ground gathers pace

Manchester United fans will be consulted and have the chance to give their view on the club's new stadium as plans continue over a new venue for the club

View 2 Images Man Utd have signalled their plans to build a new 100,000-capacity stadium (Image: Foster and Partners / SWNS)

Manchester United will involve fans in a survey as they get the chance to feedback on the club's plans for a new 100,000-seater stadium, with concept images already being released.

‌



‌



The controversial ‘circus tent’ design is only an impression of what the finished venue could look like and the plans are not set in stone, and could still be influenced by what fans say.

‌



Supporters have been invited to take part in a number of focus groups to discuss key details which could help decide on how the new state-of-the-art stadium takes shape.

‌



The survey will be distributed to season ticket holders, cup season ticket holders, executive members, official members and supporters who have purchased hospitality within the last three years. It will close at 12pm on Friday November 6, reports The Sun.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Collette Roche, CEO, New Stadium Development, said: “Our proposed new stadium is one of the most significant projects Manchester United will undertake in the next 100 years, and it is vital that we shape it together with our fans.

“Above all else, this is a football stadium built for them, so getting the details right matters. We are committed to thorough and transparent engagement, ensuring supporters help inform key decisions on atmosphere, affordability, accessibility and the traditions that have made Old Trafford so special for so long.”

‌



“By working together, we can create a world-class football stadium that supports success on the pitch, reflects the identity of Manchester United, and gives fans a home they can be proud of for generations to come.”

View 2 Images Man Utd fans will be given the chance to influence the new stadium

‌



The club have also said there will be further opportunities for fans to provide their views on other major topics, one of those being pricing, which continues to be a hot topic after some controversial decisions taken by Ineos, who have removed concession prices.

Despite the obvious emotional attachment to Old Trafford it is well documented that the stadium, once renowned as one of Europe's best, has fallen well behind the standard set by the modern stadia. That owing to a continued lack of investment, but Ineos have looked to revamp the club's infrastructure, recently presiding over major improvements to the training ground.
