Does this hero worship weaken the book? Not at all. I will return to this point in a moment.

The book is inspiring and enlightening. It is implicitly an affirmation of visionary power and a celebration of significant values. As a treasure trove of lessons in competence and commitment, Ladbone: A Life in Print is a master class for those who aspire to excellent public service. In his tribute, Steve Osuji writes that Mr Bonuola is a peculiar history that is yet to be written. This book will surely be a veritable reference to anyone who rises to the challenge of writing this peculiar history. As many of the writers tell stories of their interactions with Ladbone, they also tell plenty of stories of their own professional lives. Put differently, in honouring him they considerably honour themselves. The confluence of stories here, the narratives within narratives, give us aspects of the history of Nigerian journalism itself. In the parable of the elephant and the wise blindmen, all those who touch different parts of the huge animal draw different conclusions. But in this book, all the different perspectives return the same verdict: Ladbone is a strong breed. There are many engaging recollections here of how he was an inspiration and a spur to many readers of his most popular column in The Sunday Times — “Caught Out: A Critical Look at the Nigerian Press,” and then his Abdul Rafiu column with the ram logo in The Guardian, which is the longest running column in the history of Nigerian journalism. General Ibrahim Badamosi Babangida, a former military president; Professor Yemi Osinbajo, former vice president of Nigeria; Chief Bisi Akande, former governor of Osun State; Aremo Olusegun Osoba, former governor of Ogun State; Mr Babatunde Raji Fashola, former governor of Lagos state and Oba Masoud Oyekola Aweda Lawal, the Iba of Kishi kingdom, attest to his courage and insights as a public affairs commentator, and his pieces of advice, in private, on public policies.

The writers render in uncluttered prose Ladbone’s humble beginning in Kishi, his home town; his years at Ijebu-Ode Grammar School for his A/Levels, where he was a voracious reader and a passionate lover of good debates, and where he won the coveted zonal John F Kennedy Essay competition; his life as a secondary school teacher of English Language and Literature at Methodist High School, Arigbajo, in Ifo, and at Premier Grammar School, Abeokuta; his 55 years in journalism; how he was hired by Alhaji Babatunde Jose at The Daily Times as a sub-editor and how he rose by dint of hard work to become chief sub-editor, production editor, acting features editor, member of the Editorial Board of Daily Times and deputy editor of Spear magazine. This was where he met Prince Henry Odukomaiya, Alhaji Alade Odunewu, Dr Patrick Dele Cole, Mr Femi Kusa, Uncle Sam Amuka, Aremo Olusegun Osoba, Mr Kunle Elegbede, Prince Tony Momoh, Mr Martin Iroabuchi, Chief Tola Adeniyi, Mr Gbolabo Ogunsanwo, Mr Dele Giwa, Chief Areoye Oyebola, and Mr Tunji Oseni, the editor of Sunday Times who asked him to write the “Caught Out” column. It was here that he met his beautiful wife, Esther Iyabo Oladele, with whom he has produced and raised six daughters: Abiodun, Bolatito, Bolupe, Lolade, Kemi and Wemimo. It was also at The Daily Times, in 1977, that he earned the certificate of the Thomson Foundation Editorial Study Centre, affiliated to the University of Cardiff in Wales, United Kingdom. He then moved over to The Guardian, where he laboured for 22 years as a founding associate editor, then editor, editor-in chief and managing director.

Memories are made of the founding of The Guardian and why and how it became an instant success; of how the support for his original dummy by Mrs Maiden Ibru gave birth to the unique, attractive and winning layout of The Guardian as a high-brow newspaper; how the team of Dr Stanley Macebuh complimented that of Ladbone; and of his catchy headlines as a sub-editor. We are told of his punishing work ethic; how he became a sports enthusiast because sports reporting was selling his papers; how a well-written editorial was spiked in the dead of the night by Ladbone, just to please the publisher who had rushed down to Rutam House in his bathroom slippers to protect his business interest; Ladbone’s commitment, both in the newsroom and outside it, to those who did not have champions; the story about how he would obey the traffic light at 2 a.m. on his way home after office hours; the stories about the ethics and aesthetics of his journalistic practice; his principled positions anchored in the ethos of his upbringing and strengthened by his strong belief in God as a cross bearer; his immediate reactions to the gruesome death of Krees Imodibe and Tayo Awotusin in the Liberian civil war; his honesty and deep sense of accountability; his help in building Liberty Text School in his hometown, Kishi; his contributions to the Unique Frontline Club, Kishi; the interesting stories of how he nearly snatched Mr Ray Ekpu from Dele Giwa, but only succeeded in arresting Ted Iwere at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport and employing him at The Guardian effective immediately, beating Dele Giwa to it; the jailing of The Guardian’s senior diplomatic correspondent, Tunde Thompson, and assistant news editor, Nduka Irabor, under decree 4 by the draconian regime of Generals Muhammadu Buhari and Tunde Idiagbon; how the Simply Mr policy died; the closure of The Guardian by General Sani Abacha; the assassination attempt on its publisher, Mr Alex Ibru; the exit of Dr Stanley Macebuh, Dr Yemi Ogunbiyi, Dr Olatunji Dare, Mr Sully Abu and, eventually, Ladbone and Mr Femi Kusa. The writers reflect on Lade Bonuola’s refusal to fold when The Guardian, his beloved newspaper, was confronted with despicable regimes. Despite the terrorism of the Abacha junta, his abiding faith in a better Nigeria never wavered, as he always insisted that the future of his country was full of possibilities. Perhaps, more crucially, he believed that a nation as a community should share core values, agree on fundamental issues concerning its well-being.

Stories are also told of how, in his quiet way, with all his pleasant and courteous conversations and raucous laughter with his staff, Ladbone can be a very brutal person in his perpetual, if not obsessive, quest for excellence. This was not just in the newsroom. His children, when they were growing up, must not touch the walls of his house, which he painted every December. He washed and ironed his own clothes. He regularly went shopping for groceries, and was a terrific cook any time his wife was not around. No one stayed idle in his home.

Precisely because the meeting of the management of The Guardian with General Sani Abacha and the apology subsequently tendered to him have been reported differently by those who were not there, let me quote at length Mr Femi Kusa’s reporting of that meeting in his tribute: “When Mr Ibru became a minister in the government of General Sani Abacha, he expected The Guardian to soften on its criticisms of the regime. The newspaper did not. Abacha was tyrannical and murderous. The Guardian was not set up to support tyranny and murder. We did not come over to The Guardian to work with tyrannical and murderous leaders for pounds of porridge. Abacha closed The Guardian for one year. Mediators arranged a meeting with the dictator, at which The Guardian was to apologise. Oyinlade Bonuola declined to attend the meeting. Mr Ibru asked him to resign as managing director if he would not. Within the next second or two, Bonuola did. Mr Ibru offered me the job. Immediately, I rejected it. Mediators later proposed a meeting with Abacha at which no apology would be made. We agreed. Bonuola and I had a sleepless night before the meeting, drafting and reworking the speech he would make. The then Osemawe of Ondo, Oba Festus Adesanoye, who was Permanent Secretary at Defence Headquarters when Abacha was learning the ropes as a senior officer, joined us at the meeting on Mr Alex Ibru’s invitation behind our back. He gave Alex Ibru contracts for FESTAC 77, which he said made him. Their friendship made Oba Adesanoye a visiting consultant of The Guardian’s Editorial Board. It was he who made the apology after Oyinlade Bonuola’s speech, which made none. He was backed in the apologia by Andy Akporugo, Mr Ibru’s cousin. I spoke no words. Mr Alex Ibru did not forget our intransigence. The Guardian heated up. Soon, reprisal events unfolded, which advised us of the necessity to leave peacefully.” The utter ruthlessness of the way they were treated was one of the lowest moments in the history of The Guardian.

We have here stories about Lade Bonuola’s Spartan lifestyle; his cultivation of high-wire contacts — top people in politics, business, armed forces, etc., etc. for scoops and the verification of stories; the high premium that he always placed on archives and libraries as a newspaper administrator; his secret encouragement of some radical, left leaning journalists; his curiosity about the practice of journalism in other parts of the world, particularly in the US and the UK, for which reason he read their major newspapers everyday and religiously followed the news on their other outlets; his constant celebration of the best journalists in the electronic media, such as Christiane Amanpour, who, incidentally, announced three days ago that she would soon be leaving CNN after 43 glorious years in the place; his deep interest in books on journalism and inspiring autobiographies; and his insistence that a newspaper must be readable, inventive, truthful, and, certainly, not neutral. By and large, the book tells us about the enduring power of the Lade Bonuola effect.

Stories are also told of how, in his quiet way, with all his pleasant and courteous conversations and raucous laughter with his staff, Ladbone can be a very brutal person in his perpetual, if not obsessive, quest for excellence. This was not just in the newsroom. His children, when they were growing up, must not touch the walls of his house, which he painted every December. He washed and ironed his own clothes. He regularly went shopping for groceries, and was a terrific cook any time his wife was not around. No one stayed idle in his home. And because he woke up at 5 a.m. everyday, the children must also be awake to do house chores before they got ready for school at precisely 7 a.m. The children dared not stay out beyond 7PM. They must dress modestly well. Each time he was around, a hush fell over the house. He inculcated in the girls the hobby of reading, which, they, in turn, have passed on to his 11 grandchildren.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The huge project that the Living Archives Initiatives of the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) is embarking on, I would argue, is informed by this idea of the struggle of memory against forgetting. It is fit and proper that the organisation has started with Ladbone, who told Lasisi Olagunju, in an interview embedded in his tribute, that he is not given to blowing his own trumpet.

When Buhari and Idiagbon introduced austerity measures to the beleaguered nation, Lade Bonuola promptly introduced his own structural adjustment programme in his home. Abiodun, his first child, was taught how to measure with milk tins the rice and beans they would cook. None of the children must have more than one piece of dodo. The girls quickly learnt how to have their hair done for one another. Ladbone, who was a Sunday school teacher, never stopped delivering homilies about the responsibilities that awaited his children. Wemimo, the last child, who is now a lawyer, reports: “As children we were surrounded by animals: goats, ducks, turkeys, pigeons, 17 dogs, 15 cats, fishes, snails, chickens, rams, sheep, and so on. These animals made us very responsible people. We understood how to feed them, bath them, clean out their faeces, take the animals who could go on walks around the estate.”

Still, today, the children don’t feel unloved by him. Lolade, who now holds a PhD in Artificial Intelligence, tells all those reporters and editors in The Guardian and elsewhere who still begrudge Ladbone for pushing them so hard, for asking for stories even when they were bereaved: We shared your pains. Please, forgive him. He meant no harm. He obviously believed, and still does, that if you must deliver on excellence, you just have to be brutal sometimes. To him tough love always pays in the end. There are impeccable accounts of the failures of The Comet and The Compass newspapers under Ladbone. He is accused of unrelieved partiality to his deputy and close friend, Mr Femi Kusa, who introduced him to The Grail Message and movement, at a time that he was a senior pastor at the Redeemed Christian Church of God. Clearly, this book is not hagiography at all — writers just tell it as it is. The recollections and memories are coherent versions of the same truth.

Milan Kundera, the French-Czechoslovakian writer, in his novel, The Book of Laughter and Forgetting, says that “The first step in liquidating a people is to erase its memory. Destroy its books, its history. Then have somebody write new books, manufacture a new culture, invent a new history. Before long that nation will begin to forget what it is and what it was…The struggle of man against power is the struggle of memory against forgetting.” The huge project that the Living Archives Initiatives of the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development (CJID) is embarking on, I would argue, is informed by this idea of the struggle of memory against forgetting. It is fit and proper that the organisation has started with Ladbone, who told Lasisi Olagunju, in an interview embedded in his tribute, that he is not given to blowing his own trumpet.

Kunle Ajibade is executive editor/director of TheNEWS/PM NEWS.

This is the text of the review done at the presentation of Ladbone: A Life in Print at the Civic Centre, Victoria Island, on 22 October.

World.title: Namadi attends Hadejia development forum, inaugurates board of trustees
World.content:
The Governor of Jigawa State, Umar Namadi has highlighted education, agriculture, environmental sustainability, and youth development as critical areas requiring sustained attention and collective action in the state. The governor said this in his remarks during the inauguration of the 15-member Board of Trustees (BoT) of Hadejia Strategic Development Forum (HSDF).

While inaugurating the Board, Namadi urged the Forum to collaborate with the state government, especially the Tsangaya Board, in supporting efforts to reduce the number of out-of-school children and improve access to educational opportunities.

He expressed confidence that effective cooperation among the government, traditional institutions, community-based organisations, and other stakeholders would contribute significantly to sustainable development and improved living standards across the Emirate.

Namadi said the event marked a significant milestone in the forum’s commitment to promoting unity, sustainable development, and socio-economic transformation across Hadejia Emirate. He congratulated the newly inaugurated Board of Trustees and reaffirmed the state government’s readiness to collaborate with HSDF in advancing the development aspirations of Hadejia Emirate.

In his remarks, His Royal Highness, Dr Adamu Abubakar Maje Haruna, the Emir of Hadejia commended HSDF for its initiative and commitment by developing a long-term strategic roadmap to advance Hadejia Emirate.

The Emir said that unity, integrity, local investment, and collective responsibility are essential foundations for sustainable development. He described HSDF as a non-partisan organisation dedicated to the welfare and advancement of the people and urged the newly inaugurated trustees to discharge their responsibilities with honesty, dedication, accountability, and the fear of Almighty Allah.

He further called on wealthy individuals, entrepreneurs, and business leaders from the Emirate to invest in their home communities, create employment opportunities, empower young people, and contribute meaningfully to economic growth.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Reaffirming the importance of preserving the unity of Hadejia Emirate, the Emir encouraged all stakeholders to work together towards a shared vision of prosperity, progress, and sustainable development.

Speaking on behalf of the Board of Trustees, Professor Zubaida Nagee expressed appreciation for the confidence reposed in the members and pledged their collective commitment to advancing the Forum’s objectives through unity, strategic leadership, accountability, and purposeful action.

She emphasised the importance of a shared vision for Hadejia Emirate and assured stakeholders of the Board’s determination to contribute meaningfully to the successful implementation of the proposed 25-year development roadmap.

Nagee stressed that the inauguration marks an important step towards strengthening the Forum’s institutional leadership and establishing a solid foundation for strategic planning, effective coordination, and sustainable community development.

The HSDF Lead Group, Abbas Muhammad, described the inauguration as the fulfilment of a longstanding aspiration to promote the development and advancement of Hadejia Emirate through a coordinated and sustainable approach.

He expressed profound gratitude to Governor Namadi for his financial, moral, and institutional support, as well as to the Emir of Hadejia for his encouragement and commitment to the initiative.

He also extended special appreciation to Senator Ahmad Abdulhamid Mallam Madori for his financial contributions and donation of a brand-new vehicle to support the Forum’s operations.

Abbas Muhammad further acknowledged the valuable contributions of stakeholders, supporters, and the technical team, whose dedication and expertise have played an important role in advancing the initiative.

He reaffirmed the Forum’s commitment to working with relevant institutions and development partners to promote initiatives that respond to the needs and aspirations of the people of Hadejia Emirate.

The following 15 distinguished individuals were inaugurated into the Board of Trustees of the Hadejia Strategic Development Forum, representing various Local Government Areas, professional fields, and the Hadejia Emirate traditional institutions:

1. Isma’ila Usman — Chairman, Hadejia LGA.

2. Turaki Ibrahim — Vice Chairman I, Kafin Hausa LGA.

3. Professor Zubaida Nagee — Vice Chairman II, Mallam Madori LGA.

4. Usman Abdulaziz (Galadiman Hadejia) — Representative of the Hadejia Emirate Council and Traditional Institution Member.

5. Mrs Hauwa Umar Aliyu — Member, Birniwa LGA.

6. Muhammad Babandede — Member, Hadejia LGA.

7. Abdullahi Hudu — Member, Kafin Hausa LGA.

8. Abubakar J. Maina — Member, Guri LGA.

9. Garba Muhammad Auyo — Member, Auyo LGA.

10. Mrs Hadiza Muhammad Isa — Member, Kirikasamma LGA.

11. Ahmed Muhammed — Member, Kaugama LGA.

12. Dr Habibu Sale — Development Expert and Member.

13. Ahmed Abdullahi — Financial Expert and Member.

14. Ahmed Gambo Saleh, Esq. — Legal Expert and Member.

15. Malam Abbas Muhammad — Member/Secretary, Hadejia LGA.

The inauguration represents a significant step towards advancing HSDF’s proposed 25-year development roadmap, with key priorities encompassing education, agriculture, youth empowerment, employment generation, environmental sustainability, investment, and community welfare.

Through strategic collaboration with the Jigawa State Government, traditional institutions, political leaders, private investors, development partners, and community stakeholders, the Forum seeks to establish a sustainable development framework that addresses the needs of the people and creates lasting opportunities for present and future generations.

Realising this vision will require unity of purpose, effective planning, accountable leadership, strategic partnerships, resource mobilisation, and the sustained commitment of all stakeholders.

The inauguration of the Board of Trustees therefore represents more than an organisational milestone. It signifies a renewed commitment to collective responsibility and a shared aspiration for a united, prosperous, and sustainable Hadejia Emirate.

World.title: Inside Zamfara communities, where residents bear brunt of reprisal attacks by bandits
World.content:
On 5 October, a terror kingpin, Dankarami Gwaska, and his fighters attacked a military base and mining sites in the gold-rich Bindin ward of Dansadau Emirate in the Maru Local Government Area of Zamfara State.

His fighters killed 14 soldiers and mobile police officers at the military base and looted the armoury.

The following day, the terrorist sent emissaries to Bindin, demanding financial compensation from the community for the weapons he lost after his fighters were killed in the area several days before his gang attacked the military base.

Residents confirmed that Mr Gwaska’s men were killed in Bindin, but not by the military. They were reportedly killed by rival terror groups operating in the axis.

Mr Gwaska’s forces later killed scores of miners in Bindin ward, all to avenge the killing of his fighters. He then imposed a ₦50 million “protection levy” on Bindin and neighbouring farming communities.

Residents said the terrorist extorted about N360 million in protection levies from the communities within two weeks of sacking the military base.

According to residents and security sources, the destruction of the town’s sole line of defence—the military base—has forced nearly the entire population to flee.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

These sources shared videos and photos with our reporter showing locals and miners departing in heavily overloaded vehicles.

Who is Gwaska?

Mr Gwaska is a prominent bandit in Zurmi Local Government Area. He attacked the palace of the late Emir of Zurmi and is notorious for village raids, cattle rustling, and kidnapping for ransom in the Zurmi axis.

According to local sources, Mr Gwaska relocated to the Dansadau Emirate recently, under pressure from the military and rival terror leader Bello Turji. He had also reportedly escaped assassination in the neighbouring Niger Republic.

In Dansadau, he reportedly struck protection deals with the local mining operators, after ousting smaller gangs from key sites, including the major gold deposit in Bindin.

The deals compelled miners to share their revenues with the terrorist.

To maintain operational stability, Mr Gwaska entered into separate peace deals with the local communities, including Dan Kurmi, Bindin, Gobirawa Chali, and areas extending to Magami.

Residents and security sources told PREMIUM TIMES that the temporary peace attracted over 10,000 people to Dansadau to work as labourers at the illegal gold mines, and increased local business activities.

Under the protection arrangement over the past year, labourers keep a third of the gold they extract, while the operating entity takes the remaining two-thirds.

However, tension escalated after Mr Gwaska’s group reportedly raised its taxes on the labourers.

This led to clashes in which several of his fighters were killed. While rival bandit factions were suspected in the killings, Mr Gwaska blamed the labourers and the military, prompting the 15 October retaliatory attacks on the military base and mining grounds in Bindin.

The trouble area

Bindin sits at the edge of the ungoverned Kwiambana forest linking Katsina, Kaduna, Kebbi and Niger states. It is one of the five wards of Dansadau Emirate. The other wards are Kwiambana, Dan-Gulbi, Dan-Kurmi and Dansadau town.

The Dansadau Emirate alone covers 492 of the 1180 square kilometres of Zamfara State territory, that is, over one third of the state’s landmass.

The area’s land is suitable for farming and livestock rearing, and is believed to have vast gold deposits.

Mr Gwaska and the other bandits operate from the Kwiambana Game Reserve, which provides natural cover from security personnel and for moving rustled cattle and abducted people.

The government created the Kwiambana Game Reserve in Zamfara to preserve wildlife. The forest stretches from the ‘Dajin Rugu’ to the Kontagora Forest.

The reserve has been slated as a possible UNESCO heritage site. For now, it is a notorious hideout for criminals.

More deadly attacks

However, it is not only disagreement in peace deals that is behind violence in these troubled areas.

Residents narrated to PREMIUM TIMES how another terror kingpin, known as Rambo, moved to avenge his lieutenants killed by local vigilantes in the Yantasha community. The vigilantes also allegedly confiscated their firearms.

In a letter seen by this newspaper, Rambo detailed his grievances and ordered the community to return the confiscated rifles. But the vigilantes ignored the order, daring him to retrieve the weapons by force.

Recognising the community’s defensive capabilities, Rambo targeted other vulnerable areas, raiding communities such as Yar Gada, Mai Kogo, Magama, and Mai Rake, inflicting heavy casualties and causing mass displacement.

Rambo vowed to block the Magami–Dansadau highway until he received ₦50 million in damages.

To enforce this blockade, he planted improvised explosive devices (IEDs), forcing the road to be abandoned for three days until the military cleared the hazard on 9 October.

The success of the demining operation was confirmed in a statement by Aliyu Danja, an army spokesperson for Operation Fasan Yamma—the counter-banditry force in the state.

“Troops of Sector 2 have recovered and neutralised explosive devices planted by terrorists to cause major havoc to commuters along the Magami–Hannutara–Dansadau road in Maru Local Government Area.

“Acting on credible intelligence, the troops secured the affected area, conducted a thorough search, and identified two spots planted with explosive devices. An Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) team was subsequently deployed to detonate one device controlledly and safely recover and render another harmless,” Mr Danja stated.

However, a day after the military cleared the road, Rambo’s men ambushed a civilian convoy travelling from Dansadau to Gusau under military escort.

They killed several travellers and set their vehicles ablaze.

In an audio message obtained by PREMIUM TIMES, one of the terrorist leaders warned that the highway ambush would continue until the vigilantes returned the seized weapons.

“We burnt the vehicle because, while we were living peacefully with the people in the Magama and Yar Tashin Sahabi areas, vigilantes suddenly attacked, killed our people, and took our guns. This year, God willing, we are going to burn 250 vehicles unless you return those guns to us,” the bandit said in the audio message.

Efforts to obtain comments from the police spokesperson in Zamfara, Yazid Abubakar, were unsuccessful at the time of filing this report. Also, his colleague in the army, Mr Danja, could not be reached to comment on the developments.

Nuhu Babangida, a community leader in Dansadau and a member of the Leadway Peace Foundation for Human Rights Advocates (LPFHRA), and some community leaders spoke about the attacks with PREMIUM TIMES.

Mr Babangida said many bodies were yet to be recovered at the Bindin mining site, where he said several miners were trapped and shot by the bandits.

Mr Babangida attributed the persistent attacks in the area to the activities of local vigilantes, stating that residents ultimately bear the brunt of the fallout.

According to Mr Babangida, the escalation of violence along the route is closely tied to vigilante groups attacking bandits operating in the axis.

“The vigilantes ambush and kill the bandits even during periods of relative peace; they are fully aware that the local people—whom they claim to be protecting— end up at the receiving end of their actions,” Mr Babangida stated.

Whenever such vigilante attacks occur, bandits retaliate with raids against innocent residents along the axis, he lamented.

Mr Babangida also highlighted a political dimension to the violence, noting that such attacks tend to surge during election cycles.

“Some politicians exploit these situations to cause the cancellation of elections in areas where they are unpopular.

“In their opponents’ strongholds, they deliberately stir up insecurity so that political activities cannot take place, ultimately tipping the playing field in their favour,” Mr Babangida said.

World.title: Nigeria’s billionaire businessmen in politics and the scary future, By Adeola Akinremi
World.content:
….here is the question that Nigerians should be asking: how much do we really know about the money shaping our politics? Wealthy people will always have more resources than ordinary citizens. That is a fact of life. But when their money enters the political arena, the public deserves to know whose interests are being advanced. Nigerians should be able to scrutinise these relationships, question the motives behind political spending and organise to protect their own interests.

Nigeria’s billionaires control assets worth trillions. But now they want to control politics.

This week, Africa’s richest man and Chairman of Dangote Group, Aliko Dangote; Founder and Chairman of BUA Group, Abdul Samad Rabiu; and Femi Otedola, the billionaire son of Michael Otedola, who spent nearly two years as governor of Lagos State before General Sani Abacha forcefully truncated Nigeria’s Third Republic, met privately at a dinner with Obafemi Hamzat, Lagos State’s deputy governor and the All Progressives Congress (APC) governorship candidate tipped to win the 2027 election.

What is surprising is how openly these billionaires have allowed their private meetings to be displayed. Legacy newspapers and social media are often awash with images and video clips from their gatherings. That kind of publicity does not happen by accident. No, they are not the first billionaire businessmen to cultivate relationships with political leaders openly, and Nigeria is hardly the first country where wealth seeks political influence. Of course, rich people, like all other citizens, can exercise their right to express their views, meet elected officials and sway the direction of our politics and elections. But the openness of these encounters, and the scale of the fortunes involved, should make us pay attention. This brazenness raises serious questions about the future of politics, public policy, prosperity and poverty in Nigeria.

It is a quiet but consequential shift. Nigeria has lived with extreme inequality for decades. The difference now is how openly some of the country’s richest businessmen are stepping into the political arena. The World Inequality Report estimates that the richest 10 per cent of Nigerians owned 58 per cent of household wealth in 2021, while the bottom half owned less than 6 per cent. That is the scale of the imbalance we are dealing with. And when people who command such enormous economic resources begin to gather openly around political power, Nigerians have every reason to ask what it means for the future of our democracy.

With billionaires becoming more visible and more brazen in their political engagement, the middle class and working class across the country should begin to think about how they, too, can redefine politics. This is about opportunity and inequality. When billionaires control our politics, can ordinary Nigerians still expect to live a decent life?

The answer is neither here nor there. But think about social opportunities, education and healthcare. You don’t need a fortune-teller to know that very rich people may be more inclined to support cuts in social benefits and programmes that benefit the less fortunate members of society, especially during an economic crisis. They will advance their own interests through tax cuts, which can reduce the resources available for investment in public schools and local healthcare centres.

Many working class and ordinary Nigerians have become cynical about politics. They believe there is little difference between one politician and another. They have become doubting Thomases, questioning whether politics can produce meaningful change. But billionaires do not think that way. They understand that political decisions have consequences for their businesses, their investments and their fortunes. That is why they are choosing to engage, and they are bringing their money with them.

The outsized influence of billionaires in politics can determine what you pay for medicine, how much you pay for petrol and where you can go for recreation. They already own the assets. Now, through their financial relationships with political leaders and parties, they can influence the public policies that govern those assets. This class of billionaires is consolidating political influence, merging economic power with political power, without having to contest a single elective office. And they have their reasons for doing so.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

It is possible to admire individual billionaires for their resilience in building businesses. But to ignore the interests of capital in any economy is a grave mistake.

I have encountered a few billionaire businessmen, and I admire their creativity, energy and transformative impact. But I also know that they do not necessarily think about the working class. They are smart thinkers. They think about profit. They are all about margins. So when they enter politics, there are consequences. They are likely to favour policies that do not always align with the prosperity of the poor. For example, we have seen billionaires hobnobbing with the ruling government, suggesting that their political engagement is not evenly distributed across the political spectrum.

Our country faces serious risks when so much money is concentrated in the hands of so few people.

The role that the super-rich are playing in politics should not escape our attention. Their spending on political campaigns raises questions about the kind of democracy we are building and whose interests it will ultimately serve.

Many working class and ordinary Nigerians have become cynical about politics. They believe there is little difference between one politician and another. They have become doubting Thomases, questioning whether politics can produce meaningful change. But billionaires do not think that way. They understand that political decisions have consequences for their businesses, their investments and their fortunes. That is why they are choosing to engage, and they are bringing their money with them.

Voters deserve to know whose money is behind the prime-time messages on their television screens, who is financing political campaigns and whose interests may be served by the policies that follow. A democracy cannot function properly when citizens are expected to judge political messages without adequate information about the interests behind them, just as unequal wealth combined with secrecy in political donations can breed a toxic democracy.

Politicians and political parties should be worried, too. It may only be a matter of time before we see the corrosive effects on democracy when billionaires bring their wealth to bear on political competition. The super-rich could begin sponsoring more candidates into the House of Representatives and the Senate, where they could become a thorn in the flesh of any president whose decisions threaten their interests. They could also seek to influence the outcome of future elections, not necessarily by standing for office themselves, but by determining who gets there and what those elected are expected to do.

But here is the question that Nigerians should be asking: how much do we really know about the money shaping our politics? Wealthy people will always have more resources than ordinary citizens. That is a fact of life. But when their money enters the political arena, the public deserves to know whose interests are being advanced. Nigerians should be able to scrutinise these relationships, question the motives behind political spending and organise to protect their own interests. Without that awareness, the imbalance between wealth and political power will only deepen.

Of course, Nigeria does have laws regulating campaign finance. But the question is whether those laws give voters enough information about the money shaping their politics. The Electoral Act 2026 requires political parties to keep financial records, report contributions, and publish audited election-expense returns. Yet Section 94 raises the threshold for recording a contributor’s name and address from one million naira under the previous 2022 law to one hundred million naira. That is a significant change.

Voters deserve to know whose money is behind the prime-time messages on their television screens, who is financing political campaigns and whose interests may be served by the policies that follow. A democracy cannot function properly when citizens are expected to judge political messages without adequate information about the interests behind them, just as unequal wealth combined with secrecy in political donations can breed a toxic democracy.

Adeola Akinremi is a public policy advisor, strategic communications expert, and the founder and CEO of Hintells, an AI-powered intelligence platform serving businesses and diplomatic missions in Washington, D.C. He has extensive multilateral experience advising on governance, economic and policy reforms across global markets and can be reached at: [email protected]

World.title: State Police: 24 states approve constitutional amendment – Presidential panel
World.content:
The Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill says 24 State Houses of Assembly have approved the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026, providing for a dual policing system.

The approval meets the constitutional threshold of two-thirds of the 36 states required for the amendment to proceed.

The working group commended the state Houses of Assembly for their action and acknowledged the National Assembly for passing the amendment in both chambers.

This is contained in a statement issued by Femi Gbajabiamila, chief of staff to the President and chairman of the group, on Friday in Abuja.

“In line with Section 9 of the Constitution, the amendment can now be returned to the National Assembly for transmission to Mr President for assent.”

Mr Gbajabiamila said the approval provided constitutional backing for the policing framework outlined in the working group’s draft National Policing Bill, 2026.

READ ALSO: Akwa Ibom Assembly adopts recommendations to establish state police

He added that the draft Bills were undergoing legislative drafting review and validation at the Federal Ministry of Justice.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The Bills are expected to be returned on or before 30 October, after which the working group will give them final consideration before presenting them to President Bola Tinubu.

The working group urged stakeholders to support a smooth transition to a dual policing system aimed at improving public safety.

(NAN)

World.title: Ebola: Nigeria case highly similar to Kenya infection – Minister
World.content:
The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Muhammad Pate, has confirmed that the Ebola virus detected in Nigeria is highly similar to the virus identified in Kenya’s first imported case.

Mr Pate disclosed this on Friday during a briefing at the Federal Ministry of Health in Abuja, saying genomic sequencing showed that the viruses differed by only one mutation.

He said the analysis was conducted by sequencing teams at the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) and the Institute of Genomics and Global Health at Redeemer’s University, Ede, Osun State, with the team led by virologist Christian Happi.

However, he cautioned that the finding does not establish how the Nigerian first case acquired the infection.

“Based on the genomic analysis, there is no evidence of travel of that index case in Kenya that links it to Nigeria, but the viruses are appearing to be related,” he said.

He added that the finding could change the understanding of the route of transmission as further investigations and testing continue.

Kenya has so far recorded nine confirmed Ebola cases caused by Bundibugyo virus, including one death, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC). Eight of the cases were linked to the country’s first imported case from the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), including four healthcare workers.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Africa CDC probes link

The genomic finding came on the same day the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) said it is investigating a possible connection between Nigeria’s case and Kenya’s first imported case.

The agency said both patients had travelled through Entebbe International Airport in Uganda on 3 October, prompting investigations into whether they had shared equipment or had other contact. Africa CDC, however, stressed that no connection had been established between the infections.

The Kenyan patient travelled from the DRC through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi. He later died, becoming the first recorded Ebola death in Kenya’s current outbreak.

The Nigerian patient also passed through Uganda, but Ugandan authorities had earlier rejected suggestions that this established the country as the source of her infection.

Uganda denies active case

On 21 October, Uganda’s Ministry of Health said it had no confirmed active Ebola case and that the Nigerian patient’s transit through the country did not establish that she contracted the virus there.

The ministry said preliminary information indicated that the Nigerian woman had travelled to eastern DRC for business and passed through Uganda in early October without showing symptoms. It said the location of her exposure remained under investigation.

The new genomic finding now provides evidence of similarity between the Nigerian and Kenyan infections, although Nigerian authorities have not established that the patient was infected in Kenya.

One confirmed case

Mr Pate said Nigeria still has only one confirmed Ebola case and that authorities were continuing contact tracing, quarantine and additional testing of contacts.

Some tests have returned negative results, while others are pending, he said.

He urged Nigerians to remain vigilant but calm, saying there is no need for panic.

“We will continue to work diligently to ensure that we contain this virus as much as possible, and that we avoid a situation that spills over to the communities,” he said.

The minister said the government is also strengthening infection prevention and control measures in health facilities and would train health workers on how to identify and manage suspected cases.

He urged hospitals to notify public health authorities of suspected cases and encouraged Nigerians to observe basic preventive measures, including regular handwashing and hygiene.

Mr Pate also said Ebola is not currently known to be transmitted through the air but through close contact with infected body fluids.

He urged Nigerians to rely on information from public health authorities, including the NCDC, Federal Ministry of Health, World Health Organisation and Africa CDC, rather than unverified information on social media.

World.title: Okpebholo vows to sign death warrant against convicted kidnappers after 30 days
World.content:
Governor Monday Okpebholo of Edo State says he will sign the death warrants of four kidnappers sentenced to death by the state’s Special Criminal Court, if they fail to appeal within 30 days.

Mr Okpebholo stated this while recounting his administration’s efforts to tackle kidnapping, cultism and other criminal activities at the God’s People Worldwide Prayer Ministry, Ekpoma, on Friday.

The News Agency of Nigeria recalls that the defendants were sentenced to death by an Edo State Special Criminal Court on 29 September over the abduction of a woman at the vegetable market along Airport Road, Benin.

The governor said insecurity was a major concern when he assumed office but decided to prioritise tackling it, after raising the issue with President Bola Tinubu, who urged him to go ahead.

“When the kidnappers attacked the vegetable market area, I told the commissioner of police that I wanted them arrested without delay,” he said.

The governor said the suspects had been sentenced to death and expressed hope that they would not appeal the judgement.

“If within 30 days they don’t appeal, I will execute (it),” he added.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The governor also said he had consulted prominent traditional rulers across the state before commencing his administration’s campaign against kidnapping and cultism.

Mr Okpebholo said he warned the traditional rulers against intervening on behalf of anyone involved in criminal activities.

“I told them not to come begging me because I will not listen,” he said.

The governor recounted incidents he associated with spiritual forces following his administration’s demolition of a building linked to a cult group.

“A black bird died in my office when I demolished their building. A vulture also died in my bed while I was contesting for governorship,” he added.

Earlier, the cleric, Ehijele Umuahia, founder of God’s People Worldwide Prayer Ministry, urged his church members to vote Mr Okpebholo and his preferred candidates in the 2027 general elections.

Mr Umuahia, citing Proverbs 29:2, urged the congregation to complement their prayers for the governor with active participation in the electoral process.

He said Christians should not only pray for Governor Okpebholo but also come out to vote for him and his preferred candidates.

The cleric described Mr Okpebholo as a humble man, whose commitment to the things of God predated his emergence as governor.

“I have known him for over 15 years, dating back to the days of Chief Tony Anenih of blessed memory.

“Whenever Anenih came to visit me, he was one of those who accompanied him. That was how we came to know each other,” he said.

Mr Umuahia said Mr Okpebholo had maintained his devotion to God despite his demanding schedule before becoming governor.

World.title: Uyo remains home ground for Super Eagles for now
World.content:
The Nigeria Football Federation is not ready to move the Super Eagles’ home games from Uyo to Lagos, with a senior official saying Lagos is under consideration but Uyo stays the venue for now.

The comments followed the Super Eagles’ 3-0 loss to Guinea-Bissau in an AFCON 2027 qualifier. Nigeria have three points from two Group L games, while Guinea-Bissau lead the group on six, the outlet said.

It was earlier reported that the Super Eagles could host November qualifiers in Lagos. But the renovated Teslim Balogun Stadium is not yet ready to host an international. NFF inspectors will visit once the Lagos State Government finishes the renovation.

The federation is also considering friendlies at Teslim Balogun to test the facilities and gauge the reaction of fans, and plans to consult players before deciding, the report said.

The official argued that changing a settled home ground could hurt performance. The Super Eagles have played most of their home games in Uyo for nearly a decade.

The NFF’s stated reasoning is cautious, and the logic is easy to follow: a stadium that has not been inspected cannot host a qualifier. The harder question is the calendar. With less than a month to the November double-header against Tanzania, there is little room for inspections and approvals if Lagos were chosen.

If the stadium is not signed off in time, Uyo is the only practical option for the next home game, whatever the appetite for change. If it is, the NFF has said it would test the venue with a friendly first, which suggests a move for a competitive match would come later rather than sooner.

World.title: 2026 Ballon D’Or: Too close to call
World.content:
By Douglas Baye-Osagie

*[email protected]

Football’s Grammy night is here again. It’s the red-carpet night where the best players, coaches, legends, celebrities gathers in one theatre, and one man is called up to take the biggest individual prize in the sport. The 70th Ballon d’Or ceremony will take place on Monday, October 26, 2026. For the first time in its history, the brainchild of French journalists Gabriel Hanot and Jacques Ferran at France Football magazine, the event moves from Paris to the London Palladium in England. This is football’s Grammy night.

The Ballon d’Or is arguably the biggest individual prize in sports, given to the best footballer in a calendar year. In its early decades, the award was strictly European – only players from European clubs and European nations could win it. That changed in 1995 when eligibility expanded to include any player at a European club regardless of nationality. By 2007, the award went fully global, allowing players from any club or country to compete.

How is that hard choice made? For 2026, France Football kept it journalists only – no fan vote, no players, no coaches. The 30-man shortlist is drawn up by France Football, L’Equipe, one previous juror and UEFA ambassadors Luis Figo, Fabio Capello for the men and Nadine Kessler for the women. The final say goes to 100 specialist journalists, one from each of the top 100 FIFA-ranked nations for the men’s award, and 50 for the women’s award as of September 8, 2026. Each juror names his Top 10 in order.

This year the competition is different. Never in recent memory has the queue been this long, this loud. Not two. Not three. Five, six, seven men with a legitimate shout, a season to point to, a trophy to hold up. No one has blown the field away. No one can say, “It is mine.” And yet, with days to go, one must go home wearing the most prestigious hat in football.

Start with the favourite, Harry Kane. No footballer in the world scored more in 2025/26 than Kane – 61 goals for Bayern Munich, 36 in the Bundesliga to win his third straight Torjägerkanone and a second European Golden Shoe. He delivered a domestic treble – Bundesliga, DFB-Pokal and the Franz Beckenbauer Supercup. If I was voting, I will vote for Harry Kane.

His moment? April was brutal and beautiful. 100 Bundesliga goals in record time, then that semi-final vs PSG where he scored twice but Bayern went out 6-5 on aggregate. At the World Cup he led England to bronze with 6 goals, including a 6-4 thriller against France in the third-place playoff. Could he be the first English winner since Michael Owen in 2001?

Then Kylian Mbappe – football’s ultimate World Cup man. 38 goals in 33 games for Real Madrid before the tournament, winning the Pichichi. Then in America, 10 goals to become the World Cup’s all-time top scorer at just 27. He is now the first player in history to win the Golden Boot in the Champions League, La Liga and the World Cup in the same calendar year – a treble of scoring crowns that may never be broken.

His moment was not lifting the trophy – France finished fourth – but the way he left it all on the pitch. A breathtaking opener against Senegal to get his World Cup account going, a hat-trick vs Norway in the group stage, and four assists on top of the 10 goals. 22 goals in 22 games across three World Cups is the story of greatness. He did not win the World Cup, but he won history.

Lamine Yamal is so many people’s favourite. He and Olise at the highest level are the most entertaining footballers in the game at the moment and he already has an archive of breathtaking goals. At 19, he could become the youngest Ballon d’Or winner ever, a record held by the great Ronaldo Nazario who won it at 21 years and 96 days in 1997. Yamal’s story writes itself: La Liga champion, La Liga Player of the Year, and then World Champion with Spain.

His tournament was quiet by his standards, but he contributed to Spain’s victory which was largely a team performance. He completed 27 dribbles from 51 attempts – the highest total at the World Cup. He was Man of the Match twice, against Austria and Belgium in the semi-final – a game in which Spain were underdogs – and he won the crucial penalty that gave Spain the opening goal. For Barcelona this past season: 24 goals and 17 assists, averaging a goal contribution every 85 minutes. He is no longer the future. He is the present.

If Yamal is the present, Michael Olise is pure magic. Bundesliga Player of the Season with numbers that read like a video game – 15 goals, 19 assists in the league, 22 goals and 31 assists in 52 games across all competitions.

Two moments define him. First, the Freiburg game: Bayern down 0-2, Olise scores two and assists three in a 6-2 comeback. Then the quarter-final vs Real Madrid – 90+3, 4-3 on the night, that left-foot curler past Lunin to send Bayern through. At the World Cup he broke Pelé’s record with 7 assists in one tournament for France. As Thomas Müller said, “He has that dance-like, artistic ease you can’t learn.”

And then Lionel Messi. At 39, in what might be his last World Cup, he took Argentina to the final and lost 1-0 to Spain in extra time. Heartbreak in New Jersey. He was Player of the Tournament until the final against Spain. He single-handedly dragged Argentina to the World Cup final in a manner that clearly stood him apart from the pack.

But look at what he still did: 25 goals and 15 assists for Inter Miami this season, first player ever to record 15+ assists in three straight MLS seasons, first to have 30+ goal contributions in three different seasons. His moment? October 17th vs Atlanta – two goals, one assist, his 934th career goal. He is chasing a third straight MLS MVP. He is 39 and still top-two in the Golden Boot race.

The defending champion Ousmane Dembele wants back-to-back. PSG retained both Ligue 1 and the Champions League, and Dembele was again their engine – 20 goals in the league campaign, 7 in the Champions League.

His best moment came in the World Cup quarter-final run – 6 goals including that hat-trick against Norway. France faded late, but Dembele proved last year’s Ballon d’Or was no fluke. Can he retain it?

Rodri is the anomaly. He left Manchester City for Barcelona this summer after winning the World Cup Golden Ball. Spain’s captain, the metronome who made Spain champions again. His moment wasn’t a goal, it was control. In the final against Argentina, with Messi throwing everything at Spain in extra time, Rodri won the ball back 11 times and completed 96% of his passes. The anchor. The man who makes everyone else look good.

So who does the cap fit? If you want pure numbers, it’s Kane. If you want trophies, it’s Yamal. If you want history, it’s Mbappe. If you want beauty, it’s Olise. If you want longevity, it’s Messi. If it was just about who was the best player at the World Cup, Rodri has a real shout – World Cup winner and Golden Ball winner. On October 26th at the London Palladium, football will finally have to choose. For once, there is no wrong answer – only a hard one.

World.title: Alex Iwobi: From Arsenal prodigy to Premier League mainstay
World.content:
Iwobi

Fulham FC will today travel to the Midlands to take on Coventry City at the Coventry Arena, all eyes will be on Nigeria international, Alex Iwobi, whose lone strike against Hull City gave The Cottagers maximum points. More remarkable was the fact that it was Fulham’s first victory of the season. The Nigerian has become one of the most consistent players in Álvaro Arbeloa’s ensemble.

For much of his early career, Alex Iwobi was often viewed as a talented but inconsistent player. Critics questioned his end product, while supporters saw flashes of brilliance that hinted at something greater.

The amazing thing is that football careers are rarely linear.

Now at Fulham F.C., the Nigerian midfielder appears to be experiencing something of a renaissance. His recent performances suggest a player who has matured tactically, refined his decision-making, and become one of the most dependable midfield engines in the Premier League.

From Arsenal Prodigy to Premier League Mainstay

Born in Lagos, Nigeria, Iwobi moved to England at a young age and joined the academy of Arsenal F.C. at just six years old. His development at the club’s Hale End academy was rapid, and by the 2015-16 season he had broken into the senior team under legendary manager Arsène Wenger.

Iwobi quickly gained attention for his close control, agility, and ability to glide past defenders. During his Arsenal years, he was primarily deployed as a winger or attacking midfielder, often tasked with linking midfield to attack. Yet while his technical ability was undeniable, consistency and goal output became recurring talking points.

In 2019, Iwobi made a high-profile move to Everton F.C. in a deal reported to be worth around £28 million plus add-ons. The transfer marked a new phase in his career, one that would eventually reshape how he was perceived as a player.

When Fulham F.C. signed Iwobi in September 2023 on a five-year contract, manager Marco Silva clearly had a defined role in mind.

At Fulham, Iwobi operates as a dynamic attacking midfielder who often drifts into wide areas to create overloads. His ability to connect midfield with the forward line has made him central to Fulham’s attacking transitions.

Since joining the club, he has recorded; over 92 Premier League appearances, 18 goals and 11 assists

Those numbers highlight a player contributing far more decisively in the final third than earlier in his career. Iwobi’s resurgence is not simply about improved numbers, but also translates to tactical evolution.

Positional Versatility

One of Iwobi’s greatest strengths is his ability to play multiple roles; central midfielder, attacking midfielder, wide playmaker and advanced number eight. The versatility allows Fulham to adapt shape during matches without making substitutions.

Ball Progression

Iwobi excels at carrying the ball through midfield, breaking defensive lines with dribbles or quick combinations, and his ability to move the ball into attacking areas has become a vital part of Fulham’s transition play.

Work Rate

Across his Premier League career he has recorded about 330 tackles, 144 interceptions and 147 clearances These contributions underline his transformation into a complete midfielder rather than a purely attacking player. Another measure of Alex Iwobi’s evolution is his longevity in one of football’s most competitive leagues. Across spells at Arsenal, Everton, and Fulham, he has accumulated about 315 Premier League appearances, 35 goals and 38 assists

In fact, he has also reached a historic milestone as the Nigerian player with the most Premier League appearances, surpassing the previous record held by Shola Ameobi.

That achievement highlights both durability and consistency across nearly a decade in England’s top flight.

The Nigerian Influence

For fans of the Super Eagles, Iwobi remains an essential figure in the midfield setup. Often operating behind attacking stars like Victor Osimhen and Ademola Lookman, his creativity helps link midfield control with attacking penetration.

Footballing pedigree also runs in the family as Iwobi is the nephew of Nigerian legend, the famous Jay-Jay Okocha, whose flair and creativity inspired a generation of African footballers.

While their styles differ, the influence is indeed unmistakable.

A Career Renaissance

Iwobi’s career arc is a reminder that football development does not always follow a straight path.

Once labelled inconsistent, he has evolved into a dependable Premier League midfielder capable of influencing games through intelligence, movement, and versatility.

At Fulham, he has found a tactical environment that maximises his strengths. With his confidence growing and his productivity improving, the Nigerian international may still have his best football ahead of him.

For a player who once lived in the shadow of expectation, Alex Iwobi is now writing a compelling second chapter to his career, and this time, the numbers and performances are finally telling the same story.

World.title: Edo govt, NLC strike peace deal as Labour moves to restore electricity
World.content:
By Victor Ahiuma-Young

The Nigeria Labour Congress, NLC, and the Edo State Government have resolved their prolonged dispute, with the state government agreeing to recognise the NLC caretaker committee.

As part of the truce, the National Union of Electricity Employees, NUEE, is expected to take steps towards restoring electricity to the state that has been in total darkness since Monday.

The NLC Acting General Secretary, Benson Upah, said the resolution followed a meeting brokered by the Secretary to the Government of the Federation, SGF, at his residence on Friday, October 23, 2026.

According to Upah, the meeting was attended by the Edo State Governor, NLC President, Comrade Joe Ajaero, former Governor of the State and Senator representing Edo North, Adams Oshiomhole and the Minister of Labour and Employment.

Upah said, “The long-running dispute between the Nigeria Labour Congress and the Edo State Government on the non-recognition of the NLC caretaker committee in Edo State has been brought to an end.

“At a meeting brokered by the SGF at his residence today, Friday, October 23, 2026, between the Edo State Government, represented by the governor, and the NLC, represented by President Comrade Joe Ajaero, the governor accepted to recognise and work with the NLC caretaker committee in Edo State as the lawful representative of the NLC.

“The governor also agreed to ensure that check-off dues are remitted through the appropriate channels to the NLC.”

On the steps to consolidate the peace agreement, Upah said the Edo State governor had requested a meeting with the caretaker committee.

“As part of the peace initiative, the Edo State governor requested the Congress president to lead the caretaker committee to pay him a courtesy visit in Benin City,” he said.

Upah further disclosed that the NLC secretariat in Edo State, which had remained under lock and key amid the dispute, would reopen immediately.

“The Congress Secretariat in Edo State, which has been under lock and key by some people who presented themselves as acting for and on behalf of the governor, even as the governor denied knowledge or acquiescence of their actions, is to reopen immediately,” he said.

He added that the agreement would restore normal relations between the state government and organised labour.

“The regular or normal statutory relationship between the state government and the NLC is to resume with immediate effect,” Upah stated.

On electricity supply, the NLC Acting General Secretary said the labour movement had also undertaken to facilitate the restoration of power to the state.

“On the NLC’s part, NUEE is to restore power to Edo State as soon as practicable,” he said.

Upah recalled that the dispute had escalated over what the Congress described as anti-labour actions by the Edo State Government.

“It will be recalled that the prolonged anti-labour actions of the government, which constituted interference, intimidation and bullying, compelled the NLC to lodge a complaint against the Edo State Government at the International Labour Organisation (ILO), for which Nigeria was indicted,” he said.

The agreement is expected to pave the way for the reopening of the NLC secretariat, the resumption of normal industrial relations, the proper remittance of check-off dues and steps towards restoring electricity in Edo State.

Observers believe the full implementation of the resolutions will be crucial to sustaining the peace agreement and preventing a recurrence of the dispute between the state government and organised labour.

World.title: EBOLA: Genomics links Nigeria’s case to Kenya index case – Pate
World.content:
Ali Pate, coordinating minister of health and social welfare

…says no evidence yet of direct travel link

By Chioma Obinna

Genomic analysis has revealed a close relationship between the Ebola virus detected in Nigeria’s confirmed case and the virus identified in the index case in Kenya, raising fresh questions about the connection between the infections as health authorities intensify containment measures.

Read Also: Return of Ebola: Triumph of 2014, test of 2026

The Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Professor Muhammad Ali Pate, who disclosed this on Friday night, however, stressed that there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan index case had travelled to Nigeria.

He cautioned against drawing premature conclusions from the findings, explaining that genetic relatedness alone did not establish how the infection reached Nigeria.

“We still have only one confirmed case. The contacts have been traced, quarantined, and we are conducting additional tests, some of which are negative and others are pending,” Pate said.

He added that further genomic analysis could provide more information about the relationship between the viruses, although it might not necessarily resolve the route of transmission.

He said the findings were made possible through the laboratory infrastructure of the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention, NCDC, and research facilities led by Professor Christian Happi at Redeemer’s University, Ede, Osun State.

“That case appears to be closely related to the case identified in the index case in Kenya,” Pate said.

The minister said the government was sustaining contact tracing, laboratory testing, surveillance and case management to prevent further transmission.

He added that health authorities were also strengthening infection prevention and control measures in healthcare facilities.

As part of the response, he said, health workers would receive training to improve their ability to identify suspected cases, protect themselves and promptly notify public health authorities.

“All hospitals should be sensitised and health workers be aware and, when there are suspected cases, to notify public health authorities,” he said.

Pate urged Nigerians to remain vigilant but calm, emphasising that Ebola was not transmitted through the air but through direct contact with the body fluids of an infected person.

“Ebola is a disease that is so far not transmitted through airborne. It’s transmitted through close contact with body fluids,” he said.

He advised the public to rely on information from the NCDC, the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the World Health Organisation and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, rather than unverified reports circulating on social media.

The government is also developing and refining guidelines for mass gatherings in public spaces as part of efforts to protect public health while allowing activities to continue in line with evidence and established best practices.

Pate said the measures formed part of a broader response involving the NCDC, the ministry, laboratories and public health professionals.

Speaking, NCDC Director-General, Dr Jide Idris, said the agency would provide regular public briefings to explain the response, communicate preventive measures and encourage Nigerians to take practical steps to reduce the risk of infection.

Idris stressed the importance of environmental control, personal hygiene and handwashing, recalling the preventive practices adopted during Nigeria’s 2014 Ebola outbreak.

“It’s a contact issue. So, we need to address the issue of environmental control, personal hygiene, and hand washing,” he said.

He said containing the disease required cooperation between government agencies, healthcare workers and the public, adding that regular updates would help Nigerians understand the situation and their role in preventing transmission.

The government urged Nigerians to report suspected cases promptly, observe public health guidance and avoid spreading unverified information.

Pate said the country remained vigilant and would continue to provide updates as testing and contact-tracing activities progressed.

“There is no need to panic, but it is important to follow public health preventive measures that have been clearly identified,” he said.

World.title: How 25-yr-old Ogun farmer died in police cell; family, community demand answers
World.content:
IGP Olatunji Disu

By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta

What began as a routine arrest over an alleged petty theft of plantain has ended in tragedy, leaving a grieving family and the entire community of Ipara in Remo North Local Government Area of Ogun State demanding answers from the police.

Read Also: Full List: Names of 37 miners who died in NSCDC custody

Peter Igbang, a 25-year-old farmer and former mechanic apprentice, was pronounced dead in police custody. Police authorities claim he hanged himself inside the cell using his own clothing. His family and local leaders, however, have raised serious questions over the circumstances surrounding his death, the delayed notification of relatives, and conflicting accounts given by officers.

Peter was arrested on Saturday, October 17, following an allegation that he stole a bunch of plantain. Relatives and community members described him as an industrious young man who owned a six-acre farm planted with cassava and mature plantain crops. Despite the arrest, his family said they received no formal notification for four days. Under Nigerian law, suspects are expected to be charged to court within 24 to 48 hours. That did not happen.

“I have no other son” – Mrs. Gift Joseph, Mother

Peter’s mother, Mrs. Gift Joseph, said she only learnt of her son’s arrest the day after his death, which was Tuesday, October 20.

“Honestly, I do not know what to say. It was only Tuesday, October 20, that I heard my son had been arrested on Saturday. Nobody called me or informed me about what had happened,” she said.

“My son had gone to the farm and was arrested on the road while returning. What I want to ask is this: in all my life, I have never seen or heard of someone being arrested and taken to a police station without their clothes being removed when they moving the person inside a cell, only for him to be left fully clothed and then reportedly hang himself inside the station. I find it difficult to understand how such a thing could happen.

“I have no other son; he is my only son. I want the authorities to hear my questions and listen to what I have to say so that I can receive answers and have some peace of mind.”

Gift confirmed that Peter was about 25 years old. Though trained as a mechanic, the family could not complete his apprenticeship or set up a workshop for him, so he turned to farming on his own six-acre land.

Sister’s account of confusion and contradiction

Peter’s elder sister, Juliet, who lives in Lagos with their mother and other siblings, said she received the shocking news on the evening of Tuesday, October 20, that the young man has died.

“Yesterday evening (Tuesday, October 20), around 7 or 8 o’clock, I got a call from someone in Ogun State close to my brother saying that my brother had died,” Juliet recalled.

“She said they arrested him on Saturday October 17, for stealing plantain. I asked how the family did not hear about it.” According to Juliet, a local woman who visited Peter in the cell said he complained of hunger and lack of water or food since Saturday, October 17, that he was arrested. He had pleaded that his family be contacted so he could be bailed.

When Juliet and her mother finally reached the station on Wednesday , October 21, an officer’s first words were: “I’m sorry for your loss.”

“I asked, ‘Loss? How?’ They said my brother hung himself. I said I wanted to see the cell. Is there a rope there? What is inside that cell that he could use to hang himself? They said he used his own clothes.

“I asked, ‘But I thought when they arrest someone, they don’t allow them to go in with clothes except boxers. How come he was with his clothes?’ When they showed me a picture of him hanging on the window, he was wearing his full trousers.

That means the boy was fully dressed.

“They took me to the cell. I saw a small window that is very high. I asked how he got up there. They said he used a bucket. I asked what the bucket was doing inside the cell. They said it is normally in the bathroom beside the cell.

“The story is just somehow. I am confused. I still don’t know what to do.”

Community leaders dispute police claims

Mr. Fidelis, former Chairman of Ogoja community in Ipara, said police only contacted him after Peter was already dead.

“Yesterday they called me. When I reached the station, the man said something had happened.

He opened the cell and I saw that Peter had hanged himself, with a rope around his neck, from the window,” Fidelis said.

He said, “nobody called me until Peter died. Even me and the complainant have never seen each other. We don’t know each other.”

Mr. Joseph, current chairman of the community, questioned both the detention procedure and the official explanation.

“The question we asked at the station was: ‘Should a person be detained inside the station with his clothes?’ They said yes. But the way they showed us inside there, it does not look like the guy hanged himself.

“What shocks me is that the man was arrested since Saturday. According to the law, after 24 hours you should charge the person to court. From Saturday to Tuesday, none of the family was aware. And the person they claimed was aware said they did not call him.”

Another community member, Monday Philip, said he approached the complainant shortly after the arrest to plead for leniency.

“I went to the man who arrested the Peter to beg him. He said he just wanted the boy to go there and learn a lesson for only one month and come back. I hadn’t even finished talking when the man kicked his motorcycle and left me standing there.”

Calls for thorough investigation

The family and community leaders insisted that the circumstances of Peter’s death must be thoroughly investigated, especially the decision to leave a detainee fully clothed, the presence of a bucket that could serve as a platform, the failure to notify next of kin promptly, and the claim that the young man said he had no family.

World.title: 21-year-old butcher stabs colleague’s to death in Ogun
World.content:
IGP Disu

By James Ogunnaike, Abeokuta

The Ogun State Police Command has arrested a 21-year-old butcher, Selim Ayodele, over the alleged stabbing to death of his 26-year-old colleague, Ibrahim Wasiu, following a disagreement at their workplace in Alagbole, Ogun State.

Read Also: Family seeks justice as butcher hacks 25-year old wife to death in Ekiti

The incident reportedly occurred on Sunday, October 18, 2026, after the two men had finished work at a cow meat-selling outlet.

In a statement issued on Friday, the Police Public Relations Officer of the command, DSP Oluseyi Babaseyi, said the incident was reported at the Ajuwon Police Station at about 8 p.m., prompting a police response.

According to the police, preliminary investigations revealed that the disagreement between the two colleagues arose over who should sweep the floor after the day’s work.

The statement alleged that during the ensuing altercation, Ayodele picked up a knife and stabbed Wasiu in the left side of his chest before twisting the weapon.

The victim was subsequently rushed to Life Hospital, where he was confirmed dead on arrival.

His remains were deposited at Life Channel Private Mortuary, Lanbe, Ajuwon, pending an autopsy, the police said.

The police added that the suspect was in custody as investigations continued ahead of his prosecution.

The Commissioner of Police in Ogun State, Bode Ojajuni, reaffirmed the command’s commitment to responding promptly to criminal incidents, conducting thorough investigations and ensuring the lawful prosecution of suspects.

He also urged residents to exercise restraint when disagreements arise, resolve disputes peacefully and promptly report criminal incidents to the police.

The command reiterated the importance of peaceful conflict resolution, warning against allowing minor disagreements to escalate into violence.

World.title: Why crashes on Otedola Bridge — Lagos govt
World.content:
File photo of an accident on Otedola Bridge.

By Olasunkanmi Akoni

The Lagos State Government has absolved Otedola Bridge of any structural or engineering defects, attributing the recurring fatal crashes on the corridor to reckless driving, driver indiscipline, and overloaded heavy-duty trucks.

The State Commissioner for Transportation, Mr. Oluwaseun Osiyemi, made the remark during the annual media parley organised by the Lagos State Ministry of Transportation held at Ikeja.

The parley formed part of the updates presented by transportation agencies at the media parley, with officials outlining plans to improve public transport capacity, strengthen road safety, expand water transportation and make vehicle-related services more accessible.

​Refuting public speculation regarding the safety of the bridge’s design, Osiyemi revealed that a joint inspection conducted by team leads from both the Federal Ministry of Works and the Lagos State Government confirmed the integrity of the structure.

“Our recent joint assessment with the Federal Controller of Works in Lagos, alongside previous structural integrity tests, shows conclusively that Otedola Bridge has no engineering defects.

“The recurring accidents are largely linked to motorist behavior and the poor condition of vehicles plying the road,” Osiyemi stated.

Addressing the menace of unroadworthy and overloaded articulated trucks, Osiyemi expressed concern over indiscriminate parking along major corridors, noting that such practices obstruct traffic flow and endanger lives.

​To curb infrastructure degradation and enhance road safety, the commissioner announced plans to deploy weighbridges across strategic locations in the state. The weighbridges will monitor truck weights and enforce compliance with legal limits.

​Osiyemi also warned motorists against speeding on corridors currently under construction, specifically highlighting the ongoing coastal road project.

He urged drivers not to treat active construction zones as high-speed expressways and advised patience to prevent avoidable collisions.

​The state government reaffirmed that reducing road fatalities will require a multi-faceted approach combining driver discipline, stricter enforcement of traffic regulations, vehicle roadworthiness checks, and the upcoming weighbridge monitoring system.

​Also speaking at the parley, the General Manager of the Lagos State Traffic Management Authority (LASTMA), Olalekan Bakare-Oki, stressed the enormous pressure commercial transportation places on the state’s road infrastructure.

​Bakare-Oki noted that over 60 per cent of all cargo transported in Nigeria originates from or moves through Lagos, resulting in heavy articulated truck traffic.

“While indiscriminate movement and congestion caused by heavy-duty vehicles significantly accelerate road wear and increase crash risks, human error and excessive speeding remain the leading causes of crashes along the Otedola Bridge corridor,” he said.

Recall that there have been incessant road crashes on the Otedola bridge along Lagos Ibadan Expressway, which often results into avoidable loss of lives and property.
