Consequently, motorists and residents have called on both Federal and State Governments’ intervention for a lasting solution that would address the situation.

World.title: Ebola: FG Tightens Surveillance, Screening, Infected Woman Identified as Swiss Diplomat’s Wife
World.content:
* Kenya Reports Second Death from the disease

* WHO says source of infection remains unknown, calls for regional vigilance

* Nigeria’s NCDC begins genomic sequencing

*Edo sets up emergency response committee

Onyebuchi Ezigbo in Abuja, Ayodeji Ake in Lagos and Felix Omoh-Asun in Benin City, with agency reports

The federal government yesterday tightened Ebola control measures across Nigeria, directing ministries, departments and agencies (MDAs), public health institutions and other stakeholders to strictly enforce screening, surveillance and other approved entry protocols as Switzerland confirmed that the woman who tested positive for the virus in Nigeria was the wife of a Swiss diplomat.

The directive by the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare followed concerns raised by the Office of the National Security Adviser (ONSA) over reported breaches of government-approved Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) entry protocols at Nigeria’s designated points of entry.

The ministry’s directive was contained in circular PS/FMOH/08/VIII/48, dated October 22, 2026, and signed by the Permanent Secretary, Daju Kachollum S., on behalf of the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare, Prof. Muhammad Ali Pate.

This comes as Kenya’s Health Ministry yesterday announced a second Ebola death, adding that the 65-year-old woman had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a ‌Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.

Also yesterday, Edo State Governor, Senator Monday Okpebholo, established a committee to coordinate the state’s emergency preparedness and response.

Swiss Ministry Confirms Diplomat’s Wife Tested Positive

Switzerland’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that the woman who tested positive for Ebola in Nigeria was the wife of a Swiss diplomat.

The 42-year-old Ugandan-born woman, who lives in Abuja, tested positive on October 20, becoming Nigeria’s first confirmed Ebola patient in more than a decade.

The couple had travelled to Uganda earlier in October. Her husband is currently in isolation but has not developed symptoms, according to the Swiss Foreign Ministry.

The ministry told the BBC that all 25 staff members at its embassy in Nigeria were in good health and did not need to isolate. The decision, taken in consultation with Nigeria’s Ministry of Health and the World Health Organisation (WHO), covered eight Swiss staff members and 17 local employees.

The embassy remains open and operational, with health and safety measures in place.

The woman had reportedly spent about a week at a private clinic in Abuja experiencing symptoms before her diagnosis. She returned to Nigeria on October 3 after spending about two and a half weeks in Uganda. She developed symptoms four days after arriving in Abuja and sought treatment at two private health facilities before testing positive on October 20.

WHO said the woman was receiving treatment in isolation and showing signs of improvement.

Although there were reports that she had travelled to eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) for business, the WHO, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) and Nigeria’s health ministry said they had not received verified information confirming that she visited the country. The Swiss government had also told Reuters that she did not travel to DR Congo, contradicting accounts from Uganda.

Health officials are investigating whether she may have crossed paths with a Kenyan man who died of Ebola after travelling through Uganda’s main airport on the same day. The Africa CDC said investigators were examining whether the two could have been exposed through shared equipment or other contact.

The agency’s Head of Emergency Preparedness and Response, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, described this as one of the possible scenarios but stressed that no link had been established.

The Kenyan man had travelled from DR Congo through Uganda before arriving in Nairobi on October 3. He subsequently died, becoming Kenya’s first recorded Ebola fatality. Kenya has since confirmed nine cases and traced 135 contacts, all of whom were placed in quarantine.

Ebola has infected nearly 10,000 people and killed more than 4,600 in Congo. The disease can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhoea and, in severe ⁠cases, internal and external bleeding. Only people with symptoms can transmit the virus. The rare Ebola species behind the current outbreak has no approved treatment or vaccine.

WHO said it was too early to determine where the woman in Nigeria contracted the virus.

“The source of exposure is still not known. The travel history of the patient is still being pieced together,” said Dr Patrick Otim, a WHO emergency response official.

He said investigators had struggled to obtain a complete account of her movements because opportunities to interview her were limited while she remained in hospital.

The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) is conducting genomic sequencing to help establish whether her infection is linked to other cases. However, the woman has been confirmed to have the Bundibugyo species of Ebola, the same species responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.

“The investigation is reconstructing the full travel and exposure history. Genomic sequencing is given a high priority,” said Dr Pavel Ursu, WHO’s representative in Nigeria.

Meanwhile, Nigerian authorities are tracing additional people who may have been exposed to the woman beyond the 44 contacts initially identified.

Kenya’s Director-General of Health, Dr Patrick Amoth, said all nine confirmed infections in his country were linked to the first patient, with no evidence of wider community transmission. He urged the public to remain vigilant without panicking, while warning that the country was not yet out of danger.

He added that the eight surviving patients remained in isolation and were responding well to treatment.

The developments have renewed concerns about the movement of infected people across international borders, particularly between DR Congo and neighbouring Uganda, where thousands of people cross daily for trade, work and family visits.

WHO’s Regional Director for Africa, Dr Mohamed Janabi, called for regional vigilance and urged countries to strengthen surveillance, investigate infections and protect frontline health workers.

Ebola is a serious viral disease transmitted through direct contact with the blood or other bodily fluids of an infected person, or contaminated objects. It does not spread through the air like influenza. Symptoms can include fever, severe weakness, vomiting and diarrhoea, and the disease can be fatal. People are not considered infectious before developing symptoms.

Health authorities say rapid contact tracing, isolation of suspected cases and early treatment are crucial to preventing further transmission.

FG Orders Strict Compliance with Ebola Protocols

In the circular, the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare directed relevant institutions to ensure strict adherence to approved EVD screening, health declaration, surveillance and other applicable entry requirements at all designated points of entry into Nigeria.

According to a statement signed by the Assistant Director, Information and Public Relations, Ado Bako, the directive followed concerns communicated to the Coordinating Minister by ONSA over reported non-compliance with government-approved protocols.

The ministry emphasised the need for consistent, effective and non-discriminatory enforcement of the measures to mitigate potential cross-border transmission and protect public health and national security.

It also called for stronger coordination, communication and information-sharing among stakeholders to support effective surveillance, early detection and prompt responses to potential threats.

“All concerned institutions have been urged to promptly document and report any actual or attempted breach of approved protocols through established channels, provide necessary support to officials responsible for enforcement, and establish effective monitoring and accountability mechanisms to sustain compliance,” the statement said.

The ministry stressed that personnel responsible for enforcing the protocols should be allowed to perform their duties professionally and without undue interference.

It also directed the immediate and widespread dissemination of public advisories to relevant departments, units, field offices and personnel to ensure that they understood their responsibilities.

“All concerned MDAs are expected to accord the directive the highest priority, address identified lapses promptly and sustain compliance with approved EVD entry protocols in the collective interest of public health and national safety,” the statement added.

The directive comes amid efforts to contain the confirmed Ebola case in the Federal Capital Territory, with the government intensifying surveillance at airports, seaports and land borders.

Kenya Reports Second Death from Ebola

Kenya has recorded a second Ebola death, the health ministry said yesterday, adding that the 65-year-old woman had developed symptoms during quarantine and was a close relative of a ‌Kenyan man who died of Ebola earlier this month.

The outbreak, which started in the Democratic Republic of Congo, has now been reported in four countries across eastern, central andwestern Africa, giving it the widest geographic spread of any Ebola outbreak on the continent to date.

The Ebola victim who died yesterday, was a direct contact of the index patient, Reuters quoted the Kenyan ministry to have revealed.

“This loss brings the number of deaths to two among the nine confirmed cases. The remaining seven patients continue to receive care in the ‌two ⁠isolation facilities,” the ministry said, adding there was no evidence of community spread in the country.

Late on Monday, the US State Department advised Americans to reconsider travel to Kenya and raised its travel advisory level for the countrybecause of health risks.

Edo Sets Up Ebola Emergency Response Committee

Edo State Governor, Senator Monday Okpebholo, has established a committee on Ebola emergency preparedness and response.

The committee is chaired by the Deputy Governor, Dennis Idahosa, according to a statement issued yesterday by the Chief Press Secretary to the Governor, Dr Patrick Ebojele.

The committee is expected to coordinate the state’s preparedness and response to any Ebola threat.

Its members are drawn from the state ministries responsible for health, environment, livestock, local government, finance, and information and communication; the Edo State House of Assembly Committee on Health; the governor’s Special Adviser on Health; the State Emergency Management Agency; the Department of Port Health; and the National Orientation Agency.

Other members include personnel from the Department of State Services, Nigeria Immigration Service, Nigeria Police Force and Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps.

The committee also includes representatives of the University of Benin Teaching Hospital, Irrua Specialist Teaching Hospital, Edo State University Teaching Hospital, Federal Neuropsychiatric Hospital in Uselu, Edo Specialist Hospital, Central Hospital in Benin City and Stella Obasanjo Hospital.

Professional bodies represented include the Nigeria Medical Association, National Association of Nigeria Nurses and Midwives, and the Edo State chapter of the Association of Private Medical Practitioners of Nigeria.

Other members include a traditional ruler, a leader of the Christian Association of Nigeria in Edo State, the state’s Chief Imam and a market women’s leader.

Development partners and agencies represented on the committee include the WHO, UNICEF, Nigeria Red Cross Society, DataFi, National Primary Health Care Development Agency and Edo State Primary Health Care Development Agency.

The committee will operate through the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre, which has designated areas of responsibility covering coordination, epidemiology, surveillance, infection prevention and control, risk communication, logistics, laboratory services, case management, and safe and dignified burial. A centre manager will oversee operations.

The statement added that a stakeholders’ meeting would be scheduled for the committee.

World.title: State Police: 25 Assemblies Approve Amendment, Bill Crosses Constitutional Hurdle
World.content:
• Lagos, Ondo, Ebonyi, Kogi, Niger, Borno, Bauchi, Jigawa, Katsina, Kano, Sokoto yet to approve

Deji Elumoye in Abuja

The constitutional amendment seeking to establish State Police in Nigeria has crossed a major legislative hurdle, with 25 of the 36 State Houses of Assembly approving the 2026 Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, surpassing the two-thirds threshold required for the amendment to proceed to the next stage.

However, 11 States —Lagos, Ondo, Ebonyi, Kogi, Niger, Borno, Bauchi, Jigawa, Katsina, Kano and Sokoto — have yet to approve the amendment.

With the required constitutional threshold secured, the amendment can now be returned to the National Assembly for transmission to President Bola Tinubu for assent.

Chief of Staff to the President and Chairman of the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill, Hon. Femi Gbajabiamila, disclosed the development in a statement, commending the State Houses of Assembly for their decisive action on the reform.

He also expressed appreciation to the National Assembly for passing the amendment in both chambers.

The development came as the National Policing Bill and 29 consequential amendment bills were undergoing legislative drafting review and validation at the Federal Ministry of Justice.

Gbajabiamila explained that the approval by 25 state assemblies had provided the constitutional backing required for the proposed dual policing framework.

He stated: “The approval gives constitutional backing to the policing framework that the Working Group’s draft National Policing Bill, 2026 is designed to implement.

“The Working Group’s efforts remain on track. The draft Bills are currently undergoing legislative drafting review and validation at the Federal Ministry of Justice and are expected to be returned on or before Friday, 30th October 2026. Thereafter, the Group will give them final consideration before presenting them to Mr President.

“The Working Group urges all stakeholders to support a smooth transition to a dual policing system that makes Nigerians safer.”

The Presidency had on Tuesday disclosed that the draft National Policing Bill, 2026, was ready.

Gbajabiamila explained that the Working Group had completed the drafting stage of its assignment and formally submitted the proposed National Policing Bill, together with 29 consequential amendment bills, to the Federal Ministry of Justice for legislative drafting review and validation.

According to him, the submission was made to the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice on Monday, October 19, 2026, in accordance with the Working Group’s work plan.

He said the ministry’s review would ensure that the proposed legislation conformed to established legislative drafting standards and conventions and did not conflict with existing laws.

The Ministry of Justice, he added, was expected to return the validated draft bills to the Working Group on or before October 30, 2026.

Thereafter, the Working Group would give the bills final consideration before presenting them to the President, thereby concluding its mandate.

Gbajabiamila stated: “The proposed National Policing Bill seeks to establish the constitutional and legislative framework for a dual policing structure, comprising a Federal Police Service and State Police Services.

“The Working Group remains committed to a rigorous and transparent process that will deliver a comprehensive legislative proposal for consideration by the President and subsequent transmission to the National Assembly.

“The work on preparing the National Policing Bill is proceeding alongside the ongoing consideration of the Constitution of the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 1999 (Sixth Alteration) Bill, 2026 by the States Houses of Assembly, which must be completed before the Bill is transmitted to the National Assembly.”

The Presidency had last Thursday indicated that the National Policing Bill would be transmitted to the National Assembly within two weeks.

Speaking with journalists after a steering committee meeting at the State House, Abuja, Gbajabiamila said the proposed legislation was nearing completion.

“The National Policing Bill is more or less ready for transmission to the National Assembly. We will probably have one more meeting after this to cross the t’s and dot the i’s and make sure every area is covered. So, we are 90 percent ready.

“The governors have one or two observations, and we should be ready in about a week or so,” he said.

Gbajabiamila described the proposed legislation as “the most consequential Bill of the administration so far,” explaining that it had undergone extensive deliberations since the Working Group’s steering committee commenced its meetings on August 3, 2026.

Responding to concerns that some states might delay approval of the Sixth Constitution Alteration Bill on state police, particularly when only about six states had reportedly approved the amendment, Gbajabiamila expressed confidence that the required support would be secured.

He maintained that there was a “national consensus” among Nigerians on the need for the constitutional amendment.

“I see no reason why anyone will want to have a rethink on it,” he said.

Those present at Thursday’s steering committee meeting, held at the conference hall of the Chief of Staff’s Office at the State House, Abuja, included the Chairman of the Nigeria Governors’ Forum and Governor of Kwara State, AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq; Ogun State Governor, Dapo Abiodun; Kaduna State Governor, Uba Sani; Inspector-General of Police, Tunji Disu; and the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, represented by the Solicitor-General and Permanent Secretary of the Federal Ministry of Justice, Mrs Beatrice Jedy-Agba.

Others included the Chairman of the Policy Advisory Committee, Justice Abdullahi Liman (retd.); Head of the Nigeria Police Reform Secretariat, Professor Olu Ogunsakin; Special Adviser to the President on National Assembly Matters (House of Representatives), Dr Lanre Smart; and Senior Special Assistant to the President on Planning and Research and Secretary of the Committee, Nnadubem Moghalu.

Also in attendance were a representative of the President of the Nigerian Bar Association and AIG Abraham Nabhon Thomas, who represented the National Security Adviser, among others.

President Tinubu had, on July 7, 2026, inaugurated the Presidential Working Group on the National Policing Bill to prepare the legal framework for the implementation of state police across the country.

The inauguration followed the National Assembly’s passage of the Constitution Alteration (State Police) Bill, 2026, which provides for a dual policing structure comprising a Federal Police Service and 36 State Police Services.

Tinubu had explained that although the constitutional amendment would establish the framework for state police, the National Policing Bill would provide the legal structure necessary for its implementation.

“The Constitution Amendment Bill establishes the framework for dual policing, but it does not operationalise it. That work is left to the National Policing Bill,” the President stated.

World.title: Oramah: Africa Must Break Economic Bondage, Build Its Own Industrial Power
World.content:
· Says political independence incomplete without economic freedom

· Urges investment in manufacturing, skills, technology

Nume Ekeghe

The immediate past President of the African Export-Import Bank (Afreximbank), Dr. Benedict Oramah, has urged African countries to intensify efforts to achieve economic independence through industrialisation, deeper intra-African trade, strategic deployment of capital and investment in human development.

Oramah, who spoke in an interview on the sidelines of the recently concluded International Monetary Fund (IMF)/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, said the continent’s political independence would remain incomplete unless African countries developed the capacity to produce goods, create decent jobs and determine their economic future.

He called on governments, financial institutions, businesses and other stakeholders to see themselves as fighters for Africa’s economic freedom, warning that the continent must overcome the fragmentation and dependence that continue to constrain its development.

“Everybody in the banking business, including our governments and corporates, has to regard themselves as economic freedom fighters. We are combatants for economic freedom. Those in banking and financial services are engaged in financial guerrilla warfare,” he said.

According to him, political independence was only the beginning of Africa’s struggle, with the ultimate objective being economic self-determination.

“Political independence gives you the platform to achieve the ultimate independence, which is economic independence,” Oramah said, adding that the struggle must now be fought through ideas, industrial production, technology and human capital rather than weapons.

“The fight we are in now is not going to be fought in trenches, but on factory floors, in technology incubation centres and so on. It is not going to be fought with brute force. It will be fought with ideas. Capital is key, not bullets. That capital includes human capital,” he added.

Oramah, who recently completed his tenure at Afreximbank after two terms, said he had established Marob Strategies, a strategy and advisory firm, to continue contributing to Africa’s development by helping institutions formulate and implement strategies.

He explained that Africa’s challenge was not merely a shortage of ideas but the inability to execute them effectively and mobilise the resources required to achieve continental ambitions.

On regional integration, he lamented that Africa’s trade with external partners remained disproportionately high compared with trade among its own countries, despite the continent’s significant infrastructure assets and productive capacity.

He said existing infrastructure could support between $1 trillion and $1.4 trillion in African trade, yet intra-African trade accounted for only about $170 billion to $200 billion.

Oramah further urged African countries to develop their own artificial intelligence capabilities rather than remain mere users of technologies developed elsewhere.

World.title: Babalakin Hails Tinubu Over Resolution of 19-year MMA2 Dispute, Pledges Jobs for Nigerians
World.content:
Dike Onwuamaeze



The Chairman of Bi-Courtney Aviation Services Limited (BASL), Dr. Wale Babalakin, SAN, has commended President Bola Tinubu for facilitating the resolution of the longstanding dispute surrounding the Murtala Muhammed Airport Terminal Two (MMA2), describing the settlement as a victory for Nigeria.



Babalakin also pledged that Bi-Courtney would fulfil its obligations under the agreement and pursue projects expected to create quality employment opportunities for Nigerians.



He spoke at the signing ceremony of the settlement agreement involving the Federal Government, the Federal Airports Authority of Nigeria (FAAN), Bi-Courtney Limited and Stabilini Visinoni Limited, which resolved an impasse that had lasted more than 18 years.

The BASL chairman attributed the breakthrough to Tinubu’s intervention through the Minister of Aviation and Aerospace Development, Olorogun Festus Keyamo, SAN.



“This is not a win for us alone; it is a win for Nigerians,” Babalakin said, expressing appreciation to the President, the minister and Nigerians who had followed the dispute over the years.

He said the resolution sent a positive signal to investors that longstanding disputes between the government and private enterprises could be settled through dialogue and constructive engagement.



According to him, prolonged uncertainty over commercial agreements could discourage long-term investment, making the settlement an important step towards strengthening confidence in Nigeria’s investment environment.



The agreement is also expected to pave the way for the advancement of key development projects at MMA2, particularly the proposed hotel and conference centre, as well as the commencement of regional flight operations.



Babalakin said completing the hotel and conference centre would enhance the airport environment by providing accommodation and conference facilities for business travellers, corporate organisations and other airport users.



He added that the project could generate employment across construction, engineering, hospitality, facility management and related services.



The commencement of regional flight operations, alongside the planned expansion of the airport apron, would also create opportunities for skilled employment and commercial growth.

The settlement further addresses outstanding issues arising from the parties’ longstanding commercial relationship, including matters relating to the General Aviation Terminal (GAT), which remained under FAAN’s control and operation.



The agreement incorporates reciprocal concessions and revised obligations, providing a framework for the parties to move forward.

Babalakin acknowledged the responsibility to translate the settlement into tangible results, assuring stakeholders that Bi-Courtney would fulfil its obligations and work constructively with the relevant parties.



“We will not disappoint the President, the Ministry of Aviation and Aerospace Development, FAAN or Nigerians,” he said.

He reiterated his appreciation to Tinubu for facilitating the resolution, describing the agreement as an opportunity to renew cooperation, deliver infrastructure projects and realise the full potential of MMA2.

World.title: Atiku Accuses Tinubu of Using 90-day Cost of Living Relief to Woo Voters
World.content:
Chuks Okocha in Abuja

Former Vice President and presidential candidate of the African Democratic Congress (ADC), Alhaji Atiku Abubakar, has accused President Bola Tinubu of using the 90-day cost-of-living relief plan announced by the National Economic Council (NEC) to woo voters ahead of the presidential election.

Atiku, through his Director of Strategic Communication at the ADC Presidential Campaign Council, Phrank Shaibu, said the timing of the initiative raised questions about the government’s commitment to easing the hardship Nigerians had endured over the past three and a half years.

Addressing a press conference on behalf of Atiku, Shaibu said: “The presidential election is 86 days away. Yet President Bola Tinubu’s National Economic Council has announced a cost-of-living plan that will run for 90 days.

“The arithmetic is plain: the plan ends after Nigerians have voted. After three and a half years of hardship, this government is asking families to carry another promise into the polling booth and wait for relief until the votes are counted.

“This is election bait. Tinubu is offering hungry Nigerians the promise of affordable food, but the promised relief comes with a deadline that outlasts the election. The message is simple: vote first; relief later. Nigerians should refuse the bait and judge this government by the three and a half years they have already lived through,” Atiku added.

The plan, according to Atiku, identifies five priorities: food affordability, tax harmonisation, completion of important projects, removal of investment bottlenecks and household support. He argued that these were problems Nigerians had expected the administration to address since taking office.

“Families have cut meals. Workers spend more of their wages getting to work. Manufacturers struggle to produce, and businesses have closed. Tinubu cannot erase three and a half years of hardship with a 90-day announcement,” he said.

Atiku argued that the consequences of petrol subsidy removal on transport, food and production costs had been predictable, insisting that measures to protect vulnerable households should have accompanied the decision.

“Instead, the government imposed the costs immediately and left Nigerians to wait for the benefits. Now, after years of hardship, it has suddenly discovered that people need affordable food.

“A government cannot put a 90-day deadline on hunger, the cost-of-living crisis and insecurity and call it an economic policy,” he said.

Atiku also questioned the effectiveness of the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited’s (NNPC) petrol discount promotion, which began on October 1 and was subsequently presented by the government as part of its relief efforts.

He said he had visited NNPC Retail stations and was told that no discount was available, adding that he bought petrol at N1,405 per litre.

“With barely a week left before the offer expires, my experience as a customer was simple: a promise of relief, and a higher price at the pump. If NNPC says motorists can access a discount through an app, it must explain why customers arriving at its stations were told there was none.

“How many customers received the discount? At which stations? How many litres were sold at the reduced price? Publish the figures,” he said.

Atiku questioned the reach of the promotion, noting that NNPC had about 900 retail stations in a country where motorists bought petrol from thousands of outlets.

“What reach can a N66-per-litre promotion have when it is confined to that network? And what lasting relief does N66 offer families whose transport and food bills remain high?” he asked.

He added: “Tinubu announces relief at a podium. Nigerians arrive at the pump and pay more. Now his government expects the country to trust another announcement, this time with a 90-day deadline.”

The former vice-president said the timing of the initiative was significant because the cost-of-living crisis had become central to his campaign, which he said was focused on making Nigeria affordable again.

He accused the Tinubu administration of attempting to appropriate that message with a relief plan whose timeline extended beyond the election.

“Nigerians should not trade three and a half years of lived hardship for three months of promises,” he said.

Atiku challenged the government to provide details of the five priorities outlined in the plan.

On food affordability, he asked which costs would fall for farmers, transporters and traders, when consumers would begin to see lower market prices, and how the government would sustain affordability beyond the 90-day period.

On tax harmonisation, he demanded details of the charges to be removed or consolidated and urged the government to publish the full tax schedule, including whether the promised relief would be followed by higher charges after the election.

He also questioned which projects would be completed within 90 days, how much remained to be paid for them and when Nigerians would be able to use them.

“A project is complete when it serves people, not when it is marked complete on a government dashboard,” he said.

On investment bottlenecks, Atiku asked which barriers the government intended to remove within the period, arguing that manufacturers needed reliable power, manageable transport costs and access to affordable finance to expand operations and create jobs.

He also demanded details of the proposed household support, including eligibility criteria, the amount each household would receive, when payments would begin, the budget and the payment mechanism.

Atiku raised concerns about a registration form reportedly being circulated under the name “Arise for Tinubu 2027”. He said the form requested voter identification, bank details and telephone numbers, and questioned who was collecting the information, how it would be used and whether the exercise was linked to the government’s household support programme.

“No Nigerian should have to hand over voter or bank details to a political group to receive public relief,” he said.

He urged the government to clarify whether the registration exercise was connected to any publicly funded programme and, if not, explain how it would prevent household support from being used to recruit voters or collect their personal data.

Atiku maintained that Nigerians who had borne the burden of the government’s reforms were entitled to evidence that the promised benefits would reach them and continue beyond election day.

“People do not reject reform because they fail to understand it. They reject being told to sacrifice today for relief that never arrives—or arrives with an expiry date,” he said.

He pledged to make Nigeria more affordable through disciplined public spending, targeted household relief, lower costs of producing and transporting essential goods, and policies that would enable Nigerian manufacturers to expand and employ more people.

“Economic policy should be judged by what families can afford, not by how many deadlines a government announces,” he said.

Atiku challenged Tinubu to answer two questions: whether Nigerians were better off than they were in May 2023, and whether they would still be able to afford food on the 91st day of the proposed relief plan.

“Until he can answer both, Nigerians have every reason to see this 90-day exercise for what it is: a political timetable dressed up as economic relief.

“President Tinubu made life expensive. Atiku Abubakar will make life affordable again,” he said.

Atiku also questioned Tinubu’s record on security in Kaduna State ahead of the President’s expected visit to launch his re-election campaign today.

He said the President should reflect on the state’s experience with deadly attacks, civilian casualties and natural disasters before seeking another mandate.

“Tinubu is also expected in Kaduna to launch his re-election campaign. Before the music starts and the crowd is assembled, he should remember what the state has endured under his presidency,” he said.

Atiku cited the December 3, 2023, military drone strike on civilians attending a Maulud celebration in Tudun Biri, in which at least 85 people were killed. He said Tinubu sent the Vice-President to visit survivors but did not personally visit grieving families.

He also referred to reports by residents of Giwa in September 2024 that another military airstrike had killed at least 24 civilians.

In Kajuru, he said, families had buried loved ones and searched for relatives abducted by bandits. He also cited a kidnapping-related attack in Kachia in September 2025 that affected 152 people, with eight deaths and nine injuries recorded.

Atiku further highlighted the impact of storms and floods in the state. He said windstorms and rain in July 2025 affected 6,172 people and damaged hundreds of shelters across five local government areas, while flooding in Zaria in September affected 476 people and left dozens injured.

“When families were burying their dead, searching for their children and clearing wreckage from their homes, Kaduna needed the attention of its President,” he said.

Atiku questioned the Presidency’s account of Tinubu’s September 2025 visit to Kaduna, which he said listed a wedding and a courtesy call.

“Tinubu can find his way to Kaduna for a wedding. He can find his way there for votes. Why was he absent when grieving families needed their President?” he asked.

He urged Tinubu not to use affected families as a backdrop for a campaign event, calling on the President to explain what had been done for the victims of Tudun Biri, the outcome of investigations into civilian deaths and the measures being taken to protect communities still threatened by abductions.

“Before asking Kaduna for another mandate, he should explain what has been done for the victims of Tudun Biri, what became of investigations into civilian deaths and how his government will protect communities still threatened by abduction,” Atiku said.

World.title: Interest Rate Cut: Is Now Right Time to Take Loan?
World.content:
Omolabake Fasogbon

A cut in the Central Bank of Nigeria’s (CBN) monetary policy rate (MPR) usually raises hopes that loans will become cheaper for households and businesses. The expectation is understandable: when banks’ borrowing costs fall, customers may eventually benefit too.

In September, the CBN cut its benchmark rate from 26.5 per cent to 23 per cent amid easing inflation and relative stability in the foreign exchange market. The move aimed to make credit more affordable. For a household planning a major purchase or a business hoping to expand, this may seem like the right time to borrow.

But a rate cut does not mean banks will immediately reduce the interest charged on loans. Lower rates at the CBN do not always reach customers, and industry stakeholders have repeatedly questioned why borrowing costs remain high after monetary policy is eased.

The CBN wants cheaper credit to encourage investment, production and job creation. It can also help reduce government financing costs and improve productivity. For households and business owners, the practical question is: should they borrow now or wait?

Why Loans May Not Get Cheaper

Banks consider more than the CBN’s benchmark rate when deciding what to charge customers. Their rates also reflect funding costs, operating expenses, the risk of non-payment, available cash, regulatory requirements and uncertainty in the economy.

Another factor is the 45 per cent Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR), which requires banks to keep a portion of deposits with the CBN rather than lend it out.

Chief Executive Officer of the Centre for the Promotion of Private Enterprise, Dr Muda Yusuf, said the high ratio limits the share of deposits available for loans and raises the cost of providing financial services.

Yusuf said lower MPRs failing to reduce borrowing costs had been a longstanding concern and pointed to weaknesses in Nigeria’s financial system, including limited financial access, fragmented credit markets, high lending risks and inadequate systems for assessing borrowers.

Who Benefits First?

Even when rates fall, not everyone benefits equally. Larger companies often have stronger financial records, better collateral, lower perceived risk and greater bargaining power. Yusuf said they are better placed to negotiate cheaper loans or refinance existing debts.

Small and medium-sized businesses, despite their importance to the economy, face a tougher challenge. Many have limited assets to offer as security, fewer financing options and less power to negotiate with lenders. As a result, their borrowing costs may fall more slowly and by less.

What Businesses Should Do Now

While waiting for lower rates to reach borrowers, businesses can review their finances and borrowing plans. Finance expert Dr. Ozemoya Pedro, advised owners to assess existing loans and consider whether refinancing or renegotiating could reduce repayments.

He cautioned against taking a loan simply because rates are falling. Businesses should calculate how much they need and compare complete offers from banks, fintech companies and development finance institutions. The advertised interest rate is only part of the cost; fees, repayment periods and other conditions matter too.

Pedro also advised businesses to prepare financial statements, cash-flow records and tax documents before applying. Lenders will assess whether applicants can repay their debts. Any borrowed money, he said, should go towards activities that produce measurable returns. A loan is useful only when it supports real business growth.

Households should apply the same discipline. Before borrowing, work out whether repayments fit income and essential expenses, compare the total cost of offers and avoid taking on debt simply in the hope that rates will fall later.

Existing Loans, Savings and Investments

The rate cut may create opportunities to restructure or refinance debts, but stronger borrowers are likely to have more room to negotiate. Yusuf said customers with floating-rate loans may qualify for lower rates, depending on the benchmark and the terms agreed with lenders.

Fixed-rate loans generally retain their interest rates until maturity unless the borrower and lender agree to renegotiate or refinance.

Savings and investments may also be affected. Lower MPRs can moderate returns on bank deposits and newly issued fixed-income products. Investors may consider spreading their money across assets, including shares and property, according to their goals and willingness to take risks.

Yusuf said the cut signals a move towards less restrictive monetary conditions. This could help businesses plan with greater confidence, encourage investment and give borrowers an opening to renegotiate financing. However, the benefits depend on inflation continuing to ease, exchange-rate stability and confidence in economic policy.

He called for further reforms to ensure lower MPRs translate more quickly into affordable loans. These include gradually reducing the CRR when conditions permit, improving credit information and lending efficiency, expanding financing for small businesses, and maintaining fiscal discipline so government borrowing does not crowd out private-sector credit.

For households and businesses, a CBN rate cut may create an opportunity, but it does not guarantee cheap borrowing for everyone. Compare offers, understand the full repayment cost and borrow only when the money serves a clear purpose and repayments are affordable.

World.title: Benedict Oramah: Africa Must Build Its Own AI Models, Not Just Supply the Data
World.content:
Former President of Afreximbank, Dr. Benedict Oramah, has urged Africa to build its own artificial intelligence models rather than remain a supplier of data to foreign technology firms, stressing the need for greater economic independence. In this interview with Nume Ekeghe on the sidelines of the just-concluded IMF/World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, he argues that Nigeria can leverage its cheap gas to power data centres, establish technology parks and attract investment, while calling for massive infrastructure financing, industrialisation and deeper continental trade to drive growth and create jobs

You have completed your tenure at Afreximbank and established Marob Strategies and Consulting, what services does Marob Strategies offer and what are your plans for it?

I just completed my two terms of office at Afreximbank. You know the journey we embarked on, which I’ve been involved in for the past 30 years. Fragmentation as you know is the bane of the continent. Finishing at Afreximbank does not mean that the problem has been solved. As I moved on to other things, I kept focusing on the challenges that we had to solve, and there aren’t enough soldiers to attack that problem. Retreating when you still have energy would betray the commitment to the continent. I never saw my departure from Afreximbank as retirement because, thank God, I still have the energy and the faculties. It would be a disservice to the continent if the experience, contacts and capabilities acquired over time were lost overnight. Marob is the strategy firm we have established. I have always believed that one of Africa’s challenges is the proper articulation of strategy and its execution. That is what I created Marob to do. It is not primarily about making money, although we have to generate revenue to meet our obligations. Essentially, it is about continuing to develop strategic interventions that I believe the continent still needs, helping African institutions articulate their strategies, and mobilising the capabilities and resources required to execute them efficiently.

I believe we can do even more for the continent through Marob because it gives me greater freedom to think and challenge conventional wisdom. Once we develop and test these ideas, we can take them back to Afreximbank, other African multilateral financial institutions, commercial banks and other organisations working across the continent.

Your work with Dangote’s refinery and its subsequent share offering has attracted attention. What informed Afreximbank’s support for the project?

We expected the reception because Dangote had built a brand, and we helped him build it. We are happy that Dangote became what it is and the refinery itself. It’s all credit to Alhaji Aliko Dangote’s perseverance and determination. For us at Afreximbank, when we were supporting him, a bank can only do so much. We began by doing principal financing, but we were looking for entrepreneurs. A bank has money, but a bank is not organised to do certain things. For a bank to be effective, you need entrepreneurs who are credible, trustworthy, who can envision, execute and strategise. Dangote embodies all of this, and that refinery, for me, was a no brainer to support. I recall that initially, our first facility to the refinery was almost a billion dollars. When we went to the board, I didn’t go there to argue about credit. My argument to them was that when we see this kind of thing in other parts of the world, we say these people are doing great things. This one is here. This is our project. I told them I didn’t think this is a matter of credit, but a matter of continental pride and continental survival. Since we started that relationship, Afreximbank has provided $18 billion. Most of it was to the refinery.

I must also say it’s not just me. There was no way I was going to do it alone. The management, everybody, believed in it. It was like a mission, and I bought into it. When it got to this stage and we had to do the IPO and the private placement, I was very pleased that Alhaji recognised all of that and gave us the opportunity to participate in a big way. We worked with Afreximbank to underwrite about 25 per cent of the private placement and also about 24 to 25 per cent of the IPO. That was a significant opportunity, and I believe it shows Alhaji’s appreciation of the road we travelled together.

Afreximbank always achieves smooth transition between presidents, unlike many African institutions where former leaders are pushed out. Why is continuity important?

I think people who fight like that are small people, and people who doubt their competence. Why would you throw away a trove of wisdom that will make you stronger? I’ve done my own. I’m gone. But if I can contribute to making President Elombi successful, I think it would be stupid of President Elombi to tell me not to contribute because it’s him. I was in the bank from day one, so I know all the challenges. I was privileged to have worked very closely with all the presidents as an adviser and special assistant, handling very sensitive issues, research and strategy. That experience helped me later because there was hardly anything we went through that I didn’t know about or participate in resolving. As president, why would I throw that knowledge away? There were times when I had to go back to my predecessors for advice. I remember when we wanted to develop the idea of export trading companies. Rather than issue a request for proposals to find an expert, I told the team to bring in a former president of the bank because I knew his experience in export trading companies. He helped us undertake the study, and that work eventually led to the establishment of the African Trade and Distribution Company. If I had burnt that bridge, would I have been able to go back to him? Even if we paid him more, he might not have been willing to help us. That is how we approach continuity at Afreximbank. It is not just about presidents; it also applies to staff. Whenever we have a task that a former colleague can handle, we bring them in. It is not only because we want to support our colleagues, but because we know their capabilities and can identify who is best suited to do the job. So, I would be surprised if President Elombi discarded that experience. In fact, he has continued to involve me, and I have had to tell him that I also need to attend to other things. For us, it is about preserving institutional knowledge and using the experience of people who have helped build the bank to strengthen the work that continues.

You earlier spoke about building a continental strategy and advisory firm. What problem are you trying to solve?

The big picture for me is that we build a number one continental strategy and advisory firm, so that we no longer have a situation where our people run to someone else to do the things we can do. We are already rapidly going there because of the kind of mandates we are getting. I would rather find partnerships than tell a country, company or bank that comes to us that we are overstretched. Ultimately, we may become the nucleus of a federated advisory platform that brings credible advisory firms in different African countries under one umbrella, so that we can give our people the right advice.

Your Pan-African approach to business is quite strong. Where does this conviction come from?

Everybody in the banking business, including our governments and corporates has to regard themselves as economic freedom fighters. We are combatants for economic freedom. Those in banking and financial services are engaged in financial guerrilla warfare. Our sensibilities have been numbed by the so-called belief that things are good. We did not understand that there is still economic bondage. It is only now that we are beginning to break away from it. During the struggle for political independence, many of those who fought for it went into the bushes, fought with guns, were killed and were jailed. They were ready to sacrifice and pay the supreme price. That is why we can go around, carry flags and say we are a nation. But if you read the works of people such as Nkrumah and Nyerere, you recognise that this was just the beginning. Political independence gives you the platform to achieve the ultimate independence, which is economic independence. We were quickly sabotaged in pursuing this. There used to be a time when the issue was the struggle against neocolonialism. It quickly disappeared from the lexicon, so that we no longer remembered there was something to deal with. The fight we are in now is not going to be fought in trenches, but on factory floors, in technology incubation centres and so on. It is not going to be fought with brute force. It will be fought with ideas. Capital is key, not bullets. That capital includes human capital.

Afreximbank supported several initiatives aimed at integrating African economies. What do these initiatives say about the continent’s ability to achieve economic independence?

I’m very proud of what we did at Afreximbank during my time, and even before, under my predecessors. The first meeting of the Organisation of African Unity in May 1963 produced key decisions. The leaders asked the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa to conduct a study towards delivering a continental free trade area, an African Payments Union, a Pan-African trade fair, transit schemes and a strategy to break the technical attachment of currencies to foreign currencies. We didn’t know this until after we had done some of the things ourselves. In 2018, the AfCFTA was launched, and we supported the process. We were paying the salaries of quite a few people. Even the negotiations of protocols were supported by grants we provided. We launched the Pan-African Payment and Settlement System (PAPSS), which the African Union adopted. We introduced the Pan-African Transit Guarantee Scheme, and we organised the Intra-African Trade Fair. We never saw that 1963 resolution. We only discovered it after we had asked a team to examine the African Union’s archives and identify decisions from many years ago that were still relevant but had not been implemented. When they came back and told me what they found, I asked, why did it take 60 years? The leaders knew that after independence, we had to move quickly to integrate our economies.

At the AfCFTA signing, you said signing papers would not open borders. Why has implementation been difficult?

We have really progressed. One of the surprises for me was when we came to Rwanda to open the papers for signing the AfCFTA. We thought 21 countries would sign, based on all the discussions. But as the books were opened, I think 45 countries signed that day. The problem is that we have been divided and fragmented into these atomistic units for so long. There are vested interests and so much fear of losing authority or power that people think will happen if they open up and start implementing what they signed. To be fair, I don’t expect everybody to be so open-minded. You just need a strong nucleus to get things moving. It is moving now. I think 24 countries have created their tariff schedules, which means they can implement the agreement. Non-tariff barriers remain the biggest problem. It took the Europeans almost 50 years to achieve what they achieved. It will take time, but I always knew that businesses would push the boundaries. People always said we had infrastructure problems and that was why we were not trading among ourselves. My view was, and remains, that Africa has infrastructure challenges, but the infrastructure deficit is a generalised challenge. The stock of infrastructure on the continent today can carry, depending on the year, between $1 trillion and $1.4 trillion of African trade. The question is, why is Africa’s share of that trade only between $170 billion and $200 billion? Why is it not $800 billion? The infrastructure stock can carry more than $1 trillion, yet our share is only 15 to 16 per cent. Why is it not 30 per cent? China’s share of our trade is higher than the trade we do among ourselves. The issue is trade information. We don’t know what is going on around Africa. Our traders and businesses trust Chinese, Europeans and Americans more than they trust the person next to them because they don’t know what is happening in neighbouring countries. We have factories in Ethiopia manufacturing leather products that import semi-processed leather from New Zealand at a higher cost than Burundi exports the same product to the world. We have many such absurdities. That’s one of the reasons we created trading companies, trade information platforms and the trade fair.

How can Africa bridge its infrastructure gap when governments cannot provide all the required financing?

I always knew there was no way governments could finance the infrastructure gap. To bring African infrastructure to world standards would require investment of about $100 billion a year. That is more than a trillion dollars over time. I asked my team to aggregate the budgets of all African countries, and I found that it would amount to about 60 per cent of their total budgets. You don’t need to be a rocket scientist to know that would not work. You need private capital. The only way is to demonstrate that there are businesses. Once businesses demonstrate the opportunity, private capital will finance infrastructure. People who invest in commercial infrastructure don’t need anybody to plead with them. The business case will attract them.

What policies should Nigeria and other African countries adopt to create decent jobs?

I don’t see anything other than a better economy that grows. Then you have to invest in human capital. There are jobs people are looking for people to fill, but they cannot find them because we have so many people who do not have the training and education to fill those jobs. The birth rate is very high, which is good, but we have to invest in human capital. We have to invest in quality education right from the first year in school and produce the right calibre of skills for the decent jobs we are talking about. I went to a company in Nigeria that does additive manufacturing. They wanted me to come and help them. Initially, I was skeptical, but when I saw what they were doing, I was surprised. It is 3D printing. You need skills in computer-aided design, material science and other areas. They have to go to India to get some of these skills. When you expand a refinery, you don’t necessarily double the number of jobs because some things can still be done by the people already there. But the refinery may start looking for skilled people and not find them. There may be thousands of jobs that it can only fill partially. I am the chairman of a number of companies, and I know the challenges we face. At our hospital and African centres of excellence, we sometimes struggle to find people with the appropriate skills. We prioritise quality service. It is not charity. The economy has to grow to create opportunities, but the system has to produce the quality of human capital that the growing economy needs, through formal and vocational education and relevant skills. I must also add good healthcare because healthcare is part of human development. We have to read the trends and create financing arrangements that support young people who want to start businesses. Some will fail and some will succeed, but the few that succeed may become the Google or SpaceX of the world. Except for a few countries, our educational systems are not producing the right kind of people. Our universities are not being funded to train people, and only a few have the capabilities. We also need vocational education because quite a lot of jobs will emerge from labour-intensive manufacturing. There will be repetitive jobs, technical jobs and jobs created by expanding manufacturing. These can be decent jobs. If somebody has good skills, they will get paid well and can set up their own company.

How can African countries use artificial intelligence to drive industrialisation and economic growth?

AI is a fact of life now. But we should make sure we don’t become those who are just applying models and using what other people have done. We should also generate our own models. One of the things additive manufacturing does is shorten production time. You don’t need to keep physical inventory. You keep the computer design and use it when needed. The waiting time for certain parts can sometimes be 15 months, but they can manufacture them in days. One of the things the Nigerian company is doing is manufacturing parts for the oil industry, where equipment is very old. Some of the parts no longer have designs, so they use infrared to examine them and create the designs. They told me that what used to take months to design now takes hours with AI. China is leading in AI because of its population. They are generating data all the time. In Africa, we should not allow ourselves to be feeders of the data that people use to build models. We should build our own.

To do this, you need data centres. Data centres require huge power, and we haven’t even met the basic electricity demand. My attitude is that we can build technology parks where we concentrate energy and diversify sources, using solar, gas and whatever is available. We are working with people on an AI factory and technology park. Nigeria is in a good position because we have cheap gas. The country should make a decision to build technology parks and sell electricity at a price that attracts investment. You will see heavy investment, people who can do the civil works, people who can work in the data centres and people who bring equipment. Some investors don’t want to do the civil works. They want to set up their facilities and lease the infrastructure.

What would you consider your major legacy at Afreximbank, and how is the bank performing under your successor?

The legacy is the people you leave behind who continue the work, and the way they continue to think and do things. At Afreximbank, we amplified the mantra we work with: ‘If it is possible, it will be done; if it is impossible, it can be done.’ I believe we proved that we can be architects of our own future and not rely on anybody for anything. We were not driven by so-called international best practice. We focused on African best practice, rooted in our realities, ambitions and priorities.

The idea of people coming to exploit us and saying they are helping us is something we quickly made sure was gone. Nobody can deal with us except on a win-win basis. You are gaining, we are gaining. We are not going to beg you. If you give us something, of course we will take it, but with dignity. You cannot give it to us and make us look like beggars.

The way we do things in Afreximbank is that we have overlapping strategies. President Elombi is completing my second strategy, which ends this year. They have just completed their retreat, and they will launch a new five-year plan starting in January. Some of the things we started are multi-year endeavours. They don’t just stop. The fact that he is giving impetus to those things we worked on together is important. He was part of them, so I don’t see him suddenly repudiating what he was part of. That is not our culture in Afreximbank. We debate a lot. Everybody has a chance to bring their ideas when we conceive things. That’s why most people support whatever we commit to, and that’s why we execute them. It looks seamless because we debate things thoroughly and consider different views. Financially, so far, things are very good in my view. They are doing very well. In terms of development work, he has taken the course we set and is emphasising value addition and manufacturing. I don’t think the strategy he will announce will deviate violently from the direction of travel we had set for the continent. The Pan-African Transit Guarantee Scheme is being continued. The Pan-African Payment and Settlement System is becoming continental. The African Trade and Distribution Company has been established, and the Africa Energy Bank is expected to launch. The constitutional financing window will bring a new way of doing concessional financing. Some of the existing concessional financing arrangements make capital too dependent on governments. This window will provide concessional financing to the private sector. Take Nigeria for example, somebody wants to build a textile factory. He has to build his own power plant, water treatment plant and road to connect to the factory. When he brings the proposal, the infrastructure costs can account for 16 per cent of the project cost. If he had all these facilities, he would only need to seek financing for the actual project. His competitors in India, China, Malaysia and Indonesia have these facilities. He comes to you with a bloated project cost and is expected to compete in the global market. How can he compete? What we proposed with the constitutional financing window is to break the financing into two. Afreximbank would commercially finance the actual project, while the concessional window would finance the infrastructure that government ought to have provided. They would blend the financing to make it more patient, with a longer tenure. Then the entrepreneur can dream of competing with somebody else. That’s how we manufacture. That’s how growth will happen to create jobs.

World.title: Umahi: South-east Voted Obi In 2023 Over Marginalisation, But Will Reward Tinubu in 2027
World.content:
.Says Obi ‘can never be the best’ presidential material from region

.Lagos-Calabar coastal highway cheaper than comparable Nigerian, international road projects

.Accuses Landmark of ‘land-grabbing’ on Lagos beach, vow to take them to court

.Hitech got coastal highway contract through legal direct procurement; Seyi Tinubu not on board

Demola Ojo

Nigeria’s Minister of Works, David Umahi, has said the South-east’s overwhelming support for Peter Obi in the 2023 presidential election was driven by anger over years of marginalisation, but predicted the region would respond differently in 2027 because of President Bola Tinubu’s treatment of the region.

Umahi, who was emphatic that Obi failed to consult South-east leaders before his presidential bid, argued the region has other qualified political figures.

The former governor of Ebonyi State also defended the cost of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway, arguing that the project is cheaper than comparable road projects in Nigeria and internationally when its specifications and difficult terrain are taken into account.

The minister who accused Landmark Africa of “land grabbing” on the Lagos beachfront, threatened legal action against its chief executive, Paul Onwuanibe, over claims surrounding the impact of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway on the business.

Umahi, who defended the award of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway to Hitech Construction, also rejected claims that President Bola Tinubu’s son, Seyi Tinubu, sits on Hitech’s board, amid longstanding questions about the relationship between the President’s family and companies associated with the Chagoury Group.

Speaking in an interview on Arise News Channel, Umahi described the South-east’s 2023 voting pattern as an “accident of history,” arguing that voters were expressing dissatisfaction with the region’s treatment under the previous administration.

“In 2023, it was an accident of history,” Umahi said. “It was a demonstration of the anger of the people of South-east on how they were treated.”

The Works Minister said the region had legitimate reasons to feel aggrieved at the time, citing what he described as inadequate federal appointments and infrastructure.

“We’ve been marginalised in the past, but it’s no longer so,” he said.

Umahi argued that Tinubu had changed the political equation through increased federal infrastructure and appointments for the South-east, predicting that voters would acknowledge that treatment when they return to the polls in 2027.

“If in 2023 they demonstrated their anger, in 2027 they are going to demonstrate their joy on how the President has treated them,” he said.

Umahi maintained that the South-east would “pay the President” for what he described as Tinubu’s commitment to the region, particularly through major infrastructure projects.

He pointed to ongoing federal road projects and other investments as evidence that the region had received greater attention under the current administration.

The minister also argued that the political environment had changed significantly since 2023, saying serving governors, former governors, traditional rulers and other influential figures across the Southeast were increasingly aligned with Tinubu.

He said voters would be reluctant to abandon what he described as tangible infrastructure gains in favour of another political “gamble.”

Umahi rejected suggestions that support for Tinubu amounted to a betrayal of the South-east or Peter Obi, arguing that the region’s political interests should not be tied permanently to one candidate.

He also criticised social media supporters who insult South-east political leaders for backing Tinubu rather than Obi, saying such attacks were counterproductive.

According to Umahi, ethnic and regional antagonism would not advance Obi’s political interests or those of the Southeast.

The minister said the region’s long-term political interests required engagement and negotiation with other parts of Nigeria, particularly if the South-east hoped eventually to produce a president.

He maintained that Tinubu’s record in the region would ultimately determine the 2027 vote rather than the voting pattern recorded four years earlier.

Asked whether he believed Tinubu would defeat Obi in the South-east in 2027, Umahi was emphatic.

“Why do you say I believe?” he responded. “That is what is going to happen!”

Umahi said the South-east would not repeat its 2023 electoral choice because, in his assessment, the circumstances that produced that result had fundamentally changed.

He said Obi “can never be the best” presidential material from the South-east, arguing that the former Anambra State governor failed to adequately consult political leaders in the region before his 2023 presidential bid.

Umahi said his position was not driven by personal animosity towards Obi, but by his assessment of the political leadership available in the Southeast.

“Peter Obi is not the best of our finest in South-east,” Umahi said. “He’s not the best, he can never be the best.”

He argued that a presidential candidate seeking to represent the political aspirations of the South-east should first build consensus among governors and other political leaders in the region.

“You cannot play politics in South-east without consulting people like us,” he said.

Umahi said that if he were seeking the presidency himself, he would approach the process differently by consulting extensively with political stakeholders before presenting himself as a candidate.

“If I were contesting, I would have consulted,” Umahi said, maintaining that a presidential ambition carrying the expectations of an entire region could not be pursued in isolation.

He argued that Obi should have consulted South-east governors and other leaders before emerging as the region’s dominant presidential candidate in the 2023 election.

Umahi also challenged the suggestion that Obi should automatically be regarded as the South-east’s strongest candidate for the presidency because of his performance in the last election.

He said the region had other qualified political figures and argued that presidential politics required negotiation and engagement with other parts of the country rather than relying principally on regional enthusiasm.

Umahi said he had “nothing personal” against Obi, stressing that different political circumstances required different qualities in a leader.

The Works Minister also questioned arguments that the presidency should automatically return to Anambra State if the opportunity arose for the South-east to produce a president.

He noted that Nigeria’s first President, Nnamdi Azikiwe, came from the area now constituting Anambra State and argued that other states in the South-east should also be considered.

Umahi identified Ebonyi, Enugu, Abia and Imo as states that should have an opportunity in any future discussion about producing a president from the region.

His comments came as he defended the growing support for President Tinubu among political leaders in the South-east ahead of the 2027 presidential election.

Umahi argued that the South-east’s path to the presidency ultimately depended on political negotiation and integration with the rest of the country rather than treating support for a particular candidate as a test of loyalty to the region.

He also rejected criticism of South-east political figures supporting Tinubu rather than Obi, saying it was wrong to portray them as betraying the region because of their political choices.

The minister maintained that the South-east must negotiate and build alliances across Nigeria if it wants to produce a president, insisting that no single politician should be treated as the region’s only viable presidential option.

He rejected criticism of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway’s cost, saying comparisons should be based on equivalent carriageways and engineering specifications rather than simply dividing the contract sum by the length of the road.

“I deserve kudos for the cost of the coastal highway,” Umahi said as he compared the project with other major road developments.

Using Section One of the highway as an example, the minister said the 47.47-kilometre stretch from Victoria Island to Eleko Village had a contract value of about N1.06 trillion, but argued that the figure had to be assessed against the number of carriageways and the extensive infrastructure included in the project.

He said that when the cost was normalised to a standard two-lane carriageway, it amounted to approximately N7.3 billion to N7.5 billion per kilometre, or about $5.5 million at the exchange rate he used in his calculation.

Umahi argued that the figure compared favourably with other major road projects, including the Bodo-Bonny Road, the East-West Road and coastal road projects elsewhere in West Africa.

“You have to compare apple to apple,” he said, insisting that comparisons which ignored differences in road width, pavement type, bridges, drainage and terrain created a misleading impression of the project’s cost.

The minister said the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway was being constructed with reinforced concrete pavement and would include solar lighting, underground drainage, two-metre walkways, crash barriers and a corridor reserved for a railway line.

He also pointed to the extensive ground improvement required along the Lagos section, saying that approximately 30 kilometres involved the removal of unsuitable material to an average depth of about 10 metres, while the road level had to be raised by an average of about five metres.

“You remove the pit, average of 10 metres, and then you fill it back,” Umahi said, describing the engineering work required before the pavement itself could be constructed.

He said those features needed to be factored into any meaningful comparison of the project’s cost with conventional highways built on less challenging terrain.

Umahi also cited the changing cost of construction materials, saying the price of concrete had increased significantly since the contract was awarded without a corresponding increase in the contract price.

“When we started, concrete was N350,000 per cubic metre. Today, it is N460,000 per cubic metre,” he said. “The contract price has not changed.”

The Works Minister compared the Coastal Highway with the Bodo-Bonny Road in Rivers State, as well as portions of the East-West Road, arguing that their costs demonstrated that the Lagos-Calabar project was not unusually expensive when assessed on equivalent engineering terms.

His defence follows sustained public scrutiny of the project’s cost. Umahi has previously argued that the price approved for the Coastal Highway was lower than comparable projects and has repeatedly disputed calculations based on a simple cost-per-kilometre formula.

In October 2025, he publicly challenged Oyo State Governor Seyi Makinde to a debate after the governor questioned his explanation of the project’s cost.

Umahi said international financiers had also scrutinised the project’s pricing before committing funding to it.

He said Deutsche Bank, which led the financing for Section One, examined the project before the financing was syndicated and reached a favourable assessment of its pricing and construction quality.

“They said the project was underpriced,” Umahi said, adding that the financing was subsequently “oversubscribed by $100 million.”

Umahi has previously made the oversubscription claim publicly, saying international financial institutions regarded the project’s cost as competitive.

He maintained that the cost of one section could not simply be extrapolated across the full 750-kilometre highway because terrain and engineering requirements vary significantly along the route.

“There are no two sections that are the same,” Umahi said, arguing that bridges, soil conditions and other engineering requirements would ultimately determine the cost of individual sections.

The minister insisted that when those factors were considered alongside the highway’s specifications, the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway represented value for money rather than the excessively priced project portrayed by its critics.

Umahi also strongly disputed Onwuanibe’s account of the losses Landmark suffered following the federal government’s demolition of structures along the highway’s right of way.

“He was land grabbing,” Umahi said, referring to Landmark’s occupation of portions of the beachfront affected by the project.

The Works Minister challenged Onwuanibe to make public the company’s Certificate of Occupancy and other documents establishing its legal title to the affected land.

“Let him publish his C of O,” Umahi said.

He maintained that the federal government had deliberately adjusted the highway around Landmark’s permanent structures to prevent the destruction of its main facilities.

“We saved his permanent structure,” Umahi said, arguing that what was removed consisted largely of “shanties” erected along the beachfront rather than Landmark’s principal permanent development.

Umahi also rejected claims about the scale of Landmark’s financial losses, pointing to what he described as inconsistencies in figures publicly associated with the company.

He said Onwuanibe had previously spoken of investments worth about $250 million but had more recently cited losses of about N42 billion arising from the demolition.

The minister questioned the basis of those figures and said the government should not be portrayed as having arbitrarily destroyed a legitimate investment without regard for ownership or compensation rights.

Umahi said smaller businesses and other affected occupants who were entitled to compensation had been identified and compensated by the government.

He said the affected people were enumerated and payments made directly into their bank accounts, maintaining that the compensation process was transparent.

The minister then warned that the continuing public claims surrounding Landmark could result in legal action.

“If he doesn’t refrain from misleading the public, I may take him to court,” Umahi said.

The dispute over Landmark became one of the earliest major controversies surrounding construction of the Lagos-Calabar Coastal Highway after the federal government demolished parts of the Landmark Beach complex in April 2024 to clear the project’s right of way.

Onwuanibe had publicly maintained that the demolition caused significant losses to the Landmark ecosystem and businesses operating within it, while the federal government consistently argued that the affected structures were within the highway’s legally established corridor.

Umahi maintained that the government had gone out of its way to preserve Landmark’s principal investment, saying the highway was effectively divided around the permanent structure rather than demolishing it.

He insisted that the disagreement should ultimately be resolved on the basis of documentary evidence establishing ownership of the beachfront land.

Umahi confirmed that there was no public  or open competitive bidding for the highway, but insisted the procurement method was lawful.

When challenged if there was  or public bidding, Umahi retorted, “But there was direct procurement. It’s within the law.”

Asked specifically whether Seyi Tinubu was on Hitech’s board, Umahi responded: “He’s not.”

The minister said the government had examined Hitech’s board as part of the pre-qualification process.

“I’ve heard people that say, ‘Oh, Seyi Tinubu is on the board of Hitech’. We have the board of Hitech, because before we did pre-qualification,” he said.

Umahi explained that federal procurement rules provide different routes for awarding contracts, including open tendering, restrictive tendering and direct procurement, with emergency procurement available under particular circumstances.

“There are three kinds of procurement that are allowed,” he said. “There is a fourth one, which is emergency procurement.”
