Explaining the distinction, Umahi said open procurement involves public , while restrictive tendering allows government to invite companies considered to have the necessary expertise to pre-qualify and bid.

“And so the third one is direct procurement,” he said. “Direct procurement is where there are no competitive bids. But it’s a specialised kind of procurement.”

Umahi said the decision to use that method for Hitech was driven by the engineering challenges expected along the coastline, particularly the threat posed by Atlantic Ocean surges.

“Our job was to construct road along the coast — coastal highway — and we knew that we were going to be confronted with the ocean surge,” he said.

The minister cited the historical threat of coastal erosion to Victoria Island and the eventual development of Eko Atlantic as evidence of Hitech’s ability to undertake specialised coastal engineering.

Umahi recalled that repeated interventions by expatriate contractors had failed to permanently resolve the threat to Victoria Island before Hitech became involved.

“All over the years, the federal government would engage expatriates from Belgium, from France and all over the country,” he said. “Each time the flood came, there would be that kind of intervention. But it could not solve the problem of the VI.”

He said Hitech initially resisted undertaking the coastal protection work because of the financial and technical risks involved.

“The President called Hitech and said, ‘Please, can you invest to do this, to tame the Atlantic Ocean?’ They said, ‘No. You’re going to liquidate us. We won’t be able to do it.’”

Umahi said the company eventually developed a solution involving massive concrete structures and geotextile materials to hold back the Atlantic.

“They were almost liquidated until they came up with that method,” he said, referring to the coastal protection system. “And today we have a beauty to behold, the Eko Atlantic.”

According to Umahi, that track record became central to the government’s justification for proposing Hitech for the Coastal Highway.

“So when we knew that we were going to be confronted with this, we were going to look for that kind of technical expertise,” he said. “And that’s why we sent the name of Hitech.”

He said the government presented Hitech’s Eko Atlantic work as evidence of its performance, technical capacity and capability to the Bureau of Public Procurement.

“They put the Eko Atlantic as the attraction and the evidence of performance and capacity and capability to the BPP,” Umahi said.

The BPP, he said, considered the proposal before allowing the government to proceed with direct procurement on a section-by-section basis.

“BPP looked at it and said, ‘Yes, but procure this thing in sections,’” he said.

Umahi said the government subsequently obtained a Certificate of No Objection before taking the procurement to the Federal Executive Council for approval.

“Federal Executive Council approved: go ahead, direct procurement, but procure it in sections,” he said.

Pressed on whether this amounted to confirmation that there had been no public bidding for the project, Umahi initially objected to the framing, insisting that the central question should be whether the procurement complied with Nigerian law.

“You should ask me whether we conformed to the law of the federal government,” he said.

When the interviewer ARISE News Anchor Ojy Okpe reiterated that there had been no  or public bidding, Umahi ultimately confirmed the procurement method. He said, “It’s within the law.”

World.title: Orlando Pirates set for R12 million boost after CAF Champions League qualification
World.content:
Orlando Pirates have reached the CAF Champions League group stages for the second time in four seasons, securing a significant financial boost in the process.

The Buccaneers cruised past Namibian champions African Stars, winning 5-0 on aggregate to book their place in the group stages.

Having struggled to progress beyond the preliminary rounds in previous campaigns, Pirates will be pleased with their latest achievement as they look to establish themselves among Africa’s elite clubs.



The qualification will also provide a boost for Abdeslam Ouaddou’s men as they aim to build on their domestic success and challenge for continental honours.

How much will Orlando Pirates earn?

Pirates are set to earn approximately R12 million for reaching the group stages of the CAF Champions League.

The amount represents a significant financial reward for the Soweto giants, who will now have an opportunity to increase their earnings by progressing further in the competition.



The group-stage qualification prize is also around R2 million more than what the club would have earned for winning the MTN8 final.

With the group stages secured, Orlando Pirates will turn their attention to advancing to the knockout rounds and potentially challenging for the continental title.

Reaching the final and winning the CAF Champions League will be among Pirates’ major ambitions this season.



With reigning champions Mamelodi Sundowns having been eliminated, the Buccaneers will have an opportunity to carry South Africa’s hopes in the competition.

An improved squad could give Ouaddou’s side the depth required to compete against some of the continent’s strongest teams, although the group stages will present a significant test.

Orlando Pirates must navigate six group-stage matches and finish among the top two teams in their group to qualify for the quarter-finals.



Progressing beyond that stage would bring further financial rewards and put the Sea Robbers closer to their ultimate goal of being crowned African champions.

Will Pirates earn a second star this season?

World.title: Addo Elephant Park: What you will pay to enter from 1 November
World.content:
South African National Parks (SANParks) announced an increase entry prices to all its parks as of Sunday, 1 November 2026.

Here’s how much it cost you to visit the Addo Elephant Park in the Eastern Cape from next month.

HOW MUCH IT COSTS TO ENTER ADDO ELEPHANT PARK

Addo Elephant Park is one of the most popular parks in South Africa, located in the Eastern Cape, about 30 minutes away from Gqeberha (formerly Port Elizabeth). The park is the third-largest national park, and is not home to just the traditional Big Five, but the Big 7, which includes the Southern right whale and Great white shark in its marine environment.



Visitors planning to visit this park will pay a new entrance fee as of Sunday, 1 November as SANParks introduces its new conservation fee for the 2026/2027 financial year.

The new fee applies until 31 October 2027. According to the new tariff schedule international visitors see the biggest price hike with locals only having to fork out a couple rands extra.

South African: Adults will pay R115 per day and children aged between two and 11 will pay R57. Children under two may still enter for free.

SADC Nationals: Adults will pay R225 and children R112.

International visitors: R492 per adult and R246 per child.

SADC countries include:

Angola

Botswana

Comoros

Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC)

Eswatini (Swaziland)

Lesotho

Madagascar

Malawi

Mauritius

Mozambique

Namibia

Seychelles

Tanzania

Zambia

Zimbabwe

HOW MUCH WILL IT COST TO TAKE YOUR FAMILY TO ADDO ELEPHANT PARK?

A family of two adults and two children will pay R344 for a day visit from November, compared with R328 under the current tariffs. This means the family will spend an additional R16 on park entrance fees.

However, international families see a significant increase. Two international adults and two children will pay R1696 per day, compared with R1476 under the current rates. This is an additional R220 for the same visit.

World.title: Endangered rabbit spotted AND photographed in Karoo
World.content:
For the first time in over 20 years, a critically endangered riverine rabbit has been captured on camera for the first time in over 20 years.

The riverine rabbit (Bunolagus monticularis) inhabits dense vegetation along dry riverbeds in South Africa’s Karoo region. Unfortunately, due to habitat loss through cultivation and livestock grazing, the population of these solitary, nocturnal creatures has shrunken to worrying levels.

RABBIT CAUGHT IN CAMERA LIGHTS

In a Facebook post shared on Wednesday, 21 October 2026, the Cape Leopard Trust uploaded a candid photo of a recently spotted riverine rabbit:



Per the post, it’s the first time that a riverine rabbit’s been spotted in this area in over two decades.

“The record was captured unexpectedly on a camera trap set by the Cape Leopard Trust to monitor their Mobi-kraal (mobile predator-proof kraal) project,” the Trust writes. “It was then positively identified by the Endangered Wildlife Trust Drylands Strategic Conservation Landscape team.”

WHY HERE, WHY NOW?

The Trust questioned how and why the rabbit came to appear in this particular location. Ultimately, they theorise that flooding played a major contributing factor.

“The theory is that this rabbit moved to higher ground on these specific two days, due to the riparian area (their expected habitat) being flooded during this time,” the post reads.

“It showcases these incredible animals’ resilience and ability to adapt to changes in their environment – when the surrounding habitat is intact and allows for safe movement.”

HOW TO SUPPORT RIVERINE RABBIT CONSERVATION

It’s heartwarming to see animals like the riverine rabbit out in the wild like this. Indeed, it speaks to their perseverance and adaptability. By the same token, however, it serves as a chilling reminder that these rabbits are still incredibly vulnerable.



To support their conservation, the Endangered Wildlife Trust advises you to adhere to the following:

Implement sustainable land management practices on your property, such as using good grazing practices.

Oppose unsustainable development in your area.

Make sure that you don’t have any illegal traps on your property.

Manage dogs to prevent them from hunting wildlife.

Learn to distinguish between the different rabbit and hare species.

Report rabbit sightings to the Endangered Wildlife Trust at ewt@ewt.org.za.

In other wildlife news, a pangolin was admitted to the Johannesburg Wildlife Veterinary Hospital after being rescued from horrendous conditions. Despite a slow start, it is currently on the mend.

World.title: The Western Cape leads South Africa in inflation
World.content:
Things are getting even more expensive in the Western Cape. Image: Pexels

While the rest of the country struggles financially, the Western Cape is bearing the brunt.

According to Consumer Price Index (CPI) data released by Statistics South Africa (Stats SA), the Western Cape leads the nation with higher-than-average inflation.

The province achieved higher-than-average inflation

The Western Cape’s year-on-year inflation is one percentage point higher than the country’s average.



On 21 October, Stats SA released September’s CPI data, announcing that inflation rose for the second consecutive month to 4.5%, coming in lower than many had predicted.

However, the data revealed that, when analysed per province, the Western Cape had the highest annual increase.

Between September 2025 and September 2026, inflation rose 5.5% in the province.

The monthly increase also exceeded the national average.

Between August of this year and September, inflation in the province increased 0.5%. The national CPI for that period was 0.4%.

The only other province to report higher-than-average inflation was the Eastern Cape.



Inflation in the province reached 4.7%.

What’s Making the Western Cape More Expensive?

Data from Stats SA shows consumers in the Western Cape had very few wins.

Only one food category decreased in the province: fruits and nuts.

They dropped 6.7% between September 2025 and September 2026.

Nationally, at least 3 food categories declined in price.

Overall national CPI data shows food increased 0.7% year-on-year.

In the Western Cape, food increased 3.1%.

This includes a 0.9% increase in cereal products, compared to the nation’s -2.5% decline over the same period.

Nationally, vegetables are up 3.3%, milk and dairy are up 2.1%, and fish and seafood are up 7.7%,

In the Western Cape, vegetables are up 5.9%, milk and dairy are up 4.5%, and, shockingly, fish and seafood are up 9.1%.

Actual rentals for housing are up 5.9%, and health services are up 4.7%.

Fuel is up 29.2%, and passenger transport is up 14.2%.

Nationally, insurance is up 5.5%; in the Western Cape, it’s 6.3%.

It’s also become more expensive to get water and electricity in the province.

The CPI data shows water supply and miscellaneous services are up 10.1% in the province, and electricity is up 6.8%.

World.title: Boerewors: Here’s WHAT makes it uniquely South African
World.content:
Few foods are more closely associated with South Africa as boerewors. Whether sizzling over coals at a weekend braai or tucked into a boerie roll at a rugby match, this coiled sausage is so much more than a national favourite. In many ways it represents a taste of the country’s layered culinary history. And that’s why every South African loves it …

WHAT MAKES BOEREWORS

First, did you know it has a legal identity. South African regulations require raw boerewors to contain the five Ms:

Minimum 90% meat.

meat. Maximum fat content of 30% .

. Must contain coarsely grouns beef, pork, sheep or goat meat (or a blend) in an edible casing.

Mechanically recovered meats and added colourants are prohibited.

May also include spices, herbs, vinegar, salt, cereal or starch, certain permitted additives and water.

WHAT MAKES THAT UNIQUE BOEREWORS FLAVOUR?

So popular is boerewors that it has even crossed over into fine dining. Image: File

Then there is the distinct flavour of boerewors. When you eat it, you know you’re not eating just any other sausage. Traditional recipes typically feature coarsely ground meat, seasoned with toasted coriander seeds, black pepper, cloves and nutmeg. Allspice is another popular addition, while vinegar provides a distinctive tang.



Recipes vary between butchers and regions, but coriander seeds add the unmistakable signature. Unlike finely emulsified frankfurters, for example, boerewors has a coarse, meaty bite. It is stuffed into a long casing and sold in a continuous coil, ready to be unfurled on the braai.

COMPLEX ANCESTRY OF BOEREWORS

Its ancestry is international, too. Dutch settlers brought European sausage-making traditions to the Cape. But its distinctive seasoning reflects the Cape’s place in global spice networks. In the time of the Dutch East India company, ingredients and cooking traditions migrated around the world. And people brought to the Cape from places including Indonesia, Madagascar and Mozambique also shaped Cape food culture. It’s history is far more culturally complex than you might imagine.

And which overseas sausage comes closest to boerewors? Experts argue Britain’s Cumberland sausage is probably the closes. It shares boerewors’ coarse texture and traditional coiled presentation, and can contain pepper, nutmeg and herbs. However, it is pork-based and lacks the same coriander seed-led flavour profile. Historically, Dutch ‘verse worst’ is arguably the closer relative. Ultimately, boerewors is not defined by one secret spice or recipe. It is the combination of a legally protected composition and rich South African heritage.



But what do you think? Are you a big boerewors fan? Please share your thoughts in the comments section below …

World.title: WATCH: Uebert Angel linked to alleged fake Mnangagwa rally in UK
World.content:
Zimbabwean self-proclaimed prophet Uebert Angel has been linked to an alleged £2 600 (approximately R57 600) payment for a staged demonstration supporting president Emmerson Mnangagwa’s campaign to have Western sanctions lifted, according to a new Al Jazeera investigation.

The documentary, Contract Killers and the Far Right, examines connections between British political activists and Allan Nesbitt, a convicted criminal whom the broadcaster links to the Ulster Volunteer Force (UVF), a proscribed terrorist organisation in the United Kingdom.

The investigation revisits events surrounding the COP26 climate summit in Glasgow, Scotland, in November 2021, when Mnangagwa’s government was pursuing improved relations with Western countries.



The £2 600 fake rally

According to Al Jazeera, Turning Point UK chief executive Jack Ross arranged a demonstration intended to create the impression of grassroots British support for lifting sanctions against Zimbabwe.

Undercover footage reportedly shows Ross agreeing to pay Nesbitt thousands of pounds to organise the event.

The documentary links Angel to the £2 600 used for the operation, although the allegations should not be interpreted as proof that he personally handed over the money.



The demonstration allegedly involved participants recruited to create an appearance of public support for Zimbabwe’s campaign.

Angel attended the event while serving as Zimbabwe’s ambassador-at-large and special presidential envoy to Europe and the Americas, a position to which Mnangagwa appointed him in March 2021.

The investigation also examines allegations that Ross claimed Nesbitt and his associates could arrange violent attacks for money.



Nesbitt allegedly offered to arrange the killing of a fictitious business rival during a secretly recorded meeting with Al Jazeera’s undercover reporter.

Ross has denied the investigation’s findings, saying his statements to the undercover journalist were not intended seriously.

Al Jazeera said other parties featured in the investigation did not respond to its requests for comment.



Angel’s previous Al Jazeera controversy

The latest investigation renews scrutiny of Angel, who featured prominently in the broadcaster’s 2023 Gold Mafia series.

The four-part investigation examined alleged gold smuggling and money laundering involving individuals connected to Zimbabwe’s gold trade.

Secretly recorded footage showed Angel discussing a proposed arrangement through which large amounts of unaccounted cash could allegedly be brought into Zimbabwe under diplomatic cover and exchanged for gold.



Angel subsequently denied wrongdoing, with his representatives arguing that he had deliberately engaged with people he suspected were criminals as part of an intelligence operation.

The latest documentary raises further questions about the activities associated with Angel’s diplomatic role and Zimbabwe’s efforts to improve its international standing.

However, the allegations presented in the investigation remain distinct from any finding of criminal liability against Angel.

World.title: South Africa has definitely betrayed Tambo - Madlanga
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Have we lived up to what Tambo fought for, or have we betrayed his ideas, values, principles and convictions?

This was the question Retired Constitutional Court Justice Mbuyiseni Madlanga posed as he challenged South Africa to reflect on whether it is living up to the legacy of Oliver Tambo.

Madlanga stood firm in his answer, saying "South Africa has definitely betrayed Tambo" pointing to high levels of gender-based violence in the country.

READ | 'I want him to rot in jail' | Soweto mother speaks after alleged rape of daughter

He was delivering the OR Tambo Memorial Lecture in Johannesburg on Friday evening.

Themes for the address included "The Mirror, Map and Compass", focusing on ethical leadership, integrity, and Tambo’s enduring values.

Madlanga reflected on the string of killings in Ekurhuleni, which saw more than 10 women killed and bodies discovered.

READ | Ekurhuleni murders: Ramaphosa vows cases will not go cold

He said violent attacks and murders of women and children are not what Tambo fought for.

“The reality is that even without such publicly witnessed waves, we live in the midst of the continuous physical violation and killing of women. This is happening in the face of the constitutional promise of freedom and security of the person…”

In his keynote address, Madlanga also highlighted Tambo’s legacy of integrity and leadership in keeping the anti-apartheid movement united.

READ | Our people must never be held hostage by political instability - Ramaphosa

Praising Tambo for his incorruptible, selfless character, Madlanga said the struggle stalwart understood that public resources are not there to amass personal wealth.

World.title: Signs point to renewed major US military ops against Iran
World.content:
WASHINGTON - The United States appears to be preparing to resume large-scale strikes against Iran, but there is unlikely to be a military solution for either side in the devastating conflict, experts say.

Washington and Tehran's forces have settled into a pattern of strikes on commercial ships, with the United States seeking to enforce a blockade of Iran's ports and the Islamic republic trying to exert control over the key Strait of Hormuz waterway.

Neither country has engaged in major attacks on land-based targets since early September, but that may soon change.

"I'm banking now on the likelihood of strikes shortly after the midterms," said Suzanne Maloney, director of the foreign policy program at the Brookings Institution, referring to November 3 elections in the United States.

She pointed to potential signs including the movement of additional US military assets and troops to the Middle East, warnings issued to Americans in the region, and a high alert status for Israeli forces.

Additionally, President Donald Trump "came out publicly and said that he wouldn't strike before the midterms," and "it wouldn't seem to help him at the polls to do so," Maloney said.

The US-Israeli war against Iran -- launched in late February -- is largely unpopular in the United States, especially because it has sharply driven up fuel prices, and is likely to be a drag on Trump's Republican Party in the key vote.

"Fundamentally, the situation isn't sustainable in its current state," Maloney said, noting that the US blockade is "creating greater pain for the Iranians," while Washington has a large number of naval assets tied up in enforcing it.

"There has to be some kind of a resolution, either through diplomacy or through military action," she said.

Asked about the Iran on Friday, Trump told journalists that "we could end it very quickly," but said the question is "do we want to finish it off, or... do we just want to let it wither?"

Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy for Syria and Iraq, meanwhile said Friday that there could "absolutely" be a strike this weekend, ahead of Tuesday's Israeli elections.

- 'Impossible to predict' -

Jason Campbell, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, said there have "certainly been recent signs that renewed strikes may be in the offing," or that "the US is expecting strikes carried out by Iran" or their Houthi allies in Yemen.

He noted the planned deployment of the USS Theodore Roosevelt to the Middle East, which could at least temporarily bring the number of carrier strike groups there to three, as well as the decision to dispatch another Marine Expeditionary Unit to the region.

Campbell also said Israeli warplanes recently carried out a "show of force" mimicking previous strikes on Iran, and noted that US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had met with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in Israel.

However, "timing here is impossible to predict," he said of renewed strikes, while noting that "this is admittedly an expansive set of actions to take if the intent is to simply pressure Iran to the negotiating table."

Campbell said Trump's options are more limited than they were earlier in the conflict, with damage to US bases in the region having made any potential ground operation more difficult.

"At this point, there is no safe place to stage the thousands (in some scenarios tens of thousands) of forces that would be required for such an operation," he said.

Maloney meanwhile said that "most of the conventional military sites (in Iran) have already been heavily degraded" by previous strikes, meaning any new campaign will likely "entail more strikes on civilian infrastructure and targets that impact the Iranian population."

But that, or any type of military action, is unlikely to bring about a resolution to the conflict.

"From the start... this has been a war that can't be ended with further escalation on either side," Maloney said.

Campbell agreed, saying: "I do not see how renewed strikes on Iran akin to the first fifty days of the war will move the strategic needle for the Iranian regime."

"They have demonstrated a willingness to absorb a significant amount of physical pain and even some alterations to targeting that includes key mixed or even civilian infrastructure will not significantly change this," he added.

By W.g. Dunlop

World.title: Attorney denied bail in alleged R5.2m RAF fraud case
World.content:
KUGOMPO CITY - An attorney accused of defrauding the Road Accident Fund (RAF) of approximately R5.2million has been denied bail by the KuGompo Magistrates’ Court in the Eastern Cape on Friday.

Precious Muleya faces charges of fraud, alternating theft relating to claims allegedly submitted on behalf of at least 12 beneficiaries.

According to Eastern Cape National Prosecuting Authority (NPA) spokesperson Luxolo Tyali, Muleya, who is a Zimbabwean national, was arrested at OR Tambo International Airport on 30 September.

READ | OUTA opposes plan to slash fuel levy for RAF

He said at the time, Muleya had been arriving from the United Kingdom and had allegedly been evading arrest.

During the bail application, Tyali said the state argued Muleya was a flight risk, had no established family ties or property in South Africa and had the means to leave the country.

This was despite an affidavit filed by Muleya, who argued that she had returned to South Africa permanently to reopen her law firm and that she had a child who lives in the country, he added.

This saw the court deny her bail.

READ | SCOPA to lay criminal charges against former RAF CEO

According to Tyali, Muleya was an admitted attorney of the High Court and practised as Precious Muleya Attorneys.

The crimes were allegedly committed between 29 August 2019 and 19 February 2021 with claims reportedly lodged on behalf of road accident victims from areas including KuGompo, Centane, Butterworth, KwaBhaca, Mdantsane and Estcourt in KwaZulu-Natal.

The matter was postponed to 11 November 2026 for Muleya’s first appearance in the KuGompo Specialised Commercial Crimes Court.

World.title: eNCA News Bite | Gauteng Water Woes Deepen, Pastor Case Postponed and MK Party Sacks Secretary-General | 23 October 2026
