While the early voting data should not be overinterpreted as a predictor of final results, it shows Democrats voting at higher rates than Republicans, Miller says. Unaffiliated voters are also participating early. Democrats are generally more likely to vote early, and Republicans are more likely to turn out on Election Day, Miller says. ➡️ A federal judge in California is limiting the Department of Homeland Security's pre-election field operations. The agency says they aim to identify noncitizens who allegedly voted illegally in nine states.

The agency says they aim to identify noncitizens who allegedly voted illegally in nine states. ➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.

Trump must sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation case against the BBC, a federal magistrate judge ruled. Trump is required to comply with court rules or face sanctions, the judge said yesterday. The case centers on a Panorama broadcast from late October 2024, which allegedly edited the president's Jan. 6 speech to make it appear he incited a violent siege of Congress. Trump has described the broadcast as false, misleading and defamatory under Florida law.



Sponsor Message

🎧 It's unclear if Trump will sit for a deposition after he previously canceled for "matters of national importance" and suggested January as an alternative, NPR's David Folkenflik says. The case initially focused on the economic harm the broadcast posed to Trump's brand and financial prospects. Although the BBC apologized for the splicing, it now seeks to understand Trump's mindset during his testimony, as he may have intended to encourage violence. BBC attorneys say more than 200 defendants from Jan. 6 said Trump's speech motivated them. The BBC is actively pursuing details about how Trump has profited since regaining the White House, most likely to assess the extent of the damage he faces, Folkenflik says.

Deep dive

Julianna Conley/NPR

Trump promised to lower grocery prices in his second term. While some individual items have gotten cheaper since he returned to office, overall grocery prices have risen, driven by factors such as increased labor costs, tariffs and higher energy prices due to the conflict with Iran. Specific issues facing a single crop, animal species or geographic region can cause the price of one item to rise well above inflation, while lowering the price of another. NPR analyzed five everyday food items — ground beef, eggs, coffee, butter and chocolate chip cookies — to better understand the math behind grocery store prices.

🍔 Ground beef prices have skyrocketed, reaching $6.79 per pound last month, which is an 85% increase over the past decade, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. This surge is largely due to weather and financial pressures on producers.

🥚 Prices for eggs fell to $2.27 per dozen last month. Outbreaks like the avian flu can cause significant price fluctuations. In March 2025, the average dozen reached a record high of $6.23.

🧈 In September, a pound of butter averaged $3.96 — down 17.3% from last year. U.S. butter production has surged as dairy farms expanded their herds and boosted milk supply for popular items like Greek yogurt. This has resulted in an oversupply of butter.

🍪 Chocolate chip cookie prices hit a record $5.35 per pound this January, and last month dropped by 20 cents. The price spike is partly due to factors affecting the sweet treat's ingredients, such as higher flour costs driven by the war in Ukraine.

☕ The U.S. imports 99% of the coffee it consumes. Severe weather and climate change have affected harvests, and the price of coffee is still 44% higher than it was two years earlier, despite Trump removing tariffs on the product.

Sponsor Message

Read more about why these prices have fluctuated here.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Karen Almond/Metropolitan Opera

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: A new film version of Jane Austen's Sense and Sensibility focuses on the Dashwood family's two oldest sisters, Elinor and Marianne, who face financial insecurity due to laws that disadvantage widows and daughters.

📺 TV: Actor Sharon Horgan stars as Alex, a 50-year-old divorcée who finds herself at multiple personal and professional crossroads in HBO's new show Youth.

📚 Books: Barbara Trapido's Brother of the More Famous Jack follows Katherine Browne, who is determined to escape her stiflingly conventional upbringing and create a life with fewer constraints.

🎵 Music: NPR's New Music Friday host Stephen Thompson breaks down the best albums released today, including Anderson .Paak and Cordae's Heavy Is the Crown and Fenne Lily's Win Win. Listen to a playlist of the best songs from the new albums.

🎭 Theater: Missy Mazzoli's music brings George Saunders' Booker Prize-winning novel, Lincoln in the Bardo, to life in a stage adaptation at the Metropolitan Opera House in New York. Mazzoli is the first woman composer to have a world premiere on the Met stage.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Karl Bushby

British adventurer Karl Bushby set out from Chile with the goal of walking an unbroken path to his hometown in England. After 28 years, he has returned to the U.K. and plans to return to his mother's home in Hull by Nov. 1. At least four Trump merchandise stores closed this year as the MAGA Mall reports sales fell 30% from his presidential election years. In this week's edition of Far-Flung Postcards, NPR's Carrie Kahn recalls feeling the rare power of nature at Iguazú Falls on the Brazil-Argentina border. A rain-soaked October brought near-record water volumes crashing over the cliffs.

This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

World.title: Canadian cybersecurity exec arrested by FBI accused of working with criminals to defraud his own clients
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Toronto-area cybersecurity executive arrested by the FBI amid a high-profile hacking probe colluded with cybercriminals to extort money from his own clients, according to U.S. prosecutors.

The explosive allegations laid out in a U.S. court provide a clearer indication of how Edward Dubrovsky is suspected of being involved with "threat actors" linked to the notorious ShinyHunters cyber-gang.

ShinyHunters claimed responsibility last month for hacking an FBI jobs portal and stealing a massive trove of data. The group typically demands ransom payments in exchange for not releasing the sensitive data it's obtained.

"The defendant was actually working on behalf of the threat actors," assistant U.S. attorney Anthony Carissimi claimed before a federal magistrate judge in Philadelphia on Oct. 8, according to a court transcript obtained by CBC News.

"Given that those are the charges and that is what he's been arrested for, I suspect that his business will dry up," the federal prosecutor added.

Dubrovsky will contest the charges, his court-appointed defence said.

Dubrovsky, 54, was detained earlier this month during a trip to Philadelphia for a cybersecurity conference. He was charged with an extortion conspiracy offence and "interference with commerce by threats," according to a public docket.

At the time, FBI director Kash Patel said the agency had arrested a "suspected co-conspirator" of ShinyHunters. The RCMP said it was aware a Canadian had been arrested in connection with the case.

FBI director Kash Patel confirmed on Oct. 9 the agency had in recent days 'arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group,' the notorious cyber-gang linked to a hack targeting an FBI jobs portal. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)

During Dubrovsky's 14-minute initial hearing in U.S. District Court, the federal prosecutor provided a brief overview of the case against the Canadian. He did not directly reference ShinyHunters or the FBI cyberattack.

"The reason [Dubrovsky] is sitting here is because he was engaging in essentially a fraud involving his own clients, his own business partners," Carissimi said.

He said Dubrovsky was "clearly engaged in cryptocurrency exchanges with, among other people, a criminal element."

Carissimi told the court that Dubrovsky had been dealing in the cryptocurrency Monero, which the prosecutor said is "renowned for being untraceable." He told the court that, while Dubrovsky has a Canadian passport, he's originally from Latvia and at one point also held an Israeli passport.

Tim Wright, a court-appointed federal defender, described the allegations against Dubrovsky as "completely untested."

"He wants to fight this to clear his name because of his reputation, because he's a businessman," Wright said.

Canadian firm CyberSteward shared this picture of Edward Dubrovsky signing copies of his book Cyber Extortion: Strategic Response at the NetDiligence conference in Philadelphia on Oct. 6. (CyberSteward/LinkedIn)

Self-described 'globally recognized' expert

On his LinkedIn profile, Dubrovsky describes himself as a "globally recognized cybersecurity expert" who helps clients negotiate with ransomware attackers. He recently published the book Cyber Extortion: Strategic Response, intended for victimized companies.

The day before his arrest, Toronto-based tech firm CyberSteward posted a picture of Dubrovsky signing copies of his new book at the NetDiligence conference in Philadelphia.

Heather Osborne, NetDiligence's director of global events and programming, told CBC News in an email that "to our knowledge," Dubrovsky's arrest "did not occur at our event, which ended at 11:30 a.m. on Oct 7."

CyberSteward has not responded to multiple requests for comment on the firm's ties to Dubrovsky, and his employment status.

Wright, the defence lawyer, said in court that Dubrovsky had planned to attend another conference in Canada on Oct. 15, then return to the U.S. for an event in South Carolina.

"He is a very well known and well respected businessman in cybersecurity," Wright said.

The FBI's criminal complaint remains under seal. The document would typically contain further details of the agency's investigation into a defendant and specifics of any alleged offence.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Scott W. Reid ordered Dubrovsky held in custody until he is transported to Texas, where the charges were filed and where he will appear for a formal detention hearing.

As of Friday, public records from the U.S. Federal Bureau of Prisons showed Dubrovsky was still being held at the Philadelphia detention centre where he was taken on Oct. 7.

WATCH | Dubrovsky arrested amid FBI hacking case: Canadian ransomware negotiator arrested in connection to FBI hacking case | Duration closed caption 1:57 Edward Dubrovsky, a Canadian cybersecurity executive who negotiates with ransomware hackers has been arrested in Pennsylvania as authorities investigate a hacking group that claims to have stolen FBI employee information.

'Every system' is vulnerable, Dubrovsky once told CBC

Dubrovsky previously served as managing director at CYPFER, the firm tasked with helping the city of Hamilton, Ont., recover from a 2024 cyberattack.

The company recently told CBC News that Dubrovsky wasn't involved in the Hamilton file.

Once hired as a York University cybersecurity instructor, he appeared in Canadian media as a commentator on related issues and was previously interviewed by CBC News.

"Every organization uses vendors and service providers to do some of their business," Dubrovsky said in 2018, "so every single system in the world has vulnerabilities."

David Shipley, CEO of the Fredericton-based firm Beauceron Security, told CBC News in an interview earlier this month that Dubrovsky's case highlights his own longstanding reservations surrounding ransomware negotiators.

"We have seen people fall from grace before," Shipley recalled.

He urged ransomware victims who have backed up their data to seek to restore uninfected files, rather than paying a ransom.

"There's no guarantee that paying [the attackers] gets you out of the pain," he said.

If you have a news tip related to this story, contact CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle by email: thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

World.title: Trump to swap some tariffs on Canadian goods amid midterm pressure
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. President Donald Trump is poised to lift tariffs on some Canadian products — and hit others with new duties — as Republicans in border states lobby for relief from trade actions that have put them in a shaky political position ahead of November's midterms.

Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins said on Friday that the Trump administration will scrap tariffs on some paper and plastic products, refrigeration and packaging equipment, agricultural machinery and seaweed and algae products, among others, after she relayed how damaging these levies have been for consumers and businesses in her state.

Trump hit these products with a 50 per cent tariff in August, apparently retaliating for Canada's countermeasures on some U.S. goods that were imposed after the president first launched his trade war last year.

While removing tariffs on some products important to a politically sensitive swing state, the White House said it would levy new Section 338 tariffs on products with certain valves, carpets and waste products "to continue addressing Canada’s discriminatory treatment of U.S. commerce."

The six-page list of new Canadian products facing the 50 per cent tariff also includes shampoos, cocoa powder products, window air-conditioning units, archery equipment and canoes less than 7.5 metres long, among others.

Collins said the Canadian products that are getting a tariff reprieve are "essential" to some Maine businesses and farms and cannot be easily replaced with U.S. alternatives.

She said, for example, Maine's blueberry growers rely on Canadian-made specialized harvesting boxes that work with existing processing equipment. Plus, a U.S. supplier of cardboard totes widely used in the agricultural sector recently stopped making that particular product, "leaving producers with no choice but to turn to Canada," she said.

"I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner," Collins said in a social media statement announcing the changes.

U.S. Sen. Susan Collins campaigns in Fryeburg, Maine, earlier this month. Collins, a Republican, is in a tight race with Democrat Troy Jackson. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

Collins, a 30-year veteran of the U.S. upper house, is in a pitched battle for re-election in Maine as she tries to hold off a Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, who has made Trump's trade war with Canada a centrepiece of his campaign.

A moderate Republican who has sparred with Trump in the past, Collins had earlier pressured the administration to drop U.S. tariffs on products like road salt given her wintry state depends on Canadian supplies to keep the roads clear.

Another border state Republican Senate candidate, Michigan's Mike Rogers, has publicly called for an end to the trade war with Canada, saying the tariffs have raised prices at a time when inflation is already high.

Polls show Trump's dispute with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.

The tariff climbdown comes on the same day Trump claimed that Canada "very much wants to make a deal" with the U.S. to restore trade peace, while falsely claiming Canada has been making "$90 billion a year" from the U.S.

That's an apparent reference to the U.S. trade deficit in goods with Canada, which Trump's own U.S. Trade Representative pegs at $48.3 billion US — much of it driven by U.S. refineries buying large volumes of Alberta oil at a discount to world prices. The U.S. consistently runs a trade surplus in services with Canada.

While suggesting a bilateral deal could soon be in hand, Trump has repeatedly made it clear he is wedded to his tariff policy.

At a Friday rally in Fort Myers, Fla., one of several deep-red states where he is trying to shore up the Republican vote, Trump said "tariffs" is still his "favourite word" because they've "made us rich."

WATCH | Carney says Canada can wait for 'another administration': Carney says Canada can wait for 'another administration' if necessary for U.S. trade deal | Duration closed caption 0:35 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking in Istanbul on Friday, said a trade deal with the U.S. could be signed 'this afternoon' if the Americans 'were there.' Carney said 'we don't care about the timing.'

Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, said during a bilateral visit to Turkey that Canada is open to a mutually beneficial deal with the U.S. that protects Canadian interests — but the government is in no rush.

"We could sign it this afternoon if the U.S. were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said.

World.title: U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra offers Canada help following Wainwright tragedy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

U.S. Ambassador to Canada Pete Hoekstra says the United States has offered to help following the deadly fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta.

Four soldiers were killed and 39 injured on Oct. 17 when a fire that began during a training exercise on an anti-grenade launching range was picked up by fierce winds.

The military has said the fire took less than a minute to race about a kilometre, where a different training exercise was taking place on the base about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton.

Twenty-seven soldiers remain in hospital, including 13 in critical condition, many of them with severe burns.

In a social media post Friday, almost a week after the tragedy, Hoekstra said the U.S. government has made a formal offer of assistance and resources to Canada's federal government to help support the recovery of soldiers affected by traumatic burns "should it be deemed necessary."

The military said there are three different investigations into the tragedy and could not say when more answers will be available about how the tragedy occurred.

WATCH | Commander corrects details on deadly Wainwright fire: 'Getting the facts right' commander corrects details on deadly Wainwright fire | Duration 0:50 Maj.-Gen. Wade Rutland, commander of 1st Canadian Division, corrected information he provided in the immediate aftermath of the deadly tragedy at CFB Wainwright. Rutland initially said Sunday that the injured soldiers had been conducting a section attack range. However, he said today they were in fact setting up for a pairs range — where two soldiers attack a target, taking turns covering one another — a step before the larger-scale section attack range. Rutland also initially estimated the investigation would take a month. But on Thursday, he said he had underestimated the scope for the board of inquiry, 'which will take as long as it takes.'

Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre thanked Hoekstra for reaching out to him as MP for the riding of Battle River-Crowfoot, where the base is located.

"We deeply appreciate this gesture of support for our injured soldiers and their families at such a difficult time," Poilievre wrote in a social media post Friday.

The federal Opposition leader said his office has informed the defence minister and the Alberta government of the offer "whether these additional resources and expertise are needed."

"The safety, security and recovery of the heroes injured at CFB Wainwright are our top priority," Poilievre said.

"Our prayers remain with our heroes and their families."

World.title: 7 dead, 40 wounded after gunmen open fire during funeral at Greek Orthodox church in Jordan
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a church in Jordan on Friday, killing seven people and wounding 40 others, authorities said.

The shooting took place at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, about 180 kilometres south of the capital, Amman.

Footage broadcast on Jordanian state television showed two gunmen, apparently armed with pistols, approaching the church and firing shots. A third man, apparently carrying a semi-automatic rifle, then approached and fired before all three ran toward the church.

Video taken by witnesses showed broken glass and pools of blood on the church floor.

Unclear if any gunmen captured, killed

Dorgham Halasa, who was among the mourners inside the church, said intense gunfire erupted about 15 minutes after the funeral began and people started running.

"It was a weird situation, and heavy gunfire," Halasa said.

He did not see the gunmen but said other people reported seeing four of them. The Associated Press could not independently verify the number of assailants, and Jordan's security services did not immediately release details.

Gendarmerie forces are seen standing guard outside Al-Karak Government Hospital, where some of the injured persons are being treated. (Alaa Al-Sukhni/Reuters)

A government statement said that the attack was "carried out by unknown assailants" but did not say whether any gunmen had been captured or killed. It said "investigations are underway at full speed."

Jordan declared three days of national mourning, according to the kingdom's Petra News Agency.

Karak is home to a minority Christian population.

In 2016, gunmen ambushed police in a series of attacks in Karak, including at a Crusader castle popular with tourists, killing 10 people, including seven officers and a Canadian tourist, and wounding dozens. Jordanian security forces killed those gunmen after a long standoff.

2 people in critical condition

Jordan's Health Minister Ibrahim al-Budour said two of the wounded are in critical condition.

A view of the interior of the church is seen, through a shattered window, on Friday. (The Associated Press)

King Abdullah II said on X that Jordan "will confront the terrorist act that targeted Karak with the harshest penalties" and offered his "deepest condolences to the families of the martyrs, and our wishes for recovery to the wounded."

Jordan's Prime Minister Jafar Hassan said during a security meeting in Karak on Friday evening that the attack was the result of terrorist ideology and blind extremism. He said the assailants would be punished and legal measures taken against those who seek to introduce extremism.

Condemnation of the killings came from around the region, including from Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman.

Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein called his Jordanian counterpart and "affirmed Iraq's solidarity with Jordan in the face of terrorism," Hussein's office said in a statement.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres condemned the attack during a funeral as "especially heinous," spokesman Stéphane Dujarric said.

"The secretary-general also calls for all those responsible to be found and to be held to account."

World.title: Canadian woman dies in U.S. after fears of detainment prevented her from seeking medical care
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A 61-year-old Canadian woman living in the isolated U.S. town of Point Roberts, Wash., has died after refusing to seek medical care out of fears she would be detained or deported.

Paige Adamson made headlines last month when she was stopped at the Point Roberts border crossing, south of Tsawwassen, and interrogated for hours about whether she had unlawfully voted in a U.S. election.

The U.S. permanent resident was scheduled to appear at a deportation hearing before a federal immigration judge in Seattle on Nov. 4.

WATCH | Paige Adamson died after a fall last week: Canadian woman dies in U.S. after fears of detainment prevented her from seeking medical care | Duration closed caption 1:52

Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman said Adamson called her on Thursday night asking to borrow a pair of crutches from local nonprofit Circle Of Care.

"I took them over and found her literally debilitated on the sofa, in very, very bad pain," Norman said.

"She told me that she had slipped and fallen on her right side … she was relying on the help of a few friends to come and help her get up and take her to the bathroom."

Norman, who was also a friend and neighbour of Adamson, said she urged the distressed woman to call paramedics or visit the local Point Roberts health-care clinic.

"And she said, 'No, no, I'm afraid if I go, I won't be able to come back. They'll keep me or they'll deport me.'"

Point Roberts community support officer Annelle Norman says she urged Paige Adamson to call paramedics or visit the local health-care clinic. (CBC News)

Point Roberts is a U.S. pene-exclave at the southern tip of the Tsawwassen Peninsula, completely cut off by land from the rest of the country.

U.S. immigration lawyer Len Saunders said Adamson had mentioned not feeling well and needing to see a doctor. Residents of Point Roberts have to cross into Canada in order to get to other parts of Washington state or the U.S. and there was a risk she would be detained by ICE upon return to the U.S.

A United States border crossing is pictured in Point Roberts from Tsawwassen, British Columbia on Tuesday, July 6, 2021. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

"She was quite frankly scared about trying to drive up to Canada and come back in," Saunders said.

"There are no doctors where she lives. For all practical purposes, she was in detention," he said.

"I mentioned to her that I'd heard of people in the past maybe taking a boat or taking an airplane. But financially, I don't think she could afford it. She didn't have a lot of money."

Norman said she checked in on Adamson over the weekend, but her friend's condition had not improved.

"The next message that I got was on Monday, telling me to show up at her address," she said.

"She had died sometime in the hours previous."

In a statement, Whatcom County Sheriff public information officer Deb Slater said the death "appeared to be of natural causes."

Louise Trapp, operations manager with the medical examiner, said Adamson's body was in her office's care pending examination by a forensic pathologist.

'Absolute worst case outcome'

Adamson was a permanent resident of the U.S. who had been living in Point Roberts for more than 14 years.

According to Saunders, her status meant she was legally entitled to leave and enter the country while awaiting deportation proceedings, but border officials had the right to detain her if they saw fit.

"Officers have the right to take you into detention and send you on a one-way trip to the Northwest Detention Centre down in Tacoma," he said.

Immigration lawyer Len Saunders says Paige Adamson had been missing appointments with her doctor in Bellingham, Wash., due to fears of being detained or deported trying to cross the border. (Martin Diotte/Radio-Canada)

"I asked her to speak to the Peace Arch port-of-entry. I believe she had called them but was given no guarantees on what would happen … I could understand her concerns."

CBC News reached out to U.S. Customs and Border Protection for comment but did not hear back before deadline.

Saunders said he couldn't believe it when he was advised of Adamson's death on Sunday.

"This is an absolute worst case outcome. Here's a lady with no prior immigration violations, no criminal convictions. She was about as squeaky clean as you could get," he said.



Adamson is survived by two sons, both residents of B.C. A vigil will be held for Adamson in Point Roberts Sunday afternoon.

World.title: Calgary family finds box of Pokémon cards valued at roughly $48,000
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Calgary family is giving thanks after they discovered an old box of Pokémon cards worth roughly $48,000 during Thanksgiving dinner.

Kirk Ledene was visiting his parents on the holiday when his mother asked him to go through some of his old boxes left in the basement.

He went down and found an old wooden box he'd made in shop class. Inside were some old hockey trophies as well as items he'd purchased at an auction house he worked at in the early 2000s.

And buried amongst the long-neglected items was an unopened box of Pokémon cards.

He brought the finds upstairs to show his kids.

“I showed the trophies off to the kids, and their jaws dropped when they saw the box in my hand,” said Kirk.

An initial search online revealed the box in question — a Wizards of the Coast Night booster box from 1999 — could be worth tens of thousands of dollars.

“It basically became like a piece of China, like don't touch it, don't breathe on it,” said Kirk.

Colleen Ledene, Kirk’s wife, was skeptical at first. “The only thing we talked about at Thanksgiving dinner was this stupid box,” she said. “At first I was like, this is really silly."

But she slowly started to realize it was actually a life-changing find.

A Calgary couple found a box of Pokémon cards worth roughly $48,000 while sorting through old boxes over Thanksgiving. (Colleen Underwood/CBC)

Online world of collecting

Next, the family dove into the online world of collectible cards, something that was entirely foreign to them.

They first reached out to auction houses and started to receive messages from interested buyers via social media after their son made a TikTok about the discovery.

After a lot of messaging and searching across social media platforms the couple found a collectibles dealer in Los Angeles — Edward Heikali, who runs E&A Collectibles. Since starting the business in 2020, he has focused on sealed vintage items, just like the box of Pokémon cards the Ledenes found.

“The value of it now is somewhere around the $40,000 US range and it's been steadily going up,” said Heikali.

The value of such boxes is dictated by basic supply and demand and the possibility that the cards within are themselves valuable, said Heikali.

He says stories like the Ledenes' happen quite often.

“A lot of the business that we do is helping people like Colleen that find these things and they then find us,” said Heikali.

For the Ledenes, choosing a buyer and deciding whether to ship or travel with the box to make the sale was a lot to think about.

“There's so many, like, logistical things and you know, like, customs or tariffs and stuff you don't know about or you have to think about,” said Kirk.

In the end they felt comfortable with Heikali and agreed to ship him the box via UPS.

“We just trusted this guy a lot,” said Kirk. "He would send all the forms that would be needed at customs so that just kind of relaxed both of us, making us know that he's done this a few times.”

The fact that Heikali operates a business and is not just an individual buyer also put their minds at ease.

Timing could not be better

The box has now been shipped and the Ledenes are anxiously awaiting the wire transfer.

Heikali says he'll look to sell the box to a collector or another business.

“It'll likely go to someone who's going to open it himself or to a business that is going to open it on behalf of their customers,” said Heikali.

For Kirk and Colleen, the timing of the discovery couldn’t be better.

"It felt like a little bit of an answered prayer ... just with everything going on in our life right now," Colleen said.

They don't know exactly what they'll do with the windfall, but a down payment on a new house, a family trip, and a dinner out with the folks — to thank them for not throwing out the box years ago — are all in the cards.

World.title: Loblaw CEO apologizes to 2 million shoppers for personal data hack, offers free credit monitoring
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The CEO of Canada's largest grocery retailer is apologizing to about two million shoppers for a data breach earlier this year where hackers accessed private information, including names, addresses, phone numbers, birthdates and purchase details.

Brampton, Ont.-based Loblaw operates about 2,500 stores nationwide under its namesake Loblaws banner, as well as numerous sub-brands including No Frills, Real Canadian Superstore, Zehrs and Fortinos.

In March, Loblaw announced that unauthorized activity took place "in certain Loblaw technology systems" around Feb. 23. In an email this week to impacted customers, the company says its internal investigation found an "unauthorized third party" accessed certain personal information.

"We know you trust us to protect your information, and we take that responsibility seriously," Loblaw CEO Per Bank states in the email seen by CBC News. "We're sorry for the concern this may cause, and are committed to supporting you and helping protect your information."

WATCH | Loblaw returns country-of-origin labels to produce: Loblaw stores returning produce country-of-origin labels after backlash | Duration closed caption 1:46 Just weeks after removing country-of-origin labels from the produce section of most provinces' stores, Loblaw reversed the decision after being contacted by CBC News, and in the face of a renewed trade war with the U.S. and customer backlash.

As a precaution, Loblaw says customers were logged out of applications that use the company's PCiD credentials. These include loyalty programs like PC Optimum, the PC Express online grocery service and the PC Financial portal.

The company is offering two years of free credit monitoring and identity restoration services through TransUnion. Impacted shoppers have until Feb. 28, 2027 to enroll.

Loblaw is also advising those who receive the email to "be cautious" about unexpected emails, calls or texts asking for personal information or asking you to click a link or download an attachment.

"Keep an eye on your accounts and report any suspicious activity to the appropriate organization," the CEO says in the email.

Understanding credit monitoring services

Consumers should know that credit monitoring services offer limited protection, warned Cat Coode, a Waterloo, Ont.-based privacy and data strategist.

"It only covers if someone is going to use your information in order to apply for a credit card or apply for certain government documents. It doesn't cover the spectrum of the things that you could do with that data," she told CBC News on Friday.

"The privacy issue can never be resolved … Once your data is available, it is available. ... You can change your credit card number, but you can't change your birthdate."

More than a 'slap on the wrist'?

All organizations in Canada have a legal obligation to keep the personal information they collect safe, says Maanit Zemel, a Toronto-based lawyer who specializes in internet, privacy and cybersecurity law.

"It's a regulatory obligation imposed by both federal and provincial privacy legislation."

Federally, there is the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act. But Zemel calls PIPEDA, which officially came into force in 2001, "stuck in the 90s."

The government introduced Bill C-36, the Protecting Privacy and Consumer Data Act, in June. It proposes a major overhaul of Canada's private sector privacy framework, updating language to establish privacy as a "fundamental right" and replacing parts of PIPEDA.

The bill also requires companies to conduct a "privacy impact assessment" before transferring personal data outside of Canada.

If passed, Zemel says the new legislation will significantly up the consequences for companies found to have mishandled the personal data of customers.

"It's no longer going to be a slap on the wrist," he said. "There's going to significant consequences for a potential failure to comply with these requirements, including appropriate security safeguards."

World.title: How the Brewers and Rays got to baseball's biggest stage with small budgets and small ball
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A new World Series champion will be crowned as two of Major League Baseball's most frugal franchises — the Milwaukee Brewers and the Tampa Bay Rays — battle for supremacy.

Neither franchise has won it all before, meaning it will be a history-making outcome no matter who wins the Fall Classic.

Ahead of the first game in the best-of-seven series on Friday, we're taking a look at how the Brew Crew and the D-Rays got here, the Canadian connections, their World Series records and what it means to see two teams with relatively small payrolls make it this far into the playoffs

Tampa Bay Rays pitcher Freddy Peralta celebrates his team's Game 6 victory over the Cleveland Guardians in the ALCS. (David J. Phillip/The Associated Press)

Comparatively puny payrolls

Milwaukee and Tampa are in the bottom-half of MLB's 30 franchises when it comes to payroll spending.

The Brewers had an Opening Day roster payroll of just over $124 million US — 19th in the majors according to The Associated Press. The Rays' payroll was just $88.7 million US, ranked 26th at that time.

Compare that to Toronto's Opening Day payroll of nearly $269 million US, the fifth-highest in baseball. And yet, the Jays missed the playoffs.

The deep-pocketed Los Angeles Dodgers had a payroll of nearly $317 million US at the season's start. And while they made the playoffs, they got swept — by the Brewers.

None of this is helping the argument of the MLB owners, who are pushing for a salary cap to be established in the league, arguing that baseball's richest teams are too dominant. It's all part of negotiations taking place as b aseball's current five-year deal expires in December.

The Associated Press says this year's World Series marks the first time since 1991 that two teams with payrolls in the bottom half of the majors will compete for the title.

Brewers first baseman Jake Bauers hits a home run in Game 3 of the NLCS against the Los Angeles Dodgers. Bauers led his team with 26 homers during the regular season. (Kiyoshi Mio/Imagn Images/Reuters)

Homer drought

The Brewers were tied for the second-lowest, regular-season home-run total, with just 154 round-trippers. Only the Blue Jays hit fewer home runs (152).

Despite this power outage, Milwaukee put together a 103-59 season — the best in the game.

Tampa's lineup slugged 169 homers prior to the playoffs, which put them at 22nd in the majors. The Rays wrapped their regular season with a 98-64 record.

WATCH | Not the 2026 season Jays fans hoped for: Toronto Blue Jays leave fans with little to cheer about | Duration closed caption 2:15 After coming close to winning the World Series last fall, the Toronto Blue Jays are wrapping up this season with little to cheer about, losing more games than they’ve won and scoring the fewest runs in the league.

The power of 'small ball'

The strategy of small ball — getting runners on base and advancing them by stealing bases or putting the ball in play with sacrifice hits and bunts — was key for both Milwaukee and Tampa as they outplayed rivals in their respective leagues.

The Rays led the majors with 45 sacrifice bunts during the regular season. The Brewers had 37, the fifth-most overall.

The two teams also stole a ton of bases: The Rays swiped 164 bases prior to the playoffs, while Millwaukee claimed 162.

This year's World Series could be the first with a 104-mile-per-hour pitch, thanks to Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski. The 24-year-old threw a record 1,115 pitches of 100 miles per hour or higher in his first full major league season. (Kayla Wolf/The Associated Press)

Triple-digit heat

The Brewers' ace starting pitcher, Jacob Misiorowski, is the most prolific, hard-throwing pitcher in the game.

He's thrown more than 1,100 pitches at speeds exceeding 100 miles per hour this season.

Misiorowski has already set the record for the fastest pitch thrown in a playoff game (104.8 miles per hour) — at least, since tracking started in 2008. Amazingly, that's not the hardest pitch he's ever thrown.

He's slated to start Game 1 for the Brewers on Friday night.

Milwaukee Brewers pitcher Freddy Peralta and catcher Liam Hicks celebrate after a strikeout in Game 2 of the American League Championship Series against the Cleveland Guardians on Oct. 13. (Julio Aguilar/Getty Images)

Canadian catcher

Toronto-born ballplayer Liam Hicks joined the Rays at the trade deadline.

The 27-year-old catcher is in his second big-league season, joining Tampa in August, after first getting to the big leagues with the nearby Miami Marlins.

So far this post-season, Hicks has six hits, one run, three walks and four RBIs across nine games he's played with the Rays.

Tampa Bay Rays manager Kevin Cash has served as the team's skipper for 12 seasons — including in 2020, when the Rays played in the World Series against the Los Angeles Dodgers. (Kim Klement Neitzel/Imagn Images/Reuters)

The ex-Jays catcher

Rays manager Kevin Cash was a player before he was a manager and started out his major-league career in Toronto.

Cash appeared in 101 games for the Jays from 2002-2004. He later played for the Rays, the Boston Red Sox, the New York Yankees and the Houston Astros.

He's managed the Rays for 12 seasons, including in 2020 when Tampa lost the World Series to the Los Angeles Dodgers.

A long wait for Brewers fans

Milwaukee last made it to the World Series in 1982 — back when Ronald Reagan was in the White House, and years before any of the current Brewers players were born.

The Brewers lost in seven games to the St. Louis Cardinals.

Hall of Famer Robin Yount was part of the Milwaukee team that lost to St. Louis, and he recently said he'll "never get over it until the Brewers win one."

On Tampa's side, the Rays have been to the World Series twice, losing both times: First in 2008 and again in 2020.

Brewer Robin Yount plays in Game 4 of the 1982 World Series against the St. Louis Cardinals, which the Brewers went on to lose. (The Associated Press)

Where to watch

Canadian baseball fans can catch the World Series on Sportsnet.

Most games will air on the main Sportsnet channel — except for Games 2 and Game 7 (if necessary), which will run on Sportsnet One.

All games will also stream on Sportsnet+.
