World.content:
Foreign Minister leads Belize Delegation at CARICOM Inter-Sessional meeting

By Zoila Palma: Foreign Affairs Minister Francis Fonseca led Belize’s delegation to the 44th Inter-Sessional Meeting of the Conference of Heads of Government of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM), held virtually.

Discussions focused on key regional priorities, including the CARICOM Single Market and Economy (CSME), regional security, the ongoing situation in Haiti and climate change.

The meeting provided an opportunity for regional leaders to address shared challenges and strengthen cooperation among CARICOM member states.

World.title: Belize congratulates Grenada on becoming member of the World Meteorological Organization
World.content:
Belize congratulates Grenada on becoming member of the World Meteorological Organization

The Government of Belize, through the Ministry of the Public Service, Disaster Risk Management and Enterprise and the National Meteorological Service of Belize (NMSB), extends its warm congratulations to the Government of Grenada on its milestone achievement of becoming a member of the World Meteorological Organization (WMO).

As a fellow member of the Caribbean Community (CARICOM) and the Caribbean Meteorological Organization (CMO), Grenada’s admission to the WMO represents an important step in strengthening regional and international cooperation in meteorology, climate, and hydrology.

The Caribbean is highly vulnerable to the impacts of extreme weather events and climate variability. These shared challenges underscore the importance of countries working together, pooling resources, exchanging knowledge, and strengthening technical cooperation to improve our collective capacity to respond to the effects of climate change. Weather and climate systems transcend national borders, making regional partnerships and international collaboration essential to safeguarding our people and building resilience.

The Government of Belize, through the Ministry and the NMSB, remains committed to advancing regional and international cooperation in weather, climate, and hydrology. We look forward to continued collaboration with Grenada and our fellow CMO and WMO members to strengthen early warning capabilities, protect lives and livelihoods, safeguard property, and support the sustainable socioeconomic development of our countries and the wider Caribbean region. The Government of Belize once again warmly welcomes Grenada to the WMO community and looks forward to the continued strengthening of our collective efforts toward a safer, more resilient Caribbean.

World.title: Belize launches digital border crossing card for Mexican Nationals
World.content:
Belize launches digital border crossing card for Mexican Nationals

By Zoila Palma: Today, the Government of Belize officially inaugurated the Digital Border Crossing Card introducing a new initiative that allows eligible Mexican nationals to travel anywhere in Belize for up to seven days.

The initiative highlights continued cooperation between Belize and Mexico, with the aim of strengthening cross-border tourism and generating long-term benefits for Belize’s tourism industry. The card is being introduced as part of ongoing efforts to facilitate travel between the two neighbouring countries.

The Digital Border Crossing Card carries no application fee, and official guidelines will be made available through the Belize Immigration Portal.

World.title: Ministry of Health warns public against consuming meat from the Sandhill Truck Fire Incident
World.content:
Ministry of Health warns public against consuming meat from the Sandhill Truck Fire Incident

By Zoila Palma: The Ministry of Health and Wellness (MoHW) says that it has received reports through its hotline that meat involved in the delivery truck fire in Sandhill on October 9, 2026, is being sold to the public.

The Ministry strongly advises the public NOT to purchase, sell, distribute, prepare, or consume this meat.

“This meat is contaminated, as it was exposed to unsafe temperatures, smoke, and chemicals while being in a burning vehicle,” the Ministry said.

The Ministry warned that contaminated meat could cause:

Acute illness, such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhoea, and abdominal pain. Chemical toxicity, which may cause organ damage. Long-term health effects, which may lead to an increased risk of certain illnesses, such as cancer.

The Ministry says that while the meat may appear normal and have no unusual smell despite being contaminated.

“Washing, seasoning, or cooking it will not remove harmful chemical contaminants or make it safe for consumption,” the ministry said.

The MoHW urges the public to protect their health and the health of their families by not consuming, selling, or handling this meat.

World.title: Belize’s Psychiatric Evaluation Crisis: Defendants languish in prison awaiting mental assessments while others walk free without ever being evaluated
World.content:
Belize’s Psychiatric Evaluation Crisis: Defendants languish in prison awaiting mental assessments while others walk free without ever being evaluated

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Six months after Breaking Belize News exposed that approximately 40 inmates at the Belize Central Prison were awaiting court-ordered psychiatric evaluations, the shortage of personnel authorized to conduct those assessments remains unresolved, with the Kolbe Foundation now confirming that it has been paying private psychiatrists to assist inmates whose families cannot afford the evaluations.

Despite these efforts, criminal proceedings continue to be affected by the shortage, with some defendants spending months on remand without receiving assessments, while others have been released or had their charges dismissed before their cases could proceed to trial.

In an exclusive interview with Breaking Belize News, Francis “Cisco” Woods, Kolbe Foundation Board Member and Acting Chief Executive Officer of Belize Central Prison, confirmed that the institution has been arranging private psychiatric evaluations once it’s court mandated, sometimes at its own expense, to ensure that inmates are fit to stand trial.

“We do our best to have the family member cover the cost. But when in a case where somebody can’t cover it, we will cover it,” Woods explained.

He confirmed that Kolbe has paid for several such court mandated assessments in recent months, acknowledging that the arrangement places additional financial pressure on the foundation, which already bears substantial costs associated with operating the prison and providing healthcare services to inmates.

“It’s a cost on us and it’s financially challenging to have to do this because it’s normally something covered by the Government appointed psychiatrist who has limited time at the prison ,” Woods said.

According to Woods, the prison has strengthened its psychological and counselling services, while a government-appointed psychiatrist also visits the facility. However, he acknowledged that the available psychiatric assistance falls far short of what is needed.

He explained that when magistrates or judges specifically request psychiatric evaluations for inmates appearing before them, prison management attempts to arrange the assessments through private practitioners, particularly when families cannot afford to do so.

Woods stressed that the institution makes every effort to accommodate the courts, although he acknowledged that the arrangement is not perfect.

The latest developments follow an April 8 investigation by Breaking Belize News, which reported that approximately 40 inmates were awaiting psychiatric evaluations, with some having spent months and, in certain cases, more than a year on remand.

Then-Prison CEO Virgilio Murillo confirmed that the problem had worsened over the preceding three to four years as psychiatrists who previously worked in the public system transitioned into private practice.

While Kolbe’s decision to finance private assessments represents an effort to address the shortage, serious questions remain about how many inmates are still awaiting evaluations and whether cases predating the current prison management are being systematically reviewed.

Woods could not immediately provide an updated figure for the number of outstanding psychiatric assessments or the total number financed by the foundation.

Consequently, it remains unclear how many of the approximately 40 cases identified in April have since been resolved, how many additional defendants have entered the system requiring assessments, and whether some inmates continue to be overlooked despite the interventions.

BBN has documented several additional cases involving court-ordered psychiatric evaluations in the months since its original investigation, although those cases cannot simply be added to the original figure without determining whether they were already included or have subsequently been resolved.

One of the most troubling recent examples involved 27-year-old Kareem Anderson, who was charged with common assault and harm following separate alleged attacks on two women in downtown Belize City in December 2025.

Both incidents were captured on surveillance footage and circulated widely on social media.

Anderson spent approximately nine months on remand without receiving a court-ordered psychiatric evaluation. The court had not taken a plea from him because of concerns about his mental fitness, while his family reportedly could not afford a private assessment.

With no indication of when a government evaluation would become available, the Chief Magistrate dismissed the charges against Anderson in late September and ordered his release.

The allegations against him consequently did not proceed to trial.

When BBN raised Anderson’s case with Woods, he said he was unfamiliar with the specific circumstances and requested the defendant’s name so he could investigate.

Anderson’s case is not an isolated example of criminal proceedings being affected by the shortage.

In May, Harold Palma was released after spending more than four months on remand without receiving a psychiatric evaluation. He subsequently pleaded guilty to aggravated assault involving a police officer and was sentenced to four months’ imprisonment, resulting in his release for time already served.

In another case, Raymond Moody remained behind bars as of October 1, despite being granted $800 bail so his relatives could seek a private psychiatric evaluation. His court-ordered assessment had not been completed, and he was unable to meet his bail conditions.

The situation has also affected serious criminal proceedings before the High Court.

On October 16, BBN reported that Shedrack White, an accused murderer who was declared unfit to stand trial in 2024, had not received the periodic psychiatric reviews ordered by Justice Candace Nanton.

The court had instructed that White undergo evaluations every six months, but those reviews were not conducted as required. Although an assessment was eventually completed in June 2026, it failed to adequately address whether he was currently fit to stand trial, prompting the judge to order another evaluation.

The matter remains before the High Court, with further proceedings scheduled for November.

Similarly, in September, High Court Justice Nigel Pilgrim criticized the failure to conduct periodic psychiatric assessments in the case of Collin Francis, who was eventually sentenced for the manslaughter of Nestor Vasquez and the attempted murder of a psychiatric nurse.

“There is no excuse for failing to fulfil a court order,” Justice Pilgrim stated, stressing the State’s constitutional responsibility to provide adequate resources, including psychiatric services, for the administration of justice.

Meanwhile, Director of Public Health and Wellness Dr. Melissa Diaz-Musa has confirmed to Breaking Belize News that the Ministry of Health and Wellness continues to face challenges in providing psychiatrists authorized to conduct assessments for legal proceedings.

“We have psychiatrists working at the MOHW but they don’t have authority to deal with legal cases,” Dr. Musa explained in a written exchange with BBN.

She clarified that while forensic psychiatric training would be preferable, particularly for complicated cases, Belize currently does not have a forensic psychiatrist in the country.

Dr. Musa also explained that psychiatrists can assess a person’s mental fitness to stand trial, although more complex cases may require additional information.

Her explanation highlights an important distinction between psychiatric treatment and the specialized or authorized assessments required by the courts.

While the Ministry provides psychiatric care through healthcare facilities, community programmes and visits to the Belize Central Prison, those services do not necessarily fulfill the courts’ requirements for determining whether accused persons are mentally fit to plead or stand trial.

Dr. Musa disclosed that the Ministry was actively working to recruit someone capable of conducting legal assessments, expressing hope that the position could be filled as early as the beginning of November, provided recruitment efforts proceed successfully.

She also confirmed that the Ministry is seeking to recruit three additional psychiatrists for the country.

The continuing shortage has also drawn criticism from Public Service Union President Dean Flowers, who told Breaking Belize News that mental healthcare, particularly for vulnerable persons within the criminal justice system, must receive greater priority.

“I think it’s a very important topic, and certainly a very important conversation that keeps being swept under the rug,” Flowers said.

He argued that adequate psychiatric services should be available throughout the public healthcare system, including correctional institutions, and questioned why the shortage has persisted for so long.

Flowers also called for greater scrutiny of Kolbe’s finances and the use of public resources allocated to the institution. He suggested that a comprehensive financial review could help determine whether sufficient funding could be identified to employ an in-house psychiatrist rather than continuing to outsource assessments.

His proposal comes as Woods maintains that Kolbe is already shouldering considerable expenses, including salaries for medical personnel, healthcare services, outside medical treatment and infrastructure improvements.

Woods emphasized that the foundation continues working closely with government authorities and acknowledged the difficulties facing the Ministry of Health and Wellness in recruiting specialized medical personnel.

He welcomed the prospect of additional psychiatric assistance, describing it as a significant relief for the prison.

However, the broader issue remains unresolved.

Six months after dozens of inmates were identified as awaiting psychiatric evaluations, there is still no updated publicly confirmed accounting of how many remain in the system without the assessments ordered by the courts.

Although Kolbe has assumed the cost of some private evaluations, neither its efforts nor the Ministry’s ongoing recruitment has established that every outstanding assessment is being completed, particularly those involving inmates remanded before the current prison management took over.

The consequences extend beyond prison administration and healthcare. Defendants risk spending prolonged periods incarcerated without their cases advancing, while complainants may face lengthy delays or see criminal proceedings come to an end without the allegations ever being determined at trial.

With the Ministry hoping to recruit additional psychiatric personnel by November, the outstanding question is whether that intervention will be sufficient to address not only new cases but also the backlog that has already left dozens of accused persons caught between the prison, the courts and a system struggling to provide the psychiatric assessments it requires.

World.title: Belizeans cross into Melchor to stretch every dollar as fuel prices bite
World.content:
Belizeans cross into Melchor to stretch every dollar as fuel prices bite

By Zoila Palma: For years, Belizeans have crossed into the Western Free Zone in search of cheaper fuel. Now, that search for savings is extending beyond the Free Zone, with motorists increasingly heading into Melchor de Mencos to fill their tanks as they try to stretch every dollar.

At the western border, Guatemalan fuel peddlers can be seen selling gasoline by the gallon directly to Belizean drivers, often filling vehicles on the spot.

The cross-border trade has become a daily sight, reflecting the financial pressure many motorists say they face as fuel costs continue to weigh on household budgets.

Today, regular gasoline in Melchor de Mencos is selling for Q34.99 per gallon, equivalent to approximately BZ$9.21. The price difference has made the short trip across the border an attractive option for some drivers looking to reduce transportation costs.

The growing number of Belizeans seeking fuel across the border highlights the cost-of-living pressures affecting families and workers.

What was once largely associated with the Western Free Zone is now becoming a common scene in Melchor de Mencos, where motorists are searching for any opportunity to make their money go further.

World.title: Market Bag: Carrot for $500 as relief from rains not yet felt
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Despite recent rainfall providing relief from prolonged drought conditions and raising hopes among shoppers that food prices will ease, the cost of agricultural produce remains stubbornly high at the Coronation Market.

During this week’s visit to the downtown Kingston landmark, lettuce remained among the most expensive items, selling for $1,500 per pound. Scotch bonnet peppers were priced at $600 per pound, while carrots were being sold for $500 per pound.

Sweet potatoes were going for $450 per pound, while tomatoes, sweet peppers and pineapples were each selling for $400 per pound. Escallion was priced at $300 per pound, while onions and Irish potatoes were being sold for $250 per pound.

Shoppers expressed frustration over the high prices which continue to put pressure on household budgets. Speaking with Market Bag host Carlysia Ramdeen, a consumer expressed concern about how much he is now spending on groceries, noting that his money is buying significantly less than it used to.

“The prices this week are crazy. Right now, I came here with probably like $10,000 and just one bag, and for the items that I got for that price, [it’s] ridiculous,” he said. “This needs to be rectified and fixed because probably like say a couple months from now, it’s gonna be crazy.”

Catch the latest episode of Market Bag on all Jamaica Observer digital platforms.

World.title: Inclement weather forces postponement of schoolboy football games
World.content:
KINGSTON, Jamaica — Several ISSA Manning Cup and daCosta Cup schoolboy football matches scheduled for Friday have been postponed because of prevailing weather conditions.

The postponements affect matches in Portland, St Thomas, Kingston and St Andrew, St Catherine and Clarendon, as organisers continue to monitor the weather situation across the island.

The decision means a halt to schoolboy football action in the affected parishes, with further updates expected as the day progresses.

Organisers are continuing to assess conditions in the other parishes to determine whether the scheduled matches can proceed.

Players, coaches, officials and supporters have been urged to prioritise their safety and avoid unnecessary risks amid the unfavourable weather.

“Please stay safe and do not take any chances that may prove unsafe,” the advisory stated.

No details have been provided regarding new dates for the postponed matches. Further announcements are expected as the weather situation develops.

— Howard Walker

World.title: Gov’t halts overseas travel for public officials until March 2027
World.content:
Jamaican passport

KINGSTON, Jamaica — The Government has imposed an immediate moratorium on official overseas travel across the public sector until March 31, 2027, as it moves to contain expenditure and redirect resources towards national recovery and reconstruction following the devastation caused by Hurricane Melissa.

The directive, outlined in a government memorandum, applies to Cabinet ministers, ministers of state, permanent secretaries, senior public officers, heads of government agencies, board members, chief executive officers and other public sector employees.

The restriction will remain in effect for the remainder of the 2026/2027 financial year, subject to limited exceptions.

According to the memorandum, the unprecedented destruction caused by Hurricane Melissa has placed significant pressure on Jamaica’s fiscal resources and public sector capacity, prompting the Government to prioritise expenditure and mobilise resources for reconstruction.

“At this critical juncture, it is imperative that the Government exercises the highest degree of fiscal discipline, prioritises expenditure and ensures that the attention and efforts of ministers and senior public officials remain firmly focused on national reconstruction, economic recovery and the effective delivery of public services,” the memorandum stated.

The travel ban extends to all ministries, departments and agencies, statutory bodies, executive agencies, public enterprises and other public sector entities.

It said the restriction applies regardless of whether the proposed travel is funded by taxpayers, the budget of a public body or an external organisation or sponsoring institution.

The Government has also directed that all previously approved overseas trips that have not yet taken place be reviewed to determine whether they comply with the new restrictions. The specific circumstances under which overseas travel may be exempted were not detailed.

The memorandum also makes clear that prior approval does not automatically exempt officials from the moratorium.

“The Government must lead by example in demonstrating prudence, restraint and an unwavering commitment to directing scarce public resources towards the country’s most urgent priorities,” the memorandum added.

World.title: Blood blunder
World.content:
A woman mistakenly transfused with blood intended for another patient with the same first and last names at University Hospital of the West Indies (UHWI) in March 2006 has won nearly twice the $4 million in general damages awarded by the Supreme Court after successfully challenging the decision in the Appeal Court.

According to the Appeal Court, instead of the $4 million awarded by the Supreme Court judge, the woman should have been awarded the sum of $7,600,000 for “pain and suffering and loss of amenities”. The judges of the appeal, after hearing arguments from attorney Denise SeniorSmith, who represented the woman, said: “The complaint that the measure of damages was either inordinately low or grossly inadequate is irresistible.”

“In short, in the judgment of this court, the award made to the appellant by the learned judge was an entirely erroneous estimate of the damages to which the appellant was entitled,” the Appeal Court stated.

According to the facts contained in the record of the court, the woman was admitted to UHWI on March 4, 2006 as an emergency admission with severe thrombocytopaenia (a medical condition defined by an abnormally low blood platelet count). She was subsequently diagnosed with immune thrombocytopaenia (ITP) — a bleeding disorder caused by low blood platelets — and was required to undergo a blood transfusion as part of UHWI’s management of the condition.

That transfusion was conducted the following day (March 5, 2006) by the UHWI’s nursing staff. According to the evidence before the court, the transfusion “resulted in a mismatch with the appellant’s blood group as she was given blood intended for another patient with the identical first and last names”.

According to the evidence, the night after being transfused with the incorrect blood group, the woman experienced what she described as “intolerable pain throughout her body, high temperature and depersonalisation (a psychiatric state where the patient does not believe he/she is real). That pain and suffering, the court was told, “continued for several days, accompanied by sleepless nights”.

Two days after the transfusion, the haematology service became aware of the nursing staff’s error. The woman was informed of the transfusion blunder during a meeting with the medical team the next day (March 8).

She was discharged as an inpatient on April 10, 2006, but remained an outpatient of the hospital and filed a claim form and particulars of claim in August 2011 seeking damages against the hospital for the negligent transfusion of the incorrect blood group by its nursing staff.

In the claim she alleged that she suffered “excruciating pain, reduction of her platelet count, and trauma, amongst other injuries”, because of that negligence.

In December 2016 the Supreme Court made an award of $3,500,000 for psychological injury along with an additional sum of $500,000 to account for the further pain and suffering that the woman experienced as a consequence of the transfusion, making the total award for general damages $4,000,000.

However, the woman disputed that decision in January 2017 appeal, contending, among other things, that the judge had erred in determining the amount of the award which was “inordinately low/or grossly inadequate” and far less than the sums submitted by her attorney.

The Appeal Court, in reviewing the case, said the overarching issue was whether the sum awarded was an entirely erroneous estimate of the damages to which she was entitled as a result of the learned judge’s failure to apply comparable cases, or otherwise act on correct principles of law.

Following an assessment of arguments from Senior-Smith, attorneys representing the hospital, and various case law, the Appeal Court, in its ruling handed down on October 16, said: “A fair and reasonable quantum of damages for the psychological injury the appellant suffered should be $7,100,000, rounded up.”

“The appellant should have been awarded the sum of $7,600,000 for pain and suffering and loss of amenities. That is just shy of twice the sum the learned judge awarded ($4,000,000),” the Appeal Court stated.

In reference to the $10-million in damages sought by Senior-Smith on the basis of a comparative case, the Appeal Court, however, maintained that the two matters were “distinguishable”, while adding that, “In the assessment of damages, the object is never to provide the injured party with a windfall, but with that sum of money which will restore that party to the position she would have been in had she not suffered the wrong that gave rise to the claim”.

The court apologised for the delay in delivering the judgment and said, “The appeal is allowed. The order for general damages is set aside. Substituted therefor is the following: general damages awarded to the appellant in the sum of $7,600,000 with interest at the rate of three per cent from August 31, 2011 to December 7, 2016.”

It further affirmed the original orders of the Supreme Court for special damages and for future medical expenses.

World.title: Six charged in alleged $110-million loan fraud
World.content:
CHUNG... the activity alleged in this matter, although sophisticated, expansive and creative, was no match for the skills of our forensic investigators

THE Financial Investigations Division (FID) is reporting that six people have been arrested and charged following a joint investigation with the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF) into an alleged fraudulent loan scheme totalling approximately $110 million.

According to the FID, the loans were obtained from a prominent financial institution between January 2023 and December 2024 through applications supported by forged and fictitious documents. The agency also said that loan proceeds were then moved through bank accounts held by third parties.

The FID identified the six individuals charged as Errol Williams, 39, a business owner and accountant from St Catherine; Christine Elliot, 52, a customer service representative from St Catherine; Staisha Campbell, 24, who is unemployed and from St Catherine; Paige Dixon, 34, a labourer and farmer and Adrien Kerry-Ann Gordon, 44, a self-employed shopkeeper, both from Kingston; and Admarie Ashman, 58, who is self-employed and from the Kingston 3 area.

The FID said Williams was arrested on September 24, 2026, during an intelligence-led search operation. “He is alleged to have benefited by approximately $20 million from the scheme. He was offered bail in the sum of $1.5 million with a surety,” the FID said in a news release late Thursday evening.

Elliot and Campbell were arrested and charged on September 16, 2026, following a search operation. They are alleged to have received $1.35 million and $1.2 million, respectively in loan proceeds. Each was offered bail in the sum of $500,000 with a surety.

Dixon and Gordon were arrested on September 9, 2026, following a search operation. Each is alleged to have received $1.5 million in loan proceeds, which was withdrawn. They were offered bail in the sum of $500,000 each with a surety, while Ashman was arrested and charged on October 20, 2026, following a search operation at her home.

“All six face charges of engaging in a transaction involving criminal property under the Proceeds of Crime Act; uttering forged documents under the Forgery Act; obtaining credit by fraud under the Larceny Act; and conspiracy to defraud under common law,” the FID said.

It added that Williams is also charged with possession of criminal property.

The FID said Ashman, who remains in custody, is scheduled to appear in the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court, Criminal Division on Friday, October 23, 2026. The other five accused appeared in the Kingston and St Andrew Parish Court, Criminal Division, on October 13, 2026, each represented by an attorney.

The matter was adjourned for mention on February 16, 2027 with the following bail conditions:

• A stop order has been placed on their movement;

• They have surrendered their travel documents;

• They are to report to the police twice weekly; and

• They are not to interact or interfere with witnesses.

The FID said that on December 24, 2024, the financial institution reported to the police that documentation submitted in support of loan applications made by 79 individuals, between January 2023 and December 2024, was fraudulent.

“The institution had identified irregularities in the applicants’ files and, when it tried to verify the applicants’ stated places of employment, could not locate them at the addresses provided. By then, the loans had been disbursed and were not being repaid,” the FID said.

“It is alleged that forged job letters, utility bills, and pay advices were submitted to support the loan applications. Analysis of the bank accounts of two of the accused indicated that most of the loan funds received were subsequently transferred to third-party accounts,” the FID added.

The law enforcement agency also said it is further alleged that Williams “created fictitious documents, provided bank accounts to others and instructed that loan funds be transferred to them, and obtained a fraudulent driver’s licence and birth certificate and opened bank accounts in fictitious names to facilitate the deposit of loan funds”.

The FID said that Ashman was taken into custody following a search operation conducted on October 20, 2026, by members of the Constabulary Financial Unit, assisted by personnel of the Kingston Eastern Police Division, under a warrant issued pursuant to the Financial Investigations Division Act.

“She was held on reasonable suspicion of engaging in a transaction involving criminal property, obtaining credit by fraud, uttering forged documents and conspiracy to defraud, and was subsequently charged,” the FID said.

It added that during the search, “Ashman was found in possession of two separate forms of Government-issued photo identification, a driver’s licence and an electoral identification card, which carry different dates of birth: One in her name and the other in the name ‘Cassandra Burton’. Numerous items, including banking cards, letters and other printed documents, were seized by the police, taken into custody and entered into evidence.”

Commenting on the matter, FID Chief Technical Director Dennis Chung said: “The activity alleged in this matter, although sophisticated, expansive and creative, was no match for the skills of our forensic investigators. It spanned a long period, involved many individuals, and relied on documents, accounts and identities made to look legitimate. The investigation required close collaboration and the expertise of one of our longstanding strategic partners, the JCF.

“We also want the public to understand how easy it can be for persons to get caught up in a money mule scheme such as this. A request to receive money, or to lend an account or identification, can seem harmless, but it can make a person a pawn in someone else’s criminal activity. We urge everyone to remain vigilant, to ask questions and to refuse any such request, as you will be held criminally liable.”

Arguing that financial institutions also have a critical role to play, Chung said: “We encourage them to strengthen their due diligence capabilities, both in assessing loan applications and applicants, and in vetting their own employees, whether new hires or those with long tenures. Due diligence is not a one-time exercise. It must be sustained, as it protects institutions, their customers and the wider financial system.”

The FID also reminded the public that the charges are allegations and that each of the accused is presumed innocent unless and until proven guilty in a court of law.

World.title: It’s Timeless!
World.content:
Ricardo Smith .

What initially started as co-producing songs for some of the biggest names in the dancehall space has morphed into a various artistes rhythm project.

Jamaican label Armzhouse Records has teamed up with overseas-based Land Lawd Music for the release of the six-song project Timeless rhythm.

Maurice Linton, who alongside Everton “Rado” Minott are the driving forces behind Armzhouse Records, explained how the joint collaboration with Land Lawd Music came about.

“Our label has been somewhat of a musical mentor to Ricardo Smith of Land Lawd Music. This journey began when we collaborated on singles for different artistes, so when we decided to commence work on the Timeless rhythm, it was just to create a body of work that stood the test of time — songs that could resonate with everyone and have a longer shelf life. This was a shared vision between both entities. The aim of the collaboration was to bring our creative ideas together, develop a strong body of work, and build upon the foundation of the Timeless rhythm project. By combining our experience, creativity, and passion for music, we wanted to create something meaningful,” Linton told the Jamaica Observer’s Splash recently.

Linton added: “Our previous collaborations have done well so there is a musical chemistry between both entities. We always deliver great work, so we decided to repeat the formula.”

The Timeless rhythm features the songs God and I by I-Octane, which was included on the dancehall artiste’s 2025 album of the same name, and for which a music video has now been released.

Apologies by chart-topper Turbulence; Born Fighter by Zagga, who is best known for his #1 hit My Destination; Calling On You by Frassman Brilli; Victory by Ras Shiloh and Norris Man; and Late Night by Mr Melody.

Linton said: “After hearing the rhythm, we knew that it would be one of those rhythms that would be played many years from now. It has a longevity sound. Hence, the reason it’s called Timeless. And getting the artistes involved was quite easy. From the moment they heard it, it’s like the lyrics and melodies just started to flow out of nowhere. Every artiste on the project gravitated to it with the right energy. The rhythm truly is Timeless.”

According to Linton, the success of I-Octane’s God and I single was what prompted his team to get other artistes involved.

“The first song that we released I-Octane’s song, which is on his album, and it accumulated more than one million streams on Apple Music. And with that kind of success, we decided to open up the project to other artistes and the quality of music that we got was well-received,” he disclosed.

Smith, who says the name of his label represents his entrepreneurial mindset, and whose ultimate goal is to one day earn a Grammy Award, says he is pleased with the feedback that the project has so far received.

“I think it’s a job well done. The feedback is great, both from the artistes and listeners. With a project like this we can see it growing more in the reggae space, thanks to an incredible line-up of artistes that we worked with,” said Smith.

The video for Apologies by Turbulence has now been released.

World.title: Boys need more male teachers
World.content:
The Education Transformation Oversight Committee is arguing that the response to boys’ under-performance cannot be left to the education ministry alone, as the difficulties affecting some students were linked to circumstances both inside and outside the classroom.

AS Jamaica searches for answers to the persistent under-performance of boys in school, chairman of the Education Transformation Oversight Committee (ETOC) Dr Adrian Stokes is calling for a closer look at the gender balance among the country’s teachers, arguing that more men must be encouraged to enter the profession.

His call comes as the education ministry continues to find ways to develop preliminary measures to improve how boys learn.

Speaking during an ETOC quarterly press conference on Thursday, Stokes said the country needed to examine how it could attract more men to teaching.

“We may have to look at how much room we have to provide incentives for males to enter the teaching profession. There’s a plethora of female teachers. Sometimes when I go into a room for a meeting with anything to do with education it’s a preponderance of females. We need to have a better balance in terms of the gender mix that we have in education,” Stokes argued.

He noted that the response to boys’ under performance could not be left to the education ministry alone, as the difficulties affecting some students were linked to circumstances both inside and outside the classroom.

“For the psychosocial issues, it will have to be a joined-up approach. It’s not just the Ministry of Education. We’re talking about social work, social services, Ministry of Labour and Social Security, Ministry of National Security. It will take a holistic approach of joined-up government to really deal with the problem in the manner that it deserves,” he added.

The ministry’s preliminary approach identifies three areas for action: making classroom learning more engaging for boys, replacing punitive discipline with restorative measures, and providing support for the social and psychological challenges that may affect their education.

Stokes said the ministry had done considerable work to develop a systematic response, but stressed that the proposals were still at an early stage and had not received final approval.

He said the country needed practical measures that could be tested and improved, rather than assuming that one committee or a single intervention would solve the problem.

Acting Chief Education Officer Terry-Ann Thomas Gayle said the ministry was continuing to strengthen psychosocial support in schools, including through cluster-based guidance counsellors who serve several institutions where a counsellor is not assigned to an individual school.

She said the ministry had also incorporated a psychosocial component into its boys’ education programme and was working with teams to develop activities and support measures for male students.

Thomas Gayle said the ministry wanted to encourage more men to participate in education, including through mentoring.

“We welcome more men to really take part in education… but wherever there are males in education we’re maximising how we utilise their support in ensuring that we pull more boys into the focus. Our males in education, part of the thrust for our revisit to how we look at boys, is really to get more of our males to be mentors, and we want those boys in our schools, in our high schools specifically, and in our tertiary institutions, to volunteer to be peer mentors,” she said.

She added that the ministry intended to expand programmes already operating in some schools.

Thomas Gayle also argued that the national standards curriculum included activities designed to engage boys, particularly in subjects such as science, where practical and experimental learning can be used.

Meanwhile, minister of state in the Ministry of Education Rhoda Moy Crawford, who said boys’ education had long been one of her interests, expressed optimism that the situation could improve.

“One of the reasons why I’m very positive that all is not yet lost in terms of the education of our boys is when we look back at the top 10 PEP students, six of those students are boys… So I really know that all is not lost,” she said.

At ETOC’s previous quarterly press conference in July, Stokes warned that Jamaica had yet to find effective solutions to the long-standing gender gap in education. He cited findings from the review led by Professor Orlando Patterson, which pointed to social circumstances, abusive upbringings and cultural ideas about masculinity as factors that can discourage boys from engaging with school.

The committee has since placed the issue among its key priorities, as the ministry works to translate its preliminary ideas into practical measures.

World.title: WIGTON’S SOLAR SNAG
World.content:
WIGTON Energy has taken its concerns about delays in finalising a power purchase agreement with Jamaica Public Service Company (JPS) to the energy minister, as unresolved terms hold up financing for more than 70 megawatts of planned solar generation.

The company is aiming to break ground within six months, but told shareholders at its annual general meeting that it would not compromise their interests to get the agreement signed. The solar developments form part of a wider expansion programme under which Wigton expects to spend at least $8 billion over the next two years.

The BusinessWeek reported in October 2025 that the power purchase agreement (PPA) had been completed with JPS and submitted to the Office of Utilities Regulation, (OUR) for review. A year later, terms remain unresolved.

“We have recently met with JPS, met with the OUR and written to the minister of energy to express our concerns about how slow the process is moving. And this is not just for Wigton alone,” Wigton Energy chairman Dan Theoc told shareholders during the question-and-answer session.

“What we want to do is get that PPA executed in short order, move on to secure the financing, and then move on to construct the actual assets. And it has to happen in that order.”

Asked whether the delay effectively left the projects at a standstill, Theoc replied, “We cannot secure financing without an executed power purchase agreement.”

Wigton has leased land for the two solar developments, described at the meeting as approximately 50 megawatts and 20 megawatts. Its September interim report puts their combined capacity at 70.53 megawatts, more than the 62.7 megawatts of wind generation it currently operates.

JPS would purchase the electricity under a proposed 20-year agreement, but the terms must first be acceptable to Wigton and the lenders expected to finance construction.

Chief Executive Officer Gary Barrow acknowledged the difficulty during his presentation, saying negotiations had taken longer than anticipated.

“There are a few problematic provisions that we are working through, as we have to be sure that we represent the best interests of you, our shareholders,” Barrow said.

“And we will not expedite and compromise, notwithstanding we are aiming to break ground within the next six months.”

The provisions in dispute were not identified at the meeting. Theoc said the negotiations involve Wigton and JPS, with the OUR also participating.

“What we’re experiencing is a difficulty in finalising that PPA, which may or may not be related to the fact that JPS itself is going through a very dynamic time,” shareholders were told.

Wigton said it understood that the other successful bidder in the procurement round was similarly awaiting an agreement that would allow it to proceed with financing.

The company approaches the planned expansion with $3.26 billion in cash and cash equivalents at September 30, after fully repaying its Bond A obligation during the month. Total liabilities were down 23.7 per cent from a year earlier to $3.03 billion, while shareholders’ equity stood at $5.81 billion.

Management pointed to the investment programme when shareholders questioned the cash being held by the business.

“I see a future where in the next two to three years we will have doubled the size of the company and spent more than $8 billion in capital expenditure,” shareholders were told.

“So before the questions come about why are we sitting down on this $3 billion of cash, let me let you know right now that we plan to spend about $8 billion in the next two years. So we need that cash to help us grow the business.”

Wigton is also negotiating terms for its remaining Bond B, which has a principal balance of approximately $1.9 billion. Management said those discussions were advanced. The obligation falls due within the next 12 months, according to the September report.

Debt repayments have already reduced the cost of borrowing. Finance expenses fell 47.2 per cent to $81.2 million for the six months ended September, helping to cushion higher operating costs and a fall in other income.

The existing wind business is producing more electricity, although the improvement has not yet translated into higher profit across the full half-year.

Production rose 16.6 per cent to 94.7 million kilowatt-hours, supported by favourable wind conditions and spending on plant maintenance and repairs. Electricity sales increased 13.6 per cent to $1.51 billion.

Net profit, however, declined 11.5 per cent to $313.6 million from $354.5 million. Other income fell to $71.3 million from $210.1 million, largely because of lower insurance proceeds and foreign exchange gains. Repairs following the hurricanes of 2024 and 2025 also contributed to higher costs, while administrative spending increased as Wigton invested in staff and technology.

The July-to-September quarter showed an improvement. Net profit rose 51.8 per cent to $144.6 million, with electricity sales up 42.6 per cent to $726.5 million.

The expansion plans extend beyond the solar developments awaiting the JPS agreement. Wigton is in advanced negotiations for a solar project with a major Jamaican industrial company, part of its effort to build a business supplying commercial and industrial customers.

Management did not identify the prospective client or disclose the size of that individual project, but said the wider pipeline included 10 megawatts of capacity it could execute over the next two to three years.

Wigton is also pursuing business elsewhere in the Caribbean, with its September report confirming that it has been shortlisted to participate in upcoming regional requests for proposals. The company did not identify the markets or disclose the potential size of those projects.

Barrow said the regional expansion would involve strategic partners as Wigton broadens its energy portfolio and reduces its dependence on a single market.

“Our ultimate ambition is definitive and unwavering. Wigton will become the largest renewable energy powerhouse in the Caribbean,” he told shareholders.

World.title: Inside the cyber flaw scramble that brought the AI threat to life
World.content:
While no major hacking damage was immediately apparent, the way the incident unfolded over 72 hours showed how easily cybersecurity processes can break down and the outsized consequences of cyber risks in the AI era.

The man who set off the chain reaction with the early release — Chainguard’s CEO Dan Lorenc — quickly apologized in a LinkedIn post. But on Thursday, in an interview with POLITICO, Lorenc said he’d shared the information ahead of time because the flaw was already being exploited. Though others disputed that, Lorenc said he believed he’d seen enough evidence to invalidate an embargo set up to allow time to find a fix for the flaws.

While he disputed that his actions would have caused problems for other defenders, Lorenc conceded that the evidential threshold in these coordinated cyber defense systems is a “grey area.”

The revelation of the PHP flaw brings out into the open what cyber officials have been bracing for since the arrival of the most powerful tools of artificial intelligence, which not only can be used to discover vulnerabilities but also to exploit them at scale.

The cybersecurity world’s long-established protocols helped prevent disaster scenarios, in which hackers would have successfully exploited the vulnerabilities to take control of numerous websites and access their data. But the scale and end-of-days potential of AI-driven cyber risks are now visible for the world to see.

This “is what happens when AI turns up a flaw that’s been hiding for years,” said Eylam Milner, co-founder and chief technology officer at cybersecurity start-up Echo. The vulnerabilities, he added, are “about as serious as it gets for the web.”

World.title: What’s not on the ballot in Israel: Peace
World.content:
But campaigns by both the Arab parties and Jewish politicians have avoided talking about what the outcome might actually mean for Jewish-Arab relations in the region, for the possibility of a two-state solution and even for U.S. President Donald Trump’s vision for a comprehensive peace-through-prosperity deal between Israelis and the Palestinians.

“The election campaign has been bizarre,” said Michael Milshtein, a retired Israeli army colonel and former head of Palestinian affairs in Israel’s military intelligence agency. “The campaign has been focused on domestic and personal issues, and on Netanyahu.”

That means it hasn’t included “the very deep complicated issue of the critical relations between us and the Palestinians, and what kind of scenarios or solutions are left after the Oct. 7 Hamas attack and the Gaza War — for any kind of political settlement,” Milshtein said.

But outside of Israel there’s alarm — especially among Arab leaders — over the absence of any serious debate about how to end the multi-front conflicts Israel is engaged in and what that might foretell, said HA Hellyer, a geopolitical scholar specializing in the region.

“Netanyahu, or not, the Israelis are on a particular trajectory when it comes to foreign and security policies,”Hellyer told POLITICO.

“Opposition politicians blame Netanyahu for Israel’s increasing diplomatic isolation and loss of support in parts of Europe and North America. But when you look at what they’re actually saying, they’re not arguing with the policies when it comes to Gaza. They support the overall settlement project in the West Bank. They support the incursion in Southern Lebanon. Their proposition is that they could have done things in a better way,” said Hellyer, who’s a fellow at Britain’s Royal United Services Institute.

World.title: Ukraine and Russia each exchange 270 prisoners of war
World.content:
Moscow’s defense ministry also confirmed the exchange in a statement, saying Friday that the 270 exchanged Russian prisoners were in Belarus.

A prisoner exchange deal was brokered by U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration in May. The process is expected to involve 2,000 prisoners of war in total, Zelenskyy said at the time. The latest wave of exchanges took place soon after the end of another round of negotiations in Oslo and St. Petersburg.

“We express our gratitude to the United States of America and the United Arab Emirates, and in particular, we thank everyone who contributed to the release of Stephen Hubbard — a 74-year-old English teacher from Izium who was unlawfully convicted and subjected to torture by the Russians,” Ukraine’s Coordination Headquarters for the Treatment of Prisoners of War said in a statement.

Most of the military personnel handed over to Ukraine had been detained since 2022, authorities said. Some had even been captured in 2018 and 2020, during the war in Donbas.

World.title: French prosecutors open hate crime probe after deadly drive-by shooting
World.content:
Earlier in the day, French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced on X that at least one person had been killed and four others injured in a shooting in Trappes, a suburb west of Paris with a lower socioeconomic status and a large Muslim community. A 12-year-old was among those injured, the mayor of nearby town La Verrière told reporters.

“The main focus will obviously be on identifying the perpetrator’s motives — what drove him to attempt to carry out a massacre … to target our communities,” Trappes Mayor Ali Rabeh said on French broadcaster BFM.

“Our thoughts are with the victims, their families, and all the residents of Yvelines. During this terrible ordeal, the nation stands with them,” President Emmanuel Macron said on social media.

Marine Le Pen, the front-running far-right candidate for next year’s presidential election slammed the killing as “a barbaric act whose motives must be determined, and of which those responsible must be severely punished.”

“Racism kills,” Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leading left-wing candidate for next year’s election. “In the face of this heinous crime, all human beings are reminded that they are alike as they see themselves united in horror and outrage.”

Center-right candidate Edouard Philippe said “terrorism must be fought relentlessly, with absolute determination” and that “the investigation will have to determine the motives of the perpetrator of this despicable act.”

This is a developing story.

World.title: EU prosecutor probes EPP over consultant contracts
World.content:
It covered only the initial €110,000 payments, leaving the EPP to pay roughly €350,000 itself, according to Germany’s Süddeutsche Zeitung, Dutch investigative outlet Follow the Money and Greece’s Inside Story.

The consultants were hired to work on the party’s communications ahead of the election campaign. However, former EPP employees told reporters at the outlets that their fees were disproportionate to the work they delivered. The consultants disputed that assessment and said they had subsequently reimbursed part of the money.

The EPPO neither confirmed nor denied the investigation, saying it could not comment in case it jeopardized any ongoing proceedings or their outcome.

A spokesperson for the EPP said: “We have not been formally notified regarding this matter. The EPP fully respects the independence and mandate of the relevant authorities and remains committed to providing them complete transparency and full cooperation, should it be requested.”

World.title: Drone hits another ship in Black Sea near Romania, killing at least 1 sailor
World.content:
The incident is the latest in a string of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea. Dan told POLITICO last week that Russia’s intention was clearly to weaken Romania’s support for Ukraine in the war but vowed not to back down.

NATO allies met Tuesday to discuss the threat to Black Sea shipping and Dan said Romania would receive “additional capabilities” to help defend the area.

“Evidently, this is an incident within the broader process of escalation that Russia is pursuing in the context of its war in Ukraine,” the Romanian president said.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was “deeply alarmed” by “yet another Russian escalation in the Black Sea.” The ship was carrying Ukrainian and Azerbaijani crew, she said.

“These reckless attacks target innocent lives and openly defy international law. My thoughts are with the family and loved ones of the sailor that was killed. And with the families of the three crew members still missing.”

Over the last month, drones have hit several cargo ships and chemical tankers close to Romania and Bulgaria — both NATO members — killing more than 20 people in total.

Reuters reported that the ships hit by drones in recent weeks had been near or heading towards the Sulina Canal, linking the Danube River and the Black Sea. This has become a key export route for Ukrainian grain and food oil after Russia attacked Ukraine’s own Black Sea ports.

This article was updated.

World.title: Top ICC official urges EU to act ‘as soon as possible’ on US sanctions
World.content:
That has agonized senior figures in The Hague. Zavala Giler said the Commission's "lack of clarity" left private companies and NGOs in the dark over whether they should comply with sanctions decided by Washington — and what risks they face if they don't.

Zavala Giler's call to the Commission adds to pressure from EU lawmakers for a swift response after the Oct. 9 announcement. Kallas told the European Parliament on Tuesday that Brussels would use the next few months "to open dialogue" on the issue. The new sanctions are set to take effect in April next year.

"What I would hope is that the space for dialogue is not interpreted as a space for waiting to protect the court," Zavala Giler said, who spoke from his glass office on the eve of a visit to the Court’s headquarters by the EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas.

Damocles sword

Anticipating sweeping sanctions, the Court spent six months abandoning U.S. tech providers and moving to an open-source software environment, and 20 months to make its financial transactions dollar-proof. That move has been a huge undertaking for Zavala Giler's team, he said.

The Court initially deepened its reliance on U.S. technology after it was hit by a massive cyber attack in 2023, but what seemed a solution at that time became a problem in the face of sanctions. Even though the current regime includes a carveout for telecommunications, there is no guarantee it will remain the case.

"It becomes a sort of Damocles sword on top of our head that could be revoked at any time," Zavala Giler said. "I cannot count on U.S. tech companies anymore."

World.title: Feijóo vows conservative overhaul if he wins Spain’s Nov. 29 election
World.content:
“I cannot rule out doing what the Spanish people tell me,” Feijóo said, acknowledging the polls which currently indicate the PP would need Vox’s support to secure a parliamentary majority. “If they tell me to provide stability with [Vox], I will do so.”

If such a partnership is needed, Vox is expected to demand a deputy prime minister post and at least one ministry, as it has in regional coalitions with the PP. POLITICO’s Madrid Playbook this week reported on speculation that the far-right party could be given the agriculture portfolio, but Feijóo said he had held no formal talks on allocating ministries.

During the interview, the conservative leader vowed to revise Spain’s abortion law, which was amended in 2023 to allow minors over 16 to terminate pregnancies without parental consent. Feijóo said he was keen to involve legal guardians in the decision, arguing that “many 16-year-old girls who have their parents’ support will not want to have an abortion.”

It’s unclear whether that measure would satisfy Vox, which has sought to completely repeal the current abortion law and rejects abortion as a legal right.

The PP leader also pledged to restrict access to euthanasia, which Spain legalized in 2021 for adults with serious, incurable illnesses or severe, chronic and disabling conditions under strict safeguards. “Spain must become the country where it is easiest to sustain life,” he said.

Feijóo also promised to scrap the standalone Equality Ministry as part of a broader effort to reduce the size of government. He insisted the move did not undermine his commitment to feminism. “I grew up in a house with more women than men. How could I think that a woman doesn’t have the same rights as a man?” he said.

Feijóo declined to explicitly commit to further increase the minimum wage, which has risen eight times under Sánchez, from €735 a month in 2018 to €1,221 today. His goal, he said, was to raise “the average wage, so that people’s purchasing power improves.”

World.title: Arrest made after major fire breaks out at Hitler's 'Eagle's Nest' mountain retreat in Bavaria
World.content:
One person has been arrested after a major fire broke out at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat in the German state of Bavaria.

 

According to Bavarian police, the blaze at the alpine resort - known as the "Eagle's Nest" in English or "Kehlsteinhaus" in German - began on Friday evening.

A fire alarm was raised at around 9:15 pm, with firefighters able to see flames "clearly visible" as they approached the site, finding it "fully ablaze" on arrival, police said.

"The fire service’s extensive fire-fighting operations are still ongoing. So far, no people have been found inside the Kehlsteinhaus – at this stage, no one has been injured as a result of the fire," a statement from the force read.

"Shortly after the fire broke out, a suspect came to the attention of the investigators. This person has been taken into custody. Whether the individual is connected to the fire is currently the subject of the criminal investigation," it added.

The building, completed in 1938, was designed to be used as a retreat for Nazi officials, although it was rarely used by Hitler himself.

This is a developing story. Please check back here for details.

World.title: YouTube, AI and neurodivergent representation: How Gen Z and Gen Alpha are redefining modern storytelling
World.content:
In an era of entertainment that's dominated by nostalgia, younger generations are redefining storytelling through YouTube, TikTok, and even artificial intelligence (AI), according to the 2026 Teens and Screens report.

 

Conducted by the Center for Scholars & Storytellers (CSS) at the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), the report began five years ago as a way to analyse the media habits of more than 1,500 Americans aged 10-24.

Its latest findings highlight how much contemporary storytelling has diversified, with Gen Alpha and Gen Z finding just as much value in unconventional media formats like 30-second videos to feature-length films.

The majority of the survey's respondents (72.9%) chose YouTube as their favourite medium for storytelling, while nearly 4 in 5 said that short-form videos can tell a story too, with TikTok (64.2%) scoring highest among social media platforms.

TV shows (70.3%), movies (70.2%) and video games (68.5%) all followed closely behind, with respondents choosing the cinema as their favourite weekend activity for the third year in a row.

This mirrors recent findings across Europe, with 50% of cinemagoers in the UK under 35-years-old according to the Cinema Advertising Association. Meanwhile, CineEurope reports that 47% of young people now discover films through TikTok.

More 'relatable' characters

Stranger Things has been praised among Gen Z for its relatable characters and LGBTQ+ representation. Netflix

Despite younger audiences being a major target demographic for the entertainment industry, their actual experiences and desires are still frequently unheard or misunderstood.

A recurring theme is their desire to see more relatable stories, with 55% of those surveyed wanting to see more neurodivergent characters on screen — a number that increased among LGBTQIA+ youth.

Only 22.7% of respondents felt that current media portrayals of neurodivergence “ring true to real life” most of the time. One such portrayal that received huge backlash in 2021 was Sia's directorial debut Music, in which Maddie Ziegler, a neurotypical actress, played a nonverbal autistic woman.

The adolescents and young adults also said they wanted to see more “hopeful, uplifting stories with people beating the odds,” “friendships and social groups,” and “people with lives like mine.”

This continues the findings of previous reports that young people want less sex on screen and more platonic relationships, with 52% saying they believe that romantic relationships in media are more central to the lives of fictional characters than they are in real life.

“The call for greater neurodivergent and friendship representation is just some examples we found of the broader demand for more diverse and authentic portrayals,” said study co-author Stephanie Rivas-Lara.

Opinions on AI

From fake actors to social media slop, AI has rapidly taken over the media landscape and become a major source of contention among younger viewers.

Despite this, the survey's respondents seem more curious than worried about the technology, with 28.2% saying they were “fascinated" and 25.6% “excited". On the other hand, 22% said they felt "doomed" and 10.1% were "scared".

Opinions on AI were most positive among the youngest respondents, aged 10-13, with 44.2% describing programmes about AI as "fascinating".

The future of entertainment

'Backrooms', made by YouTube Kane Parsons, was one of 2026's most successful blockbusters. A24

While cinema attendance massively declined during the pandemic, there's been a steady increase in the years since as young people strive to escape their phone screens, find communities, and reconnect with the outside world.

Recent blockbuster hits like Backrooms and Obsession, which were directed by YouTube creators, also prove that younger audiences are craving more original stories that utilise internet formats and lore; reflecting the digital worlds they have grown up in.

“The gatekeepers have changed, and young people themselves are deciding what they want to watch and what they want to see more of in the content they choose,” said Yalda T. Uhls, founder and CEO of CSS and adjunct professor in UCLA’s psychology department.

“Industry leaders should ‘tune in’ to young people as well as the experts who have positive youth development and their well-being in mind,” Uhls added.

“This year’s report clearly illustrates that this is the key to creating quality content that wins over today’s youth.”

World.title: Booking an electric flight in Europe is only 10 years away, says influential Dutch researcher
World.content:
The Netherlands is pushing the world towards electric flight faster than most European countries.

 

One of the world’s first battery-powered passenger planes is being built by Dutch start-up Elysian Aircraft. Development is well underway: “There will be six engines. And we have folding wingtips, so that we fit into the current gates’ infrastructure of the airports, because the wings are very large,” explains co-founder Daniel Jacobson.

Cutting fossil fuel emissions is the most pressing challenge facing the world, and aviation is a big contributor. “By being able to transport 90 passengers for initially 800 kilometres and eventually 1,000 kilometres you can reduce emissions to zero, from half the world’s flights,” Jacobson says. “That is a very large amount of flight activity in the world. And you reduce total emissions from aerospace by 20 per cent.”

Development is well underway, confirms Elysian Aircraft co-founder Daniel Jacobson (at the right). Hans von der Brelie

Should the European Union be backing electric air travel? What can e-planes learn from EVs? When will ordinary passengers be able to fly in an electric plane?

Euronews Earth sat down with Maarten Steinbuch, a renowned Professor of Mechanical Engineering at Eindhoven University of Technology, to get his expert view of the future of electric flight.

Euronews Earth met with Maarten Steinbuch (at the left), a renowned Professor of Mechanical Engineering at Eindhoven University of Technology. Hans von der Brelie

We can’t leave it to the airlines to cut their own emissions

Aviation contributes six per cent to global heating, when CO2 as well as other emissions are taken into account. In wealthy countries, aviation is responsible for a much larger share, according to data seen by campaign group Stay Grounded.

The aviation industry is, of course, aware of its impact and has made promises to cut emissions. The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO), the UN agency responsible for regulating international aviation, adopted the goal of “carbon neutral growth from 2020”. However, CO2 emissions from international aviation have increased since 2020, as the goal focuses on offsetting the sector’s CO2 emissions rather than committing to real emissions reductions.

Climate Action Tracker rates the ICAO’s goal of carbon neutral growth from 2020 levels as “Highly insufficient”.

The European Commission, Professor Steinbuch says, is focused on helping “current aviation” to “become as sustainable as possible”. But rather than helping current planes to reduce the emissions they create, the Commission should be supporting a pivot to zero emissions planes – electric ones. “There is not enough attention yet to have a revolution in airspace electrification. So, it’s more an evolution and not yet a revolution.”

“There is not enough attention yet to have a revolution in airspace electrification. So, it’s more an evolution and not yet a revolution”, says Maarten Steinbuch. Hans von der Brelie

Could electric planes become as common as EVs?

Electric vehicles have been adopted across Europe, faster than many people predicted. Sales grew year-on-year from 2020 to 2025, with one in four cars sold worldwide in 2025 being electric, according to the International Energy Agency. As a result, about five per cent of the global car stock is now electrified, displacing 1.2 million barrels of oil per day in 2025.

This shift did not happen by magic but because car companies were put under pressure through government policy. “I have seen, in the electrification of passenger cars, that being strict on dates when manufacturers of cars effectively should have a sufficient number of models of electric cars available really helped,” says Professor Steinbuch.

He believes that if similar requirements were made of aeroplane manufacturers, we could see real change. “We need legislation saying that part of a fleet could be electrified in this or that year. Push that also with legislation.”

The European Commission also needs to speed up how quickly new aeroplane designs are certified. Safety must be the “first, second and third” priority, of course, but “it could help if the European Commission would put a little bit more effort in, so that those processes could be accelerated and giving space for scale-ups to build up both on the infrastructure for electrification of airflights, but also for the manufacturing and the startups who make new planes.”

In the workshop of the Dutch start-up Elysian Aircraft: the wings will be fully packed with batteries. Hans von der Brelie

When will electric flights be available to us all?

Seeing the owners of low-cost airlines become influential millionaires, it can be difficult to imagine aviation losing its grip on the market.

But Professor Steinbuch says there are plenty of reasons to be optimistic that electric flights will be common in the not too distant future – and there’s one key component.

“It’s not a dream, it is very real and the most important part of development is the batteries. Batteries are the key thing. All over the world billions of euros and dollars are spent in development. Why? Because everybody knows that batteries are the Holy Grail for the transition both in mobility as well as in energy.”

Batteries are so crucial because they power electric planes, and how long they last determines how far they can fly. “If solid-state batteries with double the capacity – up to 500 watt-hours per kilogram – come onto the market, electric flying will attract the interest of far more people. And this point will come soon.”

Euronews Earth takes a ride in an electric 2-seater: Start-ups such as E-Flight Academy already started to train pilots in electrical airplanes. Hans von der Brelie

How soon? “I think in 2032 or so, within six years, we might see the first 500 km range airplanes for cargo and for passengers, at five seats, so that's a very small scale – but still it will be a start for specialised purposes.” Three years later, in 2035, “we could see nine-seaters, maybe 20-seaters, flying with a range of 500 kilometres. 80- or 90-seaters will be more close to 2040, even maybe beyond.”

World.title: Grocery prices across Europe: Where is food most expensive and why?
World.content:
Food takes a sizeable share of household budgets across Europe, but the cost of filling a shopping basket varies widely from country to country. In the EU, food and non-alcoholic beverages account for 13.6% of household spending, compared with 23.6% for housing and utility bills, according to Eurostat.

 

Which countries are the most expensive for groceries, and what drives these differences?

According to mid-2026 data from Numbeo, a crowdsourced cost-of-living database, the grocery index ranges from 57.2 in Moldova to 189.2 in Switzerland, with the EU average set at 100. This means groceries are 89.2% more expensive than the EU average in Switzerland, while they are 42.8% cheaper in Moldova.

To illustrate the gap, a basket costing €100 at average EU prices would cost €189.20 in Switzerland and €57.20 in Moldova, based on the index.

Numbeo’s index takes New York as the base at 100. Euronews Business converted the index to use the EU average as 100.

Which are the most expensive countries?

Three of the five most expensive countries are Nordic. Iceland (183.6) ranks second, followed by Norway (154.4), Luxembourg (134.9) and Denmark (128.4). The other Nordic countries are also above the EU average: Finland (119.7) and Sweden (116.6).

Among five of Europe’s major economies, France is the most expensive for groceries, at 27.5% above the EU average. Spain (89.7) is the only one below the average. The UK (111.9), Germany (111.6) and Italy (110.2) are above it, with similar price levels.

Austria (124.5), Ireland (122), Belgium (117.6) and the Netherlands (116.4) are also among the more expensive countries, all above the EU average.

Cheapest EU country: Groceries in Romania cost a third less

Within the EU, Romania (66.7) is the cheapest country for groceries, with prices 33.3% below the EU average.

More broadly, groceries are cheaper in Eastern European and Balkan countries, including EU candidates. For example, the index is 59.8 in North Macedonia, 67.9 in Bosnia and Herzegovina and 68.8 in Serbia.

Turkey (82.1) is more expensive than several EU members, although it remains below the EU average. Turkey also has the highest food inflation in Europe.

Lower prices do not mean greater affordability

Ilaria Benedetti, an associate professor at the University of Tuscia, pointed out that while food prices are lower than the EU average in some countries, households spend a larger share of their budget on food. For example, groceries are cheaper in Romania, but households spend 23.1% of their budgets on food and non-alcoholic drinks. This share is also above 20% in Bulgaria.

“Lower prices do not necessarily mean greater affordability,” Prof. Jeremiás Máté Balogh from Corvinus University told Euronews Business.

Pointing to differences in wages and purchasing power, he emphasised that groceries can be cheaper in absolute terms but less affordable relative to what people earn after tax.

An 18-item grocery basket costs €69.84 in the EU

Numbeo lists 19 items in its “Markets” category. Euronews Business collected the prices of these items in October 2026. Adding together the listed prices of 18 items, with each counted once rather than weighted, gives an average EU basket cost of €69.84.

Cigarettes are excluded from the Euronews calculation because prices vary substantially and the share of smokers differs across countries.

As with the index, the grocery basket is most expensive in Switzerland at €137.90, while Moldova is the cheapest at €41.10.

The basket also costs more than €100 in Norway (€116.10). Other expensive countries include Luxembourg (€99), Austria (€88.10) and Denmark (€87.70).

France is still the most expensive among the five major economies compared. The basket costs €87.40 in France, compared with just €63 in Spain. These groceries cost €80 in Italy, €75.20 in Germany and €69.10 in the UK.

The 18 grocery items can be bought for less than €50 in North Macedonia (€43.90), Kosovo (€45.50), Romania (€45.90), Georgia (€46.90), Poland (€49.60), Serbia (€49.70), Montenegro (€49.80) and Bosnia and Herzegovina (€49.80).

However, these rankings are based on nominal prices. When purchasing power is taken into account, the gap narrows. The rankings may also change slightly when the basket is weighted.

The role of energy prices and labour costs

“Labour costs have likely become one of the most persistent drivers of grocery prices across Europe, but energy costs remain an important factor,” Balogh said. He noted that higher energy, fuel, and transportation costs continue to affect agricultural production, food processing, and distribution.

Benedetti said that energy is the main driver of recent rises in food prices, particularly fuel this time. She added that, since the strikes on Iran at the end of February, the average price of diesel in the EU had risen from €1.59 per litre on 23 February to €2.24 on 28 September, the highest level since records began in 2005.

“Diesel moves the whole food chain, from tractors to the lorries that supply supermarkets,” she told Euronews Business.

She also pointed out that when inflation slows, prices do not necessarily fall. If inflation remains positive, they keep rising, only more slowly, from a higher level.

Why does bread cost more than three times as much in Denmark as in Bulgaria?

“The price of food in a shop is only partly the cost of the food itself,” Benedetti said.

“It also includes wages, energy, rents, transport and taxes, which are much higher in richer countries.”

She noted that a 500g loaf of fresh white bread costs €3.18 in Denmark and €1.02 in Bulgaria — more than three times as much, according to Numbeo. A dozen eggs, a more standardised product, costs €4.52 in Denmark and €2.69 in Estonia, less than twice as much.

Balogh explained that differences in grocery prices across European countries reflect a combination of factors, including wages, land and labour costs, retail market structure, taxation, exchange rates, logistics and transportation costs, agricultural productivity and consumer preferences.
