World.title: Neurodivergentes: la etiqueta de moda para los cerebros fuera de lo común
World.content:
El término nació como eufemismo para las personas autistas, pero hoy se ha convertido en un cajón de sastre donde entra un sinfín de trastornos y peculiaridades

A Paloma le dijeron que su hija, con altas capacidades, era neurodivergente. Poco después le sugirieron que su hijo, con hipersensibilidad emocional, quizá entrara también en esa categoría, que a Paloma le sonó sugestiva y misteriosa, con un toque exclusivo, como de mente fuera del rebaño. En ambos casos se lo comunicaron en el colegio donde lleva a sus retoños, durante sendas reuniones con el equipo de psicopedagogía. Paloma se lo comentó entonces a su psicóloga, quien aportó una nueva evaluación: con dos niños así, lo más probable era que la madre fuese, asimismo, neurodivergente.

La etiqueta no solo corre como la pólvora entre profesionales. Con 20 años, Elvira es una brillante universitaria. Saca excelentes notas y discurre con una agilidad de vértigo. Hace años le hicieron un diagnóstico por TDAH. Ningún experto ha insinuado aún que sea neurodivergente, aunque ella se pregunta si encaja en esta denominación. Cuenta que así se llaman a sí mismos muchos de sus amigos. Porque se lo ha dicho algún especialista o porque, tras ver un par de entradas sobre el tema en redes sociales, han decidido subirse al carro motu propio. “Es una palabra que utilizamos con frecuencia”, confirma.

A medio camino entre el eufemismo anti-estigma y la lucha de minorías, lo neurodivergente está de moda. Arrasa en internet y en las librerías. Protagoniza decenas de eventos y mil conversaciones sobre lo heterogéneo de la mente humana. Ya es moneda corriente, otra tendencia sociolingüística al alza en psicología, otro neologismo que ha llegado para quedarse, sobre todo entre las nuevas generaciones. Y su empuje se va colando en las políticas de inclusión de empresas e instituciones. Mientras se hincha la burbuja, el fenómeno ha provocado unas cuantas polémicas con una pregunta de fondo. ¿Ayuda o perjudica a individuos con un cerebro fuera de lo común?

La idea nació en Estados Unidos —como tantas otras con frágil base científica y fuerte tirón popular— y se ha ido propagando a ritmo viral en el resto del mundo. Como concepto, fue acuñado un poco al alimón por dos mujeres autistas: Judy Singer, quien empezó a hablar de neurodiversidad a finales de los noventa, y Kassiane Asasumasu, que a principios de siglo dio con el término neurodivergente.

Este parto a dos bandas ha producido confusión, ya que, en teoría, Singer y Asasumasu hablaban de cosas distintas. La primera constató una obviedad: cada cerebro es único. En nuestros sistemas neurológicos, no hay dos casos idénticos. Singer añadió que era hora de dejar de considerar nuestras diferencias desde una óptica médica. Por su parte, Asasumasu afinó esa evidencia: en la diversidad, hay gente que no es neurotípica, es decir, que se sale de la media en cuanto a procesos cognitivos. Son los neurodivergentes. Resumiendo, todos somos neurodiversos, pero solo algunos neurodivergentes.

En la actualidad, ambas nociones se entremezclan y solapan. Se supone que el movimiento de la neurodiversidad (así se denomina a la faceta activista del asunto) defiende a las personas neurodivergentes, una aparente contradicción que ha contribuido a liar más un ámbito de por sí bastante escurridizo. Vago en su definición, plagado de demandas que en ocasiones chocan entre sí, con la ciencia y la ideología en un permanente tira y afloja.

Brumas léxicas aparte, Singer y Asasumasu sí compartían un objetivo: despatologizar el autismo. En origen, tanto la neurodiversidad como la neurodivergencia surgieron para referirse de otro modo (y con otras connotaciones) a la gente con trastorno del espectro autista (TEA). Básicamente, sin el trastorno en la ecuación. “El mensaje era claro: no queremos cura, sino derechos e integración; no tenemos una patología, sino una condición atípica en el neurodesarrollo”, explica Francisco Ortega, de la Institución Catalana de Investigación y Estudios Avanzados, quien ha seguido al movimiento desde sus inicios, cuando era coto privado de las personas autistas. Con el tiempo, añade Ortega, “se ha ido extendiendo enormemente, en parte porque los autistas, que suelen tener dificultades de sociabilidad, son muy activos en internet, donde se sienten cómodos”. Su mensaje fue calando en otras comunidades que compraron la premisa básica: donde antes había enfermedad, ahora hay mera diferencia.

En la actualidad, nadie sabe exactamente dónde se sitúan los límites de la divergencia en cuestiones neurológicas. Ni qué significa (e implica) tal idea. Muchas clasificaciones incluyen, además del TEA, el TDAH, el síndrome de Tourette y la dislexia. Otras, como la de la Cleveland Clinic, tiran de manga ancha y amplían el paraguas hasta el síndrome de Down, el TOC, el trastorno bipolar o la ansiedad social. En los listados aparecen dolencias de raíz genética y otras más sujetas a las circunstancias. Se juntan la discapacidad intelectual y el diagnóstico psiquiátrico. Conviven la enfermedad (o lo que el consenso científico dice que lo es) y lo simplemente variopinto.

Orgullo neuro

En esta difusa amalgama, la investigadora británica Nancy Doyle pone orden reservando la etiqueta en un tercio de la población, según sus datos. Matiza que el término se refiere ante todo a perfiles spiky (algo así como picudos o con altibajos): personas que destacan en ciertas habilidades y presentan dificultades en otras. Son, aclara Doyle, aproximadamente la mitad del conjunto de personas neurodivergentes. El ejemplo paradigmático sería el autista con elevado cociente intelectual, el Sheldon Cooper de The Big Bang Theory. Doyle admite que “hoy parece que todo el mundo es neurodivergente” y que esa barra libre, sumada al “elemento identitario, podría desvirtuar el movimiento”. Sin fronteras nítidas ni requisitos diagnósticos, nada impide que alguien se autoperciba como neurodivergente. Aunque a todas luces tenga un cerebro de lo más corriente.

La tensión entre lo identitario —ya hay Día del Orgullo neuro, el 16 de junio— y lo patológico (o no) ha generado la principal controversia en torno a la neurodiversidad. De un lado, los militantes más radicales del movimiento, la mayoría personas con TEA altamente funcionales. Del otro, las familias con hijos autistas en el escalón más discapacitante del espectro. “Hay padres que reprochan a esos activistas que, mientras ellos van a la universidad, sus hijos no hablan, se dan golpes en la pared o tienen incontinencia urinaria”, apunta Ortega. En estos casos, indica, más que el orgullo, les preocupa encontrar tratamientos.

Alfonso Troisi, que el pasado 2025 publicó un artículo científico sobre el debate enfermedad vs divergencia, va más allá al advertir de una cierta glamurización rodeando al concepto. “Hay algo guay en considerarse neurodivergente, como si uno fuera especial, distinto de la mayoría. Nadie quiere ser esquizofrénico, pero bipolar quizá no suene tan mal. ¡Van Gogh era bipolar!”. Tanto Troisi como Ortega han conocido casos de personas que, sin ningún indicio de TEA o síndrome de Tourette, se empeñaban en adjudicarse tales diagnósticos.

Con lo heterodoxo por bandera, batallando el estigma de lo patológico, hay quien alerta de que la lucha por normalizar la neurodiversidad podría, paradójicamente, socavar derechos entre algunos colectivos. Ortega cuenta que el propio Steve Silberman —autor de referencia tras la publicación de su obra Neurotribes (Una tribu propia, en su edición en español)— señaló que, “si los autistas salían del ámbito de la discapacidad, perderían protección”. Troisi, por su parte, traza un paralelismo con el llamado movimiento sordo. “En EEUU hay gente que aboga por que la sordera, para la que existen tratamientos muy eficaces en algunos casos, deje de considerarse una enfermedad y pase a ser el rasgo que une a una minoría cultural”.

Para Doyle, estas polémicas —nutridas casi siempre en la polarización digital— nos alejan de la senda principal del movimiento: hacer la vida un poco más fácil a la gente que no tiene una mente estándar. Se trata de lograr que ciertas anomalías cognitivas dejen de suponer un problema “por culpa de sistemas educativos rígidos, entornos de trabajo inflexibles y lugares públicos abrumadores”. Doyle anima a repensar “algunas de las normas que hemos diseñado sobre cómo estudiamos, trabajamos y vivimos” para que “esas divergencias sean menos discapacitantes”.

Esta investigadora subraya que su país, el Reino Unido, se ha situado a la vanguardia en la creación de espacios neuroinclusivos. Por ejemplo, salas de descompresión (con estímulos visuales y auditivos de baja intensidad) en las empresas. O sesiones de cine y teatro autistic friendly en las que no está mal visto que la gente se mueva o haga ruido. “Necesitamos más estudios sobre qué tipo de intervenciones resultan más beneficiosas”, subraya.

Según Alfonso Troisi, estos cambios en el ambiente, por fuerza limitados, deberían acompañarse de una reflexión sobre qué estimamos o no aceptable. Un juicio que es “siempre un constructo en el que influyen valores éticos y culturales”. Con frecuencia, argumenta, el reto de la integración no tiene tanto que ver con lo neurológico en sí, sino con ciertas conductas que tildamos de raras, extravagantes o incluso censurables. “La sociedad”, resume Troisi, “puede ser muy represiva si haces algo que a la mayoría no le gusta”.

World.title: Dafne Fernández, actriz: “Nunca me ha gustado escuchar cosas positivas de mí, quizás porque siempre me han dicho las negativas”
World.content:
Dafne Fernández (Madrid, 41 años) acapara las miradas desde un rincón. La actriz y bailarina ha entrado sigilosa en el Salón Carlos III del Teatro Real de Madrid, donde una veintena de periodistas e influencers esperan a que imparta un breve taller de danza clásica con motivo del 25º aniversario de la película Barbie en El Cascanueces (2001), del que es la embajadora en España. Ya en el centro de la sala, después de agradecer su nombramiento y de dar las primeras indicaciones, parece tan cercana que apetece seguirla. Plié, demi-plié, relevé; las presentes intentan imitar sus movimientos hasta que, de pronto, rompe la disciplina y se sienta en el suelo, animando al resto a hacer lo mismo mientras suena el emocionante Pas de Deux compuesto por Chaikovski para el ballet estrenado en 1892: “Así supe lo que era el síndrome de Stendhal. Es la música que me pongo cuando paso por un momento difícil y quiero escapar a otro lugar”, dice. Mientras, en el suelo, escucha con los ojos cerrados.

“En realidad, yo siempre he estado en otra posición; he sido alumna, no profesora”, explica Fernández más tarde, durante una entrevista con EL PAÍS en un salón contiguo, en el que confiesa haber sentido algo de miedo cuando le propusieron impartir el taller. Su papel como embajadora en este aniversario de Barbie en El Cascanueces, la primera película de animación de la franquicia, en la que la muñeca más famosa del mundo baila al compás del compositor ruso, “es un sueño hecho realidad”, asegura: “Ojalá hubiera podido coleccionar barbies de pequeña. Yo las quería todas, pero en la familia éramos tres hijos [tiene una hermana y un hermano], solo trabajaba mi padre y yo solo tenía una barbie, que era mi tesoro”. “Para mí no era un juguete, era yo misma siendo mayor, me proyectaba en ella”, matiza.

A principios de los dos mil, tras cursar danza clásica hasta los 18 años en el Conservatorio Profesional de Danza de Madrid, Fernández se hizo famosa interpretando a Marta Ramos en la serie Un paso adelante (2002), donde volvió a ser alumna, esta vez en la academia de baile ficticia Carmen Arranz. A los 11 años había debutado en el cine, en Malena es un nombre de tango (1996), y un año después, en 1997, fue Fuensanta en Pajarico, de Carlos Saura. Estos papeles fueron la continuación de un sueño que había empezado en casa, de niña, cuando escapaba de su vida a través de la música clásica y, junto a sus hermanos, creaba mundos, imaginaba personajes y confeccionaba invitaciones para sus abuelos, que vivían en el primer piso y tenían asientos reservados en primera fila para el espectáculo de su nieta. Sus padres, que supieron leerla y fomentaron sus sueños artísticos, junto a sus profesoras de la escuela pública, a las que Fernández reivindica, hicieron el resto: “Mi padre era el que me llevaba a las clases de ballet, y luego estaba pendiente de mis deberes, porque para ellos los estudios eran lo primero”, recuerda la actriz, que hasta el próximo 25 de octubre interpreta Locuras paralelas en el Teatro Pavón de Madrid.

"De pequeña, mi padre me llevaba a las clases de ballet y estaba pendiente de mis deberes", recuerda la actriz de 'Un paso adelante'. Pablo Monge

Ahora, casada desde 2017 con el fotógrafo Mario Chavarria, madre de un niño y una niña de 8 y 5 años y con el sueño de la interpretación cumplido, ella recoge el testigo de quienes le dieron alas. Lo hace a su manera, intentando estar a la altura de sus padres y, a la vez, sin cometer sus errores; o cometiendo otros: “A lo mejor lo estoy haciendo mal, pero como yo no tuve nada, a mis hijos les quiero dar todo. Por ejemplo, mi hija está ahora loca con las barbies y no tiene una, como tenía yo… No sé cuántas tiene, tiene todas... Yo creo que se las regalo porque también me las regalo a mí”, confiesa, divertida. Pero Fernández procura también otras cosas para sus hijos: “Ahora mismo lo que más me preocupa es valorar sus emociones, verlos, acompañarles en lo que sienten. Valido cada cosa que les pasa, no lo paso por encima”. Reconoce también que les exige mucho; al fin y al cabo, ella viene “de eso”, del esfuerzo y la exigencia de una carrera de ballet: “A lo mejor hacía una pirueta y me caía y me hacía mucho daño, pero mis profesoras no dejaban que el miedo me paralizara y yo acababa haciendo cuatro piruetas más”, rememora sobre su experiencia en un mundo que, aunque le encantaba y le proporcionó herramientas de vida, acabó cambiando por la interpretación: “En 2003, cuando terminé mi carrera, ya medía 1,78 y solo podía aspirar a bailarina solista”, explica sobre su decisión.

Tras mucho tiempo entregada a un esfuerzo que para la mayoría nunca tiene recompensa, Fernández ya es capaz de reconocer (y reconocerse) que ha tenido éxito en la vida: “Nunca me ha gustado escuchar cosas positivas de mí, quizás porque siempre he escuchado cosas negativas. En la danza, si me decían lo bien que lo hacía, no mejoraba; pero si se fijaban en lo que hacía mal, eso sí lo podía mejorar”, admite. Durante muchos años, también fue incapaz de apoyarse en los demás y luchó pensando que podía con todo ella sola. Hasta 2025, cuando le dijo esto mismo a su amiga Ana Gracia, también actriz, y ella le respondió: “No, cariño, tú no puedes con todo”. “Ahí me di cuenta de que iba a colapsar y de que necesitaba ayuda”, explica la actriz. Finalmente, la pidió, y aunque dice que “está siendo un proceso muy doloroso, también está siendo muy sanador”. A su lado está su marido, de quien se confiesa aún muy enamorada: “Me sigue produciendo mariposas, y no solo no es que me guste, sino que es mi compañero, me suma muchísimo. También ha evolucionado conmigo; es una maravilla de hombre y de padre, en el que sé que me puedo apoyar”, describe a Chavarria.

Dafne Fernández, sobre sus hijos: "Ahora mismo lo que más me preocupa es valorar sus emociones, verlos, acompañarles en lo que sienten". Pablo Monge

Las heridas de Fernández son tan recientes que están aún a flor de piel, desbordándose en algunos momentos de la conversación, aunque responda siempre que está bien. De cerca, la actriz es tan transparente como cuando la prensa le pone delante un micrófono y ella, rara avis, opina sobre el derecho a la vivienda, la inexistencia de una conciliación real o la brecha de género, que la hizo renunciar a un trabajo en televisión (El chiringuito de Pepe, 2014): “No podía seguir en una serie en la que sabía que era la que más trabajaba y era la que menos cobraba”, explica y, aunque reconoce que si hubiera sido madre en ese momento no se habría atrevido, lo cierto es que pagó el precio por plantarse con un tiempo sin trabajar. “Lo hago por inconsciencia”, afirma, asegurando que no quiere abanderar nada: “Cuando hablo, tengo que hablar desde lo que siento. Hay veces que me tengo que cortar porque hay gente del mundo este que me dice: ‘Tú tienes que ser blanquita y the show must go on’. Pero, ¿cómo no voy a estar con los derechos humanos? ¿Cómo no voy a estar con que todo el mundo tiene que tener una casa? Es que lo pone en la Constitución. ¿Cómo no voy a estar con el colectivo LGTBIQ+? ¿Cómo no voy a estar a favor del aborto? Yo creo que estar en el lado positivo de la historia nunca va a ser nada negativo para mí“.

Esa conciencia, dice, arraiga en su casa de la infancia, donde su abuelo le hablaba de la Guerra Civil: “Me contó de todo, yo no lo di en el colegio ni nada”, recuerda. “Como mis abuelos fueron niños de la guerra, creo que cuando criaron a sus hijos estaban sobre todo preocupados de ponerles un plato en la mesa y de que tuvieran un uniforme del colegio. Por eso creo que mis padres han valorado menos las emociones”, reflexiona, midiendo sus palabras para no dañar a nadie. Aunque reconoce el valor de su madre, quien de muy joven ya tenía tres hijos y “estaba totalmente desbordada”, Fernández también admite que le hubiera gustado entenderla mejor: “Si me hubiese explicado lo que le pasaba, igual me hubiese ayudado”. Ella, dispuesta a no repetir patrones, tiene clara su estrategia con la siguiente generación: “Por eso voy al psicólogo, porque quiero ser una mujer trabajada. Quiero saber lo que me pasa para poder darle nombre y explicarles a mis hijos por qué lloro, por qué estoy feliz, por qué todo”, sentencia.

World.title: Cooperativas para comprar vivienda a precio de coste: ¿una fórmula olvidada para aliviar la crisis de acceso?
World.content:
Viviendas en construcción en el barrio de Los Berrocales (Madrid), uno de los desarrollos donde hay un gran porcentaje de cooperativas.

Esta industria, responsable de la construcción de 2,5 millones de casas desde 1957, pide más suelo público, reducir la carga fiscal y mayor agilidad en los trámites

Solo 18 días después del final de la Guerra Civil, el 19 de abril de 1939, se creó el Instituto Nacional de la Vivienda para hacer frente a la grave escasez de casas y a la destrucción del parque residencial provocada por el conflicto. Entre las fórmulas utilizadas figuraba las cooperativas, que han permitido la construcción de más de 2,5 millones de viviendas desde 1957, alrededor del 10% del parque residencial español, según la Confederación de Cooperativas de Viviendas y Rehabilitación de España (Concovi).

Hoy las cooperativas no tienen el mismo peso, pero mantienen una actividad muy relevante: promueven desde pisos asequibles para jóvenes hasta urbanizaciones de alto nivel en algunas de las zonas más cotizadas. Actualmente se están promoviendo unas 30.000 viviendas libres y protegidas en España, por lo que representan de media un 30% de la cuota de mercado. Solo las cooperativas integradas en Concovi cerraron 2025 con 11.805 viviendas en curso promovidas por 227 sociedades cooperativas con una inversión conjunta de 3.683 millones de euros. “Son los impulsores del desarrollo de los ámbitos urbanísticos más relevantes de las capitales de provincia de este país y en algunas comunidades autónomas superan incluso este índice, como en el caso de Madrid, Valencia o País Vasco”, sostiene Juan Casares, presidente de la confederación.

Sin embargo, tanto cooperativas como gestoras consideran que su capacidad de producción está muy lejos de su potencial. “Podríamos producir tres veces más viviendas. Equilibrar la oferta con la demanda calmaría los precios”, afirma Juan José Perucho, presidente de la Asociación de Gestoras de Viviendas (AGV) y director general de Grupo Ibosa. En su opinión, “si no generamos rápido grandes cantidades de vivienda asequible el problema va a alcanzar una gravedad insostenible”.

Las cooperativas eliminan el margen de beneficio de la empresa promotora: los socios son al mismo tiempo los compradores y quienes impulsan la promoción. Esto les permite poder adjudicarse las casas a precio de coste: Galivivienda, cooperativa de ámbito nacional con más de 1.000 viviendas promovidas, calcula que un cooperativista puede ahorrar alrededor de un 20% frente a una promoción convencional.

Pero eso no significa que escapen del fuerte encarecimiento del suelo y de la construcción. La presión se refleja en los precios: el coste medio de adjudicación de una vivienda libre en cooperativa asciende a 312.022 euros, equivalente a unos 3.120 euros por metro construido, según los datos de Concovi. En Madrid, donde la escalada del suelo ha sido especialmente intensa, las cifras son muy superiores. Perucho calcula que en los desarrollos de Berrocales, Los Cerros o Ahijones (al sureste de Madrid), con las ultimas transacciones de suelo, las viviendas deberán salir a la venta en torno a 5.000 euros por metro construido debido al encarecimiento de los costes. “Son precios altos, a los que cada vez podrán acceder menos ciudadanos”, reconoce.

Precisamente por eso, cooperativas y gestoras coinciden en que el principal problema es el suelo, la lentitud de los desarrollos urbanísticos y los largos plazos para obtener licencias. Hay numerosos ejemplos de desarrollos que acumulan años, e incluso décadas, de retrasos. La cooperativa La Amarguilla, en el nuevo barrio del Jarama (Coslada), constituida en 2011, es un ejemplo perfecto del calvario que a veces sufren los socios. Amén de los cinco grandes desarrollos del surtes de Madrid, que suman hasta 26 años de demora.

“Muchas administraciones municipales se han negado a calificar o desarrollar nuevos suelos urbanizables suficientes para dar respuesta al notable incremento de población de los últimos años”, sostiene el presidente de AGV. En su opinión, España necesita una nueva ley estatal del suelo que permita acelerar los desarrollos urbanísticos y reducir los plazos.

Junto a la falta de nuevo terreno urbanizable, el cooperativismo pone el foco en el uso del suelo público. Juan Casares defiende una mayor colaboración entre las administraciones y las entidades de la economía social para impulsar vivienda asequible y critica el funcionamiento del mercado del suelo protegido. “Llevo muchos años denunciando la especulación que con el suelo calificado como protegido se hace desde el sector privado y público, impidiendo así que cumpla la función social para la que está destinado”, afirma. Casares, que pide a las administraciones que se les escuche, considera que una mayor disponibilidad de suelo público, junto con una reducción de la carga fiscal que soporta la promoción y una simplificación de los trámites urbanísticos, permitiría aumentar la construcción de vivienda asequible.

Galivivienda recuerda que la Ley 27/1999 de Cooperativas contempla la posibilidad de adjudicar directamente suelo público a cooperativas de vivienda. Sin embargo, sostiene que la mayoría de las administraciones optan por subastar esos terrenos al mejor postor, una práctica que encarece el acceso al suelo y limita el desarrollo de nuevas promociones asequibles.

El bastión de Madrid

La Comunidad de Madrid se ha convertido en el principal valedor de esta fórmula. Según Perucho, representa entre el 30% y el 40% de las viviendas que se desarrollan en nuevos ámbitos urbanísticos como Los Berrocales, Los Ahijones, Los Cerros o Valdecarros. En los nuevos barrios de otros municipios como Pozuelo de Alarcón, las cooperativas tienen en gestión y adjudicadas casi el 50% de las casas antes de iniciar las obras de urbanización. En Brunete o en San Sebastián de los Reyes, las cooperativas están en torno al 40%.

Cooperativa de viviendas Residencial Albali en Los Berrocales (Madrid), de Grupo Ibosa.

Haciendo un recuento rápido, Perucho calcula que el 95% de la vivienda protegida en venta que se desarrolla actualmente en la Comunidad de Madrid se impulsa mediante cooperativas. Muchas promociones ni siquiera necesitan grandes campañas comerciales y se cubren a través de las listas de espera que manejan las gestoras. “Son listas mayoritariamente de gente joven que no puede acceder a la vivienda libre”, afirma. Solo Grupo Ibosa gestiona actualmente más de 1.800 viviendas protegidas repartidas en cerca de una veintena de cooperativas en Madrid. La AGV, que agrupa a 18 empresas, administra actualmente 16.992 viviendas en distintas fases de desarrollo y entrega unas 4.072 al año, una cifra equivalente a un tercio de las viviendas terminadas en la región en 2025.

La fotografía es distinta a nivel nacional. La mayor parte de las promociones tuteladas por Concovi corresponden ya a vivienda libre. Según la organización, solo el 35% de las 11.805 viviendas actualmente en desarrollo están sujetas a algún régimen de protección, lo que refleja el cambio y la evolución experimentada por el cooperativismo residencial en las últimas décadas.

El sector cree que los fiascos del pasado como el de PSV, que afectó a decenas de miles de cooperativistas y dañaron la reputación, están superados. Durante el estallido de la burbuja varias cooperativas protagonizaron concursos de acreedores y paralizaciones de promociones. “Hoy hay muchos mecanismos para evitar estas situaciones. Tanto entidades financieras como promotores tradicionales o cooperativas han hecho sus deberes, se han profesionalizado enormemente y la seguridad es muy alta”, remata Perucho.

World.title: Egypt protests shut Dutch embassy over arrest of Sisi loyalist
World.content:

The Dutch embassy in Cairo has closed to the public until further notice after nine days of protests outside the building, during which staff had to be evacuated, the embassy has announced on social media.

The demonstrators are demanding the release of Ahmed Nasser, deputy head of a pro-government Egyptian youth group, who was arrested in the Netherlands on October 10.

He was reportedly detained on suspicion of threatening Anas Habib, an Egyptian activist who lives in the Netherlands, and his pre-trial detention has been extended by 14 days, broadcaster NOS reported.

Habib drew international attention last summer when he filmed himself padlocking the gates of the Egyptian embassy in The Hague, in protest at the Egyptian government keeping the Rafah border crossing with Gaza closed.

His action sparked similar protests at Egyptian embassies in more than 16 countries, after which supporters of President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi began gathering outside embassies to “protect” them.

Days after Nasser’s arrest, Egyptian foreign minister Badr Abdelatty called his Dutch counterpart to demand his release and better protection for Egypt’s embassy in The Hague.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen said on social media that the two had “discussed the need for progress on the security of our respective embassies and consular affairs.”

It is unclear exactly how Nasser is alleged to have threatened Habib.

World.title: Getting home safely: ADE festivals step up protection measures
World.content:
With the Amsterdam Dance Event (ADE), the world’s biggest electronic music event, underway, extra safety measures have been put in place by festival organisers and the city to make sure, Amsterdam says, that everyone feels “safe in the nightlife scene – free from any form of harassment, violence, discrimination, or (sexual) misconduct.”

To that end, there is a host of initiatives at various festival sites where techno lovers can recharge or get help getting home safely.

Bike buddies, hosts and Check-Ins

At the DGTL festival on NDSM island, cycling buddies will be on hand to help people get safely back and forth to the ferries. They will be working in pairs to ensure their own safety.

A Safe Check-In on NDSM wharf will be open all night for people who need physical help, feel unsafe at night or just need a breather. Phones can also be charged there.

At Awakenings in Halfweg, a Goodbye Host will be stationed at the exit, keeping a watchful eye on partygoers leaving solo. Hosts can help with route planning, and phones can also be charged here.

Both locations will also feature an Awareness Crew, trained teams identifiable by badges or vests that offer support to those feeling uncomfortable or unsafe.

Taking back the night

Some of the safety measures are not new. Last year, following the August murder of teenager Lisa while she cycled home alone and the resulting Take Back the Night campaign, the biking buddies programme was set up.

“We’ve been running social safety measures at our events since Covid, through our awareness teams and social safety hub, so this is something we’ve prioritized for a long time already,” Nikki Schuurs, who deals with Social Safety at DGTL, told Dutch News.

“Bike Buddies, however, was indeed introduced in response to the Take Back the Night campaign, following the murder of Lisa. Safety doesn’t stop at the dance floor.”

Visitors can find the Bike Buddy meeting point just outside the event. Group rides depart every 30 minutes between 21:00 and 07:00, on the hour and half-hour.

Safety concerns have again risen in the city following the violent death of 29-year-old Hajar, whose body was found in a suitcase in the Amstel River last week. She had last been seen cycling with a man near the RAI convention centre. He has since been arrested in connection with her death.

World.title: Inburgering with Dutch News: the great cycle path squeeze
World.content:
You can’t have failed to notice that Dutch cycle paths are no longer the preserve of old-fashioned cyclists. E-bikes, fatbikes, scooters, snorfietsen, speed pedelecs, disabled vehicles – a seemingly never-ending stream of other road users have moved in. But what exactly are the rules and regulations?

Lesson 64: what is allowed on the cycle path?

Fatbike

The fatbike, with its characteristic thick tyres and frequently thick riders, has become wildly popular. It’s not surprising because at the moment, riders do not need a helmet, driving licence, or third-party liability insurance. The fatbike is officially an e-bike, and therefore there is no age limit, but measures are afoot to make helmet-wearing compulsory for riders up to the age of 18.

Fatbikes are allowed to travel at up to 25 kph. However, many are doctored to go faster – as you will notice when you see them whizzing past cars that keep to the 30 kph limit, mandatory for cars in some Dutch cities.

Electric bike

The electric non-fat bike, so to speak, is literally overtaking the person-powered bike, and that is partly due to its popularity among older riders – who are also well represented in the annual traffic death toll. The same rules of the road as apply to fatbikes apply to ordinary e-bikes – none. You will, however, see more and more elderly riders with a helmet.

Electric cargo bike

The cargo bike, or moedermobiel, deserves a separate mention because of the riders’ mistaken opinion that everyone has to make way for this space-hogging vehicle because it carries cute little toddlers. A good place to spot cargo bikes is outside primary schools at 3pm, when they cause a veritable jam of their own.

Speed pedelec

Speed pedelecs are electric bikes as well, but unlike normal electric bikes, they can legally reach speeds of up to 45 kph. This makes them motorcycles in the eyes of the law, with the rules that then apply, such as mandatory helmet-wearing, a driving licence and insurance. Speed pedelecs can travel on cycle paths, but only at a maximum of 25 kph.

Snorfiets, or moped

No pedalling is needed for this motorised bike or moped, which has a maximum speed limit of 25 kph and is allowed on cycle paths. Although snorfietsen have the same speed limit as electric bikes, they are technically considered to be motorcycles, and riders need a helmet, a driving licence and insurance.

The introduction of helmets for all types of mopeds several years ago led to the downfall of the snorfiets – after all, if you need a helmet, why not drive a proper motorbike – or a fatbike?

Scootmobiel

The motorised wheelchair or scootmobiel is possibly the most dangerous vehicle on the cycle path. According to statistics agency CBS, the traffic death rate among mobility scooter riders is over six times that of motorbike riders and over 20 times that of cyclists.

Users don’t need to pass any tests or learn the rules of the road, and they can go pretty much wherever they like – shopping centre, pavement, cycle path, ordinary road – just not the motorway.

The Canta

The Canta looks like a brommobiel – a small electric vehicle with four wheels – but because it is considered a mobility aid for people with a disability, it is treated in the same way as a scootmobiel.

The Canta is not supposed to go faster than 30 kph on the cycle path and 45 kph on the road, but is allowed to mount the pavement and annoy pedestrians at 6 kph. It can also park anywhere and does not need a number plate.

The minimum age is 16, and you’ll need to take out insurance, but you don’t need a driving licence. The Canta became popular with youngsters who could not be bothered to cycle and has since spawned a surge in far hipper micro cars.

Micro cars

The Birò and its ilk are small, fashionable and, according to many, extremely annoying electric vehicles which are banned from cycle paths but whose drivers use them anyway – particularly as a sneaky escape when faced with a traffic jam.

Popular with estate agents and PR people, micro cars have a maximum speed of 45 kph. If you want one, you will need a brommobiel driving licence and must be 16 or over.

Electric scooter

The step, or scooter, used to be a children’s plaything, but since the invention of the electric version, they have been taking over cities throughout Europe. Steps which have been officially approved have been allowed on Dutch cycle paths since July 1 this year. In Dutch terminology they are known as “light electric vehicles”.

The step has a maximum speed of 25 kph, and riders have to be 16 or over. You will need third-party liability insurance, and the base must have a number plate which is clearly visible.

The e-step is predicted to rival the fatbike in popularity and ability to provoke cycle-path rage – as long as helmets are not compulsory.

World.title: Amsterdam exploring single-use packaging ban
World.content:
Amsterdam is considering banning single-use packaging, including coffee cups, fast-food containers and other single-use plastics that it says make up 30% of the city’s litter.

“Litter is a persistent problem; it is a symptom of a ‘throwaway society’ that pollutes our beautiful city and costs millions every year,” said Amsterdam executive Lian Heinhuis, who is responsible for waste and sanitation, in a statement.

“Yet the solution is within reach: putting an end to the throwaway culture.”

To that end, the city has commissioned a study into what it can legally do to tackle the problem. According to CircuLaw, which provides legal information on circular transitions, such a ban could be implemented, but only after less restrictive measures have proven not to work.

A ban also works best alongside other measures, such as a reliable supply of reusable packaging and a well-established return system.

The city says it will work with business owners and residents and also look at how other cities are managing the problem, including Copenhagen and Lisbon, the latter of which has already implemented a single-use packaging ban.

“Single-use packaging is a major problem,” the city said. “The plastics used in these items take hundreds of years to decompose – if they ever do at all. They pollute the soil and groundwater for a very long time, despite being used for an average of only about seven minutes.”

World.title: Student union furious as minister says interest cap unaffordable
World.content:
Despite a coalition promise to cap student loan interest rates at 2.5%, education minister Rianne Letschert has told parliament that the government can no longer afford to stick to its pledge.

The minister said that capping the interest rate at 2.5% is risky and expensive, and that the €40 million annual budget the coalition had set aside to cover the cap is only a quarter of what it would actually cost – €160 million – and could lead to other cuts in the education budget.

“I understand the concerns of current and former students regarding the rise in interest rates on student debt, driven by global instability and an increase in long-term interest rates,” Letschert said in a statement on Thursday.

“Unfortunately, I must conclude that it is not possible to implement a 2.5% interest rate cap with the €40 million per year that has been set aside. I find this very disappointing.”

Geopolitical costs

Since the coalition agreement was first presented at the end of January, the global landscape has significantly shifted due to geopolitical tensions and financial uncertainty. Long-term interest rates – to which student loan rates are linked – have risen from 2.7% to 3.3% and could climb higher.

“Recent shocks in the financial markets highlight just how unpredictable – and potentially financially risky – this interest rate policy is,” the ministry said.

But students aren’t buying it. “This effectively sends students out into the world burdened by an incredibly heavy backpack of debt,” LSVB, the national student union, told news service ANP. “The only certainty this cabinet offers students is the assurance that interest rates will rise even further in the coming years.”

Student union ISO added that once again, “students are the victims of empty promises.”

Letschert will discuss the issue with parliament later this month.

World.title: Cyber security centre warns PHP hacking situation could worsen
World.content:
The Netherlands’ National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC) is investigating the first signs of successful hacks on websites following the exposure of critical vulnerabilities on the web, and says the situation could “rapidly worsen”.

A spokesperson told the Volkskrant on Thursday that the signals came from the NCSC’s international network, and that there was no sign yet of abuse involving Dutch websites. The centre is still checking whether the reports are accurate.

Cybersecurity researchers, working with the help of AI, found that PHP, the programming language on which a majority of the web is built, had at least two serious vulnerabilities in its code.

Details of the weaknesses were leaked online on Monday, and the PHP developers announced they would issue an upgrade by Wednesday afternoon.

Hacking attempts began even before the leak, with Amazon reporting an attack attempt on October 17. US internet security firm Cloudflare said it saw hacking attempts run from thousands before the upgrade to millions afterwards.

Initially, the NCSC said that there were no signs of active hacks and the PHP developers said there were no indications of breaches.

Large amounts of government, healthcare and news sites were forced to go dark temporarily while awaiting the upgrade, including Dutch News.

The Netherlands was fast to act, closing a large amount of its sites and issuing warnings early on Wednesday, after which governments in Belgium, Germany, France and Finland did the same. The issue is now a global concern.

Dutch privacy watchdog AP said on Thursday it had not yet received any reports of data breaches linked to the vulnerabilities.

World.title: Weather warnings as storm Austen approaches Netherlands
World.content:
The weather office KNMI has issued code yellow warnings for Limburg, Zeeland and South Holland on Friday evening as storm Austen approaches, with gusts of at least 75 kilometres per hour expected.

The southwest and the hills of Limburg will be hit by the wind first, with the rest of the country following in the evening and overnight.

Saturday is expected to bring fewer showers, some sun and a calmer wind, before heavy rain and stronger gusts return in the evening. Very severe wind is possible along the coast.

On Sunday the wind will remain strong throughout the country, particularly in the north, where there will also be showers. The south will get more sun, but temperatures will not rise above 13° over the weekend.

World.title: Leader of junior coalition partner quits Polish government

Katarzyna Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, the leader of a junior party in Poland’s ruling coalition, has announced that her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party, the centrist Poland 2050 (Polska 2050), in protest over a parliamentary vote on Thursday. Poland 2050 (Polska 2050) is set to remain in the government, thereby maintaining Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s parliamentary majority. However, the dispute has highlighted tensions within the ruling coalition just a year ahead of parliamentary elections at which it will seek another term. Dwukadencyjność samorządów została utrzymana. Tak zdecydował dziś Sejm. Wygraliśmy! Zmiana, której chce 75% Polaków dojdzie do skutku! Stało się to jednak pomimo głosów K15X. Koalicja, w tym niestety znaczna część posłów Polski 2050, stanęła przeciw ludziom, a za politykierskimi… — Katarzyna Pełczyńska (@Kpelczynska) October 22, 2026 Pełczyńska-Nałęcz, who serves as minister for funds and regional policy, made her decision in the wake of an unusual voting result in the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, on Thursday. Another junior partner in the ruling coalition, the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL), had proposed a bill abolishing two-term limits for mayors. Those limits had been introduced in 2018 with the aim of reducing corruption and cronyism by preventing local officials from becoming entrenched in power. However, PSL, which has a strong presence in local politics, argues that the limits prevent effective, popular mayors from being re-elected, thereby denying voters the right to decide who they want to represent them. Although the government has a majority in the Sejm, the bill was narrowly defeated, with 213 votes in favour and 215 against, after 15 MPs from the ruling coalition joined with the right-wing opposition in voting against it. Pełczyńska-Nałęcz herself is not a member of parliament, so did not vote. Her party was split, with six MPs voting for the bill, three against, three abstaining, and three not voting at all. Aftewards, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz made clear that she opposed the bill and celebrated the fact that it was blocked. She also announced her resignation from the government and the leadership of her party. “The coalition, unfortunately including a significant portion of MPs from Poland 2050, stood against the people and in favour of backroom political deals,” she wrote. “I am leaving Donald Tusk’s government because values are more important to me than positions.” “I am leaving the party in the hands of its founder, who stepped away but then returned,” she added, referring to Poland 2050’s founder, Szymon Hołownia. “I hope that he remembers what values he came to power in the name of.” Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s decision follows a year of turmoil for Poland 2050. In September 2025, Hołownia, who had led the party since founding it in 2021, announced that he was stepping down. However, a first attempt to choose a new leader was invalidated in January after technical problems with voting. Hołownia then hinted that he may reverse course and seek to continue leading the party, though in the end that did not happen. In February, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz was chosen as the new leader. That prompted her rival candidate, Paulina Hennig-Kloska, to quit the party, taking half of its MPs with her. They formed a new group called Centrum (Centre). Both Poland 2050 and Centrum remain in the ruling coalition. However, Pełczyńska-Nałęcz has had an uneasy relationship with Tusk. Around half the MPs from Poland 2050, a junior member of Poland’s ruling coalition, have split from the party and formed a new parliamentary caucus. They expressed dissatisfaction with the actions of the party's recently elected new leader, @Kpelczynska https://t.co/IqU4vE1EEe — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 18, 2026 On Friday, Tusk, who is on a state visit to India, sarcastically responded to Pełczyńska-Nałęcz’s resignation by saying, “I thought she’d at least call before she left”. He admitted that “cooperation [with her] has not been the easiest for a long time”. The prime minister, however, added that he “does not think [her resignation] will have any impact on the future work of the coalition…My intuition tells me that this is her individual decision”. Hołownia, who currently serves as head of Poland 2050’s parliamentary caucus, confirmed at a press conference on Friday alongside fellow MPs that the party intends to remain in Tusk’s coalition. But he also warned that, without Poland 2050, the government would not have a parliamentary majority. W @PL_2050 dowiedzieliśmy się o decyzji @Kpelczynska z mediów. Zaskakująca rezygnacja przewodniczącej z zaufania wyborców i odpowiedzialności powierzonej jej w bardzo trudnym momencie przez ludzi (w tym mnie) zaledwie po niespełna 1/3 kadencji – dla każdej organizacji byłaby… — Szymon Hołownia (@szymon_holownia) October 22, 2026 The episode highlights the tensions within the ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right and contains parties that disagree on a number of issues. It also points to the pressure smaller coalition partners are feeling ahead of next autumn’s parliamentary elections. Only parties that win at least 5% of the vote nationally can enter parliament. But Poland 2050 has been polling at around 1% and PSL is on 3%. In the 2023 election, Poland 2050 and PSL in fact stood together as an alliance called the Third Way (Trzecia Droga), helping ensure that the two parties won enough votes to enter parliament. However, in 2025, they split from one another and confirmed that they would not stand together again. PSL and Poland 2050, the two parties that make up the Third Way alliance, have confirmed that they are splitting and will stand separately at the next elections. They will, however, remain part of @donaldtusk's ruling coalition https://t.co/NduEJY25eE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2025 The fact that the bill to end two-term limits for mayors was defeated has also caused tension between PSL and its coalition partners. In the wake of yesterday’s vote, PSL immediately announced that it would push for the introduction of two-term limits for members of parliament, arguing that the same rules should apply to national and local elected representatives. The right-wing opposition has long hoped that it could tempt PSL, the most conservative element of Tusk’s coalition, to quit the government. A recent report even claimed that US President Donald Trump had, at the behest of Poland’s opposition, suggested to PSL’s leader that he leave Tusk. Protests took place in towns and cities around Poland on Thursday evening, demanding that the government fulfil its promise to liberalise the country’s strict abortion laws. However, the demonstrations, which took place on the sixth anniversary of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) ruling that introduced a near-total abortion ban, were nowhere near the scale of the massive protests that emerged back in 2020. Było deszczowo, ale nie brakowało ludzi i emocji. Rzeszów pokazał czerwoną kartkę za aborcję rządzącej koalicji. pic.twitter.com/oJo8BiWXxS — Paweł Preneta (@pawelpreneta) October 22, 2026 In Warsaw, a few hundred people gathered in the rain outside parliament, reported broadcaster RMF. Many held up red cards, a symbol used by the protesters to warn the government that it could be thrown out of power at next year’s parliamentary elections. When Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition, which ranges from left to centre right, came to power in December 2023, it pledged to liberalise the abortion laws after eight years of rule by the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party. In particular, it wanted to reverse the 2020 TK ruling, which outlawed abortions in cases where a severe defect is diagnosed in the foetus. That means abortions can now only take place in two cases: where the pregnancy results from a crime (such as rape or incest) or if it threatens the mother’s life or health. However, in the almost three years since, the government has failed to introduce any new legislation on abortion. One effort to do so in 2024 collapsed amid disagreements between more conservative and liberal elements of Tusk’s coalition. Finally, earlier this week, the Sejm, the more powerful lower house of parliament, approved two abortion bills: one that would reverse the 2020 TK ruling; the other that would decriminalise providing help to women in obtaining unlawful abortions. However, those measures do not go far enough for many of those attending Tuesday’s protests, who are seeking abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In any case, both bills approved by the Sejm are likely to be blocked by President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the right-wing opposition and has vetoed a record number of government bills. Nawrocki has made his opposition to abortion clear. Parliament has approved two bills that would liberalise Poland's abortion laws One would reverse the 2020 constitutional court ruling that introduced a near-total ban on abortion; the other would decriminalise helping women in obtaining unlawful abortions https://t.co/nVj8SQVIsv — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 21, 2026 In Wrocław, Poland’s third-largest city, around 1,000 people attended Thursday’s protest, according to police estimates cited by the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Among the placards and banners was one showing Tusk with an extended, Pinocchio-style nose. “It’s sad that we have to engage in this fight again,” said one of the organisers. “For so long, they ignored us, only coming when they needed votes. Now let’s show that we can’t be ignored.” In Katowice, around 300 people gathered, according to the Polish Press Agency (PAP). In Poznań, around 400 or so protesters marched to the local headquarters of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, where they placed a symbolic red card and waved banners saying “You deceived Poland”. Czerwona kartka za aborcje. W #Lodz w proteście w strugach deszczu protestuje kilkadziesiąt osób @RadioZET_NEWS pic.twitter.com/okU7QjnhFw — Mateusz Szkudlarek (@m_szkudlarek) October 22, 2026 The 2020 TK abortion ruling triggered the largest protests seen in Poland since the communist era, with hundreds of thousands of people taking to the streets. That anger is seen as having played a major role in PiS losing power to Tusk’s coalition in 2023. Opinion polls consistently show that most Poles want the abortion law to be liberalised, though there remain divisions over whether there should be a return to the pre-2021 status quo or a move even further, to introduce abortion on demand up to the 12th week of pregnancy. In autumn 2027, parliamentary elections will take place, deciding who governs Poland for the next four years. Opinion polls currently show a fairly even split in support between Tusk’s coalition and the right-wing opposition. World.title: Poland charges second Georgian man over murder of Russian dissident
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Poland has charged a 22-year-old Georgian citizen with aiding and abetting the murder of Robert Kuzovkov (who went by the name of Semyon Skrepetsky), a Russian dissident killed near his home in Poland earlier this year. The suspect, who can be named only as Makhmud A. under Polish privacy law, was captured on Monday, a day after flying into Poland. Earlier this year, another Georgian citizen, Elnur A., was detained and charged with committing the murder itself. Warto przypomnieć: ▶️ Do egzekucji doszło w poniedziałek 15 czerwca 2026 roku rano na jednym z osiedli w Białej Podlaskiej, gdzie napastnik oddał do ofiary kilka strzałów z bliskiej odległości. ▶️ Zastrzelony to 44-letni obywatel Federacji Rosyjskiej, publicznie znany z… https://t.co/r1rZfsw1Bv — Jacek Dobrzyński (@JacekDobrzynski) October 22, 2026 Kuzovkov was shot five times near his home in the eastern Polish town of Biała Podlaska on 15 June. He was an artist whose work, published under the name Skrepetsky, focused on creating satirical cartoons mocking Russian leader Vladimir Putin. He had fled Russia in 2021 due to fear of political prosecution. Before his death, Kuzovkov had reported on social media that he had received death threats from supporters of Chechen leader and Putin ally Ramzan Kadyrov, who had also been the subject of the artist’s satirical cartoons. After the shooting, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said that “everything points to this being a political assassination”. He also revealed that Kuzavkov had previously been offered protection by the Polish authorities, but “for reasons unknown” had refused. On 18 June, the Polish authorities announced they had captured Elnur A. in a hostel near Warsaw. The following day, he was charged with the murder of Kuzovkov. He has remained in custody since then. Police have detained a man suspected of carrying out the murder of Russian dissident Semyon Skrepetsky, who was shot dead near his home in Poland this week. "Everything points to this being a political assassination," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/z37sBBxgJn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 18, 2026 On Thursday, Poland’s National Prosecutor’s Office revealed that Makhmud A. had been detained on 19 October by the Internal Security Agency (ABW) in a car park along the A2 motorway. The ABW itself confirmed that it detained the suspect after he flew to Poland from Georgia on 18 October. He had been travelling with two other Georgians, who will now be expelled from Poland and handed a 10-year re-entry ban. Makhmud A. was subsequently charged with aiding and abetting the killing of Kuzovkov by “undertaking a number of actions in the period from 1 to 11 June 2026 that made it easier for Elnur A. to commit the murder”. He is additionally charged with illegal possession of firearms and ammunition. Makhmud A. is accused of providing the perpetrator with a weapon, means of transportation and a mobile phone with an application enabling monitoring of the victim’s vehicle, a spokeswoman for the district court in Lublin told broadcaster TVN. The court has approved a period of three months’ detention for Makhmud A., with prosecutors saying that they fear he could otherwise “flee, go into hiding, or unlawfully obstruct proceedings”. Under Polish law, someone found guilty of aiding and abetting a crime can face the same punishment as the person who committed the crime itself, meaning that both suspects face potential prison sentences of between 10 years and life if found guilty. They have pleaded not guilty. A Russian man has been shot dead in Poland, with reports indicating that he was an artist whose work ridiculed Putin and that his killing appeared to be an “execution”. However, the authorities have not yet officially identified the victim or any suspects https://t.co/Zd2u7IE0A0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 15, 2026 The Polish authorities have not yet revealed who they believe was ultimately behind the murder of Kuzovkov. However, in June, Tusk said that, if Russia’s involvement was confirmed, it would be a case of “state terrorism”. In recent years, Poland has become a primary target for Russia’s campaign of so-called “hybrid warfare”, which has involved acts of sabotage, disinformation, cyberattacks, and airspace violations. Most known on-the-ground activity has been carried out not by Russian operatives themselves, but by so-called “disposable agents” hired through messaging service Telegram and paid in cryptocurrency. In some cases, Russia has used existing criminal networks to carry out such tasks. Four men – three Ukrainians and a Belarusian – have gone on trial in Warsaw accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on behalf of Russia https://t.co/i4czRb9DYZ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 Earlier this month, a trial began in Warsaw of four men – three Ukrainians and one Belarusian – accused of being part of a criminal group that carried out a series of arson attacks in Poland and Lithuania on Russian orders. Shortly afterwards, Germany detained two Turkish men at the request of Poland, which believes they were responsible for the recent arson attack on a satellite internet ground station in Poland used by Starlink. Poland believes that incident was also carried out on behalf of Russia. Last year, the interior ministry claimed that Poland is facing a growing wave of “imported crime”, committed in particular by immigrants from Georgia and other former Soviet states. World.title: Poland and India aim to double trade by 2030 as PMs meet in New Delhi
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The prime ministers of Poland and India have, after a meeting in New Delhi, outlined aims to double bilateral trade by 2030 and expand cooperation in mining, shipbuilding, energy, space and defence technologies. Donald Tusk’s visit, the first by a Polish prime minister to India in 16 years, follows the upgrading of bilateral ties between the two countries to a strategic partnership during Narendra Modi’s trip to Poland two years ago, which was the first by an Indian prime minister in almost five decades. During a joint press conference with Tusk on Thursday, Modi said that his Warsaw visit had acted as a catalyst for the Polish-Indian relationship to “gain speed over the last two years”. Tusk added that the two leaders had now reviewed the results of their cooperation so far and outlined priorities for the coming years. They discussed, among other things, ways to deepen economic, investment and technological ties between the two fast-growing economies. Poland’s GDP is set to grow by 3.5% this year, the second-fastest rate in the European Union, while India will see economic growth of 7%. Poland’s economy is also on the verge of becoming the 20th largest in the world, with the country hoping to join the G20. “The economic strength of both countries offers a wealth of opportunities for strategic partnership,” Modi said. Tusk, meanwhile, underlined that “Poland and India are countries that have much in common and nothing that divides them…[with] no conflicting interests or historical grievances.” Poland hopes that the boost to bilateral trade will come from an EU-India trade deal expected to be signed in December. The agreement is designed to eliminate or reduce tariffs on goods accounting for 96.6% of the value of EU exports to the Indian market. Tusk said Poland wanted to capitalise on the opportunities created by the deal, with the ambition of becoming “India’s gateway to Europe”. Modi expressed confidence that Poland’s and India’s “shared goal” of doubling bilateral trade by 2030 “will certainly be achieved”. “Today, trade between Poland and India totals just over $6 billion,” said Poland’s finance minister Andrzej Domański, who joined Tusk on the trip to India. “We want this trade to grow, and the conditions for that are very favourable.” However, “it is no secret that we have a significant trade deficit with India”, Domański added. Last year, Poland exported goods worth €1.4 billion to India, with machinery, mineral products and metals the largest categories. Meanwhile, it imported €4.3 billion, in particular textiles, machinery and metals. The United States wants Poland to become a full member of the G20 "as soon as possible". "Poland’s economic growth, combined with its growing leadership position in the international arena, make it an ideal participant," says the @StateDept https://t.co/OjpWly4FTw — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 12, 2026 According to the Polish prime minister’s office, the EU-India agreement could also help increase Polish investment in India, particularly in advanced manufacturing, food processing, biotechnology and mobility. To help facilitate such investments, Tusk travelled with almost 100 Polish business representatives, hoping the visit will help them to enter the large and rapidly growing Indian market. His office described the delegation as the largest of its kind in the history of Polish-Indian relations. Modi said he was “particularly happy” with Tusk’s decision to bring a business delegation and announced plans to strengthen links between startups in both countries, including through technology hackathons for young people. The countries plan to expand cooperation in critical minerals, raw materials and coal gasification, a process that converts coal into gas for energy and industrial use. Shipbuilding, defence, space and advanced technologies are also among the priority sectors. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians https://t.co/hNiOqmeUfX — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2026 The leaders also highlighted historical ties and people-to-people exchanges as a foundation for closer relations. Modi recalled the role of Indian Maharaja Jam Saheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji, known in Poland as the “Good Maharaja”, who provided shelter and care to around 1,000 Polish children evacuated from the Soviet Union during the Second World War. “In 2022, Poland helped our Indian students, demonstrating that same spirit of humanity,” added Modi, referring to the support Poland provided to Indian students escaping from Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Modi said he hoped that the ongoing Jamsaheb Memorial Youth Exchange Programme, which recently took place for the second time, will “introduce the next generation to this Polish-Indian friendship”. The strengthening of bilateral relations has also come amid a rapid rise in Indian migration to Poland in recent years. This year Indians became the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, numbering around 25,500, up almost 5% in a year. World.title: How will recent scandals affect Polish politics?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. By Aleks Szczerbiak Political scandals generate intense media attention and public outrage but rarely produce dramatic shifts in party support that they once did. They are now more likely to affect electoral outcomes indirectly by demobilising softer, less committed voters and influencing turnout, particularly among supporters of the government disappointed by its apparent underperformance and broken election promises. The hospital scandal Two high-profile political scandals dominated the Polish news agenda for much of this summer. The first centred on irregularities at Warsaw’s Southern Hospital (Szpital Południowy) and involved a young and relatively inexperienced doctor, Dawid Kacprzyk. In spite of his lack of a specialist qualification, Kacprzyk coordinated the hospital’s emergency department and reportedly earned a staggering 1.6 million złoty (€366,000) in the previous year alone. He also served as a Warsaw district councilor for the liberal-centrist Civic Coalition (KO) grouping, Poland’s main governing party led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk. Public outrage intensified following reports that the hospital had operated a dedicated “VIP path” or special lounge where ruling-party-linked politicians and their families were allowed faster access and medical examinations without the usual queues faced by ordinary patients. Further claims emerged, including a whistleblower surgeon alleging that supervisory failures contributed to patient deaths and of improper private business activity in the hospital morgue. Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 For its part, KO insisted that the scandal was the personal misconduct of one former party member rather than a general problem affecting the entire healthcare system. They noted that Kacprzyk quickly resigned his council seat and hospital role, and that party-aligned Warsaw mayor Rafał Trzaskowski had dismissed the hospital board and two of his deputy mayors overseeing the city’s health services. KO argued that no specific names of preferential VIP patients had been publicly confirmed, any irregularities were being fully investigated by prosecutors and independent bodies, and political and legal accountability would follow if ethical breaches or crimes were proven. The government also pledged systemic reforms including measures to curb excessive pay for doctors. Nonetheless, the scandal struck a deep chord with the Polish public, triggering massive negative media and political fallout that aligned perfectly with the right-wing opposition’s narrative painting KO as part of a “Warsaw elite” that enjoys special privileges at the expense of ordinary citizens. The cryptocurrency scandal The second major summer scandal centred on allegations of financial impropriety and political entanglement involving Zondacrypto, once Poland’s largest crypto trading platform, that claimed over a million users but earlier this year collapsed abruptly after thousands of retail investors were unable to access their funds. However, what began as a major financial scandal escalated into political warfare, providing the government with powerful ammunition to attack the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS), Poland’s ruling party between 2015 and 2023 and currently the main opposition grouping, party-aligned President Karol Nawrocki, and the broader conservative political eco-system over payments and donations made by the crypto firm. Prosecutors are investigating possible criminal offences relating to financing by Zondacrypto, a collapsed crypto firm, of organisations and individuals linked to the right-wing opposition, including the Polish version of US conservative conference CPAC https://t.co/swceV864nA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 26, 2026 For example, Zondacrypto sponsored the 2025 Polish edition of the Conservative Political Action Committee (CPAC) conference attended by the then-presidential candidate Nawrocki, advertised heavily with conservative media outlets such as the TV Republika television network, and made donations to foundations linked to high-ranking PiS figures such as former justice minister Zbigniew Ziobro. The government also tried to entangle Nawrocki, who repeatedly vetoed its cryptocurrency regulation laws, into the scandal, arguing that he was protecting the shady interests of the industry and its political beneficiaries at the expense of ordinary Poles (the Tusk administration lacks the three-fifths parliamentary majority required to overturn a presidential veto). For their part, PiS and the broader Polish right dismissed the government’s accusations as a smear campaign and sought to shift blame for the scandal onto the Tusk administration for inadequate oversight to protect investors. Figures on the right, including those connected to foundations that received money, framed these dealings as legitimate sponsorships common across the media and other organisations. The president of the Polish Olympic Committee has been detained as part of a criminal investigation into Zondacrypto, a crypto firm that collapsed earlier this year and was a major sponsor of Poland's Olympic team https://t.co/QPG7ejAImD — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 27, 2026 PiS rejected claims that the party or associated groups received funds from the firm and defended Nawrocki’s vetoes as necessary against flawed legislation. Nonetheless, opinion polls found that most respondents linked the scandal to PiS and the right-wing opposition, providing the government with numerous attack lines to force them onto the defensive. The diminishing impact of scandals It is worth recalling how an earlier era of post-communist politics scandals possessed much greater transformative, system-altering capacity and could act as catalysts for the restructuring of the electoral landscape. For example, at the beginning of the 2000s, the so-called “Rywin scandal” was widely seen as a decisive factor in the near-destruction as a political force of the previously powerful, and then-governing, communist-successor Democratic Left Alliance (SLD). The scandal erupted in late 2002 when film producer Lew Rywin allegedly solicited a large bribe from the Agora media group, publisher of the influential liberal-left Gazeta Wyborcza newspaper, in exchange for media legislation changes while claiming to act on behalf of a “group holding power” (grupa trzymająca władzę) linked to the ruling party. A high-profile parliamentary investigative commission, sustained media focus, and a series of follow-on scandals and accumulation of allegations of deep-seated influence peddling by post-communist networks created a powerful narrative of systemic bribery and corruption, completely discrediting the SLD as a competent governing force. Having won a substantial victory in the 2001 parliamentary election, securing 41% of the votes, its support collapsed to only 11% at the next 2005 poll. This helped clear the way for the rise of the KO (originally Civic Platform)-PiS duopoly that has structured the Polish party system ever since, thereby establishing a precedent that scandals were electorally fatal transgressions. The contrast with the recent hospital and cryptocurrency scandals is instructive and illustrates a broader transformation in the relationship between political misconduct and electoral politics in Poland. Whereas in the more fluid party system of the early post-communist period a cluster of major scandals or single-event shocks could rapidly destroy dominant parties and restructure competition, now – although they still generate intense, high-octane political and media outrage – such controversies appear to slide off the main political actors with remarkably little immediate consequence. Indeed, neither of these recent scandals produced the dramatic shift in headline polling numbers that some observers, drawing on historical precedent, might have anticipated given the intensity of the media coverage. Scandal-neutralising structural shifts This change stems from three interlocking shifts in the structural dynamics of Poland’s political system. Taken together, they have substantially diminished the capacity of scandals to move headline poll numbers and trigger the kind of large-scale systemic realignments seen in an earlier era of post-communist politics. Firstly, the sheer velocity of modern political communication prevents single-issue-based scandals from sustaining public focus. In the early 2000s, a major corruption scandal could dominate the news headlines for months through concentrated media attention. The Rywin scandal unfolded through prolonged televised parliamentary commission hearings, keeping the story alive and allowing public outrage to build into a sustained narrative that slowly drained the ruling party’s legitimacy. Today, digital algorithms and the 24-hour news cycle ensure that a major story, whether about healthcare management or cryptocurrency, moves at a breathtaking pace and is overtaken rapidly as public attention moves onto the next domestic controversy, international development, or strategic counter-narrative. Seven people have been charged in relation to alleged corruption in the issuing of Polish visas to foreign nationals The scandal has engulfed the government since last week, but officials say the opposition is exaggerating the scale and nature of the case https://t.co/iHnIShb1pQ — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2023 This hyper-accelerated news cycle means that even a high-profile case that generates intense short-term media coverage does not remain the dominant story for long enough to produce cumulative, system-level damage by limiting the time window in which a scandal can convert temporary disapproval into lasting shifts in voting intentions. Scandals thereby become a form of ambient “background noise” in Polish public life rather than a singular focal point for popular outrage. Secondly, and perhaps most formidably, the protective shield of deep polarisation and socio-political division renders large segments of the electorate relatively impervious to allegations against “their” side. After 2005, the Polish party system crystallised around a durable “post-transition” socio-economic divide reinforced by cultural and geopolitical fault lines. In this deeply fractured and highly polarised landscape, with large segments of the electorate embedded within hostile camps, when a scandal like the hospital crisis or cryptocurrency controversy breaks, voters interpret allegations levelled against “their” party through a tribal filter as a politically motivated hit job or the work of hostile media. So even severe scandals are shaped by, and largely confirm, existing political loyalties and rarely trigger cross-camp voter defections. This is a sharp contrast with the early 2000s, when the party system was still fluid and electoral volatility high. Our essential guide to Poland's parliamentary elections, which will take place one year from now. How does voting work? What do polls suggest the outcome will be? Which issues may animate the campaign? And what role will President Nawrocki play? https://t.co/fmdoFpBaxz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2026 Thirdly, the parties themselves have become far more professional at message discipline and crisis management. Today’s parties are centralised media machines staffed by sophisticated public relations strategists who view a scandal not as a moral crisis but a communication problem requiring aggressive damage containment. Rather than allowing a controversy to fester, they immediately launch counterattacks, accusing their opponents of far greater historical or concurrent corruption, and ruthlessly enforce internal party discipline and message conformity. They also deploy well-rehearsed crisis management playbooks including: personnel sanctions; framing the problem as local or individual responsibility, or residual rather than systemic failure; ordering visible audits, investigations, or reforms to demonstrate “taking action”; and co-ordinated messaging that seeks to close the story quickly and shift the focus back onto the other side’s weaknesses or broader policy issues. Differential mobilisation, not voter persuasion Yet while polarisation and professional crisis management allow parties to survive the immediate news cycle, this does not mean that scandals have become irrelevant. Rather, their effects are more subtle and delayed through the “slow-burn” mechanism of differential turnout by selectively demobilising specific voter segments. Although in a highly polarised polity the most committed hard-core partisans are relatively immune to negative information about “their” side, soft or conditional supporters may become disillusioned, or simply less motivated, when repeated scandals reinforce a narrative of self-interest or incompetence. The net result is a gradual, cumulative, asymmetric demobilisation of one camp that does not fully register in standard inter-election voting intention surveys, which generally show expressed party preferences among those willing to answer but not necessarily the intensity of that preference or the probability that a respondent will actually turn out to vote. In Poland’s deeply polarised political landscape, the next parliamentary election, scheduled for autumn 2027, is unlikely to be determined by persuading voters to cross the ideological divide. Rather differential levels of electoral turnout and mobilisation are likely to be the key, specifically: whichever side’s core base is more motivated to – and peripheral, less ideologically committed “softer” supporters are demotivated from – showing up on polling day. Young Poles are bucking the international trend by turning out at a higher rate than the oldest voters in recent elections. We spoke with experts and young voters to find out more about the growing frustrations that are driving this political engagement https://t.co/y1JpYYmbjb — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 11, 2025 And in a context where the election is likely to be closely fought, and relatively small differences in participation rates could prove decisive, although they may not produce dramatic changes in headline party polling preferences, scandals can still play a significant role. However, we are only likely to see the full impact of any such scandals when voters eventually go to the polls and actual turnout patterns are revealed. Given the general disillusionment with the current government and growing narrative of its underperformance and failure to deliver on its electoral promises, scandals are more likely to contribute to the demobilisation of the governing camp. It is anyway inherently more difficult for incumbent parties to mobilise their disillusioned supporters to turn out and vote than it is for motivated oppositions to rally their base to oust them. Indeed, revealed voter preferences in the summer 2025 presidential election – when Nawrocki won an unexpected victory over Trzaskowski, the ruling party-backed favourite – and more recently the severe setback for KO in the Kraków mayoral by-election, suggest that government supporters are already showing greater reluctance to vote. So, while their effects are routinely neutralised by fast-moving news, tribal shielding and professional spin, scandals still matter in Polish politics, although the battleground has shifted from voter persuasion to differential mobilisation. World.title: Court acquits Polish soldier who accidentally shot Syrian refugee at Belarus border
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work!
