"Imagine if [Final Fantasy XIV director] Yoshi-P was here; everyone would probably just drop dead!"

Geographic isolation as training weights

Perth's Ben Wu was one of many visitors to the Final Fantasy XIV Fan Festival in Berlin in July. As part of Team Fish, he took first place in a regional championship tournament, with a cash prize that was outmatched by the glee of meeting aforementioned director Yoshi-P.

Ben Wu (top row, second from right) from Australian Team Fish pictured along with Naoki Yoshida (top row, far right), known as Yoshi-P. (Supplied: Square Enix)

A retired competitive player in shooters like Counter-Strike, Valorant and Overwatch, Wu started playing Final Fantasy XIV during the pandemic, a period when the game's player count briefly overtook that of World of Warcraft.

Wu initially struggled to find other Australian players, participating in international tournaments with one local friend.

It wasn't until the Oceania server's arrival that he could marshal enough Australian players to field any team, let alone a winning one.

But its competitive scene still remains smaller than other regions.

Square Enix's unusual criteria means Oceania is grouped with Europe for fan festival tournaments. Wu found Australia's remoteness from other competitors, including the tightly interconnected network of European teams, gave Team Fish a surprising advantage against their rivals.

"We were able to hide our strategy from European teams by practising against North American and Japanese teams. We didn't only do that because we wanted to hide our strategy, it's almost impossible to practise with the Europeans," he says, explaining the high internet latency that makes executing rapid decisions impossible.

"We had to play on the North American and Japanese servers to get our practice.

" We weren't used to having low latency, so it felt like our training weights were removed when we played on stage. "

Final Fantasy XIV contains multitudes, accumulated over its 16-year existence. In-game there are the high-level competitions experienced by Wu, and the Limsa Extreme community's relaxed hangouts at the Aetheryte Plaza.

Outside it, there are real-life cosplay, sticker exchanges and entertaining spin-offs like the Taskmaster parody game show held at PAX Australia.

One player jokes it's not the gameplay that keeps them coming back; it's the community. Murouchi agrees Final Fantasy XIV's sense of player ownership is crucial.

"Players tend to feel Final Fantasy XIV as their own game. It's not an import from Japan: it's your game," Murouchi says.

"Because you don't need to visit Japanese servers or US servers, I believe people can feel Final Fantasy XIV is their home."

World.title: Two large earthquakes off coast of Vanuatu prompt tsunami warning
World.content:
A tsunami warning has been issued after two large earthquakes struck off the coast of Vanuatu.

A 6.9 magnitude earthquake struck first about 200 kilometres west of Sola at 12:31pm AEST on Saturday, according to the US Geological Survey (USGS).

It was followed shortly after by a 6.3 magnitude quake.

USGS recorded the quake at a depth of 10km.

The Pacific Tsunami Warning Centre said hazardous tsunami waves were possible for coastlines within 300km of the epicentre.

Its initial threat forecast identified Vanuatu as the area potentially affected.

"Persons located in threatened coastal areas should stay alert for information and follow instructions from national and local authorities," the warning centre said.

No threat is currently issued for Australia, according to the Bureau of Meteorology.

PTWC listed the initial magnitude of the larger quake as 7.2, but the USGS downgraded it to 6.9.

World.title: Years of conflict splits voters in former Netanyahu stronghold
World.content:
As lunchtime trade wanders through the door and with the smell of barbecued meat hanging in the air, kebab shop founder Amnon Oved smiles as he offers a rather blunt assessment of the state of Israel's leadership.

The popular businessman is a resident of Kiryat Shmona and, like many other Israelis, is preparing to vote in an election that will have a profound impact on the country after years of conflict and social upheaval.

In his mind, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, also known as Bibi, has reached his "best before" date.

"Bibi needs to go to America and sit there with [US President Donald] Trump, to smoke grass together and have a good life," he quips.

"Or he will sit here in prison, one of the two.

"Trump said to him, 'You're a liar.'

"That [was something] we knew before he said it!"

The October 27 election has essentially become a referendum on Mr Netanyahu's leadership and legacy.

An election poster for Benjamin Netanyahu that reads: "Never Surrender." (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

That includes his management of the multiple wars Israel is involved in, through to the personal corruption charges still hanging over him.

Current polling shows the longest-serving prime minister in Israel's history and his party, Likud, are facing a stiff challenge to hold on to power, with "change" candidates vying to topple him.

Israelis to vote in most seismic election in decades Here's a breakdown of Israel's upcoming general election and its complicated coalition structures.

Perhaps aware of the growing challenge against his ally, Mr Trump delivered a glowing endorsement of Mr Netanyahu as a "great warrior" ahead of the election.

Most data suggests Likud will be the second largest party in the next Knesset, behind one of Mr Netanyahu's main rivals, Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar.

But both men will still need to form coalitions post-election.

Israel heads to the polls after turmoil

Mr Oved's business is one of a handful that have consistently remained open in Kiryat Shmona, in far north Israel's Galilee region.

The view of Kiryat Shmona, with the Ramim Ridge in the background. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

The city has been a Likud stronghold for decades and sits at the foot of the Ramim Ridge, where the border between Israel and Lebanon runs.

It was one of the Israeli cities targeted by Hezbollah's rocket and drone strikes after the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attacks on Israel triggered the war in Gaza.

The 'straight' shooter looking to rule Israel Israel's upcoming election could be one of the most consequential in the country's history, with Benjamin Netanyahu's own former military chief firming as the favourite to oust the prime minister from office.

Israeli forces fired back over the border in response until an uneasy and, as some analysts described it, flawed ceasefire was struck in late 2024.

A fragile peace hung over the area until Hezbollah again opened fire earlier this year.

This time, the group acted in support of its backers in Tehran, days after the US and Israel launched a war on Iran.

The city came under attack once more, as Israeli forces pummelled Lebanese villages just a short distance away and launched a ground invasion.

"There have been wars since the world was created, and the wars will continue," Mr Oved said.

"It doesn't matter which leaders will be in power, good or bad. They are all crap in the end. They care about themselves."

At the November 2022 election, just over 49 per cent of the vote in Kiryat Shmona went to the Netanyahu-led party.

Trump endorses Netanyahu Donald Trump issues a glowing endorsement of Benjamin Netanyahu just months after an expletive-laden tirade against the Israeli prime minister.

The joint ticket led by far-right ultranationalist politicians Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich ranked second, with just under 14 per cent of the vote.

The two men would go on to become key members of the coalition government, which was later formed. They are running separately at this election.

Mr Ben-Gvir has been sanctioned by governments around the world, including Australia. But he and his Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party is making the pitch that a strong Ben-Gvir means a strong Israel.

That message was on clear display at a public bomb shelter on the main road of Kiryat Shmona, which was covered in posters for his party.

Election posters for leader of the Otzma Yehudit (Jewish Power) party, Itamar Ben-Gvir, that read: "Ben-Gvir is strong, Israel is strong!" (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

In the background of the image are handcuffed Palestinian prisoners, highlighting his role as national security minister and his demands to become defence minister in a future government.

'People are hard to move'

Only about half of Kiryat Shmona's 25,000 residents have returned since fighting in southern Lebanon calmed.

The city's former deputy mayor Shimon Kamari believed many locals would still vote for Likud out of blind loyalty, even though he believed it had "abandoned" the city.

Shimon Kamari says his political views have changed over the years and he has become more right wing. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"Those who remained in the city are traditional people, religious people, people who the support for Likud flows in their blood, and it seems to me that it's very difficult to get it out of them," he said.

" It's very hard to get out of it because it comes from home, from the parents, it comes to them from grandparents, and these people are hard to move. "

Mr Kamari was born in the city to a family of Iranian Jews, and stayed in Kiryat Shmona during the war to continue running his food distribution business.

He said his political views had shifted over the years, and he had become more right wing in recent times.

For example, he was now of the view that things like a two-state solution could not and should not happen.

"If the government does not change … God forbid, it is a death sentence for Kiryat Shmona," he said.

Mr Kamari said he would be backing Gadi Eisenkot at the ballot box.

Israeli opposition leader and former military chief Gadi Eisenkot is campaigning ahead of Israel's upcoming general election. (Reuters: Amir Cohen)

"This culture that took root in the State of Israel, the culture of lies, we have to change it," he said.

"And I believe that the four parties of change, headed by Eisenkot, will be able to bring us back on track."

Some Israelis remain loyal to PM

Simmering anger against Mr Netanyahu in the city is countered by vocal support for the prime minister, who has argued he is the only person able to keep Israel and Israelis safe from the enemies who surround it.

Herzl Ben Asher, another former deputy mayor and current editor of the Galilee News, said some voters were misguided if they thought Mr Netanyahu's lengthy time in office was a reason to replace him.

Herzl Ben Asher says the time Benjamin Netanyanhu has been in power is not a reason to vote for someone else. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"Can you tell someone who has lived with his wife for 20 years, that 20 years is enough, and to replace her with someone else? No," he argued.

"He needs to maintain his achievements, and that's not easy.

"Getting to the summit is easier than staying at the summit — everyone knows that. He needs to complete his work."

Mr Ben Asher described Mr Netanyahu's achievements as "incomprehensible" in scale and significance, and pointed to the recent war with Iran, which is still not resolved, as evidence of how influential and powerful he can be.

Yoav Sabbag is preparing to vote in the Israeli election. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

Another resident, Yoav Sabbag, lamented how empty Kiryat Shmona was but said Mr Netanyahu was the only person who could breathe life back into the city.

"We have to decide to take just Benjamin Netanyahu, because … maybe it is not [like he is] the 'Superman', but he [makes] me feel security in my country and in this area, five minutes from Lebanon."

World.title: Tasmanian football club coach charged with rape
World.content:
A former northern Tasmanian football coach has been charged with three counts of rape, leading to the resignation of the football club's president.

Police confirmed a 44-year-old man from northern Tasmania had been charged with the offences that were alleged to have occurred in April last year.

The man is believed to be former Bracknell football coach, Josh Adams.

He is scheduled to appear in the Launceston Magistrates Court early next year.

In a statement, Northern Tasmanian Football Association (NTFA) president Peter Gutwein said the association had recently been informed that a coach had been charged with "a serious criminal offence".

But he said the NTFA would not provide further comment as the matter was now before the courts.

News of charges being laid against Adams were first published by an independent media outlet.

Its reporting detailed private messages exchanged between Bracknell Football Club president Nicole Jones and the mother of Adams's alleged victim

Yesterday, Ms Jones announced via social media that she would be "standing down as president and all official club duties with immediate effect".

"I acknowledge that what I said [in the messages] was disrespectful, inappropriate and wrong, and I unreservedly apologise for these comments," she said.

In his statement, Mr Gutwein said the league was "deeply concerned" by the content of the private messages.

"The NTFA has referred the matter to the AFL for independent consideration and acknowledges that the President has unreservedly apologised for those comments and stood aside from all official club duties with immediate effect," he said.

"The NTFA recognises that individuals who report allegations of sexual violence must be treated with dignity, compassion and respect."

Adams had not re-committed to coaching Bracknell as of last month.

It is understood he has since been stood down from the role, and will be replaced.

World.title: Former Port Adelaide AFL player Daniel Stewart dies at 37
World.content:
The Port Adelaide AFL club has said it will honour Daniel Stewart at the first home game of 2027 after the former Power forward's death at the age of 37.

Stewart, who played 36 games and kicked 31 goals for Port Adelaide between 2010 and 2013, died suddenly yesterday.

The tall key forward was drafted by the Power in the 2009 rookie draft and promoted to the senior list at the end of that season.

Originally from Victoria, Stewart was recruited from SANFL team North Adelaide after playing for the Eastern Ranges and AFL Queensland club Labrador.

His best AFL return came in the final round of 2010 at Docklands against Richmond, where Stewart kicked four goals in a 10-point win for the Power.

"On behalf of everyone at the Port Adelaide Football Club, I extend our deepest condolences to Daniel's family including his mum Donna, dad Byron, wife Laura, his two sons Bernie and Lando and his brother Leigh," Port Adelaide chief executive Matthew Richardson said in a statement.

"We also extend our thoughts to his friends, including his close friend and former teammate Matt Thomas, and to all those at North Adelaide and Labrador who knew him.

"Daniel was part of the Port Adelaide football family, and he always will be. A sudden passing like this is devastating and our thoughts are with everyone who loved him, and with the teammates, coaches and staff who shared the journey with him here at Alberton.

"The club will provide support to those affected by Daniel's passing, including his former teammates and the people who worked alongside him."

The club stated it would honour Stewart by wearing black armbands at their first home game at Adelaide Oval next season.

World.title: Elon Musk has a lot to lose at US midterms as pollsters tip blue wave
World.content:
Last November, Elon Musk was looking to step away from the halls of power.

"You know, I've generally found that when I get involved in politics, it ends up badly," he told investor and YouTuber Nikhil Kamath.

"Best to avoid where possible."

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive's stint as a special government employee leading the now-defunct Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) had ended months earlier after a string of controversies.

Mr Musk also quietly shelved plans to launch a political party, which had been announced during a short-lived feud with US President Donald Trump.

But as the country's midterm elections approach, Mr Musk is making another foray into politicking.

And as control of Congress is now within reach for Democrats, the stakes for the trillionaire are higher than ever.

Trying to turn back a blue tide

With Mr Trump's approval rating at record lows, Democrats are banking on breakthrough performances at the November 3 elections.

Forecasters say the House of Representatives is all but guaranteed to flip blue, while the Senate result is, at the least, a toss-up.

Why Musk is spending millions to get Trump elected Elon Musk has promised to give away $US1 million a day leading up to the United States presidential election

Despite arguing that "they never poll us right", the president has embarked on a campaign blitz across the country.

He has also promised to pay every American adult $US5,000 (about $7,100) if Republicans retain control of Congress, reminiscent of the $US5,000 cheques cut from DOGE savings once floated in early 2025.

Mr Musk may be staying off the campaign trail, but behind the scenes, he has become the biggest known midterm donor, sinking about $US442 million into Republican groups in this election cycle.

At least $US158 million of that has gone toward a race in his home state of Texas, in which Republicans are at risk of losing a once-safe US Senate seat to Democratic candidate James Talarico.

Mr Talarico's campaign has released ads claiming Mr Musk wants to "buy his own US senator" by bankrolling Republican candidate Ken Paxton.

"So let's remind Elon: Texas is not for sale," the ads say.

Separately, Mr Musk earlier this month said he would give a SpaceX share to "every child in America" in 2027. While he did not provide details of the giveaway, Mr Trump claimed it as a victory for his Trump accounts program, through which he said the stock would be distributed.

Dems put target on Musk's back

There is a lot at stake for Mr Musk if control of the House changes over.

Democrats have been calling for investigations into several areas of his dealings, and if they win back gavels in several congressional committees, they will have the power to follow through.

Mr Musk recently landed himself in Democrats' sights after Ukraine reported its access to the SpaceX owned Starlink and Starshield services had been restricted, affecting the country's ability to defend against Russian drone attacks.

Starlink slowdown in Ukraine Ukraine says people will die as a result of throttled Starlink services in the country. Here's how its armed forces rely on the crucial service.

In response to the matter, Mr Musk said Starshield's systems were controlled by the US government.

Mr Trump and the SpaceX owner have denied responsibility, but a Wall Street Journal report cited officials and people familiar with the matter as saying Mr Musk ordered the throttled speeds.

Days prior, Mr Musk commented that Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had "gone too far" by striking Russian oil refineries.

Both Donald Trump and Elon Musk say they were not involved in restrictions to Ukraine's Starlink and Starshield access. (Reuters: Jonathan Ernst)

US Representative Pramila Jayapal, a member of the Foreign Affairs Committee, told Politico the incident raised questions about Mr Musk's power.

"What happens when one guy gets a giant contract from the government and then uses it to do something that shuts down communication in a war that has been extremely important to the United States to support Ukraine?" she said.

"There's a lot of different parts of the corruption around Musk."

Elon Musk's DOGE agency explained There has been an escalation in the legal battles over billionaire Elon Musk's new US government efficiency agency. Here's what we know about DOGE.

Democrats on several committees have also earmarked DOGE for congressional scrutiny.

Through its 10-month lifespan, the department cut an estimated 250,000 federal jobs, allegedly accessed sensitive data, and withheld congressionally appropriated funds.

Democrats have also alleged conflicts of interest between Mr Musk and the federal government.

Republicans blocked previous attempts by Democrats on the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform to subpoena Mr Musk.

"There's any number of House committees that would have jurisdiction in some respect over him," said Harry Melkonian, an honorary associate at the United States Studies Centre.

"He's a major defence contractor and NASA contractor, so his companies receive staggering amounts of federal money each year."

Democrats would be able to call congressional investigations into Elon Musk if they win back the House. (Reuters: Kylie Cooper)

In June 2025, representative Jasmine Crockett, who sits on the oversight committee, vowed to "bring Elon Musk in" once Democrats regained the majority.

"And we can have him under oath, and we can have him tell us about everything that he did," she said in an appearance on MSNBC.

In response to the Politico report that Democrats were discussing possible investigations into Mr Musk, the trillionaire threatened to retaliate against congressional investigations.

"Live by the sword, die by the sword," he wrote on X.

"Those who pick fights with me should understand that I will find out who is really pulling the strings and come for them, not just their puppets."

Testimonies, document production

Mr Musk could be called to testify at committee hearings and required to produce documents under a congressional investigation.

"For somebody like Musk, it would be truly awful to be sitting for eight hours a day, having a panel of people just questioning everything you do," Dr Melkonian said.

"It becomes television news … and he is a businessman selling consumer products."

Elon Musk switches focus back to Tesla. Is it too late? Experts say it could be too late for Tesla to "separate the man from the machine" as Elon Musk's personal brand hits an all-time low.

But refusing to cooperate would present its own problems.

"On the political side, as a major contractor, he would be reluctant to antagonise a congressional majority because his companies depend on money voted by Congress," Dr Melkonian said.

"Legally, he could be held in contempt of Congress."

The federal misdemeanour is punishable by imprisonment of up to 12 months.

If an investigation uncovers any wrongdoing, the findings can be referred to the Department of Justice for prosecution.

The US attorney would be bound to take the matter to a grand jury in Washington, DC.

Dr Melkonian said the findings could lead Congress to determine Mr Musk as unfit for further dealings with the government.

"They could say, 'We're not going to authorise any more spending [on government contracts with Musk]'. That's their ultimate power. Congress controls the dollars," he said.

"Whether or not it ever goes to a federal judge, I don't think he likes that."

World.title: Amanda Stoker to replace Amanda Camm as child safety and DV minister
World.content:
Oodgeroo MP Amanda Stoker will replace Amanda Camm as child safety and domestic violence minister, in the first major change to the government's ministry since coming into power two years ago.

She will also take on Ms Camm's former portfolios of families, seniors and disability services.

Ms Stoker said it was a privilege to play a greater role in the government.

"This is, I don't think it's a shock to say, a difficult area in which to work, but I came to Queensland parliament to do hard things," she said.

"I will leave nothing in the tank."

Government's first cabinet shake-up

The former minister advised Premier David Crisafulli she would be standing down on Thursday, saying it was her decision.

Ms Camm returned from six weeks' sick leave just a fortnight ago, after undergoing "major surgery".

The Whitsunday MP had faced months of intense scrutiny, including over children in residential care sleeping on the floor of child safety offices, and cuts to the DFV prevention sector in the latest state budget.

Amanda Camm has been under significant pressure in her portfolios for months. (ABC News)

It's the first movement in the frontbench since the LNP won government in 2024.

Ms Stoker said Ms Camm had her "deep respect".

"I think she's laid a really good foundation," she said.

"I look forward to driving the implementation of the response to the commission of inquiry."

Ms Stoker was previously the federal senator for Queensland. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

Mr Crisafulli said Ms Stoker's performance indicators were clear.

"We are not going to the next election without kids being adopted out of residential care," he said.

"That has got to happen, that is my expectation and it will happen."

'Far-right spear-thrower'

Opposition Leader Steven Miles said he was disappointed Mr Crisafulli had not chosen a more senior MP and instead appointed his "far-right spear-thrower".

"This is a woman who said sexuality was a choice, she's now in charge of this government's … LGBTQ policy," he said.

"This is a woman who said abortion should be illegal even for women who have been raped, and even today she refused to rule out advocating for changes to those abortion laws.

"David Crisafulli's government has a problem with women and Amanda Stoker will only make it worse."

Steven Miles says he's disappointed a more senior MP was not appointed to the role. (ABC News)

Shadow Child Safety Minister Corrine McMillan said Ms Camm had left the two portfolios "in an absolute mess".

"Women and children are more at risk than ever," she said.

"We hope that Amanda Stoker can fix some of the myriad of issues immediately."

Queensland Domestic and Family Violence Alliance CEO Mel Arnost said ending domestic and family violence "must remain a priority" for the government.

Mel Arnost says addressing the issue of DFV will take "a commitment to generational change". (Supplied: Britt Spring)

"It requires a commitment to generational change, an openness to innovation and sustained investment in specialist services," Ms Arnost said.

"We look forward to working with Minister Stoker on the Crisafulli government's commitment to addressing this serious issue to provide a safer community for all Queenslanders."

Queensland Council of Social Service CEO Aimee McVeigh thanked Ms Camm for her service and said Ms Stoker's appointment came at a "critical time".

"In the face of escalating cost-of-living pressures, we encourage Minister Stoker to renew the government's focus on families and work across government and with the community services sector, so every family and child has what they need to thrive," Ms McVeigh said.

Ms Stoker was assistant minister for finance, trade, employment and training, and a federal senator for Queensland from 2018 to 2022.

Thuringowa MP Natalie Marr will take over the assistant ministry.

World.title: Cattle prices hit 'a new gear' as rain tumbles down
World.content:
Cattle prices jumped this week as heavy rain fell across key production areas in Queensland and northern New South Wales.

Meat and Livestock Australia's (MLA) benchmark Eastern Young Cattle Indicator (EYCI) surged beyond 1,000 cents a kilogram, as restockers and backgrounders competed for numbers.

"The cattle market shifted to a new gear off the back of this rain," Stuart Bull, MLA's market information manager said.

" Some of these regions were in need of a good drink and this rain has really helped pushed prices, along with fewer cattle coming to market. "

Demand for younger cattle was strong this week and the processor cow indicator hit a record high. (ABC Landline)

At Roma on Tuesday, some weaner steers from the Winton region sold for an incredible $7 a kilogram, which equated to more than $1,900 a head.

At Dubbo, the local saleyard report said restocker demand "sparked a market boom".

"Restocker demand was a stand-out, with young cattle selling up to an impressive 80 cents per kilo dearer [than last week]," the report said.

"Young steers reached a top of $7.40/kg, while young restocker heifers sold to $6.50/kg, showcasing the strength of competition and confidence among buyers looking to replenish their herds."

Loading...

Scott Loughnan, who runs a mixed farming operation west of Roma, had received more than 160 millimetres of rain when he spoke to ABC News.

"We'd organised to feed cattle all summer with forecasts of a super El Niño," he said.

"It was apparently never going to rain again, but this will definitely make it easier."

Mr Loughnan was in the middle of harvesting wheat, barley and chickpeas, and said for winter crops in the area, the rain was "not very good".

"I looked at some chickpeas this morning and they might not be much good, but I'm trying to look at the positives that this rain will grow us some grass and give us moisture for the next planting."

The MLA national indicators for processor cows and heavy steers have both reached record highs this week. (ABC Landline)

Record cow and heavy steers

Meanwhile, MLA's national processor cow indicator has cracked $4 a kilogram for the first time on record, and the national heavy steer indicator has also reached a new high of $4.77 a kilogram.

Global AgriTrends livestock analyst Simon Quilty said the supply of heavy steers was tight and processors were competing against feedlots to secure numbers.

"Once upon a time, feedlot operators wanted 450 kilogram to 500 kilogram steers, that was the preferred weight," he said.

"But that's now been lifted because of the lack of supply and they're taking 550 kilograms to almost 630 kilograms, creating an overlap [in demand] between processors and their needs for slaughter-ready cattle and the feedlotters who have extended the requirements of their cattle.

" So there's competition for numbers between the north and the south of Australia, plus processors versus feedlots [and] the net effect is this incredible demand for heavy steers that I think will continue. "

Mr Quilty believes Australia's cattle industry is at the start of a herd rebuild and is forecasting cattle prices to increase next year.

He is forecasting heavy steer prices to rise by about 20 per cent to about $5.70/kg next year.

Watch ABC TV's Landline at 12:30pm on Sunday or on ABC iview.

World.title: ‘She keeps surprising me’: Payne says best yet to come from Proxima Dea
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing ‘She keeps surprising me’: Payne says best yet to come from Proxima Dea Craig Kerry October 24, 2026 — 5:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Rosehill trainer David Payne was excited for what’s to come from immature surprise packet Proxima Dea after she gave him a third group 1 Spring Champion Stakes (2000m) win to cement her place as the VRC Oaks favourite. The full sister to Queensland Oaks winner Gypsy Goddess took her unbeaten career to five, pushing to sit outside the leader in the $2 million three-year-old feature from the outside gate under Zac Lloyd before going for home on the home bend at Randwick on Saturday. The tactic paid off as Gloaming Stakes (1800m) winner Proxima Dea, unwanted with a $300,000 reserve at yearling sales and retained by her breeders, fended off favourite and Flight Stakes (1600m) champion Global Goal by a length and a half. Cormier was third. Proxima Dea after winning the Spring Champion Stakes. Getty Images She was in from $3.50 to $2.30 (TAB) for the Oaks (2500m) on November 5 at Flemington. “To look at her, you wouldn’t give much for her, but geez, she seems to have everything. She’s got guts and heart,” Payne said.



“I said to [Lloyd], ‘She’ll outstay them. We can’t have a sit and sprint. If nothing goes, you go. Otherwise, sit outside the leader and go early on her.’ “She’ll love [the Oaks], and you can give her a bit of an easier ride.” Jockey Zac Lloyd and trainer David Payne. Getty Images It was a first group 1 win for Payne, 78, since 2020 Spring Champion victor Montefilia took out the 2022 Ranvet – her fourth success at the top level – for the same ownership as Proxima Dea. Payne also won the 2017 Spring Champion with colt Ace High. “This filly keeps surprising me,” said Payne, a champion trainer and jockey in South Africa before coming to Sydney in 2002.



“Montefilia was a good filly, but I think this filly stays better than Montefilia. “I had a New Zealand filly in South Africa called Petrava, she was unbelievable [and won five group 1s]. She used to just jump and run to the front, 1600, lead all the way. She could sprint a mile. “I’ve had a lot of good fillies but this one, she’s the ugliest I think, but she keeps surprising me. She might be, the way she’s going, I mean, five in a row in her first prep, who knows? “I’ve had some good staying fillies, but she’s exceptional because she’s still not mature, when you look at her.” It was also gutsy effort from Lloyd, who battled illness to ride on a warm day at Randwick after missing the midweek meeting at Warwick Farm. He earlier won the Highway Handicap on Scott Singleton-trained Ocean Tsunami.



Guineas on map for Central Europe Chris Waller-trained Central Europe later broke through at his seventh start, sweeping to a 3¼-length win in the $1 million group 3 Callander-Presnell (1600m) for three-year-olds. The Frankel colt, an unlucky second in the Skyline Stakes and placed in the Pago Pago Stakes and Rosebud, came from second last down the outside under Jason Collett to prove a class above. “I think maybe a Sandown Guineas could be a nice race for him and then obviously aim a lot higher in the autumn,” Waller representative Darren Beadman said. “James [McDonald] was always saying he was pretty good and today he showed it with his turn of foot.”



In the Kirkham Plate (1000m) for two-year-olds to start the day, Waller-trained Exo Velocity ($13) caused an upset with a rails run from last under Kerrin McEvoy to edge out stablemate Tour De Force ($7) by a long neck on debut. Exo Velocity, a $650,000 Zoustar yearling bought by Waller and Guy Mulcaster, is the first foal out of Dalrello and Calaway Gal Stakes winner Exo Lady and looks likely to target the Magic Millions carnival in January.

World.title: ‘On the verge of breakdown’: MPs’ staff burnt out from online hate
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack ‘On the verge of breakdown’: MPs’ staff burnt out from online hate Nick Newling October 24, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Independent and minor party MPs say their staff are being inundated with threats and abuse being sent to their offices, with some resorting to private fundraising to employ enough advisers to share the significant workload. Politicians have been forced to turn off their office’s phone lines, order staff not to review constituent emails, and send their employees home to recuperate, amid a deluge of vitriol. MPs Mehreen Faruqi, Nicolette Boele, Sophie Scamps and Fatima Payman. Threats against federal politicians are at an all-time high, with MPs on alert after the shock attack on Helen Haines on Monday. In the aftermath of the attack, Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett confirmed that her force was charging one individual a week with threats to politicians. NSW Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi told this masthead: “There have been times that I have had to tell staff to not answer the phones because all we are getting is calls of hate and abuse.”



Faruqi said the emotional impact of the high volume of threats that come into her office directly challenges her ability to provide assistance to constituents, at times frustrating those who wish to speak with her. Related Article Haines attack A politician’s job is to listen. It’s becoming increasingly dangerous to do so “We’ve often had training and support from the Parliamentary Workplace Support Service. I have counselling quite a bit from PWSS. Staff see social media, emails come through. There are phone calls as well. It hinders how we do our work,” Faruqi said. Faruqi and independent senator Fatima Payman separately spoke of separate incidents this week in which pictures of human faeces had been sent to their email inboxes, distressing staff members employed to monitor legitimate correspondence from constituents. Payman said her office this week missed an email from the AFP regarding the conviction of a Queensland man who targeted her with menacing voicemails, emails and social media messages because her relevant staff member was taking a mental health day after exposure to “sustained abusive” content.



“My staff are on the verge of breakdown and there is no practical way of sharing the burden without shutting the office entirely because, Labor, the party for workers doesn’t give a s--t about safety and wellbeing of the workers in my office,” Payman told this masthead. After leaving the Labor Party to sit as an independent last term, the senator was not afforded the additional “personal staffing” allocation provided to other senators, leaving her with the equal lowest staffing allocation of any crossbencher in federal parliament. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has faced criticism for his provision of staffing allocations. Alex Ellinghausen Under federal legislation each MP is entitled to five electorate officers, but the provision of extra highly paid “personal staff” remains entirely under the prime minister’s discretion. Anthony Albanese has been criticised for the way he grants staffing allocations, after both cutting the crossbench’s staffing following the 2022 election, and the opposition’s following the 2025 election.



On the Senate crossbench, Jacqui Lambie has three additional advisers, David Pocock and Lidia Thorpe each have two, and United Australia Party senator Ralph Babet has one. Payman and One Nation senator Tyron Whitten, both representing Western Australia, are the only senators to have no additional staff. Payman has made repeated requests for additional staff, saying she cannot effectively represent Australia’s largest state without them. There has been no response to her requests. Independent MP Nicolette Boele has made similar requests for increased staffing which have been declined. A teal independent representing the inner-Sydney electorate of Bradfield, Boele has one additional staffer while the five other teal independents each have two. A reason for this discrepancy has never been provided. “As a woman in public life, I know the risks to me and my team are rising. Bradfield is also home to large Jewish and Chinese-Australian communities who are being targeted,” the MP told this masthead.



“We asked for more staff to keep my team safe and to properly support communities, and were turned down. We asked again after the Bondi attack last December, and were turned down again.” Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese granted Greens 15 staff just before party blocked inquiry into PM’s powers Boele has had to privately fund a social media staffer to monitor online threats against her office. She said the current staffing arrangement isn’t “fair, safe or sustainable” for her office or the community she represents. Both independent senator David Pocock and teal MP Sophie Scamps also use private fundraising efforts to employ staff. Scamps said young female staff in her office were on the front line of filtering threats and harassment that come into the office, saying they were often “trying to protect me from the vile abuse that comes in often based on misinformation.”



A member of Scamps’ team recently stepped back from her job after feeling burnt out because of the amount of vitriol she was faced with daily. “The aggression, the toxicity, it takes its toll, she’s now left. She was a beloved member of the team, but there’s only so much you can take,” Scamps said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: In troubled times, Finland’s public broadcaster has an answer: puppies
World.content:
WorldEuropeAnimals In troubled times, Finland’s public broadcaster has an answer: puppies Amelia Nierenberg and Lara McCoy October 24, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: Puppy Live is exactly what it sounds like. It’s a 24/7 livestream of newborn puppies. And it sometimes seems everyone in Finland is invested. Loading “It’s a form of stress relief,” said Kalle Kurittu, 32, who lives in Helsinki and has watched for years. “I love all the puppies equally,” said Mandi Salo, 9, also of Helsinki, who said she was excited when one pup opened its eyes.



Puppy Live (“Pentulive” in Finnish) – is something like The Truman Show for a litter, raised from birth to adoption in front of an adoring public. Broadcast by Yle, Finland’s public broadcaster, the stream is a phenomenon, with well over 1 million viewers. Now, in its sixth year, the show is going international. The Truman Show for dogs: Puppies and their mother, Hilkka, in a scene from the 24/7 livestream. Yle - The Finnish Broadcasting Company via AP Sweden’s public broadcaster, SVT, has started streaming it. A Dutch broadcaster has bought the rights for a spinoff (with Dutch puppies). Yle (pronounced OO-lay) has even launched a Puppy Live podcast and, in a very 2026 move, released a prediction-market game to run for the eight weeks of the season. Even though the babies sleep some 20 hours a day, there’s plenty to bet on: How much do they weigh? How long are their tails? Which will grow fastest? Players earn points, and weekly winners get a mug.



At any given minute, the puppies, currently two weeks old, are probably sleeping. They twitch on a purple blanket like furry potatoes. Mostly, nothing much happens. ‘We call it puppy therapy.’ Minttu Hahtola, podcast host And that’s the point. “I think anyone who is interested in the livestream expects to see sleeping puppies a lot of the time,” said Pietu Ruuttunen, 28, a viewer in the city of Jyvaskyla. The broadcast is a particularly cute example of “slow” television, a distinctly Nordic genre of easy, idyllic viewing. The Norwegians pioneered the form, broadcasting hours of firewood burning or the view from a moving train. Each year, Swedes flock to a livestream of a moose migration. And the Finns? They’ve got a lot of options.



There was a livestream of groceries moving down a checkout conveyor belt. Freshwater seals playing in a lake. Ospreys nesting in their eyrie. At first glance, the feeds could look like a screensaver. The genre is rooted in service television, said Annette Hill, a professor of media and communication studies at Jonkoping University in Sweden. Screensaver or lifesaver? There’s not much going on, but that doesn’t matter. Yle - The Finnish Broadcasting Company via AP Because public broadcasters do not need to advertise or sell products, they can invest in programs free from commercial demands. Viewers find it soothing – almost therapeutic. “That’s what this slow TV does,” Hill said. “It makes you be in the present, and it makes you slow down and stop this frenzy and stop scrolling and stop panicking about what’s going to happen tomorrow.”



This year on Puppy Live there are six puppies, four male and two female. The mother, Hilkka, stays calm even as her progeny kick, thrash, and scramble over one another to nurse. (Veterinarians carefully select and support the mothers, and all the puppies on the show have been born healthy, according to Yle’s website.) Puppy Live began during the pandemic to offer Finns a respite from all the doom and gloom. Yle - The Finnish Broadcasting Company via AP Puppy Live started during the coronavirus pandemic. Finns, like everyone else, needed comfort. (Kurittu said he had “fond memories of coming home drunk just in time to happen upon the mother halfway to a litter”.) But many also needed a crash course in dogs. Many people stuck at home were suddenly spending more time with their own. Others decided to adopt. Pirjo Koskinen, the show’s founder, said she had wanted to create something educational and was surprised by the response. “I really didn’t know that this would be so meaningful for mental health.”



Minttu Hahtola, one of the new podcast’s hosts, echoed the sentiment. “We call it puppy therapy,” she said. Related Article Streaming The 14 most anticipated TV shows still to come this year Last year, the livestream and video clips attracted more than 1 million unique viewers, more than a sixth of the Finnish population. This year, Puppy Live content has already been seen by 1.85 million unique viewers, with about six weeks to go. In Finland, where the job market is brutal, some fans said the puppies were a balm through the slog of unemployment. Others expressed worry about neighbouring Russia. “War is a constant threat,” said Elina Peltonen, 25. But in the puppy box, geopolitics are irrelevant. “Nothing bad happens in the puppy box,” Peltonen said.



Santeri Katainen, a self-described “dog person” with an allergic fiance, said she gets a microdose of puppy love during coffee breaks. Mikko Runolinna, who works at a hospital in the Helsinki area, said that he keeps it running on his second monitor. Jarmo Siira said he watched the puppies while giving blood. The message is simple: Puppies are cute. Nothing here is new – except, of course, for the puppies. For them, everything is a revelation. And their fans, on a 24/7 stakeout, get to watch them grow. “There’s no advertising,” said Kristine Visanen, 51, who watches from her New York City apartment. “There’s no algorithm. I don’t feel like there’s some kind of agenda.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times. World.title: First home buyer pays $1.3m for inner south warehouse conversion
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions First home buyer pays $1.3m for inner south warehouse conversion Robyn Willis Updated October 24, 2026 — 4:38pm ,first published 1:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A first home buyer paid $1,305,000 for a two-bedroom apartment in Alexandria, $55,000 over the reserve, on Saturday. Cooley auctioneer Jake Moore took an opening bid of $1.15 million for 2/145 Belmont Street in front of a crowd of 30 people gathered in the living room of the apartment in a converted warehouse. The property was one of 885 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. By evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 45 per cent from 490 reported results throughout the week, while 184 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Eleven parties registered for the chance to win the keys, with five active. Bidding went up in increments of $10,000 and $5000, jumping around at times to $6000 and $11,000. A final $5000 bid sealed the deal and the hammer fell.



The property had a guide of $1.13 million and a reserve of $1.25 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Related Article Sydney house prices ‘The downturn’s broadened’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.66m The vendors, who once lived in the property, moved interstate five years ago and have been renting it out since. The new owner, who has been renting locally, said he was attracted by the boutique nature of the building, which has just 12 apartments and the “great” area, which has cafes and parks nearby. He said cooling market conditions had stopped him from rushing into a purchase.



“It has given me confidence to wait,” he said. “You are not worried that tomorrow the property [you’re looking at] will be worth more.” Sales agent for The Agency, Brad Gillespie, said most buyers were thinking along the same lines. “They are not in any rush to make a decision,” he said. “There is a lot of window shopping, and they are happy to do the rounds, but unless it ticks all the boxes, they are just waiting.” He described the strong turnout for the auction, which was mostly made up of first home buyers, as “refreshing”. “We haven’t had a competitive auction with so many registrations like this for some time,” he said. “It felt like a normal, traditional campaign.”



Auctioneer Jake Moore extols the virtues of warehouse conversions to a captive audience. Audrey Richardson Moore said warehouse conversions were a perennial favourite with buyers. Related Article Luxury property Five of the best homes for sale in Sydney with water features to enjoy “They will always have good interest because they are not cookie cutter,” he said. “But it was also an extremely realistic price.” In Mosman, a five-bedroom home in the prestige enclave of Beauty Point passed in at $9.85 million.



Only one interested party registered to buy the well-appointed two-storey home at 36 Medusa Street but then failed to bid. Instead, there was a vendor bid of $9.85 million and the auction ended. The reserve was also $9.85 million and the property had a guide of $9.5 million to $10 million, which was revised down to $9 million to $9.5 million after the auction. The potential bidders were a couple who saw the potential in the property as a home for hosting their grandchildren. Principal of Guildea Residential, Jason Guildea, said he was surprised by the types of buyers who had shown interest in the property.



“I thought it would be someone with young children because of the space, but the interest has generally been from grandparents looking to move from steeper blocks into something more child-friendly,” he said. The potential buyers were attracted by the child-friendly nature of the property and the capacity to install a lift down the track. Domain However, he said the uncertain economic climate had given some prestige buyers pause for thought. “Twelve months ago people would turn up to [the auction of] a $10 million house with a baby on their hip,” he said. “But it’s perhaps a reflection of high interest rates and their reduced capacity to borrow [that they are absent].”



The vendors are moving out of Sydney to be closer to their adult children. In Huntleys Cove, a downsizer from Leichhardt paid $1.97 million for a ground floor apartment, $20,000 above the reserve. Three groups registered to bid for the keys to G05/12 Karrabee Avenue, with two raising their paddles. Bidding opened at $1.7 million, going up in increments of $50,000 until it reached $1.9 million when it dropped back to several bids of $10,000 before the property sold. The three-bedroom, two-bathroom property had a guide of $1.8 million and a reserve of $1.95 million.



The new owner, who is originally from the lower north shore, was attracted by the single level and the “future-proof” nature of the apartment, which was a deceased estate. Sales agent for CobdenHayson Lane Cove, George Gialouris, said there was always a market for “A-grade” properties such as this. “With properties like this [buyers] will still pull the trigger [at auction],” he said.

World.title: They’re one of the world’s most famous girl groups, but are they about to implode?
World.content:
CultureMusicPop music They’re one of the world’s most famous girl groups, but are they about to implode? Nell Geraets October 24, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Katseye: Wild Hearts wants you to know the kids are alright. Chronicling Katseye’s rapid rise, the new documentary is as flashy and upbeat as their concerts, marvelling over how they went from obscurity to the world’s biggest girl group. But their story has a darker underbelly, one the Disney+ documentary appears at pains to conceal. While the six-piece’s fame skyrocketed, two members, Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza, went on hiatus. Their hiatuses began five months apart, and both cited mental health and wellbeing concerns. The members of Katseye, left to right: Yoonchae Jeung, Megan Skiendiel, Lara Raj, Manon Bannerman, Sophia Laforteza and Daniela Avanzini. Getty Images Beyond a brief reference to therapy, this is absent from the documentary, which dropped last week. It begins and ends on a promising note, assuring fans (known as “Eyekons”) that Katseye is only getting started. But with a third of the group missing in action, could their future be bleaker? What is Katseye?





Their “unabashed pop” drove this swift success, Keith says. “While solo artists are concerned with things like authenticity and maintaining a stable image, Katseye skip between different genres, sounds and trends really quickly.” They went from SIS, a more conventional, “demure” album, to Beautiful Chaos, an “aggressively weird” EP with hits like Gnarly. Then came Wild, a TikTok-coded Gen Alpha treat. Such willingness to adapt keeps existing fans on their toes and attracts new audiences along the way. Loading Katseye has heralded the return of the girl group in Western pop music, an industry now largely dominated by solo artists. The outfit’s formation was documented in another carefully crafted documentary, Netflix’s Pop Star Academy: Katseye. “They tapped into the reality-competition show audience. Many people were invested even before the group debuted,” Keith says.



Are cracks beginning to show? In February, Katseye’s labels announced Bannerman’s temporary hiatus from group activities to “focus on her health and wellbeing”. Shortly after, Bannerman assured fans she was taking care of herself, and that “sometimes things unfold in ways we don’t fully control”. View post on X This caused some Eyekons to speculate about whether Bannerman had been quietly sidelined by the labels and whether her Swiss-Ghanaian heritage played a part. Rumours of tension within the group and with the labels intensified when Bannerman reportedly liked a social media post referencing the systemic mistreatment and racism faced by Black members in girl groups. The remaining group members have since said the situation had nothing to do with race. “We can definitely say that in our situation, in no way was it about race,” Laforteza told Vanity Fair in June. “That goes against everything that we stand for.” However, some fans still called for a boycott of Katseye pending Bannerman’s reinstatement. There’s been no mention of when this could be. Hybe and Geffen have been contacted for comment.



And then there were five... Getty Images Five months after Bannerman’s break began, Laforteza went on hiatus over mental health concerns. It has since been announced that she will return to Katseye in January, but the absences point to underlying issues within the group. Every member has said they’ve experienced racist or misogynistic abuse online, including offensive polls that rank them in order of “attractiveness”. Raj, an American with Tamil-Indian heritage, said she was falsely reported to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and other members have received death threats. “Looking back at the 00s and 90s, celebrities definitely had to deal with tabloids, but the internet is just so accessible and in your face, especially because we’re on there, too,” Megan told Dazed in August. Alongside online toxicity comes the general pressures of working within K-pop, which demands perfection. The documentary outlines Katseye’s dusk-till-dawn rehearsals, the occasionally brutal feedback from label executives, and Skiendiel’s chronic back pain. Katseye performed without Manon at the 2026 Coachella Valley Music And Arts Festival. Getty Images



These instances reasonably trigger concern among fans, Keith says. However, many of the girl groups that came before Katseye similarly evolved, including Destiny’s Child and the Pussycat Dolls. But Katseye has been subject to extra scrutiny, Keith notes, mainly from those curious whether the “K-pop-American-pop” crossover will work. “Any stumbles by the group or its members will likely be interpreted as a sign of this experiment failing.” What could this mean for Katseye’s future? Hiatuses may not be ideal, but they’re sometimes inevitable, especially in K-pop. “One of the ways K-pop has dealt with these shifting line-ups is to create subunits,” Keith says. “For example, if we have a four-member group, we might release a mini-album featuring a duo. For Katseye, four members would probably be sustainable, but it would be difficult if they had to operate with any fewer than that.”



Related Article Pop music Australian performer dumped from K-pop girl group Katseye may be fine, but the struggles of its members could diminish the initial optimism around “hybrid” groups from crossover cultural backgrounds. “K-pop agencies and Western artists and labels have been collaborating for decades, and Katseye is one of their biggest successes to date. But that doesn’t mean that any global group trained in the K-pop style will automatically succeed … I’m not sure whether we will see another hybrid group soon.” Katseye: Wild Hearts is available to stream on Disney+ now. World.title: Public backlash sparks backflip on Sydney train timetables
World.content:
PoliticsNSWPublic transport Public backlash sparks backflip on Sydney train timetables Clair Weaver Updated October 24, 2026 — 3:46pm ,first published 11:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. An unpopular train timetable shake-up that would have affected hundreds of thousands of Sydney train commuters has been abandoned following public backlash. NSW Premier Chris Minns on Saturday revealed the government’s dramatic U-turn on planned changes to the T4, T8 and South Coast lines’ timetables, which were scheduled to commence on November 15. NSW Premier Chris Minns apologised and said opposition to the timetable changes was universal. NSW Secretary of Transport Josh Murray (left) and Transport Minister John Graham (right) also acknowledged the backlash. Audrey Richardson Minns issued a public apology and promised that when future changes that affect train passengers are being considered, “we won’t jam it down their throats”. “The truth of the matter is since we released the new timetable I haven’t run into anybody who supported the change,” he said.



It’s an embarrassing backflip for the government less than two weeks after the new timetable was announced. “It’s not ideal ... but I’d rather apologise and backflip on a policy like this than implement a change that people don’t want,” Minns said. NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane accused the government of trying to “sell longer journeys and fewer express services to commuters as an improvement.” “Governments should be making people’s lives easier, not harder,” she said. Minns revealed his own local Labor MPs whose constituents would have been affected by the new timetable were among the “harshest” critics.



Liberal Oatley MP Mark Coure said the government had also been forced to reinstate bus services this month in his electorate after public outcry. “People want to get to work on time and get home to their families,” he said. “They should not have to campaign to protect the services they rely on.” The Minns government has abandoned controversial changes to train timetables. Dominic Lorrimer The rail changes – which the government had pledged would deliver more frequent services and additional capacity across southern Sydney and the South Coast – would have resulted in longer commute times for some passengers. Those travelling on the T4 between Waterfall and the central city, for example, were facing longer trip times of up to 14 minutes because of extra stops. Passengers travelling from Heathcote, Engadine and Loftus stations would have seen trip times to the city increase by about 12 minutes in the morning peak and about 14 minutes in the evening peak. South Coast passengers travelling to Sydney Airport from Wollongong would have had to go to Central and double-back on the T8 if they wished to avoid switching twice at stations on their journey.



Some services on the T4 and T8 lines would have increased in frequency. Minns said the government’s new focus was on improving reliability, pointing to a $2.1 billion investment in maintenance and incident response on Sydney’s rail network, parts of which are more than 100 years old. “I want to make it clear we will not be pursuing timetable changes unless and until reliability returns, particularly to the T4 transport line,” he said. “There are still too many signal failures, breaks in the rail and major disruptions.” There was some public consultation by Transport for NSW before the timetable was announced, he said, but “it’s not possible to speak to the hundreds of thousands of people” who use the services every day. Transport Minister John Graham said October has been a “difficult” month, including major disruptions on the T4 line on the same day he announced the new timetable, which he says galvanised his priorities.



“That day itself really focused the mind and left me in no doubt that we have got more to do in investing in the rail system, making sure this plan works, making sure this maintenance rolls out,” he said. NSW Secretary for Transport Josh Murray said commuters would be informed the new timetable was not going ahead. Related Article Updated

Sydney Metro Opening date locked in for final stage of Sydney’s M1 metro line The existing timetable will now remain in place and Transport for NSW will engage “with communities on future service improvements”. World.title: ‘She keeps surprising me’: Payne says best yet to come from Proxima Dea
World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing ‘She keeps surprising me’: Payne says best yet to come from Proxima Dea Craig Kerry October 24, 2026 — 5:18pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Rosehill trainer David Payne was excited for what’s to come from immature surprise packet Proxima Dea after she gave him a third group 1 Spring Champion Stakes (2000m) win to cement her place as the VRC Oaks favourite. The full sister to Queensland Oaks winner Gypsy Goddess took her unbeaten career to five, pushing to sit outside the leader in the $2 million three-year-old feature from the outside gate under Zac Lloyd before going for home on the home bend at Randwick on Saturday. The tactic paid off as Gloaming Stakes (1800m) winner Proxima Dea, unwanted with a $300,000 reserve at yearling sales and retained by her breeders, fended off favourite and Flight Stakes (1600m) champion Global Goal by a length and a half. Cormier was third. Proxima Dea after winning the Spring Champion Stakes. Getty Images She was in from $3.50 to $2.30 (TAB) for the Oaks (2500m) on November 5 at Flemington. “To look at her, you wouldn’t give much for her, but geez, she seems to have everything. She’s got guts and heart,” Payne said.



“I said to [Lloyd], ‘She’ll outstay them. We can’t have a sit and sprint. If nothing goes, you go. Otherwise, sit outside the leader and go early on her.’ “She’ll love [the Oaks], and you can give her a bit of an easier ride.” Jockey Zac Lloyd and trainer David Payne. Getty Images It was a first group 1 win for Payne, 78, since 2020 Spring Champion victor Montefilia took out the 2022 Ranvet – her fourth success at the top level – for the same ownership as Proxima Dea. Payne also won the 2017 Spring Champion with colt Ace High. “This filly keeps surprising me,” said Payne, a champion trainer and jockey in South Africa before coming to Sydney in 2002.



“Montefilia was a good filly, but I think this filly stays better than Montefilia. “I had a New Zealand filly in South Africa called Petrava, she was unbelievable [and won five group 1s]. She used to just jump and run to the front, 1600, lead all the way. She could sprint a mile. “I’ve had a lot of good fillies but this one, she’s the ugliest I think, but she keeps surprising me. She might be, the way she’s going, I mean, five in a row in her first prep, who knows? “I’ve had some good staying fillies, but she’s exceptional because she’s still not mature, when you look at her.” It was also gutsy effort from Lloyd, who battled illness to ride on a warm day at Randwick after missing the midweek meeting at Warwick Farm. He earlier won the Highway Handicap on Scott Singleton-trained Ocean Tsunami.



Guineas on map for Central Europe Chris Waller-trained Central Europe later broke through at his seventh start, sweeping to a 3¼-length win in the $1 million group 3 Callander-Presnell (1600m) for three-year-olds. The Frankel colt, an unlucky second in the Skyline Stakes and placed in the Pago Pago Stakes and Rosebud, came from second last down the outside under Jason Collett to prove a class above. “I think maybe a Sandown Guineas could be a nice race for him and then obviously aim a lot higher in the autumn,” Waller representative Darren Beadman said. “James [McDonald] was always saying he was pretty good and today he showed it with his turn of foot.”



In the Kirkham Plate (1000m) for two-year-olds to start the day, Waller-trained Exo Velocity ($13) caused an upset with a rails run from last under Kerrin McEvoy to edge out stablemate Tour De Force ($7) by a long neck on debut. Exo Velocity, a $650,000 Zoustar yearling bought by Waller and Guy Mulcaster, is the first foal out of Dalrello and Calaway Gal Stakes winner Exo Lady and looks likely to target the Magic Millions carnival in January.

World.title: ‘On the verge of breakdown’: MPs’ staff burnt out from online hate
World.content:
PoliticsFederalHaines attack ‘On the verge of breakdown’: MPs’ staff burnt out from online hate Nick Newling October 24, 2026 — 5:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Independent and minor party MPs say their staff are being inundated with threats and abuse being sent to their offices, with some resorting to private fundraising to employ enough advisers to share the significant workload. Politicians have been forced to turn off their office’s phone lines, order staff not to review constituent emails, and send their employees home to recuperate, amid a deluge of vitriol. MPs Mehreen Faruqi, Nicolette Boele, Sophie Scamps and Fatima Payman. Threats against federal politicians are at an all-time high, with MPs on alert after the shock attack on Helen Haines on Monday. In the aftermath of the attack, Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett confirmed that her force was charging one individual a week with threats to politicians. NSW Greens senator Mehreen Faruqi told this masthead: “There have been times that I have had to tell staff to not answer the phones because all we are getting is calls of hate and abuse.”



Faruqi said the emotional impact of the high volume of threats that come into her office directly challenges her ability to provide assistance to constituents, at times frustrating those who wish to speak with her. Related Article Haines attack A politician’s job is to listen. It’s becoming increasingly dangerous to do so “We’ve often had training and support from the Parliamentary Workplace Support Service. I have counselling quite a bit from PWSS. Staff see social media, emails come through. There are phone calls as well. It hinders how we do our work,” Faruqi said. Faruqi and independent senator Fatima Payman separately spoke of separate incidents this week in which pictures of human faeces had been sent to their email inboxes, distressing staff members employed to monitor legitimate correspondence from constituents. Payman said her office this week missed an email from the AFP regarding the conviction of a Queensland man who targeted her with menacing voicemails, emails and social media messages because her relevant staff member was taking a mental health day after exposure to “sustained abusive” content.



“My staff are on the verge of breakdown and there is no practical way of sharing the burden without shutting the office entirely because, Labor, the party for workers doesn’t give a s--t about safety and wellbeing of the workers in my office,” Payman told this masthead. After leaving the Labor Party to sit as an independent last term, the senator was not afforded the additional “personal staffing” allocation provided to other senators, leaving her with the equal lowest staffing allocation of any crossbencher in federal parliament. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has faced criticism for his provision of staffing allocations. Alex Ellinghausen Under federal legislation each MP is entitled to five electorate officers, but the provision of extra highly paid “personal staff” remains entirely under the prime minister’s discretion. Anthony Albanese has been criticised for the way he grants staffing allocations, after both cutting the crossbench’s staffing following the 2022 election, and the opposition’s following the 2025 election.



On the Senate crossbench, Jacqui Lambie has three additional advisers, David Pocock and Lidia Thorpe each have two, and United Australia Party senator Ralph Babet has one. Payman and One Nation senator Tyron Whitten, both representing Western Australia, are the only senators to have no additional staff. Payman has made repeated requests for additional staff, saying she cannot effectively represent Australia’s largest state without them. There has been no response to her requests. Independent MP Nicolette Boele has made similar requests for increased staffing which have been declined. A teal independent representing the inner-Sydney electorate of Bradfield, Boele has one additional staffer while the five other teal independents each have two. A reason for this discrepancy has never been provided. “As a woman in public life, I know the risks to me and my team are rising. Bradfield is also home to large Jewish and Chinese-Australian communities who are being targeted,” the MP told this masthead.



“We asked for more staff to keep my team safe and to properly support communities, and were turned down. We asked again after the Bondi attack last December, and were turned down again.” Related Article Exclusive

Political leadership Albanese granted Greens 15 staff just before party blocked inquiry into PM’s powers Boele has had to privately fund a social media staffer to monitor online threats against her office. She said the current staffing arrangement isn’t “fair, safe or sustainable” for her office or the community she represents. Both independent senator David Pocock and teal MP Sophie Scamps also use private fundraising efforts to employ staff. Scamps said young female staff in her office were on the front line of filtering threats and harassment that come into the office, saying they were often “trying to protect me from the vile abuse that comes in often based on misinformation.”



A member of Scamps’ team recently stepped back from her job after feeling burnt out because of the amount of vitriol she was faced with daily. “The aggression, the toxicity, it takes its toll, she’s now left. She was a beloved member of the team, but there’s only so much you can take,” Scamps said. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: In troubled times, Finland’s public broadcaster has an answer: puppies
World.content:
WorldEuropeAnimals In troubled times, Finland’s public broadcaster has an answer: puppies Amelia Nierenberg and Lara McCoy October 24, 2026 — 4:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

London: Puppy Live is exactly what it sounds like. It’s a 24/7 livestream of newborn puppies. And it sometimes seems everyone in Finland is invested. Loading “It’s a form of stress relief,” said Kalle Kurittu, 32, who lives in Helsinki and has watched for years. “I love all the puppies equally,” said Mandi Salo, 9, also of Helsinki, who said she was excited when one pup opened its eyes.



Puppy Live (“Pentulive” in Finnish) – is something like The Truman Show for a litter, raised from birth to adoption in front of an adoring public. Broadcast by Yle, Finland’s public broadcaster, the stream is a phenomenon, with well over 1 million viewers. Now, in its sixth year, the show is going international. The Truman Show for dogs: Puppies and their mother, Hilkka, in a scene from the 24/7 livestream. Yle - The Finnish Broadcasting Company via AP Sweden’s public broadcaster, SVT, has started streaming it. A Dutch broadcaster has bought the rights for a spinoff (with Dutch puppies). Yle (pronounced OO-lay) has even launched a Puppy Live podcast and, in a very 2026 move, released a prediction-market game to run for the eight weeks of the season. Even though the babies sleep some 20 hours a day, there’s plenty to bet on: How much do they weigh? How long are their tails? Which will grow fastest? Players earn points, and weekly winners get a mug.



At any given minute, the puppies, currently two weeks old, are probably sleeping. They twitch on a purple blanket like furry potatoes. Mostly, nothing much happens. ‘We call it puppy therapy.’ Minttu Hahtola, podcast host And that’s the point. “I think anyone who is interested in the livestream expects to see sleeping puppies a lot of the time,” said Pietu Ruuttunen, 28, a viewer in the city of Jyvaskyla. The broadcast is a particularly cute example of “slow” television, a distinctly Nordic genre of easy, idyllic viewing. The Norwegians pioneered the form, broadcasting hours of firewood burning or the view from a moving train. Each year, Swedes flock to a livestream of a moose migration. And the Finns? They’ve got a lot of options.



There was a livestream of groceries moving down a checkout conveyor belt. Freshwater seals playing in a lake. Ospreys nesting in their eyrie. At first glance, the feeds could look like a screensaver. The genre is rooted in service television, said Annette Hill, a professor of media and communication studies at Jonkoping University in Sweden. Screensaver or lifesaver? There’s not much going on, but that doesn’t matter. Yle - The Finnish Broadcasting Company via AP Because public broadcasters do not need to advertise or sell products, they can invest in programs free from commercial demands. Viewers find it soothing – almost therapeutic. “That’s what this slow TV does,” Hill said. “It makes you be in the present, and it makes you slow down and stop this frenzy and stop scrolling and stop panicking about what’s going to happen tomorrow.”



This year on Puppy Live there are six puppies, four male and two female. The mother, Hilkka, stays calm even as her progeny kick, thrash, and scramble over one another to nurse. (Veterinarians carefully select and support the mothers, and all the puppies on the show have been born healthy, according to Yle’s website.) Puppy Live began during the pandemic to offer Finns a respite from all the doom and gloom. Yle - The Finnish Broadcasting Company via AP Puppy Live started during the coronavirus pandemic. Finns, like everyone else, needed comfort. (Kurittu said he had “fond memories of coming home drunk just in time to happen upon the mother halfway to a litter”.) But many also needed a crash course in dogs. Many people stuck at home were suddenly spending more time with their own. Others decided to adopt. Pirjo Koskinen, the show’s founder, said she had wanted to create something educational and was surprised by the response. “I really didn’t know that this would be so meaningful for mental health.”



Minttu Hahtola, one of the new podcast’s hosts, echoed the sentiment. “We call it puppy therapy,” she said. Related Article Streaming The 14 most anticipated TV shows still to come this year Last year, the livestream and video clips attracted more than 1 million unique viewers, more than a sixth of the Finnish population. This year, Puppy Live content has already been seen by 1.85 million unique viewers, with about six weeks to go. In Finland, where the job market is brutal, some fans said the puppies were a balm through the slog of unemployment. Others expressed worry about neighbouring Russia. “War is a constant threat,” said Elina Peltonen, 25. But in the puppy box, geopolitics are irrelevant. “Nothing bad happens in the puppy box,” Peltonen said.



Santeri Katainen, a self-described “dog person” with an allergic fiance, said she gets a microdose of puppy love during coffee breaks. Mikko Runolinna, who works at a hospital in the Helsinki area, said that he keeps it running on his second monitor. Jarmo Siira said he watched the puppies while giving blood. The message is simple: Puppies are cute. Nothing here is new – except, of course, for the puppies. For them, everything is a revelation. And their fans, on a 24/7 stakeout, get to watch them grow. “There’s no advertising,” said Kristine Visanen, 51, who watches from her New York City apartment. “There’s no algorithm. I don’t feel like there’s some kind of agenda.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times.
