World.title: First home buyer pays $1.3m for inner south warehouse conversion
World.content:
PropertyNewsAuctions First home buyer pays $1.3m for inner south warehouse conversion Robyn Willis Updated October 24, 2026 — 4:38pm ,first published 1:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 Gift this free article Share full article with anyone — no subscription needed to read it. It won't deduct your gift credits. Learn more Share article as gift Share A A A

A first home buyer paid $1,305,000 for a two-bedroom apartment in Alexandria, $55,000 over the reserve, on Saturday. Cooley auctioneer Jake Moore took an opening bid of $1.15 million for 2/145 Belmont Street in front of a crowd of 30 people gathered in the living room of the apartment in a converted warehouse. The property was one of 885 scheduled to go to auction in Sydney this week. By evening, Domain recorded a preliminary auction clearance rate of 45 per cent from 490 reported results throughout the week, while 184 auctions were withdrawn. Withdrawn auctions are counted as unsold properties when calculating the clearance rate. Eleven parties registered for the chance to win the keys, with five active. Bidding went up in increments of $10,000 and $5000, jumping around at times to $6000 and $11,000. A final $5000 bid sealed the deal and the hammer fell.



The property had a guide of $1.13 million and a reserve of $1.25 million. There is no legal requirement for a vendor’s reserve to be in line with their property’s price guide. Related Article Sydney house prices ‘The downturn’s broadened’: Sydney’s median house price falls to $1.66m The vendors, who once lived in the property, moved interstate five years ago and have been renting it out since. The new owner, who has been renting locally, said he was attracted by the boutique nature of the building, which has just 12 apartments and the “great” area, which has cafes and parks nearby. He said cooling market conditions had stopped him from rushing into a purchase.



“It has given me confidence to wait,” he said. “You are not worried that tomorrow the property [you’re looking at] will be worth more.” Sales agent for The Agency, Brad Gillespie, said most buyers were thinking along the same lines. “They are not in any rush to make a decision,” he said. “There is a lot of window shopping, and they are happy to do the rounds, but unless it ticks all the boxes, they are just waiting.” He described the strong turnout for the auction, which was mostly made up of first home buyers, as “refreshing”. “We haven’t had a competitive auction with so many registrations like this for some time,” he said. “It felt like a normal, traditional campaign.”



Auctioneer Jake Moore extols the virtues of warehouse conversions to a captive audience. Audrey Richardson Moore said warehouse conversions were a perennial favourite with buyers. Related Article Luxury property Five of the best homes for sale in Sydney with water features to enjoy “They will always have good interest because they are not cookie cutter,” he said. “But it was also an extremely realistic price.” In Mosman, a five-bedroom home in the prestige enclave of Beauty Point passed in at $9.85 million.



Only one interested party registered to buy the well-appointed two-storey home at 36 Medusa Street but then failed to bid. Instead, there was a vendor bid of $9.85 million and the auction ended. The reserve was also $9.85 million and the property had a guide of $9.5 million to $10 million, which was revised down to $9 million to $9.5 million after the auction. The potential bidders were a couple who saw the potential in the property as a home for hosting their grandchildren. Principal of Guildea Residential, Jason Guildea, said he was surprised by the types of buyers who had shown interest in the property.



“I thought it would be someone with young children because of the space, but the interest has generally been from grandparents looking to move from steeper blocks into something more child-friendly,” he said. The potential buyers were attracted by the child-friendly nature of the property and the capacity to install a lift down the track. Domain However, he said the uncertain economic climate had given some prestige buyers pause for thought. “Twelve months ago people would turn up to [the auction of] a $10 million house with a baby on their hip,” he said. “But it’s perhaps a reflection of high interest rates and their reduced capacity to borrow [that they are absent].”



The vendors are moving out of Sydney to be closer to their adult children. In Huntleys Cove, a downsizer from Leichhardt paid $1.97 million for a ground floor apartment, $20,000 above the reserve. Three groups registered to bid for the keys to G05/12 Karrabee Avenue, with two raising their paddles. Bidding opened at $1.7 million, going up in increments of $50,000 until it reached $1.9 million when it dropped back to several bids of $10,000 before the property sold. The three-bedroom, two-bathroom property had a guide of $1.8 million and a reserve of $1.95 million.



The new owner, who is originally from the lower north shore, was attracted by the single level and the “future-proof” nature of the apartment, which was a deceased estate. Sales agent for CobdenHayson Lane Cove, George Gialouris, said there was always a market for “A-grade” properties such as this. “With properties like this [buyers] will still pull the trigger [at auction],” he said.

Collingwood’s horror week got worse as they were kept goal-less in a 48-point loss to Port Adelaide at Alberton Oval on Friday night, which leaves them second-last on the AFLW ladder.

Compounding a miserable week in which they learned captain Ruby Schleicher is returning to her native Western Australia, Collingwood kicked their lowest-ever AFLW score by three points with the one bright spot a 29-disposal game from young star Ash Centra.

Violet Patterson of the Magpies and Ashleigh Woodland of the Power compete for the ball. AFL Photos via Getty Images

World.title: They’re one of the world’s most famous girl groups, but are they about to implode?
World.content:
CultureMusicPop music They’re one of the world’s most famous girl groups, but are they about to implode? Nell Geraets October 24, 2026 — 4:00pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Katseye: Wild Hearts wants you to know the kids are alright. Chronicling Katseye’s rapid rise, the new documentary is as flashy and upbeat as their concerts, marvelling over how they went from obscurity to the world’s biggest girl group. But their story has a darker underbelly, one the Disney+ documentary appears at pains to conceal. While the six-piece’s fame skyrocketed, two members, Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza, went on hiatus. Their hiatuses began five months apart, and both cited mental health and wellbeing concerns. The members of Katseye, left to right: Yoonchae Jeung, Megan Skiendiel, Lara Raj, Manon Bannerman, Sophia Laforteza and Daniela Avanzini. Getty Images Beyond a brief reference to therapy, this is absent from the documentary, which dropped last week. It begins and ends on a promising note, assuring fans (known as “Eyekons”) that Katseye is only getting started. But with a third of the group missing in action, could their future be bleaker? What is Katseye?





Their “unabashed pop” drove this swift success, Keith says. “While solo artists are concerned with things like authenticity and maintaining a stable image, Katseye skip between different genres, sounds and trends really quickly.” They went from SIS, a more conventional, “demure” album, to Beautiful Chaos, an “aggressively weird” EP with hits like Gnarly. Then came Wild, a TikTok-coded Gen Alpha treat. Such willingness to adapt keeps existing fans on their toes and attracts new audiences along the way. Loading Katseye has heralded the return of the girl group in Western pop music, an industry now largely dominated by solo artists. The outfit’s formation was documented in another carefully crafted documentary, Netflix’s Pop Star Academy: Katseye. “They tapped into the reality-competition show audience. Many people were invested even before the group debuted,” Keith says.



Are cracks beginning to show? In February, Katseye’s labels announced Bannerman’s temporary hiatus from group activities to “focus on her health and wellbeing”. Shortly after, Bannerman assured fans she was taking care of herself, and that “sometimes things unfold in ways we don’t fully control”. View post on X This caused some Eyekons to speculate about whether Bannerman had been quietly sidelined by the labels and whether her Swiss-Ghanaian heritage played a part. Rumours of tension within the group and with the labels intensified when Bannerman reportedly liked a social media post referencing the systemic mistreatment and racism faced by Black members in girl groups. The remaining group members have since said the situation had nothing to do with race. “We can definitely say that in our situation, in no way was it about race,” Laforteza told Vanity Fair in June. “That goes against everything that we stand for.” However, some fans still called for a boycott of Katseye pending Bannerman’s reinstatement. There’s been no mention of when this could be. Hybe and Geffen have been contacted for comment.



And then there were five... Getty Images Five months after Bannerman’s break began, Laforteza went on hiatus over mental health concerns. It has since been announced that she will return to Katseye in January, but the absences point to underlying issues within the group. Every member has said they’ve experienced racist or misogynistic abuse online, including offensive polls that rank them in order of “attractiveness”. Raj, an American with Tamil-Indian heritage, said she was falsely reported to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and other members have received death threats. “Looking back at the 00s and 90s, celebrities definitely had to deal with tabloids, but the internet is just so accessible and in your face, especially because we’re on there, too,” Megan told Dazed in August. Alongside online toxicity comes the general pressures of working within K-pop, which demands perfection. The documentary outlines Katseye’s dusk-till-dawn rehearsals, the occasionally brutal feedback from label executives, and Skiendiel’s chronic back pain. Katseye performed without Manon at the 2026 Coachella Valley Music And Arts Festival. Getty Images



These instances reasonably trigger concern among fans, Keith says. However, many of the girl groups that came before Katseye similarly evolved, including Destiny’s Child and the Pussycat Dolls. But Katseye has been subject to extra scrutiny, Keith notes, mainly from those curious whether the “K-pop-American-pop” crossover will work. “Any stumbles by the group or its members will likely be interpreted as a sign of this experiment failing.” What could this mean for Katseye’s future? Hiatuses may not be ideal, but they’re sometimes inevitable, especially in K-pop. “One of the ways K-pop has dealt with these shifting line-ups is to create subunits,” Keith says. “For example, if we have a four-member group, we might release a mini-album featuring a duo. For Katseye, four members would probably be sustainable, but it would be difficult if they had to operate with any fewer than that.”



Related Article Pop music Australian performer dumped from K-pop girl group Katseye may be fine, but the struggles of its members could diminish the initial optimism around “hybrid” groups from crossover cultural backgrounds. “K-pop agencies and Western artists and labels have been collaborating for decades, and Katseye is one of their biggest successes to date. But that doesn’t mean that any global group trained in the K-pop style will automatically succeed … I’m not sure whether we will see another hybrid group soon.” Katseye: Wild Hearts is available to stream on Disney+ now. World.title: Public backlash sparks backflip on Sydney train timetables
World.content:
PoliticsNSWPublic transport Public backlash sparks backflip on Sydney train timetables Clair Weaver Updated October 24, 2026 — 3:46pm ,first published 11:24am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

An unpopular train timetable shake-up that would have affected hundreds of thousands of Sydney train commuters has been abandoned following public backlash. NSW Premier Chris Minns on Saturday revealed the government’s dramatic U-turn on planned changes to the T4, T8 and South Coast lines’ timetables, which were scheduled to commence on November 15. NSW Premier Chris Minns apologised and said opposition to the timetable changes was universal. NSW Secretary of Transport Josh Murray (left) and Transport Minister John Graham (right) also acknowledged the backlash. Audrey Richardson Minns issued a public apology and promised that when future changes that affect train passengers are being considered, “we won’t jam it down their throats”. “The truth of the matter is since we released the new timetable I haven’t run into anybody who supported the change,” he said.



It’s an embarrassing backflip for the government less than two weeks after the new timetable was announced. “It’s not ideal ... but I’d rather apologise and backflip on a policy like this than implement a change that people don’t want,” Minns said. NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane accused the government of trying to “sell longer journeys and fewer express services to commuters as an improvement.” “Governments should be making people’s lives easier, not harder,” she said. Minns revealed his own local Labor MPs whose constituents would have been affected by the new timetable were among the “harshest” critics.



Liberal Oatley MP Mark Coure said the government had also been forced to reinstate bus services this month in his electorate after public outcry. “People want to get to work on time and get home to their families,” he said. “They should not have to campaign to protect the services they rely on.” The Minns government has abandoned controversial changes to train timetables. Dominic Lorrimer The rail changes – which the government had pledged would deliver more frequent services and additional capacity across southern Sydney and the South Coast – would have resulted in longer commute times for some passengers. Those travelling on the T4 between Waterfall and the central city, for example, were facing longer trip times of up to 14 minutes because of extra stops. Passengers travelling from Heathcote, Engadine and Loftus stations would have seen trip times to the city increase by about 12 minutes in the morning peak and about 14 minutes in the evening peak. South Coast passengers travelling to Sydney Airport from Wollongong would have had to go to Central and double-back on the T8 if they wished to avoid switching twice at stations on their journey.



Some services on the T4 and T8 lines would have increased in frequency. Minns said the government’s new focus was on improving reliability, pointing to a $2.1 billion investment in maintenance and incident response on Sydney’s rail network, parts of which are more than 100 years old. “I want to make it clear we will not be pursuing timetable changes unless and until reliability returns, particularly to the T4 transport line,” he said. “There are still too many signal failures, breaks in the rail and major disruptions.” There was some public consultation by Transport for NSW before the timetable was announced, he said, but “it’s not possible to speak to the hundreds of thousands of people” who use the services every day. Transport Minister John Graham said October has been a “difficult” month, including major disruptions on the T4 line on the same day he announced the new timetable, which he says galvanised his priorities.



“That day itself really focused the mind and left me in no doubt that we have got more to do in investing in the rail system, making sure this plan works, making sure this maintenance rolls out,” he said. NSW Secretary for Transport Josh Murray said commuters would be informed the new timetable was not going ahead. Related Article Updated

Sydney Metro Opening date locked in for final stage of Sydney’s M1 metro line The existing timetable will now remain in place and Transport for NSW will engage “with communities on future service improvements”. World.title: Tsunami warning cancelled after magnitude 7.2 quake off Vanuatu
World.content:
A tsunami warning has been cancelled, following a 7.2 magnitude earthquake off Vanuatu on Saturday.

The quake's epicentre was around 200 kilometres north-west of Vanuatu's Port Olry, according to geological monitor USGS, which later revised the magnitude of the tremor down to 6.9. It also reported a second quake of magnitude 6.3 nearby.

"Based on latest available sea level and observational data, there is no longer tsunami threat from this earthquake to the Vanuatu coastal areas," the Vanuatu Geological Hazards Department said on Saturday afternoon.

Earthquakes are common in Vanuatu, a low-lying archipelago that straddles the tectonic Ring of Fire, an arc of seismic activity stretching through Southeast Asia and across the Pacific basin.

World.title: Luxon defends Potaka on photo with gang members
World.content:
Christopher Luxon says it would be "disingenuous" to say a photo circulating online of National MP Tama Potaka posing with gang members is the same as images of Labour, Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs.

Labour candidate for Tamaki Makaurau, Kerrin Leoni, resigned on Friday after video and an image of her campaigning in party attire, and posing with Mongrel Mob members at a fundraising event were published online.

Initially Labour leader Chris Hipkins had backed Leoni saying she was at a family event with some of her whanau who are gang members.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407315334112

But after a video circulated online on Thursday night Hipkins said it became untenable for Leoni to stay on as a candidate as she had not provided the full story of what had happened.

Earlier this month Hipkins had distanced himself from Green and Te Pāti Māori MPs and candidates who had attended an election hui at a gang pad and posed for photos with Mongrel Mob members.

On Saturday Luxon was asked whether he was aware of any images of his MPs or candidates posing with gang members and whether he would consider that acceptable given his tough criticism of opposition MPs and candidates.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407319621112

Luxon said he hadn't seen any images himself but was aware one was doing the rounds of MP and Māori Development Minister Tama Potaka.

"He's not campaigning, he's not fundraising, he's not raising funds for the Mongrel Mob," Luxon told reporters.

"And go talk to Tama - he's very much against gangs, like the rest of us in the National Party."

"I think it'd be disingenuous to suggest that they are equivalent images that we've seen."

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6407262765112

Luxon suggested media speak to Potaka, saying, "you'll get a very clear view from him about what's happened around crime and law and order".

"He represents an area in Hamilton that was very challenged … he understands the suffering that people have gone through, and he doesn't think gangs are good for society."

Potaka told RNZ the photo was taken at a "very public hui," organised by the Kiingitanga in January 2024.

"There were literally thousands of people there. A person I went to school with asked me for a photo, and I didn't want to create too much fuss. And the photo was taken," he said.

"That's about two and a half years ago, and well in advance of the gang pad patch ban being implemented, of course. Very different circumstances to what we've got today."

Asked if he was surprised to see the photo now being circulated the way it had, Potaka again said it was "very different circumstances" to Labour, the Greens, and Te Pāti Māori, who he accused of trying to "curry some favour" from the gangs.

He would not say if he would get a photo with that person he went to school with again, only that a gang patch ban was now in place and National had been "very deliberate and intentional" about making its position clear.

"We don't support gangs or the violence that often goes with them, whereas other parties are."

But Hipkins said National should be held to its own standards.

Speaking to media at Queensgate Mall in Lower Hutt, Hipkins said Luxon had made gangs a "huge issue" during the election campaign.

"He now needs to answer why he thinks National MPs should be held to a different standard to the standard he demands of others," he said.

While Luxon hadn't spoken to Potaka about the photo or its origins, National MP and Police Minister Mark Mitchell had.

Te Pāti Māori MP Oriini Kaipara, with Green candidates Hūhana Lyndon and Michel Mulipola, Te Whatanui Skipwith (far right) Ōtāhuhu Green Party candidate, along with the Mongrel Mob's Harry Tam and other members. Supplied / Facebook

Mitchell was at Saturday's media conference with Luxon and asked to speak to the issue.

"Tama was at an event three years ago, it was at the Kiingitanga for an event there when that photo was taken.

"He wasn't campaigning. He wasn't engaging gang members to ask them to get organised to vote for the National Party - in fact, he was probably getting a hard time because we were implementing our gang legislation," Mitchell told reporters.

"There is a big difference between being at a public event and attending a public event and having gang members approach you. I've had gang members approach me at public events.

"There's a big difference between that and fronting up to a gang fundraiser or a gang pad to try and ingratiate yourself with those gang members to actively campaign and try and get them to campaign and vote against a government that has made this country much safer, that has made it much harder to be a gang member in our country, and we will continue to do that," Mitchell said.

On why Potaka posed for the photo Mitchell speculated that he was trying to be "respectful and not create a scene".

"We get thousands of photos every day of people in a public place. We don't know every individual. We don't know their background. We don't know their history. That's just the nature of public life.

"There is a huge difference between that and actively going to a gang pad or a or a function organised by the gangs, a fundraiser by the rogue chapter that's very well known for violence and for peddling meth, and going along there in your party attire with your signage, standing up and actively campaigning, there is a huge difference, and I think the public can work that out very quickly," Mitchell said.

Hipkins was also asked whether he had ever taken a photo with a gang member.

"Couldn't say. Quite possibly. I mean, how would you know, some of the time?"

Mongrel Mob life member Harry Tam had posted a photo on social media of Hipkins and a man Tam said is a gang member. Tam's post called Hipkins "two face" and accused him of poor judgement. The man in the photo was not wearing a patch.

Asked about the photo, Hipkins said he could not recall it.

"It could have been some time ago. I've been a member of Parliament for 18 years," he said.

"How would you know, I mean, we're about to go for a walk through a shopping mall, where we'll have hundreds of photos, how would you know who they are?"

World.title: Recap: Fiji Bulikula too strong for Orchids at World Cup
World.content:
The Fiji Bulikula scored their first win at the Rugby League World Cup, following their 40-4 win over Papua New Guinea Orchids in Port Moresby on Saturday afternoon.

Making their debut in the world meet at the event last weekend, the win was historic for the side.

It also kept their hopes alive of securing a semi-final spot in the women's competition.

Having lost 12-18 to New Zealand in the first round, the Fijians turned the pressure on from the opening minute of the clash and led 30-0 at halftime.

They out-scored the hosts at the National Football Stadium in Port Moresby five tries to one in the first half and wrapped up the game with two more in the second half.

By the end of the 70-minute clash, they had out-scored, out-played and out-thought the Orchids, who last weekend opened their campaign with a big win over France.

Fiji speedster Tahlia Marshall recorded a hat-trick of tries in the match.

Winning head coach Jone Wesele, a former Fiji Bati international himself, said it was a great display by the Bulikula.

He said their defence stood out and their consistency on attack worked well for them in the end.

"It was a great game, am happy with what they did out there," he told RNZ Pacific.

"They improved and have set themselves with a chance for the semifinals.

"We will celebrate, go back to the board on Monday and prepare for our last game.

"One day and one game at a time is our focus."

Fiji's win gives them hope of finishing in the top two in Pool B, with France being their third and final pool opponent next weekend.

PNG will face New Zealand.

Sienna Lang opened the scoring for the Bulikula in the fourth minute, with captain Serena Naitokatoka converting for a 6-0 lead.

But the Orchids struck back with Ua Ravu's try two minutes later.

However, Fiji scored again through Lusiana Yaranamua, Taina Naividi, Losana Lutu and Marshall in the first spell of 35 minutes.

Yaranamua and Naitokatoka shared the goal kicking.

Orchids captain Elsie Albert worked hard, trying to get her women warriors to break the stubborn Fijian defence and was ably assisted by Ravu, Jafinda Sap, Vanesa Nakas, Shellie Long and Emily Veivers.

But the Fijians stood their ground and countered with their own moves, opening up and running the ball almost at will.

Their forward pack of Latisha Smythe, Naitokatoka, Leilani Ahsam, Elizabeth Naleba, Nanise Vakacavu and Talei Holmes created havoc for the Orchids, running the ball straight and crashing through for territorial gain.

Replacements Marshall, Teaghan Hartigan and the powerful running Lorren Ieli added firepower when they took the field.

Marshall got two tries within four minutes when the second spell resumed, finishing off Fiji's moves in the right corner.

While PNG tried to string moves together in the second spell, the Bulikula's defence stood and denied the home team any real reward.

World.title: Parker-Hulme murder: Pauline Parker dies in Scotland
World.content:
One of the killers behind one of New Zealand's most infamous murders has died in the Scottish Orkney islands.

Pauline Parker was 16 years old when she and her friend Juliet Hulme beat Parker's mother to death in a park in Christchurch, in 1954, before being convicted and spending five years in women's prisons.

The Orcadian newspaper reported that Parker was 88 when she died in retirement housing in the town of Kirkwall this month, where she had been living under the name of Hilary Nathan.

Author Peter Graham wrote a book about the case, published in 2011, and has told RNZ Pauline was known as Pauline Rieper when she was in school and the girls met.

"The Rieper family... her father Bert Rieper was the manager of a fish shop in Colombo Street, and her mother worked as a secretary, and the family home which was a dilapidated house in Gloucester Street, was run as a boarding house."

Parker had been hospitalised for a couple of years as a child with the serious disease osteomyelitis and still bore the scars, Graham said, and she was "something of a misfit" in school.

After speaking with various former classmates of the girls, he believed they formed their close bond initially as Hulme, who had weak lungs from childhood illness, and Parker were both allowed to sit out from sport together, and shared a love of fiction and imaginary worlds.

The plan to kill Parker's mother, who she had a fractious relationship with, came about after the girls' parents moved to put distance between them. Their defence argued their preoccupation with the imaginary had led them to construct their own sense of morality - which put their understanding of what they did to Parker's mother in a different light, Graham said. However the argument was not successful.

They served five years in different prisons, and their release included conditions that they live under new identities, Graham said.

Both remained fiercely private, even once their identities were discovered in their later lives.

Some UK media have reported Parker worked at a stable in the Orkney Islands, before retiring.

Juliet Hulme became best-selling crime writer Anne Perry, and died in 2023, aged 84.

World.title: LIVE: Rugby League World Cup: PNG v Samoa
World.content:
After a close first half, Toa Samoa were runaway winners over PNG in the Rugby League World Cup.

World.title: Coach Arch Jelley, who coached John Walker to mile record, dies aged 104
World.content:
Legendary running coach Arch Jelley, who guided John Walker to Olympic gold in Canada, has died at the age of 104.

Athletics New Zealand says Jelley's coaching career spanned more than five decades and shaped generations of New Zealand middle-distance running.

His coach-athlete partnership with Sir John Walker saw Walker crack the world mile record, running it in 3 minutes 49.4 seconds in 1975, the first sub 3:50 mile in history.

Walker also won the gold medal in the 1500 metres at the 1976 Summer Olympics in Montreal under the guidance of Jelley.

Their relationship continued until Walker retired from competitive running in 1992.

Jelley was born in Dunedin on 13 August 1922 and joined the Mornington Harrier Club at 18 years old.

Athletics New Zealand says his running was put on hold by the Second World War, when he served in the navy, including Russian Convoy duty aboard HMS Bermuda. He went on to a long career in education, spending more than 20 years as principal of Sunnybrae Normal School on Auckland's North Shore.

Sir John Walker and coach Arch Jelley, in 1980. www.photosport.nz

Jelley began coaching in 1960 at Owairaka Harriers, which was the home to runner and athletics coach Arthur Lydiard. Athletics NZ says he admired and adapted some of Lydiard's methods.

Jelley coached dozens of other leading athletes, among them Olympians Christine Pfitzinger and Robbie Johnston; 1990 Commonwealth Games 10,000m bronze medallist Barbara Moore; and American miler Steve Scott, whom he guided to fifth in the 1988 Olympic 1500m final.

After stepping away from coaching in 2000, he returned at the age of 93, to guide Hamish Carson to the 2016 Olympic Games in Rio.

Jelley brought the best out of athletes, Athletics NZ chief executive Cam Mitchell said, and his partnership with Sir John Walker was one of the great partnerships in New Zealand sport.

"They achieved so many good things together, obviously the Olympic gold medal in Montreal was probably the highlight," Mitchell said.

"But I think the critical thing with Arch was he was much more than just one coach of one athlete - he coached generations of New Zealand athletes."

Jelley was awarded an OBE for services to sport and made a Life Member of Athletics New Zealand in 2024.

He once said he held the firm belief that a bad race was never the athlete's fault.

World.title: Two men take over person's vehicle in Rotorua Aquatic Centre car park and flee in it
World.content:
No arrests have been made after two men allegedly took over a member of the public's vehicle before fleeing in it.

Police said they were called to the Rotorua Aquatic Centre car park following a report of the robbery.

"Around 6.40pm, it is reported that a person was approached by two men who demanded the victim's vehicle, which they then used to flee the area.

"Thankfully, the victim was not injured, however, they are understandably very shaken by the incident."

Police said the suspects continued to flee from Police.

"Police immediately conducted area searches for the vehicle, which was spotted twice, but the alleged driver fled both times - due to the manner of driving, Police did not pursue on either occasion."

The Police Eagle helicopter was deployed, and the vehicle was found abandoned on Kanahi Place.

Police confirmed they were still looking for the two suspects.

"Enquiries are ongoing, and anyone with information is urged to make a report through 105, either online or over the phone, referencing file number 261023/6817.

World.title: Former AFLW coach says likely player exodus to go 'well beyond Collingwood'
World.content:
Former AFLW player and coach Lauren Arnell has slammed the standard of Collingwood, while emphasising the responsibility of coaches to "put on a show" to grow the game.

The Magpies slumped to a new low on Friday night after failing to kick a single goal against Port Adelaide.

The 48-point defeat to the Power was the club's 10th loss this season out of 11 games. Under head coach Sam Wright, the Magpies have won just five games since the start of 2024.

"Overall, it was not the best standard of AFLW football that we would expect to see at this point of season 11," Arnell said on ABC Radio.

"Ash Centra was one of the first to walk off the ground in tears right in front of us. Totally fair. I would probably be about the same level."

Sam Wright took over as head coach at the end of 2023 and has struggled to get wins on the board since. (Getty: Mark Brake)

The pioneer of women's football and former captain of Carlton said while the AFLW continued to play 16 a side in venues open to conditions, unlike protected stadiums the MCG, Perth Stadium and Docklands in the men's game, if teams did not have high skill levels or offensive systems, they would not be able to put goals on the board.

"If you're Sam Wright, you've made some clear decisions where you want to play plus two behind the ball for a lot of the game. And my personal belief is that if you do that in AFLW, you're giving up score, and that's what we saw again tonight," Arnell said.

"And having coached against Collingwood in 2024, we beat them here at Alberton, and it was quite frustrating as a coach and someone who's been invested in women's sport and AFLW for a period of time, [as] you know that broadcast relies on high scoring.

"People who forever criticise AFLW as a sport, or a league, will always point to the lack of score and short quarters … and I'm a firm non-believer in heavy defensive systems for all of those reasons, not just because you can't score, but because we have a responsibility if you're coaching to grow the game and put on a show."

Ruby Schleicher, captain of Collingwood, will leave the Magpies at the end of the AFLW season. (Getty: Martin Keep)

Last week, Collingwood CEO Craig Kelly fronted the AFLW playing group after media reports of player unrest and concerns with the operation of the women's program.

Kelly told News Corp that when AFLW was to be introduced in 2017, Collingwood put its hand up to be an inaugural club, but now he often wondered if the Magpies would have been better off waiting to enter the women's competition at a later date.

He conceded being a foundation AFLW club might have been a mistake, while ruling out any prospect of an independent review into the women's program, which other struggling clubs have done, such as Carlton in 2023, Richmond in 2025 and St Kilda following this season.

Former player and coach Lauren Arnell slams non-offensive styles of play in the AFLW. (Getty: Russell Freeman/AFL Photos)

To Arnell, those remarks from Kelly screamed a lack of understanding between the executive and the playing cohort.

"That statement just immediately tells me you have never sat down with enough of your women's players and even asked them questions of their perspective and where they've come from," Arnell said.

"Like you've got no understanding of your playing group and potentially your coaching group."

Despite being one of the biggest sporting clubs in Victoria, Collingwood players are reported to feel behind local rivals in Melbourne, North Melbourne and Carlton, and are unhappy with multiple aspects of the program, including coaching, high performance and list management.

Collingwood is not alone down the bottom of the ladder, with St Kilda and Essendon also entering round 11 having won only one game this season.

Essendon players have looked frustrated and dejected after losses this season. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"And I'll guarantee you, off the back of that, there's going to be a lot of movement in the trade period coming up in the next month and a half," Arnell said.

There is an expected player exodus from Collingwood at the season's end, with captain Ruby Schleicher already announcing she'll be leaving to head back to Western Australia. It is reported the West Coast Eagles offered her a four-year deal, while the Magpies' initial offer was a one-year contract extension, then upped to two.

On top of Schleicher, the high-profile players such as Tarni White, Brianna Davey, Sarah Rowe and Lauren Butler are all out of contract at season's end. Vice-captain Jordy Allen tried to exit last trade period for Brisbane but Collingwood blocked her attempts.

"I think the washout of this whole storyline will be well beyond Collingwood, and we're going to see evidence of it across the trade period coming in December, and it will be really clear which players feel like their club's not invested in the environment," Arnell said.

World.title: Aussie Picklum aglow on top of WSL standings after Portugal win
World.content:
Molly Picklum has hit peak form riding the celebrated Supertubos waves to win the Rip Curl Pro Portugal event and move back to pole position to retain her world surfing title.

"Right now I'm on top of the world … literally!" roared the 23-year-old Australian after her victory over America's former world champion Caitlin Simmers in Friday's final sent her back to the top of the World Surf League standings.

Picklum's triumph at one of surfing's most famous venues gave her the maximum 10,000-point haul to ensure she overhauled Hawaiian Carissa Moore at the top.

The win came at the perfect post-season moment with just two events left.

The Gosford star has enjoyed a shiny nickname since she referred to herself as like "a glow worm in a cave" riding inside a deep barrel wave.

So she was quick to offer a shout-out to her friends and family at home, whom she knew would be watching her first triumph of the season in the early hours.

"I just want to say thank you to all of them. I know they stayed up for this one. The glow worm absolutely did it and I love you all so much!" Picklum said.

The Australian was given a triumphant ride on a jet ski after clinching the final win before she threw herself into the water to celebrate.

"I just love it when I get to win in front of them and actually do it for them," she said.

"So many people support me and put so much energy into me. I just love winning to give back to those ones that give to me.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

"I wanted to do well here. It was a dream of mine for me. Supertubos, it's like a cross between the Brazil energy and then (Hawaiian) Pipeline and those two together are like my two favourite things.

"So, oh my God, I'm so so grateful to win here. It was literally a dream of mine, and dreams come true. It's so baffling."

Picklum was delighted to "kind of hit my stride right at the right time" as she now sits atop the leaderboard on 48,950 points to Moore's 47,065, with another Hawaiian, Gabriela Bryan, third on 44,865 with two events left, the Philippines Pro and Pipeline.

Picklum didn't have a great record against 2024 world champ Simmers, having lost six of their previous eight head-to-head contests, but she was in control of the final from the moment she delivered a superb 7.83-point effort on her third wave to build on her opening 5.50.

Simmers couldn't respond, offering Picklum's fans on the beach a belated scare when she managed a best of 6.67 on the ninth of her 11 rides, but the Australian, who only had a half-dozen rides, eventually triumphed with her combined two-wave score of 13.33 to the American's 12.84.

AAP

World.title: Wallaroos send retiring pair out with win over Scotland
World.content:
The Wallaroos have completed their three-game Scottish sweep in a spicy Canberra contest that featured biting accusations and a string of yellow cards.

Australia produced plenty of classy moments in Friday night's 38-31 win but again lacked discipline in tackles and around the ruck to keep the tourists in it.

The hosts copped four yellow cards, retiring centre Cecilia Smith earning two of those to finish her 34-Test career on a red.

Scotland had two players sin-binned and it could have been far uglier if Wallaroos centre Georgina Friedrichs's accusations of biting had been verified on review.

'You can't be what you can't see' As she prepares for her final Test appearance, Emily Chancellor reflects on the legacy she leaves in Australian women's rugby.

But the officials saw no evidence and there were no bite marks on Friedrich's forearm, so the referee waved the complaints away.

Fifty-game prop Eva Karpani was yellow-carded for a high shot in her milestone game, while impressive flyhalf Waiaria Ellis was marched for slowing down a Scottish charge late in the first half.

The win came as a relief for retiring pair Emily Chancellor and Smith, with the latter smiling as she received a standing ovation after being sent off.

"I'm really sorry about that, just wanted to go out with a bang I guess," Smith said as she embraced her daughter Ruby post-match.

"She's been there since day one [of Smith's Wallaroos career].

"Having her there at trainings, camps, on the sideline, means so much and I just want to be that role model and show you can do anything if you put your mind to it and the hard work in."

A teary Chancellor, former captain and two-time World Cup member, signed off with a win in her 42nd Test after debuting in 2018.

"It's created so much opportunity for me, so much purpose in my life. I love these girls and what we play for," she said.

"I love what this game has given us: travel the world with great people and create opportunity. You can't be what you can't see."

Victory for Australia followed wins in Sydney and Edinburgh against the same opponents, the side now out of action until the Wallaroos program transitions to a full-time operation next year under new coach Sione Fukofuka.

Piper Duck scored one of the Wallaroos' five tries in their 38-31 win over Scotland. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

The hosts led 14-0 early but trailed 17-14 at half-time after a string of penalties led to three successive Scottish tries.

The Wallaroos regained the ascendancy and surged back ahead 38-24 when captain Siokapesi Palu Sekona finished a long-range effort.

But Karpani and then Smith were marched, keeping Scotland interested until the final play, but they were unable to find the match-tying converted try.

AAP

World.title: One-time minnows Tonga and Samoa now star World Cup attractions
World.content:
At Western Sydney Stadium last week, Toa Samoa had a moment of pure elation, a crushing 78-4 victory over France at the men's Rugby League World Cup.

It was capped off with an extraordinary final play that saw a penalty goal attempt from Stephen Crichton ricochet off the post.

The ball bounced towards Benaiah Ioelu who scored a try after the full-time siren had sounded, delivering Samoa's largest-ever victory.

What was more extraordinary was that a game with a kick-off time of 5:45pm on Friday, playing out what was likely and ultimately proved to be a walkover, still drew a crowd of 13,000.

It was a horror slot to play in: a workday, outside school holidays, in a busy part of Sydney where traffic was banking up across the many arterial roads that led to it.

Yet the crowd, largely comprising Western Sydney's large Samoan population, bellowed Ua fa'afetai — a traditional song of thanks and gratitude.

Fiji and the Cook Islands played each other on Sunday in Newcastle; there was a tick over 10,000 in the stands and another 1.7 million watching on television across Australia, outrating several flagship current affairs shows, news bulletins and reality programs.

These are just two examples that show this is a World Cup transformed by Pasifika passion.

Big Pasifika populations in Australia are bringing a challenge to local rugby league dominance. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

The growing strength of Samoa and Tonga's men's teams has been no secret, but now more than ever the iron grip of dominance largely held by Australia on international rugby league, occasionally disrupted by New Zealand, could be under threat.

What has also been clear to those at the grounds or watching from home is that this World Cup in Australia, New Zealand and Papua New Guinea is one where diaspora communities have breathed life into a tournament that has previously lacked the same level of excitement or prestige compared to other international sporting events.

Australia's migration story tracks with this

The shift will be most obvious on November 1, when Samoa and Tonga play each other in Sydney, in a game that was the first to sell out despite being in the third week of the tournament.

Already a series of ex-players and pundits have raised the call to move the game to the larger Stadium Australia to accommodate a crowd beyond the 30,000 that Western Sydney Stadium holds.

The interest should come as no surprise though, as the Pasifika population in Australia has been steadily increasing.

In 2011, 165,000 Australians identified as being from Pasifika communities; by 2021, that number had almost tripled to 415,033.

Data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics shows outer suburban areas of Sydney and Brisbane have burgeoning communities.

It is no surprise that Tonga vs Samoa is the first game to sell out at the Rugby League World Cup. (Getty Images: Paul Kane)

Sierra Keung, a senior lecturer in sports leadership and management at Auckland University of Technology, said she was not surprised by the fan turnout.

"The pride for our cultures, for our people, it's more than just a jersey for our Pasifika communities," Dr Keung told ABC Sport.

She cited a distinctive moment on the field that set this explosion in motion.

In 2017, the International Rugby League changed the rules to allow players with cultural ties to multiple nations to play for the country of their choosing.

The most famous change in allegiance was Jason Taumalolo.

Jason Taumalolo's choice to change allegiance to Tonga made headlines in the rugby league world. (Getty Images: Hannah Peters)

That rule change is on full display at this tournament.

Of the listed starting line-up for Tonga's match against Lebanon last night at Western Sydney Stadium, none of the players were born in Tonga, but all have deep familial ties to the island nation.

Tonga beat Lebanon 36-0 to keep its campaign on track.

"This is years in the making, and it's come down to people making bold decisions, like Jason Taumalolo to be the first to say, 'I'm going to go home and represent my people,'" Dr Keung said.

Salesi Foketi is one of a number of Tongan players that chose to represent his familial roots over his country of birth, New Zealand.

"Right from when I was a boy, it was always Tonga," he said.

Winger Jojo Fifita made his debut last weekend for Tonga and it was a moment to acknowledge his forebears.

"Being able to represent my dad's side was something I'd always wanted to do when I was older and I finally got that opportunity," he said.

Extension beyond Pasifika diaspora may be the future

There is another team outside the South Pacific that is relying on heritage and cultural ties as the bind for players to represent it.

Lebanon's winger Jason Saab has potentially the most unique ties to the country.

His stepfather, whose name he took, is Lebanese, and Saab is now lining up for the Cedars.

Jason Saab says he was brought up in the Lebanese culture through his stepfather Pierre. Now he's playing for the Cedars. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

Saab told ABC Sport in September of the sincere ties to Lebanese culture through his stepdad Pierre.

"That's the culture that raised me ultimately, that whole community of people. That's kind of where I found my identity to be," he said.

While all players in the Cedars squad were born in Australia, Lebanon coach Michael Cheika, who is also Lebanese Australian, said the small but dedicated rugby league community in Lebanon was driving the entire playing group, especially for those with family in Lebanon where strikes from Israel continued amid a broader conflict in the region.

"With everything that's going on over there … you've got to understand that they may not have enough petrol to get to the games, let alone field markings, fields that are available," he said.

As Samoa and Tonga have brought a genuine competitiveness to the tournament, there are other countries with large populations in Australia, such as Fiji and the Cook Islands, that could also challenge the Kangaroos, who have won 12 world titles, including six of the last seven.

Fiji and the Cook Islands, like Samoa and Tonga, have large diaspora populations in Australia. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

"The talent is just through the roof right now, both men's and women's," Dr Keung said.

"So I'm really excited for this World Cup, but also for future World Cups too, because it's just going to get better and better each time it comes around."

There is no doubt rugby league has cottoned on to its international life blood, and it seems the public is following suit.

World.title: Bayern Munich manager Vincent Kompany hospitalised after training collapse
World.content:
Bayern Munich coach Vincent Kompany was hospitalized on Friday after collapsing during a training session.

The German Bundesliga champions said the 40-year-old Kompany was observing a training session for the reserves team when the incident occurred.

"Kompany will undergo comprehensive examinations at the hospital and remain under medical care," the team stated. "In the meantime, his coaching staff will manage training and match-related activities."

Board member for sport Max Eberl said that Kompany, who is one of global soccer's leading younger coaches, will be given "all the time he needs" to recover as Bayern prepares to play Freiburg in the Bundesliga on Sunday.

"Vincent Kompany's health is our top priority," Eberl said. "We at FC Bayern will do everything we can to ensure that he recovers quickly. Vinnie will receive all the necessary medical care and support, as well as all the time he needs."

Kompany had been dealing with a viral infection since last week, and his assistant Aaron Danks said on Tuesday it affected the Belgian's legs.

The usually animated Kompany remained seated throughout Bayern's 6-1 win over Leipzig last week and then missed a training session and a pre-game news conference on Tuesday, when Danks said he needed time to rest at home.

However, Kompany returned to the dugout for Wednesday's 2-2 draw against Arsenal in the Champions League.

Following that match, Kompany acknowledged he tried to push through the illness and failed to heed the signals from his body.

Kompany joined Bayern in 2024 from Burnley and has won the German league twice since then. Kompany's team also reached the Champions League semifinals and won the German Cup last season.

Among a raft of teams wishing Kompany well was Manchester City, where he was the long-time captain and won the Premier League four times.

"Everyone at Manchester City is wishing a speedy recovery to our former captain and Club legend, Vincent Kompany," City posted on X. "Get well soon, Vinny."

AP

World.title: Sydney marathon champion Jepchirchir provisionally banned over EPO finding
World.content:
Kenya's world marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir has been provisionally suspended after testing positive for the banned blood booster EPO ​in a sample taken before her Sydney Marathon victory, the Athletics Integrity Unit (AIU) said on Friday.

The AIU added that the out-of-competition sample collected in Kenya returned an adverse analytical finding for EPO (erythropoietin), which boosts the production of ​red blood cells.

"I can only ‌say that I feel terrible about what happened and I think it's only right that an athlete who uses the performance enhancing drugs should be disqualified," her agent Gianni Demadonna said in an ‌emailed statement.

The 33-year-old is one of the most decorated women in the sport, having ⁠won gold at the Tokyo Games in 2021 and having claimed ‌major marathon victories in New York (2021), ​Boston (2022), London (2024) and Sydney (2026). She ‌previously held the half marathon world record.

Jepchirchir is the latest in a long string of Kenyan athletes to fall foul of doping rules. More than 140 Kenyan athletes have been sanctioned since the AIU was established in 2017.

"So much of what I see ​when ‌I'm on a broadcast call I do not believe. I'm not surprised by this," said Olympic 10,000 metres silver medallist and broadcaster Kara Goucher, who was a whistleblower ⁠in the Nike Oregon Project case.

"I am, however, ‌sad for all the athletes ‌who finished behind her and were screwed out of a podium."

Jepchirchir dominated the women's race in ‌Sydney in August, pulling clear of the field to finish in 2:18:31, more than 3 minutes ahead of second-placed compatriot Irine Cheptai.

The Sydney Marathon, which ‌was added ​to the list of ⁠world majors beginning in 2025, said it was "extremely disappointed" by the news.

"Our commitment to clean sport is unwavering. Every athlete who lines up in Sydney deserves to race on a level playing field," it said in a statement.

Last year, Kenya's ⁠women's marathon world record holder Ruth Chepngetich was banned for three years after admitting anti-doping rule violations involving hydrochlorothiazide (HCTZ), a ‌prohibited diuretic, though ‌her world record of 2:09:56 remained on the books because it ​was set before her positive test.

Reuters

World.title: In the wreckage of World Cup blowouts, hope is where you find it
World.content:
As it enters its second round of matches, just about every game of the Rugby League World Cup has become a battleground between true believers and sceptics.

The former point to the games of the opening week that attracted bumper ratings and healthy crowds for blockbuster contests like Australia against New Zealand or Tonga's clash with England.

Test football is better than ever, they cry, and these numbers prove it.

The latter scoff at the blowouts, feeling ever more justified in their derision as the scorelines mount when powerhouses old or new collide with teams who have been left behind.

Test football is a waste of time, they sneer, and these numbers prove it.

With the tournament entering a weekend where a close game will be hard to come by, the truth is firmly in the middle but hope is always where you find it, even among the wreckage of a smash-up.

For proof, look no further than Tonga's match against Lebanon in Parramatta last night.

The Cedars were 23-1 to win, making them the second-shortest-priced underdogs of a round when Australia will play Fiji, England take on France, Papua New Guinea host Samoa and Cook Islands do their best against New Zealand.

It will rain tries and apart from perhaps PNG-Samoa it will be a surprise if any match is closer than Tonga's 36-0 win over the spirited Cedars.

But you'd be hard-pressed to find a single one of the 25,605 strong crowd — the third highest of any match in history between two second tier nations — who'd call it a waste of time.

If you can pack that many people into a stadium for a result that was never really in doubt you've got something worth having.

Tonga's superior athleticism and cohesion across the field won them the day, with veteran halfback Tui Lolohea and rising fullback Lehi Hopoate both enjoying fine nights amid the rowdy atmosphere.

Western Sydney is a stronghold of both communities and Parramatta Stadium was awash in red, white and green, as it was drowned in cheers and buried in flags.

The only part of the ground that wasn't awash in colour and noise was the empty corporate sections which was fitting because this was not a game for the suits.

All through the 80 minutes beating of the Lebanese drums were answered by a chorus of Tongan voices, many of whom stayed well after fulltime to revel in their victory.

They have confirmed their place in the semi-finals but first must face their ancient rivals Samoa next week.

Tonga have established themselves as one of Test rugby league's new superpowers. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

It will be a highlight of the tournament no matter who wins or what happens next, a meeting of the two new powers in these waters and it was not so long ago that they were copping the beatings rather than handing them out.

Back in 1999, Tonga lost to New Zealand 74-0 and nine years later, boasting a full team of NRL and Super League players, the Kiwis repeated the dose 56-8.

If those big losses killed Tonga off they never would never have transformed into what they are now, which is one of Test rugby league's apex predators.

Sticking with it despite heavy losses meant there was something for Tonga and Samoa's star players to come back to when they decided to choose their heritage and the result is what we have now — two extra high quality teams in Test football, making a gang of five where for years there was only three.

If you're outside that five, life can be much harder. With the streamlined World Cup format there will be fewer meetings of the high and the low, but some of them are unavoidable.

Lebanon fought hard despite a lack of star power. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

A team like Lebanon is trapped in a land of wolves and asking for them to undergo a Tongan style transformation into a heavyweight is not realistic.

They are at the mercy of what talent they can gleam from Australia's Lebanese communities and getting them all together for matches is difficult amid an already packed rugby league schedule, but they have found a way to make the most of it.

Young Canterbury halfback Alex Conti lost no admirers, nor did Tigers lock Alex Twal and some strong scrambling defence stopped the scoreline from getting to embarrassing territory.

What they wouldn't have given for a half like Mitchell Moses, who instead represented Australia, or Adam Doueihi, who is injured, given they only had one fewer tackle inside the 20 than Tonga but could not find a point to show for it.

It might be Lebanon's last big dance for a while. Since the last World Cup they were demoted to affiliate status by the International Rugby League and only qualified this time around because they were quarter finalists in 2022.

Major infrastructure changes will need to be made at a domestic level if Lebanon are even to be given a chance to qualify for 2030.

Their diaspora talent, which is considerable, will not be enough to shepherd them through and their tournament finale next week against France could be their last World Cup game for many years.

Lebanon could be in their last World Cup for some time. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

If that's so the tournament will be poorer for their absence but they could finish with a flourish.

Next week's game against les Chanticleers is winnable for them and will be played in a double-header with Samoa-Tonga.

It will give Sydney's vast Lebanese community one more opportunity to show their pride and love through their national side in a major sport, which is a chance they are rarely offered and one they made the most of on Friday night against long odds.

That still means something, which means the game is worth something, as sure as the Pasifika blockbuster will be and as sure as this game was.

Scorelines always matter and not every blow-out is created equal. Sometimes you can squint so hard looking for a silver-lining you may as well be blind.

But other times it's right in front of you, so clear you cannot miss it, as loud as the drums that hammered out into the night and as striking as the sea of red in the stands.

World.title: How the Western Bulldogs engineered a return to AFLW finals
World.content:
It's a story that's been told countless times. The Western Bulldogs hit rock bottom in 2023, opted to undertake a review into their program, and made wholesale change. Since then, they've made steady improvement, but that hasn't been without some rocky moments along the way.

Now, the Bulldogs are locked into finals for the first time since 2022 and present as a genuine threat in the post-season, rather than simply making up the numbers.

And while their off-field changes have been immense, and an easy starting point when it comes to analysing their improvement, what has happened on field is even more interesting.

Rock bottom

The Bulldogs finished 2023 as wooden spooners, winning one game from 10 rounds of footy just a year after reaching its second ever final. Across that season they gave up control in-game easily, and relied heavily on a small handful of players to carry the load.

This required a personnel change to start the improvement spike. A new head coach, head of footy and list manager were certainly key to the shift, but change on field was also essential.

From the playing list that reached a final in 2022 just 12 players remain, and while the club has largely focused on careful draft selections, it has also engaged in trades to add experience on top of the youth.

Listed in 2022 S7 Added since Elle Bennetts Deanna Berry Ellie Blackburn Alice Edmonds Jess Fitzgerald Elisabeth Georgostathis Isabella Grant Britney Gutknecht Sarah Hartwig Isabelle Pritchard Rylie Wilcox

Heidi Woodley Lauren Ahrens (trade) Brooke Barwick (draft) Mizuki Brothwell (draft) Cleo Buttifant (draft) Mikala Cann (trade) Dom Carruthers (draft) Ellie Gavalas (trade) Maggie Gorham (free agent) Elaine Grigg (draft) Keeley Hardingham (draft) Kaylee Kimber (replacement) Vaomua Laloifi (trade) Emma McDonald (draft) Analea McKee (trade) Charlie O'Connor Moreira (draft) Sarah Poustie (draft) Jasmyn Smith (trade) Lou Stephenson (trade) Amaia Wain (draft)

This list build has happened quietly. There are no boom recruits among the incoming trades, no premiership players or All-Australians in the mix as other clubs have targeted, but they have been specific choices to work toward the game plan.

Mikala Cann has been one of those players. Little more than a role player at Collingwood, albeit a very good one, Cann has been exactly the kind of midfielder/forward required at the Dogs to elevate the team as a whole.

The stat changing Geelong in 2026 When Geelong made the move to bring Mick Stinear to the cattery, it made a bigger difference to their 2026 season than any player movement could.

Outside of this, the club's capacity to improve some down-and-out senior players has also been important.

Mua Laloifi has emerged on the other side of an ACL injury in close to her best career form, offering important intercepting strength behind the ball, and Ellie Gavalas has spent a couple of years in the wilderness but now adds some leadership and ground-level speed in the forward half.

And the draftees have been carefully selected. Although some choices haven't quite come on in the way the club would have hoped — every club has been burned by a speculative pick here or there — others have been the ideal slow burn.

Emma McDonald and Elaine Grigg were arguably the Dogs' biggest-name draftees across this period, but others like Cleo Buttifant and Dom Carruthers have complemented the growth of the list.

The Bulldogs are becoming a team that is clearly greater than simply the sum of its parts. The puzzle as a whole works well together.

Build defence

The traditional route for a club's rebuild is to start with defence, then add attack, and that's exactly the direction the Bulldogs went once Tam Hyett was appointed coach in 2024.

They were coming off a base that was easy to win the ball against, easy to maintain momentum against, and ultimately far too easy to score against.

Taking back control

Finding that defensive mindset isn't simply about establishing a strong backline, rather as the numbers above suggest, it is about making the game scrappy at times to prevent the opposition from clean access at the footy.

No longer are the Bulldogs walkovers around the footy, or easy to maintain possession against around the ground. When a team plays the Bulldogs, they are to expect a battle around the contest and pressure on the outside.

This, then, leant into tightening up on the scoreboard.

Becoming harder to score against

To get here they played some admittedly ugly footy (everyone remembers that 2024 game against the Bombers), but the first step in the plan has been the foundation upon which everything else has been built. And although some of those numbers have swung slightly back up (specifically inside 50s and marks inside 50 conceded), this has been a result of now working to find the balance between defence and attack.

Learn to attack

In Hyett's first year at the helm, the Bulldogs had their worst year in attack since the AFLW began, averaging just 26.5 points per game. Things seemed bleak and the end of the tunnel felt a long way away. But steadily, on top of that tightening defence, they have also found their own confidence to attack.

As with the defensive tightening, the first part is establishing more control through the middle of the ground, then the next layer is engaging those forwards close to goal to actually get scores on the board.

Winning the footy

Getting their hands on the footy has been a key part to winning back control throughout games, but part of that has also been a shift in how they want to use the ball.

Instead of dump kicking the ball long to escape danger or opting for long down-the-line kicks to a contest where they can compete again, the Dogs are now establishing a clear handball game; moving neatly from layers around the contest via hand and looking for the running handball receive option to add speed on the ball.

That outside ball has been a huge growth area as they develop more confidence in their game style, and for the first time since 2022 the club is averaging a positive uncontested possession differential.

Kicking a winning score

A whole new forward line has been built, with Sarah Hartwig becoming the club's all-time leading goalkicker back in round nine, and Emma McDonald posting the most goals of any Dog in 2025, her debut season.

It has been a calm, steady club-wide build that has flown under the radar in the context of the wild swings that occur in the AFLW, but it has been done for the long haul.

And in a fortnight, the Dogs will get a chance to show their wares in finals, and are a good chance of winning their first final since their flag in 2018.

Tech.title: Xbox’s first chief operating officer is out after just a few months
Tech.content:
Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Xbox’s first chief operating officer (COO) is leaving after the new role was created just a few months ago. Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today, according to an internal Xbox memo seen by The Verge. Chiang has been at Microsoft for 21 years, serving as the head of Minecraft before being promoted to Xbox chief operating officer in July.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced Chiang’s departure in a surprisingly short memo today. “Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I’m grateful for her years of service and wish her well,” said Sharma. As Chiang is departing today, her immediate responsibilities are being split up between other Xbox leaders for now, and Sharma notes that “We’ll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalized.”

That sounds like the COO position isn’t going away after just a few months, but it’s not clear why Chiang is departing after such a short stint in the role. At the time of Chiang’s promotion, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma described the new chief operating officer role as a first for Xbox, “with end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services.” The role was created as part of Xbox’s big “reset.”

Chiang reported directly to Sharma, and was promoted to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”

Chiang departs amid rumors that Xbox is preparing more layoffs this month, in November, and January. The sudden and short memo from Sharma, coupled with Chiang’s responsibilities being assigned to other Xbox leaders, makes it seem like this wasn’t a resignation.

I asked Microsoft to comment on Chiang’s departure, and the company refused to discuss the circumstances of her exit. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters,” says Kari Perez, Xbox vice president of communications. “We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

Tech.title: OpenAI now trains its frontier AI models with no internet access
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is now training its most advanced AI models without internet access following a string of rogue hacking incidents. In a blog post on Friday, OpenAI says it built an offline testing environment where AI models can interact with indexed and cached web content “without risk of affecting external systems.”

OpenAI paused training its frontier AI models in September, after disclosing several incidents in which its AI agents broke out of their testing environments to hack third-party companies and government agencies, or swarm obscure websites. On October 1st, OpenAI resumed reinforcement learning training and internal inference with tighter security measures, the blog post says.

Even with these safeguards in place and no internet access, OpenAI found that agents “do not always need a network connection in order to communicate.” One test performed by the company asked AI models on separate virtual machines to exchange secrets without a network connection. To bypass this restriction, the AI agents found a way to communicate using the processor’s cache:

Reading data from the cache is faster than retrieving it from main memory, and the agents used this timing difference to communicate. One agent encoded information by evicting selected data from the cache. Another timed how long it took to reload that data, using the difference between fast and slow reads to recover the message. Once the agents agreed on a protocol for encoding and decoding these signals, they could exchange the synthetic secrets without changing a shared file or opening a network connection.

OpenAI says it has added checks to its monitoring system to detect this type of communication. It will also continue training its frontier AI models without a network connection until improved safeguards “justify broader internet access.”

In the meantime, OpenAI says it will work to improve the security of its virtual machines, while testing for weaknesses in its testing environments. It’s also going to continue testing its monitoring systems, which were recently undermined by its AI agents during internal coding projects.

Tech.title: Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army
Tech.content:
Remember Popcorn Time, the app that served as an easy-to-use front end for streaming torrents of movies and TV shows? Development of the MPAA’s least-favorite app of the 2010s has been abandoned for years, but the “Netflix of Piracy” software is still installed on millions of devices that are just waiting to join a bot army. Researchers at Eye Security found the updater for a Popcorn Time fork called “Time4Popcorn” still running on tons of Windows, macOS, and Android devices located around the world, phoning home to now-abandoned web domains over unencrypted HTTP and running an outdated, insecure version of Chrome.

Eye Security’s Niels Teusink says the updater could have been used to install and run basically any kind of software with full privileges, easily enabling someone to create a botnet just by taking over one of the domains, using a man-in-the-middle attack to target specific devices, or perform surveillance by identifying the machines running the software.

Their solution was to register one of the domains and use it to send their own update that instructed the updater to disable itself. Despite ethical concerns about the fix, the researchers say their only alternative “was to do nothing,” pointing out, “The update process wasn’t doing anything functional anyway, it was only creating risk for users.”

Eye Security said on Windows devices, their update “simply stops and disables the service via the Service Control Manager” without deleting any files or anything else. On macOS, it uses a shell script to execute a command that blocks the update process from starting. They didn’t address the software on Android devices, where installing the update would still require actual user interaction first.

They had to tweak their update after it was uploaded to VirusTotal, causing security programs to flag it as malware and block it while leaving the vulnerable updater running. It’s unclear exactly how many devices were at risk, but Eye Security says it “sent out over 2 million update downloads” by March, when they stopped sending the update and transferred the domains they used to the Shadowserver Foundation, a web security non-profit.

Tech.title: Jack Dorsey’s Block made an AI model that talks to you like an awkward new friend
Tech.content:
Babies learn to talk without ever seeing a word written down. We wanted to see if a model could too. It can. It’s just very hard.

Speech is the most natural interface to any intelligence, super or otherwise, and today’s voice AI wastes it. It flattens what we say into text and can’t keep up with human timing.

AI keeps gaining power and independence, and it’s still nearly deaf to the emotion in our voices. Imagine being in serious pain while a voice AI has no idea and just keeps going. That’s the safety problem. Dessa is a step toward fixing it.

Tech.title: Soundcore’s latest noise-crushing headphones are on sale for a new low price
Tech.content:
My colleague John Higgins considered Soundcore’s Space One some of the best budget noise-canceling headphones you could buy when they launched in 2023 — and their successor has only improved upon their winning formula, albeit with a $30 price increase. Thankfully, the Soundcore Space 2 are currently on sale at Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart in all three colors for an all-time low of $106.49 ($23 off), making them even easier to recommend.

The Space 2 builds on the original with improved active noise cancellation, particularly when it comes to the low-frequency sounds associated with trains and airplane engines. They also deliver more accurate sound performance thanks to various design upgrades, while retaining many of the same features that made the Sound One sound so good for the price, including support for high-resolution LDAC audio. You also still get access to HearID 3.0, which lets you personalize the sound by listening to a series of samples and adjusting accordingly.

Battery life is another welcome improvement. The Space 2 can last up to 50 hours with ANC enabled or 70 hours with it switched off, up from 40 and 55 hours, respectively, on the original. And when your battery dies, you can still use the equipped 3.5mm jack for wired listening. They’ll also automatically pause playback when you take them off, which is handy when you need to step away without losing your place in a song or podcast.
