Tech.title: Elon Musk Just Dumped Another $76 Million Into the Midterms
Tech.content:
Elon Musk gave his personal political committee, America PAC, more than $76 million in the first two weeks of October to boost Republicans in the final stretch of the midterms, according to a pre-election report the PAC filed Thursday evening with the Federal Election Commission.

The group spent nearly $43 million in the first two weeks of October, and entered the campaign’s last leg holding nearly $47 million in cash.

The Texas Senate race dominated the new spending. It drew $15.2 million, double what the PAC spent there all summer. That spending included $12.4 million to attack Democratic candidate James Talarico and $2.8 million to promote Republican Ken Paxton.

Daily filings since then show $9.1 million more against Talarico, bringing the PAC’s spending against him this cycle to nearly $28 million, about 40 percent of everything it has spent supporting or opposing candidates. The PAC also shifted toward online ads, spending $11.4 million on digital ads in the same two weeks, which is close to what it spent on mail and texting combined.

All told, Musk has given more than $445 million to Republican political groups this election cycle, according to WIRED’s analysis of FEC filings, making him the biggest known individual donor in the midterms. More than $165 million of that has gone to America PAC since July alone.

America PAC declined to comment.

Musk—who has several companies, including Tesla and SpaceX, based in Texas—has also been posting online about the race. On Wednesday, Musk posted on X that “there is something deeply wrong with Talarico,” then called him “a creep” and claimed, without evidence, that he “would vote to take away your kids and transition them.” Earlier this month, Musk amplified a false claim that Talarico had been treated at a mental health facility. Talarico shot back the same day: “There is something deeply wrong with a political system that allows one trillionaire to buy his own personal US Senator.”

The Texas race remains a toss-up. An Emerson College poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters, conducted October 17 to 19, found Talarico at 48 percent and Paxton at 46 percent, within the poll’s 3-point margin of error.

The stakes for Musk reach well beyond Texas. If Democrats win the House, the lawmakers in line to lead its committees have signaled they will investigate his role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), his companies’ federal contracts, and what Zoe Lofgren, a California Democrat, called an “astounding” number of conflicts of interest. Unified Democratic control of Congress would pose even more problems for him.

Silicon Valley Democrats added another target on Friday: restrictions on SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service in Ukraine. In a letter to the White House demanding an investigation, Representatives Sam Liccardo, Jimmy Panetta, and Ro Khanna vowed that the next Congress “will closely scrutinize federal funding awarded to Mr. Musk’s businesses.”

Tech.title: How Many Billions Would It Take to Hold Meta Accountable?
Tech.content:
Earlier this week, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay a $25 billion fine for violating consumer protection laws dating back to the Cambridge Analytica scandal. $25 billion is a massive fine, the largest Meta has ever faced, but it still had us folks at WIRED wondering: Would Meta even feel the pain?

A quick recap of the case: Filed in 2021, the suit alleged that the company violated the state’s Unfair Practices Act by lying to Meta users about the way it handled their data. (Later, New Mexico’s attorney general also made claims against Meta’s content moderation policies.) In September, a jury ruled in favor of the state. Then came the multibillion-dollar penalty.

“This ruling, and the Attorney General's approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” C.J. Mahoney, Meta’s chief legal officer, said in a statement. “At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal.”

Meta’s legal troubles have proliferated so much this year that it’s hard to keep track of them. Earlier this year in New Mexico, a jury ruled that the social media company should pay $375 million for violating the state’s Unfair Practices Act. That trial was related to child safety. A second phase of the case resulted in Meta being ordered to pay $567 million.

Meanwhile, a Los Angeles County superior court found Meta—and Google-owned YouTube—liable for harming a user’s mental health with the addictive design features of their apps. The plaintiff, a young woman, was awarded $6 million; Meta is on the hook for the bulk of that payment. Then in August, Meta settled a landmark federal case brought against the company by the majority of US states. This suit, once again, centered on addictive features in its apps that were alleged to be harmful to kids. As part of that settlement, Meta will pay the states between $17 and $18 billion over 10 years.

Tech.title: Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8 Review: The Littlest Smartphone That Could
Tech.content:
While it’s very capable, the Z Flip8 is only average when it comes to battery life, another drawback of its size. Samsung put in a 4,300-mAh silicon-carbon battery that’s good enough for casual use. If you’re on your phone a lot, you’ll want a power bank handy. Charging speeds are disappointing at 25 watts wired and 15 watts wireless, and I’m annoyed by Samsung’s refusal to implement the magnetic feature of Qi2.

Snap Shot

If you’re a keen photographer, you can get many better camera systems in a range of Android phones for the same money or less. That said, the main 50-megapixel shooter is perfectly good in many situations, and most folks will be happy with the photos it captures. Some noise creeps in when it’s dark. The 12-megapixel ultrawide is useful when you want to cram a lot in or take a group selfie, but it’s a definite step down in quality. Sadly, there’s no telephoto lens, but you can emulate 2X zoom without losing detail by cropping, and it offers passable results in good lighting up to 10X.





Photograph: Simon Hill Samsung Galaxy Z Flip8, main camera.

I don’t see much reason to use the 10-megapixel punch-hole selfie camera outside of video calls, since you can flip it to get a cover-screen preview and use the main camera for selfies (a big benefit of this design). I also love Samsung’s Horizon Lock, which lets you shoot video with a steady horizontal plane no matter how you turn or move the phone.

Another new AI feature from Samsung is My FanCam, which lets you pick a subject to focus on in group videos and reframes them as though your chosen subject is the star. Handy for school plays or soccer games, if you remember to use it. (You can also apply it to old videos.) Speaking of AI, Samsung offers Now Brief to float up calendar events, reminders, and useful info like local weather, and Now Nudge to suggest adding dates to your calendar from messages, sharing locations or photos, and auto-filling forms.

Compact Competition

The cover screen, or FlexWindow, has been a weakness for Samsung’s Flip line, and it’s still limited in the Flip8. On the plus side, you can use more apps with the cover screen, including most of Samsung’s apps (Health, Calendar, Browser), YouTube, Netflix, Google Maps, and Messages. But if you want other third-party apps, you still have to install Good Lock, then the MultiStar plug-in, and select the apps you want to use. It’s stupidly convoluted, and I don’t understand why it isn't preinstalled, especially since Samsung has virtually all its other apps on there, along with a few third-party apps I never asked for (Facebook, Spotify, and Instagram). This is admittedly a bugbear of mine, but it's disgraceful that Samsung is including bloatware on a phone this expensive.

Tech.title: Split Tunneling Is Your VPN’s Best Feature. Here’s How to Make the Most of It
Tech.content:
While you may well be familiar with virtual private network apps, you might not have come across one of the best features available inside these privacy protectors: a feature called split tunneling.

In simple terms, split tunneling lets you choose which apps or sites use the protection of a VPN and which don't. While VPNs are worth using for extra security and privacy online—foiling trackers, spoofing your location, and stopping your internet provider from seeing your browsing—they do by their nature come with some compromises in speed.

If, for example, you want to get the fastest possible speeds with your online games, you might want to leave your games outside of the VPN's remit. Likewise, since VPNs typically obfuscate your actual location, if you want to make sure you can always check movie showtimes in your local area, you can use split tunneling to keep those ticketing apps outside your VPN. Putting a VPN in place can also interfere with access to other devices on your local network, like smart home gadgets and printers.

For all these reasons, you might want the extra control that split tunneling gives you, and it's available in a lot of VPN packages. Here's what you need to know about it.

How VPN Split Tunneling Works

Split tunneling on Android. Courtesy of David Nield

VPNs work by offering an encrypted bridge for data going to and coming from the web. This bridge means your internet provider, law enforcement agencies, and people connected to the same Wi-Fi can't see what you're doing online. Split tunneling lets you route some online traffic away from that bridge, without you having to constantly turn your VPN on and off.

Tech.title: Turtle Beach Vulcan II XP Review: Clicky Compromise
Tech.content:
Unfortunately, unlike Turtle Beach’s earlier Vulcan II TKL Pro, the keys here aren’t Hall effect, but they are hot-swappable—another trade-off, exchanging long-term reliability and accuracy for the ability to replace or upgrade keys easily. The board supports three-pin or five-pin mechanical switch keys and makes swapping them easy. The flat keycaps also pop off without trouble, which makes cleaning simple. Turtle Beach claims the switches last 50 million keystrokes, which should be plenty, but only a third of the TKL Pro's 150 million.

In gaming, the Vulcan II XP offers a 1,000-Hz polling rate for a 1-millisecond response time, which is competition-grade but falls short of the higher-end 8,000-Hz keyboards on the market. Hopping back to Swarm II, you can activate its more advanced features, like Easy-Shift, allowing for key duplication—basically putting commonly used features within easier reach—and ReacTap, assigning two commands to the same key, useful for games that require very swift inputs. (This might be banned in some competitive scenes under automation rules, though.)

These features can be a little fiddly to set up and map, but with a little experimentation, you can build layouts and input fields that work exactly as you want or need. I tailored a bunch of controls for Borderlands 3 and was dropping Psychos like never before. A minor annoyance, though: Reverting a specific input while trying to create a custom setup would sometimes revert the entire profile, which meant I had to redo everything.

Back to the Drawing Board

Photograph: Matt Kamen

While the Vulcan II XP offers great performance for the price, I do have concerns about the overall build quality. On the unit I received, the media wheel was inverted by default—turning it counter-clockwise toward the minus symbol turned the volume up. This was even after I updated the board’s firmware through the Swarm II app, and I had to remap the inputs for it to work as intended. It’s good that the Vulcan II XP’s customization is specific and nuanced enough to remap even the dial direction, but I shouldn’t have had to.

I also found that the LEDs below the “0” and “.” keys on the NumPad don’t seem to work properly, glowing a stubborn, glaring white no matter what color or pattern is assigned. I even tried turning off every other key’s light and manually assigning colors to just those—to no avail.

It’s another reason the board feels middle-of-the-road. Like the shiny metallic top plate hiding the cheaper plastic base, the Vulcan II XP dazzles at a glance, but the closer you look, the more flaws and small annoyances are revealed.

For the price, some of those annoyances are forgivable. For anyone who hasn't upgraded to a mechanical keyboard, this is a decent entry without breaking the bank, delivering a lovely typing experience backed up by enough pro-tier gaming features to feel like a real upgrade—but more demanding or professional players will want to aim higher.

Tech.title: TDM Neo Hybrid Headphones Review: Two-in-One Woes
Tech.content:
Unveiled at CES 2026, the TDM Neo is a pair of on-ear headphones that transform into a Bluetooth speaker. It caught the imagination of the attending media, won a handful of awards, and inspired countless column inches.

Given the current state of the portable audio industry, it's easy to understand why. Most designs seem to revolve around incremental updates and new colorways rather than genuine technical innovation. Neo is an exciting alternative, and it’s little wonder the startup brand went on to smash its Kickstarter targets.

I’ve spent the past couple of weeks listening to the headphones and Bluetooth speaker, and have lost count of the number of times I’ve showed off the clever twist-and-fold mechanism to friends. But has TDM managed to produce a genuine tech twofer, or designed a novelty product that gives you the worst of both worlds?

Twist and Shout

Video: Chris Haslam

The twist-and-fold mechanism on the Neo is clever and addictive. Rotate the ear cups around the cushioned but flexible headband, bring them together, and strong magnets snap everything firmly in place. Once connected, the headphone drivers disable, and the outward-facing Bluetooth speakers kick in. Twist them apart and you've got your headphones back.

It’s innovative, and the engineering is impressive. Once in speaker mode, the two rubber TDM logos sit closely together and form a protective base, while the asymmetrical twisted headband cocoons the ear cups together. It works well—it never once popped open accidentally. The action is smooth, the connection reassuringly solid, and switching between modes works exactly as intended.

The Neo has four 40-mm drivers—two for the headphones and two for the speakers. The outward-facing speakers are each rated at 5 watts (for a total of 10). Ten watts is not a lot for a modern Bluetooth speaker, but wattage doesn't automatically tell you how loud or good a speaker will sound, especially in the current age of digital signal processing. The highly regarded $55 JBL Go 5 has just 4.5 watts of output, for instance.

Tech.title: Call of Duty Modern Warfare 4 Review: A Dolphin Dive in the Right Direction
Tech.content:
The Call of Duty series needed a win this year. Last year’s Black Ops 7 was a clown car of bad decisions, featuring an always-online campaign mode with ridiculous zombie bosses and open-world Warzone. Worse still, the multiplayer mode (the only reason that many people buy the game) was entirely forgettable. Developer Treyarch was tasked with putting out Call of Duty games two years in a row — that crunch was a recipe for disaster.

On the other hand, that means Modern Warfare developer Infinity Ward had plenty of time to cook up the fourth and final entry in its own series. Thankfully, the studio used that extra runway to its advantage. Modern Warfare 4 may not have returned Call of Duty to the highest highs of the original trilogy that ended in 2009 (and which Infinity Ward rebooted over the last decade), but this is a leap in the right direction for a series that has become increasingly sloppy in recent years.

Players will find plenty of cinematic action in the single-player campaign, and the multiplayer mode has slowed down just a touch, which I think the game largely benefits from.

More from CNET

More importantly, Modern Warfare Zombies has been completely dropped in favor of DMZ, an accessible player-versus-player-versus-AI extraction shooter experience. The experimental swing feels like a lifeline for the series, and DMZ is the standout mode for the game.

The campaign identity crisis is (mostly) resolved

Modern Warfare 4 is a tighter game than Infinity Ward’s previous project, and it’s leagues better than Black Ops 7.

At the same time, it has a complicated campaign to crack open (and not because the plot is hard to follow). Players flit back and forth between the perspective of Captain John Price, longtime protagonist of the series, and South Korean soldier Park Hyun-Jun, a newcomer whose squad is fighting for his homeland. A battle rages against a united coalition of Russian and North Korean ultranationalists, who are blazing a path into other territories.

Russian bad actors have been the primary antagonists of every Modern Warfare game, and it’s actually really cool to see South Korea’s positive representation in a Call of Duty title. But the propaganda is laid on thick — Russia and North Korea are presented as sneering colonialist powers, while the Western world’s soldiers are a shield on every front.

Americans spearhead the fight against imperialism; forget about the Strait of Hormuz and gun down these unambiguously bad guys. The whole plot hinges on a somehow less-subtle Red Dawn-type of scenario, and the gung-ho military politics are absolutely nauseating this time around. Sure, Price is framed as morally gray — he’s working with a cartel to achieve his goals, and there’s boring melodrama where he comes to blows with his former allies — but he’s vindicated in the end because he is the type of Call of Duty leader that prevents global conflict.

Captain Price’s arc feels like a vague indictment of Western military overreach, but it ultimately amounts to nothing. Activision-Blizzard

Modern Warfare 4 also features an obligatory shockingly graphic mission, which is something of a tradition for the series. In it, you play as a North Korean soldier rounding up and executing the occupants of a small village for hiding a defector. During my playthrough, I earned an achievement for successfully interrogating a villager without beating them down. The whole affair is gratuitous, gross and gamified in a problematic way, exacerbated by the bizarre decision to continue making this kind of mission a mainstay in each game.

It’s a shame that the story is so trite and icky because the tentpole action is really good. The best mission takes place early in the campaign, when Price infiltrates a New York nightclub to search for a Russian oligarch. Bright lights and pulsing music contrast with brutal fistfights and gunplay — it’s like playing through the climax of a John Wick film. From there, the highlights keep coming: There’s a fight in a train yard where the cover moves on rails, a chase scene across Mumbai rooftops, a high-stakes nighttime penthouse raid and a full-out assault on a dictator’s compound.

But the worst mission in the campaign repeats the mistakes of other modern Call of Duty games. When the player’s squad initially counterattacks North Korean airspace, they’re shot down and have to survive behind enemy lines with scavenged gear. It’s an interesting setup that is completely wasted on a Warzone-like, open-world mission with a checklist of more than 50 optional collectibles to seek out.

The few puzzles that exist are mind-numbingly easy — despite my best efforts, I checked out after completing around half of the activities. I focused on the main objective to end the mission as soon as possible, which is just about the worst feeling to have while playing a game.

I don’t know if there’s an edict from up top to put one of these open-world missions in each new game to funnel players into Warzone, but they don’t work at all and are the worst part of any campaign.

Still, the folks that play the campaign will probably have a good time here. Players can explore tons of cool locales, and the enemies are surprisingly difficult this time around. Still, if you care about the loose narrative implications of a Call of Duty campaign, it’s tough to wash the bad taste out of your mouth.

DMZ is full of the same thrills as other extraction shooters, but it’s much easier to jump into. Activision-Blizzard

DMZ is better than Warzone and a welcome reprieve from Zombies

DMZ, a fairly accessible extraction shooter game mode, returns with new content for the first time since its “beta” ended in 2023. Players have been mourning what could have been for years, but it seems like the developers at Infinity Ward have been tinkering with it in the background for quite some time.

And their hard work has paid off because I’m confident that DMZ is the standout mode for Modern Warfare 4.

This extraction shooter is perhaps simpler than even ARC Raiders, but that’s part of the appeal. Players drop into North Korea to loot, fight each other and take down key targets throughout the map.

Everything is streamlined and easy to understand, including the loot. During play, you will come across several types of scrap, an assortment of healing items and tons of weapons, so you don’t have to think too hard about what to grab. Just move, shoot and pull out high-value items, then run the loop again.

The enemy AI is surprisingly aggressive and fun to battle against, especially when you run into an overwhelming number of troops. Armored vehicles and helicopters will try to smear you into the dirt. It’s an adrenaline rush, and as far as I’m concerned, Infinity Ward nailed the really important part of DMZ. It’s tough to get the player-versus-AI balance right, but these enemies feel like a real threat.

Other players might also come for your loot, which is what sometimes puts folks off of the extraction genre altogether. But DMZ’s in-depth bounty system provides a foil to player-versus-player gameplay.

Folks who hunt down other players rack up a bounty and appear on the map, so pacifists have a better chance to steer clear while bounty hunters stalk them down. It’s a pretty genius compromise that encourages the player-versus-player enjoyers to butt heads while the player-versus-environment crowd hides away because the tension of a potential run-in with aggressors is never truly alleviated.

I’m concerned that the pared-down simplicity of the gameplay loop could hurt DMZ’s long-term success, but Infinity Ward seems committed to adding new world bosses. That could really shake up how matches play out, even if there’s nothing as over-the-top as Marathon’s Cryo Archive boss.

DMZ isn’t perfect, but I see the groundwork laid for one of the better extraction shooters I’ve played. Depending on how the development team builds on this game mode, I can see it becoming something special (and maybe even a Call of Duty mainstay for years to come).

New traversal options are available in Modern Warfare 4, but they’re tame compared to other modern Call of Duty games. Activision-Blizzard

Multiplayer remains quick, but it’s heavier and grounded

Call me an oldhead, I don’t care: Black Ops 7’s omnimovement system, which allowed players to run, jump and slide around while looking in any direction, was disastrous for Call of Duty game balance.

Treyarch’s update to the formula might work for massive Warzone maps where there’s plenty of open space and a higher time-to-kill for other players, but the smaller multiplayer maps become impossible to breathe on. Call of Duty is, first and foremost, an arcade shooter, but the multiplayer formula still works best when there’s time to recoup and recover, make tactical flanks and call in your scorestreaks.

Infinity Ward’s Modern Warfare 4 removes the omnimovement system, but it still allows players to sprint, slide and dolphin dive around at appreciably high speeds. The new mantling mechanic adds some traversal options, but everyone feels a little heavier.

The slightly slower six-versus-six matches feel great, and the larger modes are a bit less chaotic. The Modern Warfare games have always skewed closer to classic boots-on-the-ground Call of Duty, and the latest entry doesn’t disappoint in that regard.

Still, the fatal flaws of the modern Call of Duty formula have gone untouched. There remain more than 70 attachments for many weapons. Many modes have maps cut out of larger Warzone areas. The seemingly mandatory 24/7 Shipment playlist is being added soon to prey upon your nostalgia. Progression needs to synergize across a complete Modern Warfare 4 product, so unnecessary bloat exists everywhere you look.

This is a solid modern Call of Duty game, but the overall quality is still a far cry from the series’ heyday. In a post-Warzone world, this is about as good as it gets — but if that formula doesn’t work for you, it might be worth steering clear of Modern Warfare 4.

Tech.title: Apple’s iPod Turns 25: The Song Catalog That Rode Wit You
Tech.content:
In 2001, some of the top songs included Fallin’ by Alicia Keys, Ms. Jackson by Outkast and Nelly’s Ride Wit Me. When people wanted to listen to those songs and they weren’t near a car stereo or their audio equipment at home, most carried music with them on skip-prone portable CD players, boomboxes or maybe even a homemade mix cassette.

Sure, some early adopters were already carrying a small collection of songs on a portable MP3 player (MP3s: the new-new thing!) like the Diamond Rio or Creative’s Nomad Jukebox. But these weren’t common, and you didn’t see them that often; there was no ubiquitous sign yet that, musically, the times were changing.

Enter Apple with its original iPod, a small hard drive encased in smooth white plastic that could stash between 1,000 and 2,000 songs, a sum that seemed godly at the time. Who would ever need to listen to 1,000 songs (or have access to that many) at their fingertips? What mortal would dare?

More from CNET

Apple Music’s website has an Easter egg: a first-generation iPod that works and can play music in your browser. Credit: Apple Apple

The device, which was released on Nov. 10, 2001 at a starting price of $400, heralded in the smartphone era before smartphones were a thing, making portable electronics more tactile, user-friendly and information-forward. The white earbuds that were bundled with the device were the beacon of that era: Before long, it seemed everyone had white cables coming out of their ears.

For the 25th anniversary of Apple’s game-changing music player, the device’s own creators are getting nostalgic about its silver anniversary. On Apple Music’s website, you can find at its 404 Not Found page a playful mockup of the OG iPod with its pleasing-to-use scroll wheel and a selection of songs you might have had in your iPod at some time or another.



As Tony Fadell looks back, collectors and new fans are still listening

If the iPod can be primarily credited to one person — leading a team of many — it’s widely acknowledged to be Tony Fadell, who came to Apple as a contractor and ended up heading one of its most successful product divisions. These days, Fadell is thinking a lot about the future of AI assistant devices, but he took time on his LinkedIn to acknowledge the iPod anniversary this week.

“We took it from approval to shipping in less than eight months,” he wrote. “There wasn’t time for endless refinements. We had to make decisions, trust our experience and stay focused on one clear promise: 1,000 songs in your pocket.”

While Fadell says that the iPod took a few generations to really take off and eventually come in iterations like the Nano and the Touch, some music fans who still love the original iPod design have been using the device for decades. If you have any hard drive-based gadget that lasts that long, count yourself lucky.

In addition to those old enough to remember what a Hoobastank is, iPods are also getting popular again with younger generations on a nostalgia kick, many of whom would rather carry around a separate physical device for their music than stream their Spotify accounts on their phone for the millionth time. Axios reports that iPods and MP3s are back in a big way in a trend called “friction-maxxing.” You don’t have to use that term to indulge, we promise.

Old iPods, new life

Getting into the hobby isn’t cheap: Working iPod models can cost several hundred dollars on Ebay. And one that’s never been opened? Try $25,000–$60,000.

A cheaper route may be to keep the familiar outside trappings but replacing the guts with a new motherboard. A group called Crowd Supply promises in a YouTube video a new way to bring nonworking iPods back to life. It hasn’t launched yet, but you can keep an eye on the project at Crowd Supply’s website. Other tinkerers have had years and years to work up hundreds of iPod hacks; you can find many of them on Hackaday.

Alternatively, it may be the function that a modern MP3 enthusiast seeks, not necessarily the Apple branding or hardware. Other companies, such as Fosi Audio, have their own takes on the modern music player, like the $80 DAP Neo. CNET has a list of the best MP3 players of 2026, with devices like the Shanling M0s and the Android-based HiBy R4 coming out on top.

Lastly, if you want to relive the iPod glory days, you don’t necessarily need new (or old) hardware at all; your phone can do it with iOS apps such as RetroPod, My Classic – Retro Console or, if you’re feeling saucy on Android, ClassiPod.

Tech.title: YouTube Is Letting Us Vibe Our Video Feeds, and I’m Liking It
Tech.content:
Let’s face it — we love scrolling through videos. Maybe you’re OK with what YouTube feeds you, maybe you’re not. Either way, you’ve now got more control over it.

YouTube this week added a feature to the mobile app home page that enables you to create your own video feeds for whatever topics you want. The feed helps you home in on the subjects that appeal to you instead of necessarily relying on the algorithm. The custom feed option appears as a plus sign on the horizontal menu at the top of the app’s home screen.

YouTube said in its announcement that it wants to help users “dive straight into” their favorite content. “We know that viewers come to YouTube with incredibly unique interests, moods, topics to explore, and favorite ways to watch,” the YouTube team said.

More from CNET

The horizontal menu is also new. It includes tabs for your custom feeds, subscribed channels, music and live streams. There’s also a Music & TV button for people who subscribe to YouTube TV or Primetime Channels.

To see it for yourself, go to the app’s home screen on your phone. At the top, you’ll see the menu. If you click on Subs, you’ll see your subscribed channels. The Music tab will show videos from your favorite artists, and the Live button will show livestreams from your favorite creators. The More button shows a menu of YouTube features.

Trying out the new YouTube settings

But the most intriguing addition was the custom feed feature, and I gave it a go. On the YouTube home screen menu, I clicked on the plus sign. Then, under the “Add a custom feed for any topic or mood,” I typed San Francisco 49ers, and voila, a new tab appeared on the menu — SF 49ers. I also added a feed for the 2026 midterm elections. Both of those feeds now appear in the menu.

You can create a YouTube video feed for any topic. YouTube

You can also modify or delete a feed. If you click into a feed, you’ll see buttons at the top to edit the prompt, rename the feed or delete the feed.

I decided to modify my 49ers feed. Since I’m also a fan of the Golden State Warriors NBA team, I changed the feed topic to include both the 49ers and the Warriors. That feed then showed videos for both teams.

For non-Premium users, you get three feeds. You get up to eight if you subscribe to YouTube Premium ($9 per month).

The custom feed feature was already available on desktop — added by YouTube last month. It’s not yet available on tablets, and YouTube owner Google hasn’t said when it will be.

You must be 13 or older to get the custom feeds feature, and you also must have both watch and search history enabled.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo Is Now in Our Custom-Made Foldable Phone Test Machine. Will It Beat the Galaxy Z Fold 8?
Tech.content:
We want to know how many times you can fold an iPhone Duo before it breaks. After waiting over three hours at the Apple store on Friday, we bought one of the coveted iPhone Duo foldable phones in Louisville, Kentucky, and brought it back to CNET’s lab, a bespoke facility where I oversee hardware and software testing as the director of lab operations.

The goal is simple. As of Friday afternoon, my team and I have loaded the iPhone Duo into a proprietary machine we built to test foldable phones like Apple’s and Samsung’s rival Galaxy Z Fold 8, which we’ve already started testing. I’ve overseen the methodology and build of this testing rig for months in anticipation of Apple’s long-rumored foldable iPhone. (Read on for how CNET tests foldable phones.)

We even named our machine to match its purpose: Meet the Fold-a-Phone.

Now, my team of engineers and testing experts will watch the iPhone Duo open and close, open and close, to rigorously and systematically monitor the durability of Apple’s hinge and two screens.

After all, repeatedly folding a phone with bare hands can only get you so far in understanding the complex forces at play between the magnetics that snap the screen shut and the all-critical hinge.

CNET’s Senior Technology Reporter, Abrar Al-Heeti, has done a beautiful job capturing the iPhone Duo’s pros and cons in her smart, thorough review. Our Fold-a-Phone machine will add a deep data foundation to complement her real-world experience.

Since Apple hasn’t publicly shared claims of the iPhone Duo’s foldable lifespan, CNET’s Fold-a-Phone machine is poised to provide a wealth of valuable data about Apple’s first foldable phone and competing models in the foldable market.

And yes, you’d better believe we will use our treasure trove of in-house data to share status updates and comparisons during our ongoing testing window with the Duo.

Join CNET’s iPhone Duo livestream on YouTube on Monday from 1-5 p.m. ET, where you can follow along live and ask questions about our iPhone Duo testing process.

The importance of this moment is hard to overstate. Apple’s appearance on the foldable smartfold frontier lags Samsung by seven years (the first Galaxy Fold went on sale in the US in September 2019). Motorola and other phone-makers have long experimented with foldable phones in every shape and size, including a trifold accordion foldable phone we first demoed in 2019.

Matthew Murray/CNET

CNET’s mobile experts, including Al-Heeti and Editor at Large Andrew Lanxon, have discussed the legitimizing effect of the iPhone Duo’s existence on the entire foldable phone landscape, which has previously felt like a new-wave fantasy rather than a mainstream riptide.

In many ways, Apple’s newfound competition with existing foldable phones completes the portfolio. That is precisely why we’re building the Fold-a-Phone now, and why our proprietary machine, methodology and test data will enrich our collective understanding of the capabilities – and yes, limitations – of foldable phones as our true next-generation mobile device.

How CNET’s Fold-a-Phone tests foldable phones like the iPhone Duo

Most current foldable phones are rated for 200,000 to 500,000 folds. As such, we knew we needed to create a robust and adaptable machine that could accommodate book- and flip-style foldable phones of any size, dimension and hinge orientation. (Note: The Fold-a-Phone was not built for trifold phones, which present a unique element to the engineering challenge.)

Moreover, we wanted to test the phone the way people would actually use it. No one just sits around opening and closing their foldable phone at top speed all day. Rather, you open it naturally, spend a few minutes watching a video, browsing a web page, or using an app, close it, and then put it in your pocket. This may happen dozens of times per day.

Mimicking this usage on the Fold-a-Phone limits undue stress on the phone hinge and avoids generating excess heat compared to a test built for speed.

We determined that a cadence of roughly 4 seconds could sidestep technical hurdles while also being reasonably fast. The foldable phone takes 1 second to open, 1 second to fully open, 1 second to close and 1 second to fully close. This cycle counts as a single completed fold. Then, the cycle repeats until either the hinge or the screen gives out.

In conceptualizing and building the Fold-a-Phone, our team has used standard, off-the-shelf components to simplify the machine’s development. The essential design consists of two armatures, distinctly designed to perform the opening and closing movements with both force and grace.

Matthew Murray/CNET

An industrial-grade stepper motor drives each armature, with the host software (running on a connected computer) deterministically adjusting the torque to complete each step of the process while also protecting the phone. If any of the several proximity sensors fail to detect the armature in the correct position, the machine stops immediately.

We also monitor the motors’ power usage to track how well the foldable phone opens and closes over time. We have set up cameras to capture images and video of the test from multiple angles, and we will analyze regular status updates from the computer to determine the current status of the phone and the test.

To ensure we never miss a major development, the entire rig is connected to an EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus power station to guard against electricity outages, and all the output data is saved to multiple locations.

To secure each phone to the machine, we use our CNET Lab Test-winning 3D printer, the Prusa Core One, to 3D-print a custom “sled” that matches each phone’s exact dimensions. We secure the phone to the sled with heavy-duty double-sided tape (yes, it works!) and then screw the sled onto the machine.

There’s always room for improvement. We’re constantly looking for ways to make the machine run more smoothly and quietly without disrupting the folding rhythm.

Apple’s presence is already changing the game and could very well spur innovation in ways we can’t predict today. But until then, our Fold-a-Phone machine will continue to test the iPhone Duo and its competitors, and CNET’s writers will report on how well these individual hinged devices stand up to the challenge – or fold under pressure.

Tech.title: Please Don’t Let an AI Bot Log Into Your Bank Account
Tech.content:
Whatever you do with AI, don’t give AI bots your banking information.

Agents like Meta’s Muse, OpenClaw and OpenAI’s dots are all the rage in the AI world these days. They promise to go beyond a chatbot that gives you information, becoming a tool where you can tell it to do something for you and it goes and does it.

When you first 

More from CNET

“The intention might be something simple, like managing a calendar. But that access can give the agent the ability to do much more than the person intended,” said John Strand, the owner of the cybersecurity firm Black Hills Information Security. While you may be giving the agent access to simple smart home routines or getting help planning a trip, your banking information may also be accessible.

The risk outweighs the reward

It might be tempting to think you can automate your financial chores and have more time for other things, but handing over your account credentials to an agent opens you up to many different things that can go wrong.

For one, AI agents might not be as secure as you think. This technology is very new — these kinds of always-on, persistent agents have really only been available for less than a year, and big companies like Meta and OpenAI have just put out their own versions in the last couple of months. These aren’t polished products that have had all the kinks worked out.

One of those challenges is that they don’t always behave in the way you expect or do what you want them to. Recent news stories about AI agents hacking other websites — including the AI platform Hugging Face and Australian government sites — have involved agents acting in unexpected ways to achieve an assigned goal. You don’t want AI to act like that with your checking account.

There are also plenty of reasons to be worried about the privacy of data shared with agents. Your agent might not meddle in unwanted ways with your money, but it could compromise your login info, letting someone nefarious meddle with your money.

When agents use your login info, “a bank cannot tell an authorized agent from an attacker using the exact same login,” said Ted Miracco, CEO of the mobile security firm Approov. “That is more of an identity failure than an AI failure. Until agents carry verifiable identities, scoped permissions and an audit trail, blocking them is the best defensible control a bank has.”

Banks are trying to block meddling AI agents

Many banks are aware of the risks and are already cracking down on unauthorized use of agentic agents. Charles Schwab’s CEO Rick Wurster told Bloomberg that bots are taking the liberty to move clients’ money.

“I get a report on how many times we’ve blocked clients from using one of these agents in a week, and it’s in the tens and twenties — per week — that the big agents are being blocked,” Wurster said in a Bloomberg TV interview. “What that tells me is that while people love AI, they’re not willing to turn their financial accounts over to them just yet.”

But that number is likely growing, and with bots going mainstream, it could grow rapidly. More banks are taking action against bots to protect you. A spokesperson from Wells Fargo said in an email to CNET that Wells Fargo the bank has already taken steps to block unauthorized agents from accessing customer accounts, too.

Banks aren’t completely against AI, though. Some just want you to use their features and tools instead. Wurster added in his interview that he recommends for Schwab customers to use Charley, Charles Schwab’s proprietary AI tool, to gather market insights, ask about personal financial information like balances and manage everyday financial tasks like transfers and payments. These measures make it much safer, but in the meantime, it may be best to keep your banking business to yourself.

If you want to check to see if bots have been meddling in your banking, look at your login history and account activity. Strand suggests looking for activity that doesn’t match your pattern — like multiple logins in a short period or access happening at the same time every day. That may not mean it’s your AI agent, but it’s worth keeping track of. If you notice anything suspicious, contact your bank immediately for assistance.

Strand also recommends enabling two-factor authentication now as a preventative step to safeguard your financial data, but it’s also a good time to reevaluate the access you’re giving AI. Strand also recommends restricting which applications and sites AI agents can access.

“Check the permissions. Make sure they’re limited to what it needs to do the job you gave it, and remove anything beyond that,” he added.

Shang Saavedra, founder of personal finance platform Save My Cents, suggested you regularly revisit your AI agent’s access to apps and data and require it to ask for permission before accessing new data, apps and features.

If you decide to use AI for personal finance purposes, set limitations. “I’ve tested AI with some basic questions and basic calculations, and the information it provides is good for a beginner plan that gives you some pointers as to where to go,” said Saavedra. “I also like using AI to search for book and resource suggestions.”

But the actual handling of money? Maybe do that yourself.

Tech.title: A ‘Fallout’ Competition Series Is Coming to Prime Video
Tech.content:
Good news, Vault Dwellers. Prime Video on Friday announced that a new reality competition series, inspired by Fallout, Bethesda Game Studios’ hit video game franchise and Amazon’s sci-fi drama, will launch on its platform early in the new year.

Fallout Shelter: The Experiment is the official title, and its 10-episode season will drop the first four episodes on Wednesday, Jan. 13, 2027, with three new episodes dropping weekly through Wednesday, Jan. 27.

“The world is ending,” the Pip-Boy animation in the short video announcement says. “The competition is just beginning.”

More from CNET

According to Amazon, Fallout Shelter: The Experiment will invite “everyday participants to test their aptitude for the apocalypse in Vault-Tec’s state-of-the-art bomb-proof vault shelters.” The series will pit the competitors against each other in “a series of high-octane drills, psychological dilemmas and morally challenging behavior trials” until there’s one person remaining to receive the grand prize of $1 million.

The timing of the announcement adds extra special meaning to Fallout fans, as Oct. 23, 2077, is known as Fallout Day in the fictional world of the video games and Prime Video’s series. This is the day that the bombs dropped, marking the beginning of the Great War that turned America into an irradiated wasteland.

If you’ve ever wanted to live the Vault Dweller lifestyle, this show will probably be your cup of tea. Fallout Shelter: The Experiment is also the latest in a string of competition shows inspired by established genre properties; Netflix’s Squid Game: The Challenge and Wonka’s Golden Ticket come to mind.

Beyond the reality series project, Bethesda has announced fun global partnerships to commemorate the day, including a Fallout-inspired exhibit at the National Atomic Testing Museum in Las Vegas and the return of the Fallout Cafe to Tokyo’s Tower Records. The game studio also has a new collaboration with Jones Soda, titled Project T.W.I.S.T. (which stands for Taste-Worthiness Initiative for Shelter Transition), inviting people to help select the flavor for Nuka Twist — which will also reflect the Nuka Twist flavor, once it’s revealed in-game.

As for Fallout Shelter: The Experiment, the new spinoff project arrives at the beginning of 2027, which marks the 30th anniversary of the video game franchise (Fallout dropped on Oct. 10, 1997). With season 3 on the horizon, something tells me it’s going to be a big year for all things Fallout.

Tech.title: 7 iPhone Duo Apps That Take Full Advantage of the New Foldable Phone
Tech.content:
The iPhone Duo is easily the most experimental iPhone that Apple has released. That’s both good news and bad news.

On one hand, the shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos.

On the other hand, the device is so new to iOS that some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s getting an iPhone Duo today (or soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested.

1. Netflix

Netflix on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent.

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

2. NYT Cooking

NYT Cooking on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

3. Fantasical

Fantastical on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

4. Edits by Instagram

Edits on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

5 and 6. TikTok and Instagram

Instagram on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

7. Toastie

Toastie on the iPhone Duo. Kerry Wan/CNET

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster.

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

There are many ways to pair up apps on the iPhone Duo for your convenience. Celso Bulgatti/CNET

Bonus: Your duo of choice

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-sized phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other.

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

Tech.title: The iPhone Duo Is Here, and Only That Device Will Run iOS 27.1
Tech.content:
Apple released the iPhone Duo on Friday, Oct. 23, and the tech giant released iOS 27.1 alongside the device. However, only the foldable iPhone will run that iOS version.

“This version of iOS builds on the foundation of iOS 27 but introduces features that were purpose-built for the new foldable design,” Apple told CNET in an email in September.

So unless you preordered the iPhone Duo, or were able to buy one in stores, you won’t see iOS 27.1 on your device.

The Duo is Apple’s first foldable phone, a long-anticipated move into a device category that’s still pretty niche. Launching it alongside a version of iOS tailored to that foldable design could help smooth out the debut of what is likely to be many buyers’ first foldable phone.

However, Apple did say all devices, including the iPhone Duo, will be able to update to iOS 27.2 later this year. So Apple likely won’t stagger iOS releases in the future in this way. And since Apple released the iOS 27.2 release candidate on Monday, Oct. 19, folks likely won’t have to wait long for that update to land on their foldable and nonfoldable iPhones.

For more on Apple, here’s what you should know about the iPhone Duo as well as iOS 27. You can also check out what iOS 27.2 might bring to your iPhone soon.
